The magnetic vector potential $\mathbf{A}$ is a gage-dependent vector field characterizing the electromagnetic state of a plasma. It enters fundamental physics through the canonical particle momentum $\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v} + q\mathbf{A}$, where $m$ is particle mass and $q$ is particle charge, and it governs inductive electromagnetic effects in both equilibrium and perturbed plasma states.

The defining relation connecting $\mathbf{A}$ to the magnetic induction $\mathbf{B}$ is:

$$
\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic induction. Only the curl of $\mathbf{A}$ is directly physical; the vector potential itself is gage dependent. Its time derivative contributes to the inductive electric field via $\mathbf{E}_\mathrm{ind} = -\partial\mathbf{A}/\partial t$, which is central to Faraday's law in electromagnetic plasma models.

Specific projections serve distinct physical roles. The field-aligned component $A_\parallel = \mathbf{A} \cdot \hat{b}$, where $\hat{b}$ is the equilibrium field unit vector, governs Alfvénic dynamics and is the component retained in gyrokinetic and reduced-MHD formulations; [its normalized perturbed amplitude] is used in eigenmode studies. Cylindrical components in the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — radial, toroidal, and vertical — are natural for equilibrium and MHD calculations, while the poloidal projection in flux coordinates $(\psi, \theta, \phi)$ arises in neoclassical transport analyzes. In vacuum regions, $\mathbf{A}$ is generated solely by external coil currents, with no plasma-current contribution.

Momentum convection velocity is an effective velocity coefficient for advective, non-diffusive transport of momentum carried by a specified neutral species. Its neutral-species form aggregates momentum over all resolved neutral internal states and is distinct from the material bulk velocity.

For a resolved transport direction $i$ and transported momentum component $j$, the advective contribution to the momentum-flux tensor is defined by:

$$
\Pi^{\mathrm{adv}}_{ij}=V_iP_j
$$

where $P_j$ is the selected momentum-density component, $\Pi^{\mathrm{adv}}_{ij}$ is its advective flux, and $V_i$ is the corresponding effective transport velocity. For a vector quantity, the resolved $V_i$ values form the effective transport-velocity vector.

The coefficient applies only to the selected neutral species, momentum component, and transport direction; it excludes diffusive transport, external source terms, and the material bulk velocity. It is the neutral-species realization of [momentum convection velocity]. The [toroidal neutral-species form](name:toroidal_neutral_species_momentum_convection_velocity) and [vertical neutral-species form](name:vertical_neutral_species_momentum_convection_velocity) show that the component label identifies the transported momentum in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, not necessarily the direction of the effective velocity.

Plasma pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure of the plasma, the scalar part of the kinetic pressure tensor in a fluid or magnetohydrodynamic description. It represents equilibrium mechanical stress from the plasma populations included in the pressure model and is not a perturbation amplitude.

The scalar pressure is the one-third trace of the kinetic pressure tensor:

$$
p = \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{P}
$$

where $p$ is the plasma pressure, $\mathbf{P}$ is the kinetic pressure tensor, and $\operatorname{tr}$ denotes the tensor trace. For locally isotropic Maxwellian populations, an included population $s$ contributes $n_s k_B T_s$, where $n_s$ is the number density of population $s$, $T_s$ is its temperature, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant.

The unqualified quantity applies to equilibrium scalar kinetic pressure; it is additive over the included plasma populations and does not imply normalization, volume integration, or selection of only a bulk-thermal, fast-particle, or perturbed population subset. It excludes magnetic pressure, dynamic ram pressure, anisotropic pressure components, and any individual component of the pressure tensor.

[Total plasma pressure](name:total_plasma_pressure) is the specialization in which all represented equilibrium kinetic pressure contributions are included, while [thermal plasma pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure) is restricted to bulk thermal electron and ion populations. [Perturbed plasma pressure] denotes a first-order variation about an equilibrium pressure and is not part of the equilibrium quantity defined here. In magnetohydrostatic equilibrium, the pressure gradient satisfies $\nabla p = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$, where $\nabla p$ is the spatial gradient of plasma pressure, $\mathbf{j}$ is the electric current density, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field; on nested magnetic flux surfaces this pressure may be expressed as a function of the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) $\psi$, where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux.

This quantity is the net local volumetric energy exchange caused by Coulomb collisions for a designated target population. It is positive for energy deposited in the target and negative for energy transferred from it.

$$
P_a^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_b Q_{a\leftarrow b}^{\mathrm{coll}}
$$

where $P_a^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the target power density in W m$^{-3}$, $Q_{a\leftarrow b}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional energy-transfer rate per unit volume from partner population $b$ to target $a$, and the sum includes the collision partners and subpopulations specified by the quantity's aggregation scope.

The target may be a broad population, as in [particle collisional power density], or a species, ion charge state, internal state, or electron population. Aggregated electron and ion quantities include the designated contributing species and states, whereas resolved quantities retain only their specified target, as in [ion charge-state collisional power density](name:ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) and [internal-state collisional power density].

Sign convention: Positive when the designated target population gains energy from its collision partners.

This quantity is the volume-integrated net rate of energy transfer into the complete ion population from Coulomb scattering interactions with all colliding plasma constituents. As a structural abstraction within the collisional-power family, it aggregates thermal and fast ion receiving populations across all ion species and charge states without resolving which ion sub-population receives the energy.

The volume-integrated ion collisional power is defined as:

$$
P_{\rm ion,coll} = \int_V Q_{\rm ion,coll}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $Q_{\rm ion,coll}$ is the local [ion power density due to collisions](name:ion_power_density_due_to_collisions) into the aggregate ion receiving population and the integral extends over the plasma volume $V$.

The receiving population is charge-state-summed for each ion species and species-summed over the ion population. Collisional exchanges among ion sub-populations contained in this aggregate cancel in the all-ion sum; the retained value is the net transfer between the aggregate ion population and populations outside that aggregate, including the complementary [electron power due to collisions]. Population-resolved components include [fast ion power due to collisions](name:fast_ion_power_due_to_collisions), [thermal ion power due to collisions](name:thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions), and the charge-state-resolved [ion-state power due to collisions](name:total_ion_charge_state_power_due_to_collisions); [power due to collisions](name:power_due_to_collisions) is the corresponding population-abstract parent.

Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb scattering interactions transfer net energy into the complete ion population.

Signed poloidal magnetic flux of a flux loop is the magnetic flux linked by an individual flux loop and threading an oriented surface whose boundary is that loop. It is the finite-surface flux linkage associated with the loop as a whole, not a local magnetic-field component.

The loop-linked flux is defined by the surface integral of the magnetic-field vector over a spanning surface of the loop:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{loop}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{loop}}} \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the signed poloidal magnetic flux of the flux loop, $S_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is an oriented spanning surface bounded by the flux loop, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $d\mathbf{S}$ is the directed surface element on that surface.

The scope is one specified flux loop and the total flux through its complete spanning surface; no averaging over multiple loops or loop segments is implied. The quantity is distinct from a point-locus evaluation such as [poloidal magnetic flux at a sensor attachment point](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop), which evaluates a flux function at a specified position rather than integrating over a finite loop-bounded surface.

The defining surface is any oriented spanning surface with the same loop boundary and orientation; the absence of magnetic monopoles makes the linked flux independent of the particular spanning surface. This quantity is related to [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) as a loop-bounded flux linkage, and it must not be identified with [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which uses a different flux-surface geometry; a reconstructed counterpart, [reconstructed poloidal magnetic flux of flux loop], shares the same magnetic quantity but represents a distinct value type when that distinction is made.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic-field vector has a positive net projection on the oriented surface element selected as positive for the flux loop.
documents.after:

Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density is the toroidal conventional current density assigned to a closed magnetic-flux surface. It represents the total toroidal current-density component on that surface, expressed with the geometry weighting that provides the effective toroidal current source for the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux distribution.

The defining flux-surface average is

$$
j_{\phi,\mathrm{FSA}} = \frac{\left\langle j_\phi/R \right\rangle}{\left\langle 1/R \right\rangle}
$$

where $j_{\phi,\mathrm{FSA}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density, $j_\phi$ is the local toroidal component of the conventional current-density vector projected on $\hat{\phi}$, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes an average over the closed magnetic-flux surface.

The scope is closed magnetic-flux surfaces in an axisymmetric equilibrium, and the aggregation is over the total conventional current carried by the plasma unless a population-specific qualifier is present. This quantity is not the unweighted flux-surface average of $j_\phi$, not a local current-density component at a point, and not a field-aligned or parallel current density.

It is the toroidal counterpart of the [parallel flux-surface-averaged current density] and a member of the [flux-surface-averaged current density] family. In equilibrium, this weighted toroidal average is the scalar source coupled to the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) in the Grad-Shafranov balance.

Sign convention: Positive when the conventional current-density vector has a positive projection on $\hat{\phi}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Diagnostic aperture area is the geometric extent of the designated limiting surface through which radiation or particles are admitted or collected. It may describe a clear aperture opening or a collecting face when that face defines the aperture.

The area is defined by the surface integral

$$
A = \int_S dS
$$

where $A$ is the diagnostic aperture area, $S$ is the designated aperture surface, and $dS$ is the differential area element on that surface.

This quantity applies to the specified aperture surface of the diagnostic and is not an automatically aggregated area for unrelated apertures. It is a geometric area, excluding surrounding housing, supports, and other structures unless they form the designated aperture surface; it is not an effective area weighted by transmission, sensitivity, or angular response.

The area is distinct from the [radius of a diagnostic aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture) and the [width of a diagnostic aperture], which describe linear dimensions. For a circular aperture of radius $r$, where $r$ is the geometric distance from the aperture center to its boundary, the area satisfies $A = \pi r^2$, with $\pi$ denoting the circle constant.

Wavelength of a filter is the vacuum-wavelength spectral coordinate identifying the nominal center of the filter transmission band. It is a property of the filter transmission response and denotes the central or nominal wavelength of the passband selected for spectral transmission.

For a filter characteristic associated with temporal frequency $\nu_f$, the vacuum wavelength $\lambda_f$ is defined by:

$$
\lambda_f = \frac{c}{\nu_f}
$$

where $\lambda_f$ is the wavelength of the filter, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\nu_f$ is the corresponding temporal frequency.

This quantity applies to the filter passband response, not to radiation after propagation in a material medium and not to the rest-frame wavelength of an emitted or absorbed spectral feature such as the [wavelength of a spectral line](name:wavelength_of_spectral_line). It is distinct from the [lower wavelength of a filter](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter) and [upper wavelength of a filter](name:upper_wavelength_of_filter), which identify the short-wavelength and long-wavelength bandpass edges.

The wavelength of a filter is also distinct from the [width of a filter]: that related quantity denotes a geometric extent of the filter window, not a spectral passband interval. The lower and upper wavelength quantities bound the transmitted spectral band, while the wavelength of a filter identifies its nominal central spectral coordinate.

Flux-surface-averaged number density of deuterium-tritium pseudo-species ions at the plasma boundary (separatrix) is the particle density of the effective deuterium-tritium fuel species averaged over the last closed magnetic flux surface. The pseudo-species represents the deuterium-tritium fuel mixture as a single ion constituent with effective mass number 2.5; as a species-level density, it is summed over all charge states.

Using the poloidal-contour representation of a flux-surface average in an axisymmetric equilibrium, the boundary value is defined by:

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{DT}} \rangle_b =
\frac{\oint_{\psi=\psi_b} n_{\mathrm{DT}}(l)\, dl / B_p(l)}
{\oint_{\psi=\psi_b} dl / B_p(l)}
$$

where $\langle n_{\mathrm{DT}} \rangle_b$ is this boundary average, $\psi_b$ labels the plasma-boundary flux surface, $l$ is poloidal arc length along that surface, and $B_p$ is the [poloidal magnetic-field magnitude]. The local pseudo-species density is $n_{\mathrm{DT}} = n_{\mathrm{D}} + n_{\mathrm{T}}$, where $n_{\mathrm{D}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{T}}$ are the corresponding charge-state-summed deuterium and tritium ion densities.

This quantity is the plasma-boundary member of [flux-surface-averaged deuterium-tritium density](name:flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary) and the flux-surface-averaged counterpart of [deuterium-tritium density at the plasma boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary), which retains variation around the same boundary surface. The single-isotope boundary analog [flux-surface-averaged deuterium density at the plasma boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary) separates one isotope contribution, while [volume-averaged deuterium-tritium density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density) averages the same effective fuel population over the confined-plasma volume. It excludes scrape-off-layer and material-limiter densities, including [deuterium-tritium density at a limiter](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_limiter).

The toroidal plasma current $I_p$ is the net electric current flowing in the toroidal $\hat{\phi}$ direction, integrated over the full poloidal cross-section of the plasma column. It is a primary global parameter governing poloidal magnetic field generation, MHD equilibrium, plasma confinement, and stability thresholds including the Kruskal-Shafranov $q = 1$ condition.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
I_p = \iint_{\mathcal{S}} j_\phi \, dA
$$

where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the current density, $dA$ is the area element, and $\mathcal{S}$ is the poloidal cross-section of the plasma.

$I_p$ is measured by Rogowski coils encircling the torus, or inferred from flux-loop and magnetic-pickup-coil arrays as a primary constraint in equilibrium reconstruction. The closely related [toroidal_total_plasma_current](name:toroidal_plasma_current) explicitly labels this as the total aggregated current. It should be distinguished from [current_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:current_of_toroidal_field_coil), which drives the external vacuum toroidal field, and from [current_of_plasma_filament](name:current_of_plasma_filament), which represents current in discrete plasma filament elements.

Typical values range from a few hundred kA in small research tokamaks to approximately 15 MA in ITER-class reactors, scaling roughly with the product of toroidal field strength and minor radius.

Sign convention: Positive when the plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The toroidal plasma current $I_p$ is the net electric current flowing in the toroidal $\hat{\phi}$ direction, integrated over the full poloidal cross-section of the plasma column. It is a primary global parameter governing poloidal magnetic field generation, MHD equilibrium, plasma confinement, and stability thresholds including the Kruskal-Shafranov $q = 1$ condition.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
I_p = \iint_{\mathcal{S}} j_\phi \, dA
$$

where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the current density, $dA$ is the area element, and $\mathcal{S}$ is the poloidal cross-section of the plasma.

$I_p$ is measured by Rogowski coils encircling the torus, or inferred from flux-loop and magnetic-pickup-coil arrays as a primary constraint in equilibrium reconstruction. The closely related toroidal_total_plasma_current explicitly labels this as the total aggregated current. It should be distinguished from [current_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:current_of_toroidal_field_coil), which drives the external vacuum toroidal field, and from [current_of_plasma_filament](name:current_of_plasma_filament), which represents current in discrete plasma filament elements.

Typical values range from a few hundred kA in small research tokamaks to approximately 15 MA in ITER-class reactors, scaling roughly with the product of toroidal field strength and minor radius.

Sign convention: Positive when the plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The polarization angle at a constraint position is the angle of linear polarization of Stark-split Balmer-alpha emission from fast neutral beam ions traversing the plasma, evaluated at a discrete spatial site where this measurement serves as an input constraint in equilibrium reconstruction. The motional Stark effect (MSE) diagnostic exploits the Lorentz electric field experienced by injected beam neutrals to align the polarization plane of the emitted light in a direction encoding the local magnetic-field pitch angle.

The MSE polarization angle $\gamma$ is related to the local magnetic field components by:

$$
\tan(\gamma) = \frac{B_Z}{A_1 B_R + A_2 B_\phi}
$$

where $B_Z$ is the vertical field component, $B_R$ is the radial field component, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal field component, and $A_1$, $A_2$ are dimensionless geometric weighting factors determined by the beam trajectory and sightline orientation.

During equilibrium reconstruction, the measured value at each constraint position is compared against the corresponding reconstructed [polarization_angle](name:polarization_angle_at_constraint_position) to form residuals that enter the least-squares cost functional. The motional_stark_radiance provides complementary spectral intensity data from the same beam-emission event. MSE polarization angles in conventional-aspect-ratio tokamak configurations span a few degrees to roughly 20 degrees, varying with local field pitch, beam geometry, and viewing-sightline angle.

The radial derivative of poloidal magnetic flux is the rate at which the signed poloidal magnetic flux changes across nested equilibrium magnetic flux surfaces. It is a metric coefficient relating the poloidal-flux and toroidal-flux coordinate descriptions.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{d\psi}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $\psi$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal-flux radius that labels the nested surfaces.

This quantity is evaluated as a function of the toroidal-flux radius, with one derivative value associated with each nested equilibrium surface. It is not a surface integral or average, and it is distinct from a derivative with respect to the cylindrical major radius, minor radius, or a normalized flux coordinate.

Relative to [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), this quantity describes how the flux label changes in the outward toroidal-flux-radial direction. It has the same independent coordinate as the [derivative with respect to toroidal flux coordinate of area of flux surface], but differentiates poloidal magnetic flux rather than enclosed surface area.

Sign convention: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux increases as $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

Toroidal diamagnetic magnetic flux at an inside flux surface is the diamagnetic contribution to the [toroidal magnetic flux] through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a selected closed flux surface. It is a surface-dependent cumulative flux inside the plasma boundary, not only a boundary value.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height, let $S_\chi$ be the constant-$\phi$ poloidal cross-section enclosed by the flux surface labeled by $\chi$. With $d\mathbf{A}_\phi = \hat{\phi}\,dA$ oriented toward increasing $\phi$, the enclosed diamagnetic toroidal flux is defined by:

$$
\Phi_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}}(\chi) = \int_{S_\chi} \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}(R,Z) \cdot d\mathbf{A}_\phi = \int_{S_\chi} B_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}}(R,Z)\,dA
$$

where $\chi$ identifies the selected flux surface, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic contribution to the equilibrium magnetic field, $B_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is its toroidal component, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle, and $dA$ is the positive scalar area element on $S_\chi$.

This quantity includes only the diamagnetic magnetic-field contribution. It is distinct from the total [toroidal_magnetic_flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which includes all magnetic-field contributions, from [toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which is evaluated at the plasma boundary, and from [toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary_due_to_poloidal_current](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary_due_to_poloidal_current), which isolates the poloidal-current contribution at that boundary.

Sign convention: Positive when the net diamagnetic magnetic-field contribution through the enclosed poloidal cross-section points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

This quantity is the toroidal component of the lithium-ion bulk-flow velocity, flux-surface averaged over the separatrix, which is the last closed magnetic flux surface at the plasma boundary. Lithium ions comprise Li+ through Li3+, combined using their particle densities.

$$
\left\langle v_{\phi,\mathrm{Li}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}} = \frac{\sum_{q=1}^{3}\left\langle n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}v_{\phi,\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}}{\sum_{q=1}^{3}\left\langle n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}}
$$

Here, $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}$ is the toroidal bulk-flow velocity of lithium charge state $q$, $n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}$ is its number density, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes averaging over the separatrix. The toroidal component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The related [flux-surface-averaged lithium density at the plasma boundary] supplies the corresponding charge-state-summed density, not a velocity.

Flux-surface-averaged toroidal krypton velocity is the density-weighted mean over all krypton ionization states on the plasma boundary, identified with the last closed magnetic flux surface. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
\left\langle v_{\phi,\mathrm{Kr}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS},b} = \frac{\displaystyle\oint_{\psi=\psi_b} \left(\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}} v_{\phi,\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}\right)\frac{dl}{B_p}}{\displaystyle\oint_{\psi=\psi_b} \left(\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}\right)\frac{dl}{B_p}}
$$

Here $q$ indexes krypton ionization states, $n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}$ is the number density of state $q$ in m$^{-3}$, $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}$ is its toroidal bulk velocity, $dl$ is poloidal arc length, $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude, and $\psi_b$ labels the boundary surface. This species-resolved quantity differs from the total-ion quantity [toroidal flux-surface-averaged ion velocity at the plasma boundary]; its locus differs from [toroidal krypton velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).

This quantity is the number density of tungsten ions averaged over the last closed magnetic flux surface, with all positive ionization states included and neutral tungsten excluded. $$

where $\psi_b$ is the flux label of the plasma boundary, $n_{\mathrm{W}}$ is the local summed tungsten-ion density, $d\ell_p$ is poloidal contour length, and $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude. The quantity is distinct from [volume-averaged tungsten density](name:volume_averaged_tungsten_density), which averages over the enclosed plasma volume.

The quantity is the flux-surface average over the separatrix of the toroidal component of the helium-4 ion bulk-flow velocity. The helium-4 value includes all helium-4 charge states through a density-weighted mean, rather than a sum of their velocities.

For charge-state-resolved density $n_{4,q}$ and toroidal velocity $v_{\phi,4,q}$, the species velocity is defined by

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{FS}} = \left\langle \frac{\sum_q n_{4,q}v_{\phi,4,q}}{\sum_q n_{4,q}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{sep}}
$$

where $q$ indexes helium-4 charge state, $n_{4,q}$ is its number density in m$^{-3}$, $v_{\phi,4,q}$ is its toroidal velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{sep}}$ denotes the flux-surface average over the separatrix. The toroidal component is taken along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This averaged quantity is distinct from the local [toroidal helium-4 velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_helium_4_velocity_at_plasma_boundary); the corresponding isotope-specific construction for helium-3 is [toroidal flux-surface-averaged helium-3 velocity at the plasma boundary].

The wave electric field is the complex vector phasor representing the oscillatory electromagnetic-wave contribution to the local [electric field](name:electric_field). It retains the wave amplitude, phase, and polarization before any spatial projection or spectral mode decomposition.

For a single angular frequency, the physical wave field is defined by

$$
\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{r},t)=\operatorname{Re}\left\{\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{r},\omega)e^{-i\omega t}\right\}
$$

where $\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the complex wave-electric-field phasor, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, $t$ is time, and $\omega$ is angular frequency. Its projections include the [parallel wave electric field](name:parallel_wave_electric_field) and [vertical wave electric field](name:vertical_wave_electric_field); its toroidal Fourier components are represented by the [per-toroidal-mode electric field]. The quantity excludes electrostatic and non-wave contributions unless they are explicitly part of the identified electromagnetic wave.

Alfvén frequency at a given radial position for a single toroidal mode number is the complex local shear-Alfvén continuum angular frequency for perturbations propagating along the magnetic field on the flux surface at that radial position. Its [real part](name:alfven_frequency_real_part) is the oscillatory component, and its [imaginary part](name:alfven_frequency_imaginary_part) is the temporal growth or damping component.

The ideal shear-Alfvén continuum relation defining the underlying continuum frequency is

$$
\omega_A = |k_\parallel| v_A
$$

where $\omega_A$ is the real continuum angular frequency, $k_\parallel$ is the component of the wave vector parallel to the magnetic field, and $v_A$ is the Alfvén speed, $B/\sqrt{\mu_0\rho_m}$ with $B$ the magnetic-field magnitude, $\mu_0$ the vacuum permeability, and $\rho_m$ the plasma mass density.

This quantity denotes the full complex frequency $\Omega_A=\operatorname{Re}(\Omega_A)+i\operatorname{Im}(\Omega_A)$, not either component alone, and it is an angular frequency rather than a cyclic frequency. The radial position is a flux-surface label in explicitly named flux coordinates such as $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ or $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$, not a cylindrical vector component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. At fixed [toroidal mode number], $k_\parallel$ is determined by field-line pitch, magnetic geometry, and poloidal harmonic content, with the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) entering common single-harmonic specializations.

Sign convention: Positive when $\operatorname{Im}(\Omega_A)$ makes perturbations proportional to $\exp(-i\Omega_A t)$ grow exponentially in time.

The right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field is the E-minus complex phasor obtained by projecting the electromagnetic-wave electric-field phasor onto the circular polarization basis transverse to the local equilibrium magnetic field. It retains the amplitude and phase of this polarization component.

For orthonormal transverse unit vectors $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$, with their ordered orientation defining the circular-polarization handedness, the E-minus component is defined by

$$
\widetilde{E}_{-}=\mathbf{e}_{-}^{*}\!\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}},\qquad
\mathbf{e}_{-}=\frac{\mathbf{e}_1-i\mathbf{e}_2}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

where $\widetilde{E}_{-}$ is the complex E-minus electric-field phasor, $\mathbf{e}_{-}$ is the right-hand circular polarization unit vector, $\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the complex vector phasor of the wave electric field, the superscript $*$ denotes complex conjugation, and $i$ is the imaginary unit. The vectors $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ are real orthonormal unit vectors spanning the plane perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field.

This quantity covers the transverse right-hand circular polarization of the coherent electromagnetic-wave contribution at a physical location and frequency. It is one polarization component rather than the full vector [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field); no summation over polarization components, spatial locations, frequencies, or Fourier modes is implied. Electrostatic and non-wave electric-field contributions are excluded unless explicitly included in the identified wave.

The quadrature components [right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field real part](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part) and [right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field imaginary part](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part) are respectively the in-phase and quadrature parts of this complex phasor. Its toroidal Fourier decomposition is represented by [per-toroidal-mode right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field], while the complementary circular component is the [left-hand circularly polarized wave electric field](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field).

The parallel wave electric field is the complex phasor obtained by projecting the electromagnetic-wave electric-field phasor onto the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. It retains both amplitude and phase and is a component of the [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field).

The parallel component is defined by

$$
E_{\parallel}=\mathbf{E}_{w}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{b}}=\frac{\mathbf{B}_{0}}{|\mathbf{B}_{0}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}_{w}$ is the complex wave-electric-field phasor, $\mathbf{B}_{0}$ is the local equilibrium magnetic field, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is its unit direction. The phasor carries the phase of the harmonic field under the selected time convention.

This quantity is the complex component rather than its magnitude. Its modulus gives the [parallel wave electric field amplitude], while its quadratures include the [parallel wave electric field imaginary part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part) and the corresponding real part.

Sign convention: Positive when the electric-field component is directed along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

E_{\parallel}=\mathbf{E}_{w}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{b}}=\frac{\mathbf{B}_{0}}{|\mathbf{B}_{0}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}_{w}$ is the complex wave-electric-field phasor, $\mathbf{B}_{0}$ is the local equilibrium magnetic field, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is its unit direction. The phasor carries the phase of the harmonic field under the selected time convention.

This quantity is the complex component rather than its magnitude. Its modulus gives the parallel wave electric field amplitude, while its quadratures include the [parallel wave electric field imaginary part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part) and the corresponding real part.

Sign convention: Positive when the electric-field component is directed along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

The signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ is the equilibrium flux function evaluated at a physical measurement position. It labels the nested magnetic surface passing through that position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the poloidal magnetic-flux function is defined by

$$
\psi(R,Z) = \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi(R,Z)$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at cylindrical coordinates $(R,Z)$, $B_Z(R',Z)$ is the vertical magnetic-field component, $R$ and $R'$ are major-radius coordinates, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\pi$ is the circle constant. The toroidal angle $\phi$ completes the right-handed cylindrical frame; axisymmetry makes $\psi$ independent of $\phi$.

This quantity applies to the equilibrium magnetic field at one physical measurement position and has no species or population restriction. It is a point evaluation, not a sum, average, or integral over multiple measurement positions. It is not a normalized flux coordinate and does not represent a perturbation or fluctuation of the equilibrium flux.

The same flux-function definition is used for [poloidal magnetic flux at a beam-tracing point](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_beam_tracing_point), but that quantity differs in evaluation locus. A normalized surface label at the same type of location is [normalized poloidal flux coordinate at a measurement position], which is derived by applying axis and boundary references to the signed flux value.

Sign convention: Positive when the net vertical magnetic flux through the defining horizontal disk is directed in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The global thermal-fusion neutron emission rate is the total count of neutrons produced per unit time by thermonuclear reactions between fuel ions whose velocity distributions are Maxwellian at the local ion temperature. It aggregates all neutron-producing isotope-pair channels—D-D, D-T, and T-T—while excluding contributions from beam-target or beam-beam fast-ion reactions.

The total rate is the plasma-volume integral of the summed channel emissivities:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{th}} = \int_V \sum_{a,b} f_{ab}\, n_a\, n_b\, \langle \sigma v \rangle_{ab}(T_i) \, dV
$$

where $n_a$ and $n_b$ are the reacting species number densities, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{ab}(T_i)$ is the Maxwellian-averaged fusion reactivity at local ion temperature $T_i$, and $f_{ab} = 1/2$ for identical-species pairs to avoid double-counting. Channel-resolved contributions are provided by [deuterium-deuterium thermal flux] and [tritium-tritium thermal flux]; the D-T channel is described by [neutron flux due to thermal fusion](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion).

Measured using neutron detectors—activation foils, fission chambers, or scintillator arrays—positioned outside the vacuum vessel and absolutely calibrated with activation samples or time-of-flight spectrometry. The companion quantity [total neutron flux] includes non-thermal beam-target and beam-beam contributions in addition to this thermal channel.

In pure DD plasmas the rate is of order $10^{14}$–$10^{16}$ s$^{-1}$; in DT-burning reactor-scale plasmas the 14.1 MeV DT channel dominates and rates reach $10^{18}$–$10^{20}$ s$^{-1}$.

Sign convention: Positive when neutrons are emitted from the plasma at a net outward rate.

Fusion power density is the local energy-release rate generated by nuclear-fusion reactions per unit volume. It may represent a specific reaction channel or the channel-summed quantity, with unqualified fusion power density understood as the sum over included channels.

The defining reaction-rate sum is

$$
P_{\mathrm{fus}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{n_{a,r}(\mathbf{x})\,n_{b,r}(\mathbf{x})}{1+\delta_{a_rb_r}}\,\langle\sigma v\rangle_r\,E_r
$$

where $r$ indexes fusion channels, $n_{a,r}$ and $n_{b,r}$ are reactant number densities in m$^{-3}$, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_r$ is the reaction-rate coefficient in m$^{3}$ s$^{-1}$, $E_r$ is the energy released per reaction in joules, and $\delta_{a_rb_r}$ is one for identical reactants and zero otherwise. The deuterium–deuterium and deuterium–tritium instances are represented by [deuterium-deuterium fusion power density](name:deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion) and [deuterium-tritium fusion power density](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion). This energy-release quantity includes neutron and charged-particle product energy and is distinct from [fusion neutron emissivity].

The refractive-index vector describes electromagnetic phase propagation relative to propagation in vacuum. It preserves the direction of the wave phase gradient while expressing its magnitude relative to the vacuum reference.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{k}}{k_0}, \qquad k_0 = \frac{\omega}{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ is the refractive-index vector, $\mathbf{k}$ is the [wave vector], $k_0$ is the vacuum wavenumber, $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency, and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum.

Directional representations include the projection parallel to the local magnetic field, represented by [parallel_refractive_index](name:parallel_refractive_index), and the magnitude of the perpendicular projection, represented by [perpendicular_refractive_index](name:perpendicular_refractive_index). The same normalized phase-propagation concept applies to propagation through an [optical element].

The plasma temperature is a fundamental thermodynamic state variable in fluid and single-fluid MHD models, quantifying the mean random kinetic energy of the charged particle population. In a single-fluid description it is linked to [thermal pressure] via the equation of state

$$
p = n k_B T
$$

where $p$ is the scalar pressure, $n$ is the total particle number density, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant.

In multi-species plasmas an effective plasma temperature may be obtained as a density-weighted combination of electron and ion contributions; applications requiring species resolution use explicitly qualified forms such as particle_temperature or [neutral_temperature](name:neutral_internal_state_temperature). This quantity also appears as the equilibrium background in linear MHD stability analysis, where its first-order perturbation is represented by the complex eigenfunction perturbed_plasma_temperature, encoding the amplitude and phase of the temperature fluctuation for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic. The total isotropic pressure of the plasma, including contributions summed over all species, is captured by plasma_pressure.

This quantity is the geometric area of a complete closed toroidal magnetic flux surface. It includes the full surface swept out by the corresponding poloidal contour during one toroidal revolution.

For an axisymmetric surface, the area is defined by

$$
A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\xi) = \oint_{C(\xi)} 2\pi R\,dl_p
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\xi)$ is the toroidal-surface area, $\xi$ is the magnetic flux-surface label, $C(\xi)$ is the closed poloidal contour for that surface, $R$ is the major radius, $dl_p$ is differential arc length along the contour, and $\pi$ is the circular constant. The contour is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one selected nested magnetic flux surface, with local surface elements aggregated over the complete toroidal revolution. This is distinct from the area enclosed by a poloidal contour, represented by the [poloidal-plane cross-sectional area of a flux surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), and from the enclosed [volume of a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface).

As a specialization of the broader [area measure associated with a flux surface], this quantity selects the total toroidal-surface area rather than a poloidal cross-sectional area or an area derivative with respect to a flux coordinate.

This quantity is the signed separation along the [major-radius direction] between a measurement position mapped along its magnetic flux surface to the [outboard midplane] and the separatrix at that locus.

The separation is the mapped position's major radius minus the major radius of the separatrix intersection:

$$
\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}} = R_{\mathrm{map,mid}} - R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}
$$

where $\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the mapped separatrix separation, $R_{\mathrm{map,mid}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the mapped measurement position, and $R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the [separatrix intersection at the outboard midplane]. The latter two coordinates are instances of [radial coordinate at outboard midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane).

Flux-surface mapping preserves the measurement position's flux-surface label. This is a major-radius separation, not the shortest geometric distance to the separatrix or a local flux-surface-normal separation; it is zero at the separatrix and negative for mapped positions inside it. For a separatrix-bounded plasma, the reference radius is the outboard-midplane value of the [radial plasma-boundary outline](name:radial_outline_of_plasma_boundary).

Sign convention: Positive when the mapped measurement position lies outside the separatrix in the scrape-off layer, at greater major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The low-field-side equatorial midplane: the point of maximum major radius on the flux surface in question. For a value at the separatrix intersection use outboard_midplane_separatrix. Where $R = \max_{S} R,\quad R > R_{\mathrm{axis}}$, $S$ is the magnetic flux surface the point lies on; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is major radius of the magnetic axis.

This quantity is the relative phase of a complex reflected radio-frequency power-wave phasor at a selected antenna strap or module with respect to the complex forward radio-frequency power-wave phasor of the same strap or module. It specifies the element-local reflection phase of an ion-cyclotron heating launcher rather than an absolute phase or an inter-element phase.

For element $i$, the reflected phase is defined by

$$
\phi_{\mathrm{ref},i} = \arg\!\left(b_i^{\mathrm{ref}} (a_i^{\mathrm{fwd}})^*\right) \pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $\phi_{\mathrm{ref},i}$ is this reflected phase, $b_i^{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the complex reflected power-wave phasor at element $i$, $a_i^{\mathrm{fwd}}$ is the complex forward power-wave phasor at the same element, $(a_i^{\mathrm{fwd}})^*$ is its complex conjugate, and $\arg$ extracts the phase angle. The phase is defined modulo $2\pi$.

The scope is a single selected launcher strap or module and the pair of forward and reflected traveling power waves at the same element reference plane. The forward wave propagates toward the antenna element, and the reflected wave propagates away from the antenna element toward the feeding network. The first launcher element is not the phase reference for this quantity, and the quantity is not averaged or summed over launcher elements.

This quantity is a reflected-wave member of the broader [phase of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna] family. It is distinct from the [wave phase of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:wave_phase_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna), which describes inter-element phasing, and together with the [reflected power of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) it specifies the phase-and-magnitude state of the reflected power wave without including the magnitude itself.

Sign convention: Positive when the reflected-wave phasor at the selected element leads the forward-wave phasor at the same element in phase under the adopted temporal phasor convention.
documents.after:

Current-weighted average external poloidal magnetic flux is the poloidal magnetic flux generated by conductors outside the plasma, averaged over the plasma poloidal cross-section with the toroidal plasma current density as the weighting function. External sources include the central solenoid, poloidal-field coils, vertical-stabilization in-vessel coils, passive conducting structures, and eddy currents; the flux generated by the plasma current itself is excluded. The qualifier denotes current-weighting of a poloidal flux by toroidal plasma current density, not weighting by poloidal current.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, over a plasma poloidal cross-section $\Omega_p$ at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining average is:

$$
\langle \psi_\mathrm{ext} \rangle_{j_\phi} = \frac{\int_{\Omega_p} \psi_\mathrm{ext}(R,Z)\, j_\phi(R,Z)\, dS}{I_p}
$$

where $\langle \psi_\mathrm{ext} \rangle_{j_\phi}$ is this current-weighted average, $\psi_\mathrm{ext}$ is the external-circuit contribution to the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), $j_\phi$ is the toroidal plasma current-density component taken positive in the direction of increasing $\phi$, $dS$ is the area element in the poloidal cross-section, and $I_p$ is the signed [plasma current](name:plasma_current).

The scope is the current-carrying plasma region represented by $\Omega_p$; the aggregation convention is a signed toroidal-current-density-weighted mean normalized by the signed total plasma current, so the definition requires nonzero $I_p$. It is distinct from a geometric area average and from any total poloidal magnetic flux that includes the plasma self-flux.

Relative to [current-weighted average external magnetic flux](name:current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux), this name makes explicit that the averaged scalar is the poloidal magnetic flux. The shorter related name [poloidal_average_external_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux) denotes the same current-weighted external poloidal-flux average, and the [tendency of poloidal current-weighted average external magnetic flux] is its time derivative.

Sign convention: Positive when the $j_\phi$-weighted integral of $\psi_\mathrm{ext}$ over $\Omega_p$ has the same sign as $I_p$, with positive $I_p$ flowing in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the relative phase of a complex radio-frequency phasor at a selected antenna strap or module feed with respect to the first reference element. It specifies inter-element phasing of an ion-cyclotron heating launcher rather than an absolute phase.

For selected element $i$, the relative phase is defined by

$$
\Delta\phi_i = \arg\left(A_i A_1^*\right) \pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $\Delta\phi_i$ is the relative phase of element $i$, $A_i$ is its complex radio-frequency voltage or wave phasor, $A_1$ is the phasor of the first reference element, $A_1^*$ is the complex conjugate of that reference phasor, and $\arg$ extracts the phase angle. The reference element has zero relative phase, and the result is defined modulo $2\pi$.

The quantity applies independently to one selected antenna element or module feed and is not summed or averaged over modules. It describes the radio-frequency signal associated with the antenna feed, not a phase belonging to a plasma population or integrated over a plasma region. It excludes absolute phase, amplitude, power, and reflection coefficient, although the phase may characterize a complex feed voltage or traveling-wave quantity.

The family parent [phase of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna] provides the common relative-phase meaning. Propagation-specific instances retain this definition while selecting the wave direction, as in the [forward wave phase of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:forward_wave_phase_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) and the [reflected phase of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:reflected_phase_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna).

Sign convention: Positive when the selected element's radio-frequency phasor leads the first reference element in phase under the adopted temporal phasor convention.

where $\Delta\phi_i$ is the relative phase of element $i$, $A_i$ is its complex radio-frequency voltage or wave phasor, $A_1$ is the phasor of the first reference element, $A_1^*$ is the complex conjugate of that reference phasor, and $\arg$ extracts the phase angle. The reference element has zero relative phase, and the result is defined modulo $2\pi$.

The quantity applies independently to one selected antenna element or module feed and is not summed or averaged over modules. It describes the radio-frequency signal associated with the antenna feed, not a phase belonging to a plasma population or integrated over a plasma region. It excludes absolute phase, amplitude, power, and reflection coefficient, although the phase may characterize a complex feed voltage or traveling-wave quantity.

The family parent phase of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna provides the common relative-phase meaning. Propagation-specific instances retain this definition while selecting the wave direction, as in the [forward wave phase of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:forward_wave_phase_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) and the [reflected phase of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:reflected_phase_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna).

Sign convention: Positive when the selected element's radio-frequency phasor leads the first reference element in phase under the adopted temporal phasor convention.

Local total magnetic-induction vector is the magnetic flux-density vector at a point, carrying both the local field direction and field strength. It is the unqualified parent quantity before selecting a source contribution, perturbation state, component, scalar reduction, spatial aggregation, or evaluation locus.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the vector resolves into radial, toroidal, and vertical components as

$$
\mathbf{B} = B_R\hat{\mathbf{R}} + B_\phi\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + B_Z\hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is this local total magnetic-induction vector; $B_R$ is its radial projection, $B_\phi$ is its [toroidal magnetic-field component](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), and $B_Z$ is its [vertical magnetic-field component](name:vertical_magnetic_field); and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ are the corresponding basis vectors. The frame is right-handed with $\hat{\mathbf{R}} \times \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} = \hat{\mathbf{Z}}$; $R$ is major radius measured from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies wherever a local magnetic induction is defined, including confined plasma and surrounding vacuum regions, and no particle species or population is selected or aggregated. It is pointwise and vector-valued: it is not the [magnetic field magnitude], a [flux-surface-average magnetic field], or an extremum such as the [maximum magnetic field](name:maximum_magnetic_field). No cylindrical component, source contribution, perturbation state, or named locus is implied by the unqualified name.

When a [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential) $\mathbf{A}$ is used, $\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}$; $\mathbf{A}$ is the magnetic vector potential and $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator, and a gage change affects $\mathbf{A}$ without changing $\mathbf{B}$. Source-qualified fields such as the [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field) and [plasma magnetic field](name:plasma_magnetic_field) are vector contributions of the same kind and add vectorially when they belong to the same electromagnetic state; the [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field) is the toroidal projection of the vacuum contribution. The [reference magnetic field](name:reference_magnetic_field) is a reference total magnetic-induction vector of the same kind, not a source-specific contribution; the [toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis) is the toroidal projection evaluated at the magnetic-axis locus.

Sign convention: Positive when the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field component is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the local number density of a selected charged plasma population at the plasma-facing side of a limiter. The selection may be electrons, an ion species summed over its ionization states, or a defined fuel pseudo-species formed by combining constituent ion populations.

$$
n_s(\mathbf{r}_L)=\frac{dN_s}{dV}
$$

where $n_s$ is the selected population number density in m$^{-3}$, $N_s$ is the number of counted particles, $V$ is volume in m$^3$, and $\mathbf{r}_L$ is the limiter-side evaluation position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The position is immediately adjacent to the plasma-facing limiter, on the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance.

Population aggregation is part of the specialization: ion species quantities may be summed over positive ionization states while excluding neutrals, electrons count the electron population, and the deuterium–tritium pseudo-species combines the corresponding ion densities. Concrete members include [electron density at a limiter](name:electron_density_at_limiter), [ion density at a limiter], and [deuterium-tritium density at a limiter](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_limiter). The bare quantity does not imply a sum over all charged populations.

This quantity is the local number density of a selected plasma population at the flux-surface location assigned to an internal transport barrier. It applies to electrons, individual ion species, and compound fuel populations treated as effective species.

The number density is defined by

$$
n = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n$ is the number density in m$^{-3}$, $N$ is the number of counted particles, and $V$ is volume in m$^{3}$. For an ion species, the count is summed over its ionic charge states and excludes neutral atoms; electrons are counted directly. The [ion density at the internal transport barrier] and [electron density at the internal transport barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) are specific population instances, while the [deuterium-tritium density at the internal transport barrier](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) treats the fuel mixture as one effective population. The internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep density gradients.

Recombination power is the heat load delivered to plasma-facing materials when ions recover electrons and transition to neutral states, releasing ionization potential energy and residual kinetic energy at or near material surfaces. Two principal channels contribute: sheath-accelerated plasma-ion recombination at target surfaces, and surface recombination of neutral atoms into molecules, which deposits the molecular binding energy directly into the wall or divertor plate material.

The integrated power from recombination events over a wetted area $A$ is:

$$P_\text{rec} = \sum_s \int_A \Gamma_s \, E_s \, dA$$

where $\Gamma_s$ [m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$] is the incident particle flux density for species $s$ and $E_s$ [J] is the energy released per recombination event for that species, including ionization potential and kinetic contributions.

This power channel is intrinsically non-negative and becomes particularly significant in detached and partially detached divertor regimes, where volumetric ion-electron recombination upstream of the strike point redistributes energy deposition away from the target. Location-specific realizations include [power deposited on a single divertor target](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination), the [total over the full divertor assembly](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination), and [power at first-wall surfaces]. The neutral recombination particle flux produced in these processes is characterized by [neutral_energy_flux_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination).

Flux-surface-averaged parallel current density is the field-aligned conventional electric-current density assigned to a closed magnetic-flux surface. It is the parallel member of the [flux-surface-averaged current density](name:parallel_flux_surface_averaged_current_density) family.

The defining relation for a surface of constant poloidal magnetic flux is:

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{FSA}} = \frac{\langle \mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}\rangle}{B_0}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}$ is the conventional electric-current-density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes the flux-surface average over the same closed magnetic-flux surface, and $B_0$ is the [signed reference toroidal magnetic field], the signed reference value of the $\hat{\phi}$ component of $\mathbf{B}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. For a scalar $f$ on surfaces labeled by poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, the average satisfies $\langle f\rangle = \partial(\int_{V(\psi)} f\,dV)/\partial V$, where $V(\psi)$ is the volume enclosed by the surface.

This quantity is distinct from [toroidal flux-surface-averaged current density](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_current_density), which uses the geometric toroidal $\hat{\phi}$ component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with $1/R$ weighting rather than the field-aligned scalar product. [Parallel total current density](name:parallel_total_current_density) uses the same flux-surface average of $\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}$ and the same signed-reference-field normalization for total current density; it is a closely related naming context, not an unaveraged precursor.

Sign convention: Positive when the field-aligned conventional current has a positive toroidal projection in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

A momentum source density represents the directed transfer of momentum caused by physical processes acting on a plasma population or one of its resolved states. It may retain vector direction or represent a selected component of the momentum-transfer rate.

The area-normalized source is defined by

$$
\mathbf{S}_{p} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{src}}}{\mathrm{d}A\,\mathrm{d}t}
$$

where $\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{src}}$ is the momentum transferred by the source processes, $A$ is the surface over which the source is normalized, and $t$ is time. Concrete variants may resolve a radial component, an internal state, or an ion charge state, as in [radial momentum source] and [ion charge-state momentum source](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_source). Population-level quantities may sum the corresponding state-resolved contributions, as for [ion momentum source](name:ion_momentum_source).

Normalized toroidal plasma beta, conventionally denoted $\beta_N$, is the ratio of toroidal plasma beta times plasma minor radius and reference toroidal magnetic field to total plasma current, including the conventional factor 100. It is a whole-plasma equilibrium beta metric based on the volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure entering toroidal beta.

The defining relation is:

$$
\beta_N = 100\,\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}\,\frac{a B_0}{I_p}
$$

where $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is [beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta), the unnormalized toroidal plasma beta; $a$ is the plasma minor radius; $B_0$ is the reference toroidal magnetic field; and $I_p$ is the total plasma current. The factor $100$ and the prescribed numerical normalization of $a$, $B_0$, and $I_p$ are part of the definition.

The scope is the whole plasma. The pressure population is the total perpendicular plasma pressure represented by $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$, with the volume averaging inherited from [beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta); it is not restricted to thermal pressure.

This quantity is distinct from [beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta), which is the unnormalized toroidal pressure ratio, and from a thermal-pressure-only normalized toroidal beta. Within the global beta-metric family, $\beta_N$ rescales [beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta) by plasma size, reference-field, and current factors, whereas [poloidal_beta](name:poloidal_beta) uses a poloidal-field/current normalization.

Source rate due to injection is the instantaneous rate of electron-equivalent particles supplied by active injection. It is an additive material source for the plasma particle inventory, formed by weighting each injected particle by the total nuclear charge associated with that injected particle.

The electron-equivalent aggregate is defined by

$$
S_\mathrm{inj}(t) = \sum_j Z_j \frac{dN_{j,\mathrm{inj}}}{dt}
$$

where $S_\mathrm{inj}$ is this source rate, $N_{j,\mathrm{inj}}$ is the cumulative count of injected particles of species $j$, $Z_j$ is the total nuclear charge number carried by one injected particle of species $j$, and $t$ is time.

The sum is over active injection only and excludes changes to free-particle populations caused after injection by ionization, recombination, charge exchange, recycling, pumping, or plasma reactions. For an elemental species not resolved by charge state, the contribution is charge-state-summed before the nuclear-charge weighting is applied; species-resolved injected source rates such as [deuterium source rate due to injection](name:deuterium_source_rate_due_to_injection) are unweighted summands until this weighting relation is applied. The electron-equivalent convention makes [electron source rate due to injection](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_injection) the nearest electron-population counterpart, while [electron source rate] is broader because it is not restricted to active injection. A [gas source rate at wall](name:total_particle_source_rate_at_wall_due_to_gas_injection) is wall-referenced rather than a species-weighted aggregate; a [total particle source rate] includes additional source mechanisms when defined with a compatible counting convention.

Argon density is the number of argon ions per unit volume, summed over all ionization stages from singly charged Ar+ through fully stripped Ar18+. Neutral argon is excluded.

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar}} = \sum_{Z=1}^{18} n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{Z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the total argon-ion number density, $Z$ is the integer argon charge state, and $n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{Z+}}$ is the number density of argon ions in that charge state.

The definition applies to a local value and to averages over a specified chord or confined plasma volume, including the [line-averaged argon density](name:line_averaged_argon_density) and [volume-averaged argon density](name:volume_averaged_argon_density). It is distinct from [argon count], which represents an equivalent-electron inventory rather than particles per volume.

Parallel net ion momentum source is the net force-per-area source for the total ion population projected along the local magnetic field. It is the field-aligned scalar component of the net vector source and represents the algebraic addition or removal of ion momentum by all contributing physical processes.

The field-aligned projection is defined by

$$
S_{\parallel i}^{\mathrm{net}} = \hat{b} \cdot \mathbf{S}_{i}^{\mathrm{net}}
$$

where $S_{\parallel i}^{\mathrm{net}}$ is the parallel net ion momentum source, $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{S}_{i}^{\mathrm{net}}$ is the [net ion momentum source] vector for the total ion population.

The quantity is summed over all charge states of the total ion population; [parallel ion charge-state momentum source](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_source) is the corresponding charge-state-resolved parallel source. The [ion momentum source](name:ion_momentum_source) is the broader ion-momentum-source quantity, whereas this name fixes both net aggregation over contributing processes and projection along $\hat{b}$. The area normalization is the transport-surface area associated with the source term; it is not an area defined along a magnetic field line.

Sign convention: Positive when the net source adds momentum to the total ion population in the direction of $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

Global emission rate of fusion reaction products produced by beam-thermal fusion reactions between neutral-beam-injected fast ions and thermal plasma ions is the scalar rate at which the counted products are created over the emitting plasma volume. The counted products and included reaction channels are those selected by the specific member of this quantity family.

For a selected set of reaction channels $C$ and counted product set $P$, the rate is defined by the velocity-distribution average of the beam-thermal fusion source:

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{bt}} = \int_V \sum_{c \in C} \nu_{P,c} \int f_{b,c}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}_b) f_{t,c}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}_t) \sigma_c(v_{\mathrm{rel}}) v_{\mathrm{rel}} \, d^3v_b \, d^3v_t \, dV
$$

Flux due to beam-beam fusion is the volume-integrated production count rate for a specified counted fusion product or reaction-branch event in reactions where both fuel-ion reactants belong to nonthermal fast-ion distributions. It is a count-rate quantity, not an energy flux and not a vector flux through a surface.

For a specified included branch set $S$, the counted beam-beam contribution is defined by the fast-ion phase-space integral:

$$
\Gamma_{bb}^{(S)} = \int_V \sum_{c \in S} \frac{m_c}{1 + \delta_{a_c b_c}} \iint f_{a_c}^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}_1) f_{b_c}^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}_2) \sigma_c(v_{\mathrm{rel}}) v_{\mathrm{rel}}\, d^3v_1\, d^3v_2\, dV
$$

where $\Gamma_{bb}^{(S)}$ is the flux due to beam-beam fusion for branch set $S$, $c$ indexes included fusion reaction branches, $a_c$ and $b_c$ are the reacting fuel-ion species in branch $c$, $\delta_{a_c b_c}$ is one for identical reactant species and zero otherwise, $m_c$ is the count multiplier for the selected product or event, $f_{a_c}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ and $f_{b_c}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ are nonthermal fast-ion distribution functions, $\sigma_c$ is the fusion cross section, $v_{\mathrm{rel}} = |\mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2|$ is the relative speed, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

The branch set $S$ and multiplier $m_c$ define the counting scope: product-specific quantities count the selected emitted products with their branch multiplicity, while reaction-pair quantities count the selected branch events. The [deuterium-deuterium beam-beam fusion flux] and [deuterium-tritium beam-beam fusion flux] restrict the reacting isotope pair, whereas the [neutron flux due to beam-beam fusion](name:neutron_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion) counts neutron products from beam-beam branches. Reactions with one fast reactant and one bulk reactant, or with only bulk reactants, are outside this fast-fast population scope; the [neutron source rate due to fusion] may aggregate neutron production from multiple fusion population classes.

Kinetic temperature of a specified plasma particle population evaluated at the plasma-facing wall is the scalar temperature associated with random particle motion in the plasma immediately on the plasma side of the wall interface. It is a plasma quantity at the boundary, not the thermodynamic temperature of the solid wall material.

For an isotropic wall-adjacent population, the kinetic temperature is related to the mean random kinetic energy per particle at the wall by:

$$
\left\langle \epsilon_{\mathrm{th}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{wall}} = \frac{3}{2} k_B T_{\mathrm{wall}}
$$

where $\left\langle \epsilon_{\mathrm{th}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the mean random kinetic energy per particle of the specified population at the plasma-facing wall after subtracting mean flow energy, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, and $T_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is this temperature.

The scope is the specified plasma-facing wall region and the plasma population represented there. When one scalar value represents an extended wall region, it is a representative effective temperature for the wall-adjacent plasma over that region; the name does not prescribe a particular surface weighting beyond representing the same specified population.

Because no species token is present in the name, this quantity is population-generic unless the surrounding semantic context specifies the particle population. It is distinct from a species-specialized wall quantity such as [electron temperature at wall], and distinct from temperature evaluated at other loci such as [temperature at plasma boundary] or [temperature at outboard midplane].

Poloidal angle is the geometric angular coordinate assigned pointwise to each position on the poloidal cross-section of a specified magnetic flux surface. It is measured from the geometric center of that cross-section rather than from magnetic-field-line distance.

At a point on the surface, the angle $\theta$ is defined by

$$
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(-(Z-Z_0),\,R-R_0\right)
$$

where $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed principal angle, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, $Z$ is the vertical coordinate, and $(R_0,Z_0)$ is the geometric center of the flux-surface cross-section. These coordinates belong to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

The quantity applies to individual points on one magnetic flux surface and has no averaging or summation over the surface. The surface is identified by a constant [poloidal magnetic flux at a flux surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface) value; the angle therefore parameterizes position around that surface rather than assigning one unique angle to the entire surface. It is a geometric angle, distinct from a straight-field-line poloidal angle.

This quantity specializes [poloidal angle](name:poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface) by making the flux-surface locus explicit and provides the angular coordinate used to distinguish positions around the surface's poloidal cross-section.

Sign convention: Positive when the point advances clockwise from the low-field-side midplane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

Radial neutral-state velocity due to diamagnetic drift is the signed particle-flow velocity component assigned to a specified neutral atomic or molecular state and attributed to the diamagnetic, pressure-gradient part of transport. For an uncharged neutral state, it is an effective contribution in a modeled velocity decomposition rather than a direct single-particle Lorentz-force drift.

For neutral state $a$, the radial component is defined by

$$
v_{a,R}^{\mathrm{dia}} = \hat{R} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{a}^{\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{a}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the effective diamagnetic velocity contribution for state $a$, and $\hat{R}$ is the radial unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity is the radial projection of the parent [neutral-state velocity due to diamagnetic drift] and complements the poloidal projection [poloidal neutral-state velocity due to diamagnetic drift](name:poloidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

Energy flux at the wall due to recombination quantifies the rate at which recombination-associated energy is emitted from a plasma-facing surface per unit area as a result of incident plasma ions recombining or neutralizing at the material boundary. It is the total outgoing energy flux carried by emitted recombination products or quanta, not the incident plasma energy flux or heat deposited in the wall material.

The total recombination energy flux at wall location $\mathbf{x}_w$ is defined as the product-energy moment of the outgoing recombination source:

$$
Q_\mathrm{rec}(\mathbf{x}_w) = \sum_{i,\,\zeta,\,c,\,a,\,k}\int E_\mathrm{out}\,\frac{d\Gamma_{i,\zeta,c,a,k}}{dE_\mathrm{out}}(\mathbf{x}_w,E_\mathrm{out})\,dE_\mathrm{out}
$$

where $i$ identifies the incident-ion species, $\zeta$ the incident-ion charge state, $c$ the surface recombination or neutralization channel, $a$ the emitted product species, $k$ the product internal state or emission class, $E_\mathrm{out}$ the energy carried into the plasma-facing half-space by an emitted product or quantum, and $d\Gamma_{i,\zeta,c,a,k}/dE_\mathrm{out}$ the corresponding outgoing recombination-product flux distribution with respect to product energy. For discrete product energies, the integral is replaced by the corresponding sum.

This quantity is the energy-weighted counterpart of [particle flux at the wall due to recombination], which counts the same surface recombination source without energy weighting, and is the energy-flux realization of [flux at the wall due to recombination](name:flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination). The incident-ion decomposition is charge-state-summed in this total: [ion charge-state energy flux at the wall due to recombination](name:ion_charge_state_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination) resolves a specified incident-ion species and charge state, while [ion energy flux at the wall due to recombination](name:ion_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination) is the corresponding ion contribution after summing over charge states. Neutral-product particle specializations such as [neutral particle flux at the wall due to recombination](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination) partition emitted-product counts and do not by themselves include energy weighting.

Sign convention: Positive when recombination-associated energy is emitted away from the plasma-facing wall surface into the plasma-facing half-space.

The ion absorbed power of a beam-tracing beam is the total electromagnetic wave power transferred from a single coherent beam to one selected ion species along the beam trajectory. It is a species-resolved contribution to the [absorbed power of a beam-tracing beam](name:absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam), distinct from the electron contribution represented by [electron absorbed power of a beam-tracing beam](name:electron_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam).

The species partition of the beam power balance is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{abs}} = P_e + \sum_s P_{\mathrm{ion},s}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{abs}}$ is the total absorbed beam power, $P_e$ is the electron contribution, $P_{\mathrm{ion},s}$ is the power absorbed by ion species $s$, and the sum is over the contributing ion species. This quantity denotes one term $P_{\mathrm{ion},s}$; its charge-state-resolved counterpart is [ion charge-state absorbed power of a beam-tracing beam](name:ion_charge_state_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam). It excludes residual wave power represented by [power of a beam-tracing beam] and differs from volume-integrated [ion absorbed wave power](name:ion_absorbed_wave_power).

The quantity is the signed fraction of a beam-tracing wave vector directed along the toroidal axis at each point of its propagation path. It is a direction cosine, not a gyroradius-scaled wave-vector normalization.

The normalized toroidal component is defined by:

$$
k_{phi,\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{k_\phi}{\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert}
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the local wave vector, $k_\phi$ is its projection onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$, and $\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert$ is the wave-vector magnitude. The projection is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity is defined only where $\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert$ is nonzero and lies between -1 and 1. It represents the same toroidal direction-cosine concept as [toroidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam], with normalization explicitly taken by the total wave-vector magnitude.
