Incident neutral particle flux at a plasma-facing wall quantifies the arrival rate of neutral atoms or molecules in one specified electronic, vibrational, or rotational internal state per unit wall area. It is an incoming surface flux, not an emitted or net flux.

$$
\Gamma_{n,s} = \frac{dN_{n,s}}{dA\,dt}
$$

where $\Gamma_{n,s}$ is the state-resolved neutral particle flux, $N_{n,s}$ is the number of arriving neutral particles in internal state $s$, $A$ is wall-surface area, and $t$ is time.

Unlike the state-summed [neutral particle flux at the wall], this quantity resolves the internal-state contribution. It has no process attribution; the recombination-specific subset is [incident neutral internal-state particle flux at the wall due to recombination](name:incident_neutral_internal_state_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination).

Outgoing neutral internal-state particle number flux density at a plasma-facing wall due to recombination is the surface flux density of neutral atoms or molecules in a specified internal quantum state that are produced by recombination at the wall and cross the wall surface away from the wall. It is resolved by neutral product species and by the internal quantum state of that product.

For neutral product species $n$ in internal state $\alpha$, with $\hat{\mathbf n}_w$ the unit normal directed from the wall material into the adjacent plasma, the outgoing recombination contribution is defined by

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{rec,out}}_{n,\alpha} = \int_{\mathbf v \cdot \hat{\mathbf n}_w > 0} (\mathbf v \cdot \hat{\mathbf n}_w)\, f^{\mathrm{rec}}_{n,\alpha}(\mathbf v)\, d^3\mathbf v
$$

where $\mathbf v$ is neutral-particle velocity and $f^{\mathrm{rec}}_{n,\alpha}$ is the velocity-space distribution function at the wall for neutral recombination products of species $n$ in internal state $\alpha$, normalized so that its velocity integral gives the corresponding local neutral-product number density.

This quantity includes only the emitted, outward wall-normal component of neutral recombination products in the specified internal state. Aggregating over internal states for the same neutral product species gives the [neutral particle flux at wall due to recombination](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination); the broader internal-state-resolved recombination-flux family is [internal state particle flux at wall due to recombination]. The distinct inward wall-normal counterpart is [incident neutral internal-state particle flux at wall due to recombination](name:incident_neutral_internal_state_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination) and is not included here.

Sign convention: Positive when neutral recombination products cross the wall surface in the direction of the wall normal from the wall material into the adjacent plasma.

Neutral internal-state pressure is the state-resolved scalar kinetic pressure of neutral atoms or molecules occupying a specified internal quantum or excitation state. It is a partial pressure, not a sum over all internal states, and can include thermal and nonthermal velocity-space contributions.

For state $a$, the pressure is the one-third trace of the central second velocity-space moment:

$$
p_a = \frac{m_a}{3}\int \lvert\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_a\rvert^2 f_a(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $m_a$ is the particle mass, $f_a(\mathbf{v})$ is the velocity distribution of neutrals in state $a$, and $\mathbf{u}_a$ is its mean velocity. The central moment excludes dynamic pressure from directed bulk flow. Thermal and suprathermal contributions may be separated, while [total neutral internal-state pressure](name:total_neutral_internal_state_pressure) combines them. The quantity is a neutral-specific instance of [internal-state pressure], and its associated kinetic temperature is [neutral internal-state temperature](name:neutral_internal_state_temperature).

This quantity is the net particle source or sink for a neutral species in a specified internal state. It includes all processes that create or remove particles from that state and is distinct from an aggregate neutral source that combines states.

The state-resolved density balance is written as

$$
\frac{\partial n_s}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s = S_s
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of the specified neutral internal state, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s$ is its particle flux density, and $S_s$ is this net volumetric source rate. The quantity is analogous to the charged-state [ion state source rate](name:ion_state_source_rate) and is more specifically state-resolved than the general [particle source rate].

Sign convention: Positive when particle creation exceeds particle destruction for the specified neutral internal state.

This quantity is the parallel component of the kinetic pressure contributed by fast neutral particles in one specified internal quantum or excitation state. It is the centered second velocity moment projected along the local magnetic-field direction.

The defining relation is

$$
p_{\parallel,\alpha}=m_\alpha\int\left(v_\parallel-u_{\parallel,\alpha}\right)^2 f_\alpha(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $p_{\parallel,\alpha}$ is the state-resolved parallel pressure, $m_\alpha$ is the mass of the neutral species in internal state $\alpha$, $v_\parallel$ is a particle velocity component parallel to the local magnetic field, $u_{\parallel,\alpha}$ is the corresponding mean parallel velocity, $f_\alpha(\mathbf{v})$ is the velocity distribution of that state, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

The scope is restricted to the fast, non-thermal neutral population in the specified internal state and to the field-aligned component. Contributions from other internal states are not included; this quantity is not the sum over internal states represented by [parallel fast-neutral pressure](name:parallel_fast_neutral_pressure).

It is the parallel component of the anisotropic tensor quantity [fast-neutral internal-state pressure](name:parallel_fast_neutral_internal_state_pressure), while the corresponding perpendicular component is represented by [perpendicular suprathermal neutral internal-state pressure](name:perpendicular_suprathermal_neutral_internal_state_pressure).

This quantity is the particle diffusivity of neutral particles resolved to a specified internal state and projected along the local magnetic-field direction. It describes particle-number transport rather than momentum transport or an aggregate over internal states.

The parallel diffusive particle flux is defined by Fick's law:

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,s} = -D_{\parallel,s}\nabla_{\parallel} n_s
$$

where $\Gamma_{\parallel,s}$ is the field-line-parallel diffusive particle flux for internal state $s$, $D_{\parallel,s}$ is this diffusivity, $n_s$ is the number density of that state, and $\nabla_{\parallel}=\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla$ is the derivative along the magnetic-field unit vector $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

This is the directional counterpart of [neutral internal-state diffusivity]; it excludes the separate momentum-transport quantity [parallel neutral internal-state momentum diffusivity](name:parallel_neutral_internal_state_momentum_diffusivity).

documents.before:
Field-aligned effective velocity for convective transport of the energy density of a specified neutral internal state is the component of the effective convection velocity parallel to the local magnetic-field vector. It is the field-aligned realization of [neutral internal-state energy convection velocity](name:neutral_internal_state_energy_convection_velocity), complementary to the [radial](name:poloidal_neutral_internal_state_energy_convection_velocity) and [poloidal](name:poloidal_neutral_internal_state_energy_convection_velocity) realizations.

For the field-aligned direction, the convective energy-flux component is defined by

$$
q_{E,\nu,\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}} = u_{E,\nu,\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}} w_{E,\nu}
$$

where $q_{E,\nu,\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the field-aligned convective energy-flux component, $u_{E,\nu,\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is this effective convection velocity, $w_{E,\nu}$ is the energy density of the neutral internal state, and $\nu$ identifies that state.

The quantity applies to the specified internal state and does not sum over all neutral states. By contrast, [neutral species energy convection velocity] represents the corresponding energy transport aggregated over a neutral species.

Sign convention: Positive when the effective velocity points in the direction of the local magnetic-field vector, making the field-aligned convective energy flux positive in that direction.

documents.before:
Parallel neutral internal-state momentum diffusivity is the coefficient governing down-gradient transport of momentum for neutral particles resolved by internal state. It is the field-aligned directional component of [neutral internal-state momentum diffusivity](name:toroidal_neutral_internal_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient). The parallel qualifier identifies the direction of diffusive momentum flux and of the momentum-density gradient along the local magnetic field, not a projection of the transported momentum onto that direction.

The defining Fick-type relation for the diffusive contribution along the magnetic field is:

$$
\mathbf{F}_{P,\parallel}^{\mathrm{diff},(n,s)} = -D_{\parallel}^{(n,s)} \nabla_{\parallel}\mathbf{P}^{(n,s)}
$$

where $\mathbf{F}_{P,\parallel}^{\mathrm{diff},(n,s)}$ is the diffusive field-aligned flux of neutral momentum for neutral population $n$ in internal state $s$, $D_{\parallel}^{(n,s)}$ is this diffusivity, $\nabla_{\parallel}=\hat{\mathbf{b}}\cdot\nabla$ is the derivative along the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, and $\mathbf{P}^{(n,s)}$ is the neutral momentum-density vector for that population and internal state. The operator $\nabla_{\parallel}$ acts component-wise on the vector momentum density.

The quantity is resolved by internal state and does not aggregate over neutral internal states. It describes momentum transport rather than particle transport, which distinguishes it from [parallel neutral internal-state diffusivity](name:parallel_neutral_internal_state_diffusivity); its state resolution distinguishes it from [parallel neutral momentum diffusivity], and its field-aligned direction distinguishes it from [vertical neutral internal-state momentum diffusivity](name:vertical_neutral_internal_state_momentum_diffusivity).

The parallel neutral internal-state momentum flux density is the magnetic-field-parallel transport component of linear momentum carried by neutral particles restricted to one specified atomic, molecular, charge, or excitation state. It is a momentum-flux tensor component, not a particle flux or a local momentum source.

For the state-resolved neutral distribution, the parallel component is defined by

$$
\Pi_{\parallel\parallel}^{(s)} = \hat{b} \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}^{(s)} \cdot \hat{b} = \int m_s v_\parallel^2 f_s(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $s$ identifies the internal state, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{(s)}$ is its momentum-flux tensor, $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field, $m_s$ is the mass of a neutral particle in state $s$, $v_\parallel=\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{b}$ is the velocity component along $\hat{b}$, and $f_s$ is the state-resolved velocity distribution.

The parallel direction is the local magnetic-field direction, not the radial, toroidal, or vertical direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This component is the parallel member of the parent [neutral internal-state momentum flux], differs from the [radial](name:radial_neutral_internal_state_momentum_flux), [toroidal](name:toroidal_neutral_internal_state_momentum_flux), and linear internal-state components, and is the state-resolved counterpart of [parallel neutral momentum flux](name:parallel_neutral_momentum_flux).

Sign convention: Positive when magnetic-field-parallel linear momentum is transported in the local magnetic-field direction.

Poloidal effective velocity for convective transport of the energy density of a specified neutral internal state is the component of the effective convection velocity along the tangent direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. It is the poloidal directional realization of the [neutral internal-state energy convection velocity](name:neutral_internal_state_energy_convection_velocity).

For the poloidal transport direction, the convective energy-flux component is defined by

$$
q_{E,\nu,\theta}^{\mathrm{conv}} = u_{E,\nu,\theta}^{\mathrm{conv}} w_{E,\nu}
$$

where $q_{E,\nu,\theta}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the poloidal convective energy-flux component, $u_{E,\nu,\theta}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is this poloidal effective convection velocity, $w_{E,\nu}$ is the energy density of the neutral internal state, and $\nu$ identifies that state.

The quantity applies to the specified state and does not sum over all neutral internal states. It is the poloidal member of the directional set that also includes the [radial neutral internal-state energy convection velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_internal_state_energy_convection_velocity) and the [field-aligned neutral internal-state energy convection velocity](name:parallel_neutral_internal_state_energy_convection_velocity); by contrast, [neutral species energy convection velocity] represents the corresponding energy transport aggregated over a neutral species.

Sign convention: Positive when the effective velocity points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, making the convective energy flux positive in that direction.

documents.before:
Fick's-law poloidal neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient is the scalar poloidal diffusivity for energy transport by neutral particles in a specified internal state, and is the poloidal component form of the [neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient). It is resolved for one internal state, not summed or averaged over internal states, and relates only the poloidal projection of the diffusive thermal-energy flux to the poloidal temperature gradient of those same particles.

The poloidal projection is taken along the tangent obtained by increasing the poloidal angle $\theta$ at constant flux coordinate $\rho$ and toroidal angle $\phi$ in a chosen flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. The Fickian poloidal contribution is defined by

$$
q^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,n,s,\theta} = - n_{n,s} D^{\theta}_{E,n,s} \, \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}\cdot\nabla T_{n,s}
$$

where $q^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,n,s,\theta}$ is the poloidal component of the diffusive thermal-energy flux carried by neutral particles in internal state $s$, positive in the direction of increasing $\theta$; $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}$ is the corresponding unit poloidal tangent; $n_{n,s}$ is the number density of those particles; $D^{\theta}_{E,n,s}$ is this coefficient; and $T_{n,s}$ is their temperature.

The coefficient includes only the diagonal Fickian term driven by $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}\cdot\nabla T_{n,s}$ and excludes convective energy transport, sources, sinks, cross-gradient tensor terms, and effective coefficients that absorb non-diffusive contributions. The factor $n_{n,s}\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}\cdot\nabla T_{n,s}$ is the temperature-gradient contribution to the poloidal gradient of internal thermal-energy density; an energy-density-gradient form using $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}\cdot\nabla(n_{n,s}T_{n,s})$ is equivalent only when the density-gradient contribution along the poloidal tangent is absent.

It specializes the [internal-state energy diffusion coefficient] to neutral particles and the poloidal projection. It is distinct from the [radial neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:radial_neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient), where radial denotes the $\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and is the internal-state-resolved counterpart of the [poloidal neutral energy diffusivity](name:poloidal_neutral_energy_diffusivity).

Radial effective velocity for convective transport of the energy density of a specified neutral internal state is the component of the effective convection velocity along increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is a directional realization of the [neutral internal-state energy convection velocity](name:neutral_internal_state_energy_convection_velocity).

The radial convective energy-flux component is defined by

$$
q_{E,\nu,R}^{\mathrm{conv}} = u_{E,\nu,R}^{\mathrm{conv}} w_{E,\nu}
$$

where $q_{E,\nu,R}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial convective energy-flux component, $u_{E,\nu,R}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is this radial effective convection velocity, $w_{E,\nu}$ is the energy density of the specified neutral internal state, and $\nu$ identifies that state.

The quantity applies to one specified neutral internal state and does not sum over all neutral states. By contrast, [neutral species energy convection velocity] represents the corresponding energy transport aggregated over a neutral species; [poloidal](name:poloidal_neutral_internal_state_energy_convection_velocity) and [parallel](name:parallel_neutral_internal_state_energy_convection_velocity) members resolve the same state-specific coefficient in different directions.

Sign convention: Positive when the effective velocity points toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, making the radial convective energy flux positive in that direction.

Fick's-law radial neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient is the scalar radial diffusivity for energy transport by neutral particles in a specified internal state, and is the radial component form of the [neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient). Here radial denotes projection along $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is resolved for one internal state, not summed or averaged over internal states.

The radial Fickian contribution is defined by

$$
q^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,n,s,R} = - n_{n,s} D_{E,n,s,R} \frac{\partial T_{n,s}}{\partial R}
$$

where $q^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,n,s,R}$ is the radial component of the diffusive thermal-energy flux carried by neutral particles in internal state $s$, $n_{n,s}$ is their number density, $D_{E,n,s,R}$ is this coefficient, and $T_{n,s}$ is their temperature.

The coefficient includes only the Fickian term driven by $\partial T_{n,s}/\partial R$ and excludes convective energy transport, sources, sinks, and effective coefficients that absorb non-diffusive contributions. It specializes the [internal-state energy diffusion coefficient] to neutral particles and is the internal-state-resolved counterpart of the [neutral energy diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient); it is distinct from the [poloidal neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient).

Sign convention: Positive when a negative radial temperature derivative produces a diffusive thermal-energy flux in the $+\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the toroidal component of the torque density transferred to the plasma by neutral particles occupying a specified internal state. It is the state-resolved toroidal projection of [neutral internal-state torque density], rather than a sum over all neutral internal states.

$$
\tau_{\phi,s}=\hat{\phi}\cdot\left(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{f}_s\right)
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,s}$ is the toroidal torque density, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector relative to the machine symmetry axis, and $\mathbf{f}_s$ is the force density exerted on the plasma by neutrals in internal state $s$.

Summing this state-resolved quantity over all neutral internal states gives [toroidal neutral torque density](name:toroidal_neutral_torque_density); it is distinct from the direction-independent [neutral torque density].

Sign convention: Positive when the torque points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

This quantity is the toroidal component of the torque density transferred to the plasma by neutral particles occupying a specified internal state. It is the state-resolved toroidal projection of neutral internal-state torque density, rather than a sum over all neutral internal states.

$$
\tau_{\phi,s}=\hat{\phi}\cdot\left(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{f}_s\right)
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,s}$ is the toroidal torque density, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector relative to the machine symmetry axis, and $\mathbf{f}_s$ is the force density exerted on the plasma by neutrals in internal state $s$.

Summing this state-resolved quantity over all neutral internal states gives [toroidal neutral torque density](name:toroidal_neutral_torque_density); it is distinct from the direction-independent [neutral torque density](name:neutral_torque_density).

Sign convention: Positive when the torque points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The vertical neutral internal-state momentum flux density is the vertical transport component of linear momentum carried by neutral particles restricted to one specified atomic, molecular, charge, or excitation state. It is the $ZZ$ component of the state-resolved momentum-flux tensor, not a particle flux or a local momentum source.

For the state-resolved neutral distribution, the vertical component is defined by

$$
\Pi_{ZZ}^{(s)} = \hat{Z} \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}^{(s)} \cdot \hat{Z} = \int m_s v_Z^2 f_s(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $s$ identifies the internal state, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{(s)}$ is its momentum-flux tensor, $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical basis direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $m_s$ is the mass of a neutral particle in state $s$, $v_Z=\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{Z}$ is the vertical velocity component, and $f_s$ is the state-resolved velocity distribution.

The vertical direction is the $Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; it is not the radial, toroidal, or magnetic-field-parallel direction. As a diagonal $ZZ$ tensor component formed from $v_Z^2$, this quantity is nonnegative for any nonnegative state-resolved velocity distribution.

This component is the vertical member of the parent [neutral internal-state momentum flux], differs from the [radial](name:radial_neutral_internal_state_momentum_flux), [toroidal](name:toroidal_neutral_internal_state_momentum_flux), [parallel](name:parallel_neutral_internal_state_momentum_flux), and linear internal-state components, and is the state-resolved counterpart of [vertical neutral momentum flux](name:vertical_neutral_momentum_flux).

Plasma heating power is the rate at which heating processes deposit energy in the plasma as particle internal energy. It represents a source term in the plasma energy balance rather than an energy content, loss rate, or stored-energy derivative.

Using the local volumetric heating source $q_\mathrm{heat}$, the total plasma heating power is defined by

$$
P_\mathrm{heat} = \int_{V_\mathrm{plasma}} q_\mathrm{heat}(\mathbf{x}) \, dV
$$

where $P_\mathrm{heat}$ is the plasma heating power, $q_\mathrm{heat}(\mathbf{x})$ is the [plasma heating power density] at spatial position $\mathbf{x}$, $V_\mathrm{plasma}$ is the plasma volume over which the heating source is defined, and $dV$ is the differential volume element.

The scope is the plasma as a whole: contributions are summed over all plasma species and all heating mechanisms unless a species-resolved or mechanism-resolved quantity is explicitly named. Internal energy exchange between plasma species is not an additional net plasma heating contribution. This quantity is the volume-integrated total, not the local heating power density; it excludes launched or generator power not deposited in the plasma, radiated or conducted losses, and the time derivative of stored energy.

In a global energy balance, plasma heating power is a source term for [thermal plasma energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), while losses and work terms determine how that energy changes. Mechanism-specific deposited powers add to this quantity when they refer to mutually exclusive heating channels over the same plasma region.

This quantity is the effective particle-number advection velocity of neutral particles in a specified internal quantum state, projected onto the cylindrical radial direction. The corresponding full vector is [effective neutral internal-state velocity due to convection].

Effective advective drift velocity of neutral particles in a specified internal state for convective momentum transport is the vector transport coefficient that multiplies the population's momentum-density vector to give the convective momentum-flux tensor. It represents the advective velocity appearing in a momentum-transport closure for that resolved neutral internal-state population.

The convective momentum flux is defined by the outer-product relation

$$
\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\alpha} = \boldsymbol{g}_{\alpha} \otimes \boldsymbol{u}^{\mathrm{eff,mom}}_{\alpha}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\alpha}$ is the convective momentum-flux tensor of neutral particles in internal state $\alpha$, $\boldsymbol{g}_{\alpha}$ is their momentum-density vector, and $\boldsymbol{u}^{\mathrm{eff,mom}}_{\alpha}$ is this effective convective momentum velocity.

The effective qualifier means the coefficient is defined by this momentum-flux closure and need not equal the neutral population's microscopic mean particle velocity. It is the momentum-transport analog of [effective neutral internal-state velocity due to convection], which enters the convective particle-flux relation, and is distinguished from the non-effective counterpart [neutral internal-state momentum velocity due to convection](name:neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection). This name denotes the full vector; [radial effective neutral internal-state momentum velocity due to convection](name:radial_neutral_internal_state_momentum_convection_velocity) denotes its cylindrical $\hat{R}$ projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Sign convention: Positive when a vector component of $\boldsymbol{u}^{\mathrm{eff,mom}}_{\alpha}$ is aligned with the positive direction of the corresponding explicitly chosen basis vector.

This quantity is the signed projection along the vertical direction of the E×B drift velocity for a specified neutral-species internal state. It is the vertical component of the vector quantity [neutral-species internal-state E×B drift velocity], not the drift speed or full vector.

The component is defined by projecting the crossed-field drift onto the vertical axis:

$$
v_Z = \left(\frac{\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}}{B^2}\right) \cdot \hat{Z}

The quantity is specific to the stated internal state and contains no aggregation over other neutral species or internal states.

Sign convention: Positive when the drift velocity points in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

Effective particle energy is a gyrokinetic velocity-space energy assigned to a particle species through a kinetic-energy-like weight. It provides the energy coordinate used to order that species in velocity space and is the unnormalized concept underlying [normalized effective particle energy](name:normalized_effective_particle_energy). It differs from [particle energy](name:particle_energy), which denotes the energy content of the full distribution.

The effective energy is defined by the selected velocity-space weight:

$$
\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{eff},s}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = w_s(\boldsymbol{\xi})
$$

where $s$ labels the species, $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ denotes its velocity-space variables, and $w_s$ is a kinetic-energy-like weight, such as the total kinetic energy or a directional component. A normalized specialization divides $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{eff},s}$ by a strictly positive species reference energy. This quantity is distinct from [perturbed particle energy], which describes a moment of a distribution perturbation rather than the effective energy coordinate itself.

Current due to ohmic induction is the scalar current component produced by an inductive electric field acting through the Ohmic conductivity of a conducting medium. The drive mechanism is changing magnetic flux, equivalently the loop voltage around the current path, not pressure-gradient-driven bootstrap current or externally applied non-inductive current drive.

The current is the flux of the Ohmic current-density component through an oriented surface that cuts the current channel:

$$
I_\mathrm{Ohm} = \int_S \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{Ohm} \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $S$ is the oriented cutting surface, $d\mathbf{A}$ is its vector area element, and $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{Ohm}$ is the current density produced by the inductive electric field. In a magnetized plasma, the constitutive Ohmic transport component is field-parallel, with $j_{\mathrm{Ohm}\parallel} = \sigma_\parallel E_{\mathrm{ind}\parallel}$.

This quantity is a drive-mechanism component and equals the total current only when Ohmic induction is the only current source. It excludes [current due to non-inductive current drive](name:current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive); [plasma current due to ohmic induction](name:plasma_current_due_to_ohmic_induction) is the toroidal plasma-current specialization, and [parallel plasma current due to ohmic induction] denotes the field-parallel plasma specialization.

Sign convention: Positive when $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{Ohm}$ flows through the oriented surface in the direction of $d\mathbf{A}$.

Effective neutral internal-state energy diffusivity is the scalar transport coefficient for the diffusive thermal-energy flux carried by neutral particles of a specified species and internal state. It represents the direction-independent Fickian response to the local temperature gradient of that neutral-state population.

In a scalar effective closure for the conductive part of the energy flux, the defining relation is:

$$
\mathbf{q}^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,a,s} = - n_{a,s}\,\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}_{E,a,s}\,\nabla T_{a,s}
$$

where $\mathbf{q}^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,a,s}$ is the diffusive thermal-energy flux carried by neutral species $a$ in internal state $s$, $n_{a,s}$ is the [neutral internal-state number density], $\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}_{E,a,s}$ is the effective neutral internal-state energy diffusivity, and $T_{a,s}$ is the [neutral internal-state temperature](name:neutral_internal_state_temperature). The minus sign denotes down-gradient diffusive transport in this closure.

This is a scalar effective coefficient, not the full anisotropic diffusivity. In an anisotropic formulation a second-rank tensor $\boldsymbol{\chi}_{E,a,s}$ maps $\nabla T_{a,s}$ to $\mathbf{q}^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,a,s}$; this quantity is the direction-independent value used in place of that tensor, such as through $\boldsymbol{\chi}_{E,a,s}=\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}_{E,a,s}\mathbf{I}$ or another specified scalar contraction. A projection along a particular direction vector, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\chi}_{E,a,s}\hat{\mathbf{e}}$, is a directional component and is not this quantity unless it is explicitly adopted as the scalar effective representation.

It includes only the energy flux represented by the temperature-gradient term; convective energy transport associated with neutral particle flow and local source or loss terms are excluded. It is the effective scalar counterpart of [neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient) and is distinct from [neutral internal-state heat diffusivity], which denotes the heat-diffusion coefficient for the same neutral-state population when the heat channel is specified separately from the energy channel.

The alpha angle is the oriented inclination of the alpha-side lateral face of an oblique trapezoidal ICRH antenna-strap cross-section, measured from the directed strap base edge. It specifies the alpha-side geometry complementary to the beta-side quantity represented by [angle of antenna strap].

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\hat{n}\cdot(\hat{b}\times\hat{a}),\,\hat{b}\cdot\hat{a}\right)
$$

where $\hat{b}$ is the unit vector along the directed strap base edge, $\hat{a}$ is the unit vector along the alpha-side lateral face, and $\hat{n}$ is the positive normal to the oriented cross-sectional plane. The angle is restricted to the alpha-side face and is distinct from the beta-side inclination.

Sign convention: Positive when rotation from the directed strap base edge toward the alpha-side lateral face follows the positive normal of the oriented strap cross-section.

Area of a neutral beam injector is the source cross-section of the active ion-source emission face that forms the extracted beam before neutralization. It represents the open or emitting part of the ion-extraction face through which extracted ions enter the beamline; for a multi-aperture source it aggregates only apertures that contribute to the extracted beam.

The area is defined as the projected geometric area of the active emitting or open aperture set onto the plane normal to the nominal extracted-beam direction:

$$
A_\mathrm{NBI} = \int_{S_\mathrm{open}} \left|\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r})\right| \, dS
$$

where $S_\mathrm{open}$ is the active open or emitting aperture surface on the ion-source extraction face, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the nominal extracted-beam direction, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local unit normal of that aperture surface, and $dS$ is the surface-area element.

This quantity is the geometric source area used to normalize extracted beam current density to total extracted current, as in $I_\mathrm{ext}=\langle j_\mathrm{ext}\rangle A_\mathrm{NBI}$ for area-averaged extracted current density $\langle j_\mathrm{ext}\rangle$ and extracted current $I_\mathrm{ext}$. It is not a downstream neutral-beam cross-section, propagated beam footprint, or an area of a neutralizer, duct, collimator, or target. The related [beam area of neutral beam injector] denotes the same active beam-forming source cross-section from the beam side of the source, while aperture dimensions such as [neutral-beam aperture width](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_aperture) specify component geometry rather than the aggregate active area.

Neutral-beam-driven plasma current is the net toroidal current produced when injected neutrals ionize and their fast ions transfer momentum to the plasma. It includes both the directed fast-ion contribution and the associated collisional electron return-current contribution.

The current is defined by integrating the net neutral-beam-driven toroidal current density over the plasma cross-sectional area:

$$
I_{\mathrm{NBI}} = \int_{\mathcal{A}_{p}} j_{\phi,\mathrm{NBI}}(R,Z)\,d\mathcal{A}
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{NBI}}$ is the neutral-beam-driven plasma current, $j_{\phi,\mathrm{NBI}}$ is its toroidal current-density contribution, and $\mathcal{A}_{p}$ is the plasma cross-sectional area in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This source contribution is distinct from [absorbed power of a neutral beam injector] and is combined with other current sources, including [plasma current due to ohmic induction] and [current due to electron-cyclotron current drive](name:current_due_to_electron_cyclotron_current_drive).

Sign convention: Positive when the net toroidal current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

I_{\mathrm{NBI}} = \int_{\mathcal{A}_{p}} j_{\phi,\mathrm{NBI}}(R,Z)\,d\mathcal{A}
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{NBI}}$ is the neutral-beam-driven plasma current, $j_{\phi,\mathrm{NBI}}$ is its toroidal current-density contribution, and $\mathcal{A}_{p}$ is the plasma cross-sectional area in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This source contribution is distinct from absorbed power of a neutral beam injector and is combined with other current sources, including plasma current due to ohmic induction and [current due to electron-cyclotron current drive](name:current_due_to_electron_cyclotron_current_drive).

Sign convention: Positive when the net toroidal current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

Wave-driven current is the toroidal plasma current attributable to momentum transfer from externally applied electromagnetic waves through wave–particle interactions. It excludes inductive current and non-wave non-inductive current sources.

For a selected poloidal cross-sectional area, the current is defined by

$$
I_{\mathrm{wd}} = \int_A j_{\mathrm{wd},\phi}(R,Z)\,dA
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{wd}}$ is the wave-driven current, $A$ is the selected poloidal area, $j_{\mathrm{wd},\phi}$ is the toroidal component of the [wave-driven current density], and $(R,\phi,Z)$ is the right-handed cylindrical frame. For a flux-surface-enclosed area, this gives the cumulative quantity represented by [toroidal current due to wave-driven current drive](name:toroidal_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive); the same current may be decomposed into [per-toroidal-mode current].

Sign convention: Positive when the wave-driven plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The antenna-strap height is the full vertical extent of the rectangular conductor cross-section, measured parallel to the $Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is a geometric cross-section dimension, not the antenna elevation or its distance from the plasma.

$$
H = Z_{\max} - Z_{\min}
$$

where $H$ is the strap height and $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the vertical coordinates of the upper and lower cross-section boundaries. The dimension is non-negative and complements the [toroidal width of the antenna strap] and [thickness of the antenna strap](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap), which describe the other conductor extents. For an annular cross-section, the radial boundaries are specified by the [inner radius of the antenna strap](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap) and [outer radius of the antenna strap](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap).

The quantity is the geometric distance accumulated along a beam-tracing ray from its designated reference point to a point on the ray. It follows the ray trajectory and therefore differs from the straight-line separation of the endpoints.

For a ray position $\mathbf{r}(\lambda)$ parameterized by a monotonically increasing path parameter $\lambda$, the arc length is

$$
s(\lambda_0,\lambda_1)=\int_{\lambda_0}^{\lambda_1}\left\lVert\frac{d\mathbf{r}}{d\lambda}\right\rVert\,d\lambda
$$

where $\lambda_0$ identifies the reference point, $\lambda_1$ identifies the endpoint, $\mathbf{r}$ is the ray position, and $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ is the Euclidean norm. The resulting length is non-negative and may include segments in both vacuum and plasma. The electron-cyclotron-specific counterpart [length of electron-cyclotron beam] uses the same geometric path-length concept.

The upper mechanical travel limit is the greatest permitted value of the mirror’s signed rotation angle, bounding the accessible steering range of the launcher. It is a limit of the mechanical actuator, not the mirror angle during a particular operating condition.

Let $\theta$ denote the signed mirror angle defined by [angle of electron-cyclotron launcher mirror]. The upper limit $\theta_{\max}$ is defined by

$$
\theta_{\max} = \sup\{\theta \mid \theta\text{ is mechanically accessible}\}
$$

The quantity excludes the lower travel limit and does not describe the mirror’s position unless that position equals the upper boundary of the allowed range.

Sign convention: Positive when the mirror rotates in the positive sense defined for [angle of electron-cyclotron launcher mirror].

Neutral-beam injection energy is the full kinetic energy acquired by one atom of the injected species during acceleration through the complete ion-source potential difference before neutralization. It defines the characteristic birth energy of the full-energy neutral-beam component.

The energy gain is defined by

$$
E_{\mathrm{NBI}} = |q_{\mathrm{ion}}|\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{acc}}
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{NBI}}$ is the neutral-beam injection energy, $q_{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the charge of the precursor ion, and $\Delta V_{\mathrm{acc}}$ is the magnitude of the complete accelerating potential difference.

This quantity applies per atom of the injected neutral species and to one selected neutral-beam unit. It represents the full injection energy rather than a spatially resolved plasma energy, a charge-state sum, or an energy accumulated over multiple beam units. It excludes the beam particle rate and therefore is distinct from power transferred to the plasma.

The injection energy sets the initial fast-ion birth energy and contributes to the beam penetration and heating profile. It is distinct from [absorbed power of the neutral beam injector], which describes the rate of energy transferred from the injector to the plasma, and it enters the physics of [current due to neutral beam injection](name:current_due_to_neutral_beam_injection).
documents.after:

The ordinary-mode fraction is the share of launched electron-cyclotron wave-beam power carried by the ordinary electromagnetic polarization eigenmode. It distinguishes this polarization component from the complementary mode contributions represented by the parent quantity [fraction of wave beam].

$$
f_O = \frac{P_O}{P_{\rm launch}}
$$

where $f_O$ is the ordinary-mode power fraction, $P_O$ is the launched power in the ordinary mode, and $P_{\rm launch}$ is the total launched wave-beam power. The fraction is bounded by zero and one when the polarization-mode powers are nonnegative and exhaust the launched power; it excludes power introduced or lost after launch.

Parallel per-toroidal-mode current density due to wave-driven current drive is the component of the current-density contribution from one toroidal Fourier harmonic that is parallel to the local magnetic field. It represents the field-aligned part of the non-inductive current generated by wave-driven current drive for the specified harmonic.

The defining projection is

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{wcd}}^{(n_\phi)} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{wcd}}^{(n_\phi)} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{wcd}}^{(n_\phi)}$ is the parallel per-toroidal-mode current density due to wave-driven current drive, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{wcd}}^{(n_\phi)}$ is the vector [per-toroidal-mode current density due to wave-driven current drive], $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, and $n_\phi$ is the integer toroidal Fourier mode index associated with variation in toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height.

This quantity is a field-aligned scalar projection, not the vector current density and not the $\hat{\phi}$ component that defines [toroidal current density](name:toroidal_current_density) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It includes only the wave-driven non-inductive contribution for the specified $n_\phi$; it excludes inductive, bootstrap, neutral-beam-driven, and other non-wave current-density contributions. It is distinct from the integrated [per-toroidal-mode current due to wave-driven current drive](name:per_toroidal_mode_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive) and the [toroidal current due to wave-driven current drive](name:toroidal_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive).

Sign convention: Positive when the wave-driven current-density contribution from the specified toroidal harmonic points along $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

Toroidal mode current due to wave-driven current drive is the cumulative toroidal plasma current enclosed by a magnetic flux surface and attributed to one toroidal Fourier mode. It represents the wave-particle-interaction contribution only; inductive and non-wave non-inductive current sources are excluded.

The cumulative mode current inside the surface labeled by normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is defined by:

$$
I_{\mathrm{wcd},n}(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}) = \int_{S(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}})} \widetilde{\mathbf{j}}_{\mathrm{wcd},n}(R,Z) \cdot \hat{\phi}\,dR\,dZ
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{wcd},n}$ is the mode-resolved current, $n$ is the dimensionless toroidal Fourier mode number, $\widetilde{\mathbf{j}}_{\mathrm{wcd},n}$ is the corresponding wave-driven current-density coefficient in A m$^{-2}$, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector, $R$ is major radius in m, $Z$ is vertical height in m, and $S$ is the enclosed poloidal cross-section.

At the outer closed surface, this quantity is the single-mode contribution to [current due to wave-driven current drive](name:current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive). Unlike [toroidal current due to wave-driven current drive](name:toroidal_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive), it is not summed over toroidal Fourier modes; its local density counterpart is [per-toroidal-mode current density due to wave-driven current drive].

Sign convention: Positive when the specified mode's net current contribution flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity measures the transverse spatial variation of the radio-frequency wave launched by an ion-cyclotron heating antenna, relative to the local equilibrium magnetic field.

The perpendicular wave-vector magnitude is defined by

$$
k_\perp = \left|\mathbf{k} - (\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}})\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the local RF wave vector, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, and vertical bars denote vector magnitude.

Only the component transverse to the magnetic field is included; the parallel component is excluded. The result is non-negative and has no propagation-direction sign. It is the antenna-specific counterpart of the general [perpendicular wave-vector magnitude].

Power of a beam-tracing beam is the residual electromagnetic wave power still carried by a single coherent beam at the endpoint of the traced trajectory. It represents power remaining in the wave after propagation and after modeled transfer of wave energy to the plasma.

The single-beam power balance relates the residual power to the initial and absorbed powers:

$$
P_{\mathrm{res}} = P_0 - P_{\mathrm{abs}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{res}}$ is [power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:power_of_beam_tracing_beam), $P_0$ is [initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam), and $P_{\mathrm{abs}}$ is [absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam) over the same beam trajectory.

This quantity excludes power already transferred to plasma particles; deposited power is represented by absorbed-power quantities, including species-resolved forms such as [electron_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:electron_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam). The more general wave-beam power concept is power_of_wave_beam.

Forward power of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna is the forward-traveling RF power at a defined reference plane on the feed line, directed from the generator toward the antenna. It is the incident power arriving at the antenna before reflection at the antenna–plasma interface and before power is coupled into the plasma.

The quantity applies to one antenna or antenna module at its feed-line reference plane and includes only the forward-traveling component; it is not summed over an antenna system. It excludes backward-traveling [reflected power](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) and power already coupled into the plasma.

At a common reference plane, forward and reflected power determine the net [launched power]: the launched component is the forward power less the reflected power when intervening feed-line losses are excluded.

Forward power of a lower-hybrid antenna is the nonnegative RF power propagating toward the antenna input reference plane from the transmission line. It is one per-antenna component of the wave-power budget represented by [power of a lower-hybrid antenna].

The per-antenna power components satisfy:

$$
P_\mathrm{launched} = P_\mathrm{forward} - P_\mathrm{reflected}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{forward}$ is the incident power arriving at the reference plane, $P_\mathrm{reflected}$ is the power returning toward the transmission line, and $P_\mathrm{launched}$ is the net power entering the vacuum vessel. Thus, forward power includes the portion subsequently reflected and is distinct from [reflected power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) and [launched power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna). The quantity applies to one antenna and is not an aggregate over multiple antennas.

P_\mathrm{launched} = P_\mathrm{forward} - P_\mathrm{reflected}

Launched power is the net cycle-averaged electromagnetic power crossing the vacuum-vessel entry plane in the propagation direction of one coherent RF or microwave beam.

At the launch reference plane, it is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{launch}} = P_{\mathrm{forward}} - P_{\mathrm{return}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{forward}}$ is the forward beam power after transmission losses, and $P_{\mathrm{return}}$ is the power propagating back toward the launcher at that plane; both are cycle-averaged powers in W.

This quantity is a stage-specific form of [power of a wave beam]. It excludes generator or source power, load power, and power subsequently absorbed by the plasma; therefore, it is distinct from plasma-absorbed power.

Pressure associated with an ion-cyclotron-heating antenna module represents the compressive normal stress or contained-gas pressure acting at its hardware components.

At a surface, pressure is defined as the normal force distributed over the loaded area:

$$
p = \frac{F_n}{A}
$$

where $p$ is pressure, $F_n$ is the force normal to the surface, and $A$ is the area over which that force acts. For contained gas, the same scalar represents the isotropic normal stress exerted by the gas.

The scope is the antenna module and its associated hardware components, including local mechanical or gas-pressure conditions at individual sensing locations. The quantity is not a plasma pressure, a pressure amplitude, a pressure variation, or an aggregate sum or average over the module.

Pressure is a mechanical or fluid-state property and is independent of electrical properties such as the antenna's [resistance](name:resistance_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) and [strap current].

Reflected power of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna is the backward-traveling radio-frequency wave power at a defined reference plane on the feed line, directed away from the antenna toward the source. It is the returned component of the antenna-associated power and represents incident power rejected by antenna-plasma coupling.

At a common reference plane, the reflected and forward traveling-wave powers are related by

$$
P_{\mathrm{ref}} = |\Gamma|^2 P_{\mathrm{fwd}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reflected power, $\Gamma$ is the complex wave reflection coefficient, and $P_{\mathrm{fwd}}$ is the [forward power](name:forward_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) traveling toward the antenna.

This quantity applies to one ion-cyclotron heating antenna and represents the aggregate returned power associated with that antenna at the defined reference plane. When an antenna contains multiple modules, it is distinct from reflected power assigned to an individual module; it also excludes forward power, power coupled into the plasma, and source power not present at the reference plane.

It complements [forward power](name:forward_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) as the opposite traveling-wave component at the feed-line reference plane. The [launched power] is power delivered from the antenna into the plasma, so it is physically distinct from returned reflected power; the two quantities must not be identified or substituted for one another.

Reflected power of a lower-hybrid antenna is the nonnegative RF power propagating toward the transmission line from the antenna input reference plane. It is one per-antenna component of the wave-power budget represented by [power of a lower-hybrid antenna].

The per-antenna power components satisfy:

$$
P_\mathrm{launched} = P_\mathrm{forward} - P_\mathrm{reflected}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{forward}$ is the incident RF power arriving at the antenna input reference plane, $P_\mathrm{reflected}$ is the RF power returning toward the transmission line, and $P_\mathrm{launched}$ is the net RF power entering the vacuum vessel. Thus, reflected power is the portion of [forward power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:forward_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) not coupled into the plasma load and is distinct from [launched power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna). The quantity applies to one lower-hybrid antenna and is not aggregated over multiple antennas; it excludes forward power that is absorbed or otherwise transmitted into the plasma-coupling load.

Resistance of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna is the real part of the effective radio-frequency loading impedance presented by the antenna at its feed reference plane. It characterizes the component of the antenna load that absorbs radio-frequency power, including plasma loading and intrinsic dissipative losses, distinct from the reactive energy storage represented by antenna capacitance or inductance.

The antenna loading impedance is decomposed into resistive and reactive parts as:

$$
Z_\mathrm{ant} = R_\mathrm{ant} + i X_\mathrm{ant}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{ant}$ is the complex antenna loading impedance, $R_\mathrm{ant}$ is the antenna resistance in ohms, $X_\mathrm{ant}$ is the antenna reactance in ohms, and $i^2=-1$.

For a sinusoidal strap current, the resistive power associated with this load is $P_\mathrm{res}=R_\mathrm{ant} I_\mathrm{rms}^2$, where $P_\mathrm{res}$ is in watts and $I_\mathrm{rms}$ is the [root-mean-square wave current of the antenna strap] in amperes. This quantity is a feed-plane impedance component and is not itself a forward, reflected, or net power; those powers describe traveling-wave energy flow in the connected radio-frequency circuit.

documents.before:
Thickness of an ICRH antenna strap is the full, non-negative extent of the strap conductor cross-section in the direction perpendicular to the central segment of the strap rectangle in the thick-line geometric approximation. It is a geometric length of the strap conductor, not an oriented displacement.

For a strap conductor cross-section $C$ and a unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ along the modeled thickness direction, the thickness $t$ is the range of projected positions:

$$
t = \max_{\mathbf{r}\in C}\left(\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\right) - \min_{\mathbf{r}\in C}\left(\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\right)
$$

where $t$ is the thickness of the antenna strap, $C$ is the conductor cross-section, $\mathbf{r}$ is a position vector for a point of that cross-section, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is a unit vector in the cross-section perpendicular to the central segment of the strap rectangle.

The scope is a single ICRH antenna strap represented by the thick-line strap-rectangle geometry. The aggregation convention is the complete max-minus-min extent over the conductor cross-section along the modeled thickness direction; it is not an average thickness, a local surface separation, a half-thickness, or a signed offset.

Thickness is an independent strap-geometry extent that complements the [width of the antenna strap], [height of the antenna strap](name:height_of_antenna_strap), and [length of the antenna strap]. Those quantities describe separate geometric extents of the same strap rather than projections along the thickness direction.

Total ion-cyclotron radio-frequency power is the aggregate power launched into the vacuum vessel by the complete ion-cyclotron heating-antenna system. It represents the net launcher-array power directed toward the plasma, rather than power ultimately absorbed by plasma particles.

The system total is defined by summing the launched power from each antenna:

$$
P_{\rm total}=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\rm ant}} P_i
$$

where $P_{\rm total}$ is the total ion-cyclotron radio-frequency power launched by the system, $N_{\rm ant}$ is the number of contributing ion-cyclotron heating antennas, $i$ is an antenna index, and $P_i$ is the net power launched by antenna $i$, corresponding to the antenna-resolved [ion-cyclotron heating power].

The quantity applies to the complete heating system and is aggregated over all ion-cyclotron heating antennas. It has no individual-antenna, species, charge-state, or volumetric deposition resolution. Reflected power and losses upstream of the vacuum-vessel launch boundary are excluded, and the quantity does not represent the portion subsequently absorbed by plasma particles.

This system-level total is the aggregate counterpart of [launched power due to ion-cyclotron heating], while [launched power of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:launched_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) represents the corresponding launcher-oriented power for an individual antenna.

Vertical coordinate of the geometric center of an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror is the $Z$ coordinate of that center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The coordinate is defined by projecting the mirror geometric-center position onto the vertical coordinate axis:

$$
z_m = Z(\mathbf{r}_{m,c})
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_{m,c}$ is the position of the electron-cyclotron launcher mirror geometric center and $Z(\mathbf{r}_{m,c})$ is its vertical coordinate.

Together with the [radial centroid of the electron-cyclotron launcher mirror] and the [toroidal coordinate of the electron-cyclotron launcher mirror](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror), this quantity specifies the mirror geometric-center position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is distinct from coordinates defined for other mirror reference points, such as a sphere center or a surface point.

Wave frequency is the non-negative temporal carrier frequency of a coherent electromagnetic wave interacting with a plasma. It describes the rate of phase oscillation and applies to waves at launch or during propagation, independent of the wave amplitude or absorbed power.

The frequency $f$ is related to the angular frequency by

$$
f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}
$$

where $f$ is frequency in hertz and $\omega$ is angular frequency in radians per second. The launch-specific quantity [launched wave frequency] uses this same definition as the absolute reference for a launched wave, while [frequency of electron cyclotron heating antenna](name:frequency_of_electron_cyclotron_beam) is a device-specific instance.
documents.after:

Aperture width is the non-negative clear extent of an aperture along its first local tangential direction. The aperture is described in a right-handed aperture-local frame $(\hat{t}_1, \hat{t}_2, \hat{n})$, where $\hat{t}_1$ and $\hat{t}_2$ are the first and second local tangential unit vectors in the aperture plane, $\hat{n}$ is the local normal, and $\hat{t}_1 \times \hat{t}_2 = \hat{n}$.

For a clear opening region $\mathcal{A}$, the width is the maximum-minus-minimum span of the first-local-tangential coordinate:

$$
w = x_{1,\max} - x_{1,\min}
$$

where $w$ is the aperture width, $x_{1,\max}=\max_{\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{t}_1)$ and $x_{1,\min}=\min_{\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{t}_1)$ are the maximum and minimum first-local-tangential length coordinates over the clear opening, $\mathbf{r}$ is a position vector relative to any fixed origin in the aperture plane, and $\mathcal{A}$ is the clear opening region.

This quantity is a full aperture span, not a radius, semi-width, material width, support-structure dimension, or beam-envelope width. It uses only the first local tangential direction; the orthogonal in-plane extent along $\hat{t}_2$ is a different aperture dimension. For a circular aperture, this full span is the diameter and is twice the [radius of aperture].

Fast ion power density is the local rate per unit volume at which coherent RF wave-particle interactions add energy to the nonthermal fast-ion channel. It is the absorbed-wave contribution associated with the broader [ion power density], while excluding energy deposited into bulk thermal ions or electrons and spatial transport terms.

The species- and charge-state-summed quantity is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{fi}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{F}} \sum_{Z \in \mathcal{Z}_a} P_{\mathrm{fi},a,Z}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{fi}}$ and $P_{\mathrm{fi},a,Z}$ are local power densities in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of included fast-ion species, and $\mathcal{Z}_a$ is the set of included charge states for species $a$.

The quantity represents the total local wave-energy transfer to fast ions, without resolution by toroidal harmonic. Its mode-resolved counterpart, [per-toroidal-mode fast ion power density](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power_density), partitions this transfer by toroidal mode number.
documents.after:

The left-hand circularly polarized electric field $E_+$ is the complex scalar phasor obtained by projecting an electric-field phasor onto the left-hand circular polarization basis perpendicular to the local magnetic-field direction. It represents the perpendicular component whose instantaneous electric-field vector co-rotates with positive-ion gyromotion about the magnetic field.

Let $(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_2, \hat{b})$ be a local right-handed orthonormal basis with $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ along the local magnetic-field direction and $\hat{e}_1\times\hat{e}_2=\hat{b}$. For complex amplitudes defined by $\mathbf{E}(t)=\Re\{\tilde{\mathbf{E}}\exp(-i\omega t)\}$, the left-hand component is

$$
E_+ = \frac{\tilde{\mathbf{E}}\cdot\hat{e}_1 + i\,\tilde{\mathbf{E}}\cdot\hat{e}_2}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

where $\tilde{\mathbf{E}}$ is the complex electric-field phasor, $i$ is the imaginary unit, and $\omega$ is the angular frequency. Only the components perpendicular to $\hat{b}$ enter this projection.

This scalar is the circular-polarization projection of an electric-field phasor, not the full vector [electric field](name:electric_field) or the vector [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field). When the phasor is specifically a wave field, this is the same local left-hand projection represented by [left-hand circularly polarized wave electric field](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field); the complementary polarization is [right-hand circularly polarized electric field]. Its modulus and rectangular decompositions are [left-hand circularly polarized wave electric field amplitude], [left-hand circularly polarized wave electric field real part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part), and [left-hand circularly polarized wave electric field imaginary part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part).

Sign convention: Positive when the zero-phase instantaneous perpendicular electric field of a pure real $E_+$ phasor points along $+\hat{e}_1$ and subsequently rotates toward $-\hat{e}_2$ as time increases in the local right-handed orthonormal basis $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{b})$, with $\hat{b}$ along the local magnetic-field direction.

documents.before:
Power-deposition-weighted flux-surface average of the complex left-hand circularly polarized component of the wave electric field perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field, for a single toroidal Fourier mode. The left-hand circular component is the projection that rotates in the same sense as the ion gyromotion about the equilibrium field, and this quantity preserves its complex phase.

For radial flux label $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the weighted average on flux surface $\Sigma(\rho)$ is:

$$
\left\langle E_{+,n_\phi}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{dep}}(\rho) = \frac{\int_{\Sigma(\rho)} E_{+,n_\phi}(\mathbf{x})\, w_{\mathrm{dep},n_\phi}(\mathbf{x})\, d\mu_\rho}{\int_{\Sigma(\rho)} w_{\mathrm{dep},n_\phi}(\mathbf{x})\, d\mu_\rho}
$$

where $n_\phi$ is the toroidal mode number, $\mathbf{x}$ is position on the flux surface, $E_{+,n_\phi}$ is the toroidal Fourier coefficient of the left-hand circular component, $w_{\mathrm{dep},n_\phi}$ is the non-negative deposited-power density weight for the same mode, and $d\mu_\rho$ is the positive flux-surface integration measure including the geometric Jacobian associated with the flux label. The average is defined only where the denominator is nonzero.

The physical left-hand circular field is the real part of $E_{+,n_\phi}\exp(i n_\phi \phi - i\omega t)$, where $\omega$ is angular frequency and $t$ is time. With $\hat{b}$ along the equilibrium magnetic field, $\hat{e}_1 = \nabla\rho / |\nabla\rho|$ positive toward increasing $\rho$, and $\hat{e}_2 = \hat{b} \times \hat{e}_1$, the circular component is $E_+ = (E_1 + i E_2)/\sqrt{2}$ for perpendicular projections $E_1 = \mathbf{E}\cdot\hat{e}_1$ and $E_2 = \mathbf{E}\cdot\hat{e}_2$. The opposite handedness is [per-toroidal-mode right-hand circularly polarized electric field].

Sign convention: Positive when a real zero-phase value of $\left\langle E_{+,n_\phi}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{dep}}$ with phasor dependence $\exp(i n_\phi \phi - i\omega t)$ gives an instantaneous electric field in the $+\hat{e}_1$ direction at $\phi = 0$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and $t = 0$.

This quantity is the complex left-hand circular polarization electric-field phasor for one toroidal Fourier mode, averaged over a magnetic flux surface with local wave-power deposition as the weighting function. It is a weighted component of the [left-hand circularly polarized wave electric field](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field), not a separate polarization state.

The defining weighted average is

$$
\mathcal{E}_{+,P}^{(n)}(\psi)=
\frac{\left\langle P_{\mathrm{dep}}^{(n)} E_{+}^{(n)}\right\rangle_{\psi}}
{\left\langle P_{\mathrm{dep}}^{(n)}\right\rangle_{\psi}}
$$

where $\mathcal{E}_{+,P}^{(n)}$ is the requested phasor, $E_{+}^{(n)}$ is the left-hand circularly polarized wave electric-field phasor, $P_{\mathrm{dep}}^{(n)}$ is the local deposition weight for toroidal mode number $n$, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes a flux-surface average on the surface labeled by $\psi$. The denominator must be nonzero.

The result retains amplitude and phase. Its phase is referenced to the selected zero-phase toroidal location, with toroidal angle $\phi$ defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and represented on the interval $(-\pi,\pi]$. It differs from the unweighted [per-toroidal-mode left-hand circularly polarized electric field] through the deposition weighting.

Thermal electron power density is the time-averaged volumetric rate at which a coherent wave transfers energy to the bulk thermal electron population. It represents electron heating by wave absorption, distinct from power deposited directly into fast electrons, ions, or other nonthermal populations.

For a monochromatic wave, the cycle-averaged absorbed power density is defined by

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},e}=\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},e}(t)\cdot\mathbf{E}(t)\right\rangle_t = \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathrm{th},e}\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{E}}^{*}\right]
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th},e}$ is the thermal electron power density, $\mathbf{E}$ is the wave electric field, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},e}$ is the induced current density associated with thermal electrons, $\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ denotes an average over a wave period, tildes denote peak-amplitude phasors, and $^{*}$ denotes complex conjugation. If rms phasor amplitudes are used instead, the factor $1/2$ is omitted.

This quantity is the thermal-electron channel of coherent-wave power absorption and is a component of the aggregate [electron power density] when the energy balance includes coherent-wave transfer to thermal electrons. It excludes coherent-wave power deposited directly into [fast electron power density](name:fast_electron_absorbed_wave_power_density), ions, or non-electron species. The cumulative thermal-electron wave power in a plasma volume is the volume integral of $p_{\mathrm{th},e}$; for a flux-surface-bounded volume this corresponds to [thermal electron power at inside flux surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

Sign convention: Positive when coherent-wave energy is transferred from the wave field to the bulk thermal electron population.

This quantity is the field-aligned component of the oscillatory magnetic perturbation carried by a coherent electromagnetic wave. It excludes equilibrium and other static magnetic-field contributions.

The component is defined by

$$
B_{\rm parallel}^{\rm wave} = \delta\mathbf{B}_{\rm wave} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}_{\rm eq}
$$

where $\delta\mathbf{B}_{\rm wave}$ is the wave magnetic-field perturbation and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{\rm eq} = \mathbf{B}_{\rm eq}/|\mathbf{B}_{\rm eq}|$ is the local unit vector along the equilibrium magnetic field. It is a component of the parent [wave magnetic field], not its magnitude or a complex-quadrature part. Unlike [parallel magnetic field](name:parallel_magnetic_field), it does not include the equilibrium field.

Sign convention: Positive when the wave magnetic-field perturbation points in the direction of the local equilibrium magnetic-field unit vector.

Effective charge at a divertor target is the local charge-squared-weighted ionic content of the plasma adjacent to the target, evaluated at the sheath entrance. It characterizes impurity content relative to the total positive charge density.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{\sum_i n_i Z_i^2}{\sum_i n_i Z_i}
$$

where $n_i$ is the local number density of positive-ion species $i$ and $Z_i$ is its positive integer charge state. The sums include all positive ion species and charge states represented in the local plasma. The quantity equals unity for a pure singly charged hydrogenic plasma and increases when higher-charge ions contribute.

This effective-charge interpretation is the charge-moment form of [charge at the divertor target], with the same target-local plasma scope; it is not a density or a charge-state-specific abundance.

Number density of the hydrogen species at the divertor target is the local particle count per volume at the sheath entrance immediately upstream of the target-facing plasma boundary. It is the hydrogen-specific member of [density_at_divertor_target](name:density_at_divertor_target).

The local hydrogen-ion number density is defined by the differential particle count:

$$
n_{\mathrm{H}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{H}}}{dV}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the number of free hydrogen ions in a small plasma volume $V$ whose center approaches the sheath entrance from the plasma side at the divertor target, and $n_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the corresponding local hydrogen-ion number density.

This quantity applies to the free hydrogen-ion population immediately adjacent to the divertor target. It is summed over all positive hydrogen ionization charge states, counting each ion once without charge weighting; neutral hydrogen atoms and molecules, electrons, and other ion species are excluded.

As a species-specific local component, it uses the same sheath-entrance locus and charge-state-summed convention as [deuterium density at the divertor target](name:deuterium_density_at_divertor_target), but represents hydrogen ions rather than deuterium ions. Unlike the flux-surface-averaged [hydrogen density at the plasma boundary], it is evaluated locally at the divertor target rather than averaged over a flux surface.

Ion fluence at a divertor target is the cumulative number of incident ions per unit target area over a specified time interval. It is the ion-only component of [fluence at the divertor target], including all ionic species and charge states while counting each incident ion once.

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{ion}} = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \left[\sum_{s\in\mathcal{I}} \Gamma_{\perp,s}(t)\right] \, dt
$$

Here, $\Phi_{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the ion fluence, $t_1$ and $t_2$ are the interval endpoints in seconds, $\mathcal{I}$ is the set of included ion species and charge states, and $\Gamma_{\perp,s}$ is the incident normal particle-flux density for state $s$, in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. The flux is directed from the plasma toward the target surface. Neutral atoms, molecules, and nonparticle channels are excluded.

documents.before:
The peak power flux density at the divertor target quantifies the maximum local heat load per unit area deposited anywhere on the divertor target surface under a given plasma condition. It is the spatial maximum of the heat flux distribution across the strike zone and governs the thermal stress, erosion rate, and component lifetime of divertor plasma-facing components.

For a heat flux profile $q(\mathbf{x})$ distributed over the target surface, the peak value is:

$$
q_\mathrm{peak} = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in S_\mathrm{target}} q(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position on the target surface $S_\mathrm{target}$ and $q$ is the local power per unit area from combined particle and radiation loads.

The spatial heat flux distribution on target tiles is resolved primarily by infrared thermography, with the peak extracted from the measured surface temperature rise and the known surface thermal diffusivity of the tile material. In numerical simulations, the peak is determined as the maximum over the computed deposition profile on the strike zone.

Steady-state peak heat flux values in H-mode operation range from 1-20 MW/m² in present-day devices; reactor design limits for tungsten monoblock divertor components are set near 10 MW/m² for continuous operation, with transient events exceeding steady-state limits by large factors. Analogous peak loads on other plasma-facing surfaces are captured by [peak power density at the limiter], [peak power density at the first wall](name:peak_power_density_at_first_wall), and the device-level [peak power density at the wall], while [power at the divertor target due to radiation] quantifies the integrated radiative contribution to the total target heat load.

documents.before:
Power at a divertor target is the rate at which energy is deposited on one divertor target by a specified physical deposition channel, integrated over the target's wetted strike-zone surface. The specified channel denotes a particular physical contribution to deposition and does not by itself imply an all-channel target total.

The deposited power for target $t$ and channel $c$ is defined from the channel-resolved energy-flux-density vector over that surface:

$$
P_{t,c} = -\int_{A_t} \mathbf{S}_{E,c}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_t(\mathbf{x}) \, dA
$$

where $P_{t,c}$ is the deposited power on target $t$ due to channel $c$, $A_t$ is the target's wetted strike-zone surface, $\mathbf{S}_{E,c}$ is the energy-flux-density vector for channel $c$, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_t$ is the normalized surface normal directed from the target material toward the plasma-facing side, $\mathbf{x}$ labels a point on the target surface, and $dA$ is the surface element. The leading minus sign makes flux directed from the plasma toward the target material contribute to the deposited target power.

The channel label may distinguish conductive, convective, particle, radiative, or other deposition mechanisms, but this name does not prescribe a decomposition. For a complete mutually exclusive set of channel contributions on the same target, the channel sum equals the surface integral of the total [energy flux at a divertor target](name:energy_flux_at_divertor_target); all-channel target powers at the inner and outer divertor targets are represented by [power at inner divertor target] and [power at outer divertor target]. Conductive and convective channel contributions are represented by [power at divertor target due to conduction](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction) and [power at divertor target due to convection](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_convection), respectively.

Electron power at the inner divertor target is the rate at which energy carried by incident electrons is deposited on the high-field-side divertor target surface. It is the electron-channel contribution to the total target load, rather than the combined contribution of all incident energy channels.

The deposited electron power is defined by the surface integral

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{inner}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wet,inner}}} q_{e,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x})\,dA
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{wet,inner}}$ is the wetted inner-target area, $q_{e,\mathrm{dep}}$ is the electron energy-deposition flux density in W m$^{-2}$, and $dA$ is an element of target surface area in m$^2$. The result is the electron contribution to [power at the inner divertor target]; ion energy is represented separately by [ion power at the inner divertor target], while neutral and radiative contributions are excluded.

Maximum power at the inner divertor target is the greatest total rate at which energy is deposited on the high-field-side target surface during a specified time interval. It includes electron, ion, neutral, and radiative contributions integrated over the wetted strike-zone area, rather than a local heat-flux density.

The maximum is defined from the instantaneous quantity [power at the inner divertor target](name:power_at_inner_divertor_target) by

$$
P_{\mathrm{max,inner}} = \max_{t \in [t_1,t_2]} P_{\mathrm{inner}}(t)
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{max,inner}}$ is the maximum target power, $t$ is time, $t_1$ and $t_2$ are the interval endpoints, and $P_{\mathrm{inner}}(t)$ is the total instantaneous deposited power. The total includes the ion contribution represented by [ion power at the inner divertor target].

This quantity is a temporal maximum, not the energy deposited over the interval and not the power at a particular target location.
