Electron power deposited on the outer divertor target by incident electrons integrated over the wetted strike-zone surface is the target-integrated electron energy-transfer rate to the material surface of that target. The outer divertor target is the target on the larger-major-radius side in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The deposited electron power is the surface integral of the local electron energy-flux density directed into the wetted outer-target area:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{outer}} = \int_{A_{w,\mathrm{outer}}} q_{e,\perp}\,dA
$$

where $P_{e,\mathrm{outer}}$ is the electron power at the outer divertor target, $A_{w,\mathrm{outer}}$ is the wetted strike-zone area, $dA$ is a target-surface area element, and $q_{e,\perp}$ is the electron energy-flux density directed from the plasma into the target material.

This is the electron-channel component of [power at the outer divertor target]; ion, neutral, radiation, and other non-electron contributions are excluded. It is the outer-target counterpart of [electron power at the inner divertor target](name:electron_power_at_inner_divertor_target).

This quantity is the local number density of all positive ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target surface. It is the all-ion aggregate of [ion density at the divertor target], rather than a species-specific or charge-state-resolved density.

The total ion density is defined by

$$
n_{i,total} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \sum_{Z \in \mathcal{Z}_s} n_{s,Z}
$$

where $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ is the total ion number density, $s$ indexes the included ionic species, $Z$ indexes their positive charge states, and $n_{s,Z}$ is the number density of species $s$ in charge state $Z$. The sums include all positive-ion populations evaluated at the entrance to the electrostatic sheath.

Neutral atoms and molecules, as well as free electrons, are excluded. A density resolved for one charge state is represented separately by [ion charge state density](name:ion_charge_state_density).

where $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ is the total ion number density, $s$ indexes the included ionic species, $Z$ indexes their positive charge states, and $n_{s,Z}$ is the number density of species $s$ in charge state $Z$. The sums include all positive-ion populations evaluated at the entrance to the electrostatic sheath.

Neutral atoms and molecules, as well as free electrons, are excluded. A density resolved for one charge state is represented separately by [ion charge state density](name:ion_charge_state_density).

This quantity is the ion-carried contribution to power deposited on the inner, high-field-side divertor target. It includes the thermal energy entering the electrostatic sheath and the directed kinetic energy acquired by ions across the sheath potential drop, while excluding electron, neutral-particle, photon, and halo-current contributions. It is the ion-resolved component of [ion power at the inner divertor target] and is distinct from the all-channel [power at the inner divertor target].

The deposited ion power is defined by

$$
P_{i,in} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wetted,in}}} \mathbf{q}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{t}\, dA
$$

where $P_{i,\mathrm{in}}$ is the integrated ion power, $A_{\mathrm{wetted,in}}$ is the wetted inner-target surface, $\mathbf{q}_i$ is the total incident ion energy-flux density summed over ion species and charge states, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{t}$ points from the plasma toward the target material.

Rate at which particles are returned to the edge plasma by recycling on all divertor target surfaces, expressed on a particle-number basis. For this total quantity, molecular and compound-particle carriers are resolved to their constituent-particle multiplicity before summation, so a released molecule contributes the number of atoms it delivers rather than a single carrier count, and the contributions of neutral, atomic, molecular, and ionic recycled products are then summed over the divertor target set.

The total recycled particle rate is the plasma-ward surface integral of the recycled particle flux density, summed over all divertor targets:

$$
\Phi_\mathrm{rec,tot}^\mathrm{div} = \sum_{t} \int_{S_t} m(\mathbf{r}) \, \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\mathrm{rec}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{p,t}(\mathbf{r}) \, dA
$$

where $S_t$ is the material surface of divertor target $t$, $dA$ is its surface area element, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\mathrm{rec}$ is the local recycled carrier flux-density vector (in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$), $m$ is the particle multiplicity of each carrier that converts carrier count to returned-particle count, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{p,t}$ is the unit normal directed from the target material surface toward the plasma.

This is the multiplicity-resolved, particle-number specialization of the recycling return rate [particle flux of divertor due to recycling], and it is a component of the general recycling return rate [flux of divertor due to recycling]. It excludes non-recycling sources such as external gas injection, sputtered impurity production, and pumping removal, and it is distinct from the energy, power, and momentum fluxes associated with the same surface processes.

Sign convention: Positive when the local recycled particle flux density is directed from the divertor target material surface toward the plasma.

This quantity is the e-folding distance for electron number density that decreases outward from the confined plasma into the open-field-line scrape-off layer. It is the electron-density member of the [decay-length family](name:decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer), distinct from the [ion decay length].

$$
L_e = \left|\frac{d\ln n_e}{dx}\right|^{-1}
$$

where $L_e$ is the electron-density e-folding length, $n_e$ is electron number density, and $x$ is outward distance normal to magnetic flux surfaces. The quantity is defined locally where the logarithmic gradient is nonzero; the magnitude gives the positive distance associated with the outward decrease. It does not denote the decay length of temperature or heat flux, which are separate members of the family.

This quantity is the local free-electron number density at the geometric launching position, such as a wave launcher aperture or waveguide mouth where an injected electromagnetic wave first contacts the edge plasma. It is the electron-specific component of [number density at the launching position].

The density is defined from the electron velocity-distribution function by

$$
n_e(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{launch}})=\int f_e(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{launch}},\mathbf{v})\,d^3\mathbf{v}
$$

where $n_e$ is electron number density, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{launch}}$ is the launching position, $f_e$ is the electron velocity-distribution function, and $\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity.

This is a local value for free electrons at the launching position, not a density summed over plasma species, a flux-surface average, or a wave-power quantity. It is distinct from [electron number density at the plasma boundary](name:electron_density_at_plasma_boundary), which is evaluated at the last closed flux surface.

Diffusion coefficient due to diffusion is the scalar transport coefficient that relates a transported scalar field to the diffusive part of its flux. It represents local gradient-driven spreading by diffusion, independent of directed advection or explicit source production.

The diffusive flux in a scalar Fick-type closure is defined by:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{\mathrm{diff}} \, \nabla f
$$

where $D_{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusion coefficient due to diffusion, $f$ is the transported scalar field, $\nabla f$ is its spatial gradient, and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive flux of $f$.

This quantity applies to the scalar, isotropic or effective coefficient of the diffusive component of transport for a density, concentration, or analogous transported scalar. It excludes tensor diffusion coefficients, component-resolved anisotropic diffusivities, convective or pinch velocities, fluxes themselves, and source or sink rates.

With the minus sign in the defining relation, a positive $D_{\mathrm{diff}}$ gives flux down the gradient of $f$; an effective negative value denotes up-gradient transport relative to that gradient. For particle transport, the same relation connects this coefficient to [particle flux due to diffusion] when $f$ is [number density].

Electron thermal pressure at the plasma boundary is the isotropic momentum-flux density produced by random electron motion on the last closed magnetic flux surface. It is the electron-specific contribution to [thermal pressure at the plasma boundary], not the total plasma pressure.

For an isotropic electron population, the pressure is defined by

$$
p_e = \frac{2}{3} n_e \langle E_e \rangle
$$

where $p_e$ is electron thermal pressure, $n_e$ is electron number density, and $\langle E_e \rangle$ is the mean random kinetic energy per electron. The quantity is related to [electron temperature at the plasma boundary](name:electron_temperature_at_plasma_boundary) through $p_e = n_e T_e$ when $T_e$ is expressed as thermal energy per particle.

The definition excludes directed electron bulk-flow momentum and nonthermal stress contributions; the plasma boundary denotes the separatrix between closed and open magnetic field lines.

Electron temperature at the pedestal top is the kinetic temperature of the electron population evaluated at the core-side shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier. It is the electron-specific instance of [temperature at the pedestal top].

For an isotropic electron population, the kinetic temperature is defined by

$$
T_e = \frac{2}{3}\langle E_{\mathrm{kin},e}\rangle
$$

Flux at wall due to pumping is the net particle-transfer rate across the plasma-facing wall boundary caused by pumping for the counted particle population. It is evaluated on the wall boundary and represents a boundary-integrated removal flux, not a local surface flux density.

The wall-integrated pumping flux is defined from the local pumping flux density by the oriented surface integral:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{wall,pump}} = \int_{\partial V_{\mathrm{wall}}} \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{pump}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{out}} \, dA
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{wall,pump}}$ is the flux at wall due to pumping, $\partial V_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the plasma-facing wall boundary included in the pumping surface, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{pump}}$ is the local particle flux-density vector due to pumping for the same counted population, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the unit normal directed out of the plasma domain toward the wall or pumping region, and $dA$ is the surface element.

The scope is the pumping contribution at the wall boundary only. The aggregation convention is the algebraic surface integral over the included pumping boundary, so local inward and outward contributions are combined with the stated boundary orientation.

This quantity excludes non-pumping contributions to at-wall flux, such as recycling, sputtering, or other wall-source processes. It is the pumping component of the total [flux at wall], and it is related to the local [particle flux density] by the boundary integral above.

Sign convention: Positive when the pumping contribution carries particles across the plasma-facing wall boundary from the plasma domain into the wall or pumping region.

Number density of helium-4 ions at the plasma boundary is the local particle count per physical volume for the helium-4 ion population evaluated on the last closed magnetic flux surface. It represents the charge-state-summed helium-4 ion population at that locus.

The defining charge-state-summed zeroth velocity-space moment is

$$
n_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He}}(\mathbf{x}_b,t)=\sum_q\int f_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},q}(\mathbf{x}_b,\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3\mathbf{v}
$$

where $n_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He}}$ is the helium-4 ion number density, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a point on the plasma boundary, $t$ is time, $q$ is the ionic charge-state index, $f_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},q}$ is the velocity distribution function of helium-4 ions in charge state $q$, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $d^3\mathbf{v}$ is the velocity-space volume element.

The plasma boundary is the last closed magnetic flux surface, also called the separatrix, separating confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. This quantity applies only to helium-4 ions, is evaluated locally at the boundary, includes all helium-4 ionic charge states, and excludes neutral helium-4 atoms.

As a species-specific instance of [particle number density at the plasma boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary), it fixes the otherwise unspecified population to helium-4 ions. It differs from [flux-surface-averaged helium-4 density at the plasma boundary], which averages the same charge-state-summed population over the boundary surface, and from [helium-3 density at the plasma boundary](name:helium_3_density_at_plasma_boundary), which selects a different helium isotope.

Poloidal magnetic flux at the pedestal top is the signed value of the poloidal magnetic flux function on the H-mode pedestal-top flux surface. The pedestal top is the core-side top of the steep edge pedestal and may be identified by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the value can be represented as the flux through a horizontal disk bounded by a point on that flux surface:

$$
\psi_\mathrm{ped} = \int_0^{R_\mathrm{ped}} B_Z(R', Z_\mathrm{ped})\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi_\mathrm{ped}$ denotes this quantity, $(R_\mathrm{ped}, Z_\mathrm{ped})$ is any point on the pedestal-top flux surface with $R_\mathrm{ped}$ and $Z_\mathrm{ped}$ in meters, $R'$ is the disk-integration radius in meters, and $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component in tesla. The integral fixes the additive reference to the zero-radius disk on the toroidal symmetry axis; only differences in $\psi$ are invariant under an added constant.

This dimensional flux value is related to [normalized poloidal magnetic flux at the pedestal top] through the normalization $(\psi_\mathrm{ped}-\psi_0)/(\psi_b-\psi_0)$, where $\psi_0$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and $\psi_b$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary). It is not a radius-like coordinate such as [toroidal flux radius at the pedestal top](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_pedestal_top), and it is distinct from values at the pedestal center or maximum-gradient surface unless those loci are defined to coincide with the pedestal top.

Sign convention: Positive when $B_Z$ on the horizontal integration disk points in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Poloidal particle diffusivity is the effective transport coefficient for particle spreading driven by a number-density gradient along the poloidal direction of the flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. It is the poloidal component of the generic [particle diffusivity] quantity.

For physical poloidal arclength, the diffusive particle flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{pol}} = -D_{\mathrm{pol}}\frac{1}{h_\theta}\frac{\partial n}{\partial \theta}
$$

Electron pressure over the scrape-off layer is the volume-averaged thermal pressure of electrons in the open-field-line region between the last closed flux surface and the material plasma-facing components. It represents the electron partial-pressure contribution to [pressure over the scrape-off layer](name:pressure_over_scrape_off_layer) over that volume.

The volume average is defined from the local electron thermal pressure over the scrape-off-layer volume:

$$
\langle p_e \rangle_{\mathrm{SOL}} = \frac{1}{V_{\mathrm{SOL}}} \int_{V_{\mathrm{SOL}}} n_e(\mathbf{x}) T_e(\mathbf{x}) \, dV
$$

where $\langle p_e \rangle_{\mathrm{SOL}}$ is the volume-averaged electron pressure over the scrape-off layer, $n_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local electron number density, $T_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local electron temperature expressed as thermal energy per electron, $V_{\mathrm{SOL}}$ is the scrape-off-layer volume, $dV$ is a volume element, and $\mathbf{x}$ is position.

This quantity excludes ion partial pressures and the neutral-gas pressure described by [neutral pressure over the scrape-off layer](name:neutral_pressure_over_scrape_off_layer). It is a SOL volume average, not the [electron pressure at the plasma boundary](name:electron_pressure_at_separatrix), and it is related to [electron density over the scrape-off layer] through the same averaging domain but is a density-temperature moment rather than a number-density average.

The radial plasma momentum diffusion coefficient is the effective kinematic coefficient governing down-gradient transport of bulk plasma momentum along $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. The radial direction specifies the transport direction, not the component of momentum being transported.

In a Fickian closure, the coefficient is defined component-wise by the relation between radial diffusive momentum flux and the major-radius gradient of the corresponding momentum density:

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{\mathcal{P}_j,R} = -D_{\mathcal{P},R}\,\frac{\partial \mathcal{P}_j}{\partial R}
$$

where $D_{\mathcal{P},R}$ is the radial plasma momentum diffusion coefficient, $\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{\mathcal{P}_j,R}$ is the diffusive flux of the $j$-th component of bulk plasma momentum through a surface of constant $R$ and is positive in the $+\hat{R}$ direction, $\mathcal{P}_j$ is the bulk plasma momentum density component, and $j$ denotes any chosen momentum-vector component. The derivative is taken with respect to $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The leading minus sign fixes the down-gradient diffusion convention: a positive $D_{\mathcal{P},R}$ transports each component from larger toward smaller $\mathcal{P}_j$ along $R$.

Bulk plasma momentum density means the charge-state-summed ion-fluid momentum density, $\mathcal{P}_j = \sum_{a,z} m_a n_{a,z} u_{a,z,j}$, where $a$ indexes ion species, $z$ indexes charge state, $m_a$ is ion mass, $n_{a,z}$ is ion number density, and $u_{a,z,j}$ is the corresponding ion fluid-velocity component. Electron inertial momentum and neutral momentum are excluded.

This quantity is the $R$-directed member of the bulk plasma-momentum diffusion-coefficient family anchored by [plasma momentum diffusion coefficient], with the $Z$-directed counterpart [vertical plasma-momentum transport coefficient](name:vertical_plasma_momentum_diffusivity). It is distinct from a flux-surface-normal momentum-transport coefficient such as [radial momentum transport coefficient](name:radial_momentum_diffusivity), from the charge-state-resolved [radial ion charge-state momentum transport coefficient](name:radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity), and from the neutral-fluid analog [radial neutral momentum diffusion coefficient](name:radial_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient). In an anisotropic tensor representation, it corresponds to a radial diagonal transport coefficient; related ion-momentum tensor-family quantities include [ion momentum diffusion coefficient](name:ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient) and the toroidal diagonal component [toroidal ion momentum diffusion coefficient](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient).

Toroidal argon velocity at the pedestal top is the $\phi$ component, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, of the density-weighted mean bulk flow of argon impurity ions where the H-mode pedestal transitions to the confined core. As an intensive species-level quantity, it is the density-weighted mean over all argon charge states, not a charge-state-summed velocity.

The charge-state aggregation is defined by the density-weighted mean at the pedestal top:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ar}}^{\mathrm{ped}} = \frac{\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}^{\mathrm{ped}} v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}^{\mathrm{ped}}}{\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}^{\mathrm{ped}}}
$$

where $q$ indexes argon ionization state, $n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}^{\mathrm{ped}}$ is the local number density of that charge state, and $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}^{\mathrm{ped}}$ is its toroidal velocity component at the pedestal top.

It is inferred primarily from Doppler spectroscopy of argon emission, often charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy when suitable neutral-beam excitation is available. The observed line shift and viewing geometry determine the velocity projected onto the $\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; estimating the all-charge-state mean may require emissivity modeling, ionization-balance information, or collisional equilibration assumptions.

Because pedestal argon rotation is sensitive to external torque, radial electric-field shear, neoclassical friction, turbulence-driven momentum transport, and charge-state distribution, no device-independent numerical range is implied. This value is commonly interpreted with same-species values at other loci, including [toroidal argon velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), [toroidal argon velocity at the internal transport barrier](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier), [toroidal argon velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), and [toroidal flux-surface-averaged argon velocity at the plasma boundary].

Sign convention: Positive when the density-weighted mean argon flow points in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the local toroidal component of the argon-ion bulk-flow velocity evaluated at the plasma boundary, identified with the last closed flux surface. It is a pointwise boundary value rather than an average over that flux surface.

The charge-state-aggregated toroidal velocity is defined by

$$
V_{\mathrm{Ar},\phi} = \frac{\sum_z n_{\mathrm{Ar},z} v_{\mathrm{Ar},z,\phi}}{\sum_z n_{\mathrm{Ar},z}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{Ar},\phi}$ and $v_{\mathrm{Ar},z,\phi}$ are toroidal velocity components in m s$^{-1}$, $n_{\mathrm{Ar},z}$ is the argon-ion number density in m$^{-3}$, and $z$ indexes argon ion charge states. The toroidal component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The local value is distinct from the [toroidal flux-surface-averaged argon velocity at the plasma boundary], which averages the same component over the boundary flux surface. Neutral argon is excluded from the ion bulk-flow aggregation.

Sign convention: Positive when the argon-ion bulk velocity projects onto the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The carbon impurity-ion toroidal velocity at the plasma boundary is the local density-weighted mean of the bulk-flow velocities of all included carbon ion charge states on the last closed magnetic flux surface. It is not a flux-surface average; that distinct quantity is the [toroidal flux-surface-averaged carbon velocity], while the magnetic-axis counterpart is [toroidal carbon velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).

The defining local component is

$$
V_{\phi,C}(R,Z)=\frac{\sum_{q\in Q} n_{C^{q+}}(R,Z)\,\mathbf{V}_{C^{q+}}(R,Z)\cdot\hat{\phi}}{\sum_{q\in Q} n_{C^{q+}}(R,Z)}
$$

where $Q$ is the set of included carbon ion charge states, $n_{C^{q+}}$ is the corresponding number density in m$^{-3}$, and $\mathbf{V}_{C^{q+}}$ is its bulk velocity in m s$^{-1}$. The component is resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$; $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Sign convention: Positive when the carbon-ion bulk flow has a component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

As a species-level intensive quantity, it is the density-weighted mean over all krypton ion charge states, not a sum of charge-state velocities. The toroidal direction is the $\hat{\phi}$ basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

$$

$$

The toroidal nitrogen velocity at the pedestal top is the density-weighted mean flow of ionized nitrogen ions over all nitrogen charge states at the core-side shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier. It describes flow rather than abundance, which is represented by [nitrogen density at the pedestal top].

For nitrogen charge states $q=1,\ldots,7$, the species velocity is defined by

$$

where $n_q$ is the number density of charge state $q$ in m$^{-3}$ and $v_{\phi,q}$ is its toroidal velocity in m s$^{-1}$, measured in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Sign convention: Positive when the density-weighted velocity points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

Toroidal plasma momentum at the pedestal top is the cumulative toroidal component of plasma linear momentum contained inside the flux surface located at the top of the H-mode pedestal, summed over electrons and all ion species. The toroidal component is taken in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Let $\rho_{\mathrm{ped}}$ denote the radial flux-surface label of the pedestal-top flux surface and let $V(\rho_{\mathrm{ped}})$ be the plasma volume enclosed by that surface. The quantity is the radial cumulative [toroidal_total_plasma_momentum](name:toroidal_total_plasma_momentum) evaluated at the pedestal-top endpoint:

$$
P_{\phi,\mathrm{ped}} = P_\phi(\rho_{\mathrm{ped}}) = \int_{V(\rho_{\mathrm{ped}})} \sum_s m_s n_s(\mathbf{x}) v_{\phi,s}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_\phi(\rho)$ is the cumulative toroidal plasma momentum inside the flux surface labeled by $\rho$, $s$ indexes electrons and all ion species, $m_s$ is the species particle mass, $n_s$ is the species number density, $v_{\phi,s}$ is the signed toroidal velocity component, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $dV$ is the volume element.

This quantity is an endpoint value of a volume-integrated radial function: it is not the local toroidal momentum density $\sum_s m_s n_s v_{\phi,s}$ on the pedestal-top surface, and it is not a flux-surface average. It is also not toroidal angular momentum; the angular-momentum integral would include the moment arm $R$ multiplying the toroidal linear-momentum density. The same cumulative quantity has related endpoint values at the [magnetic axis](name:toroidal_plasma_momentum_at_magnetic_axis) and at the [plasma boundary].

Sign convention: Positive when the net toroidal plasma momentum points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The toroidal tritium velocity at the plasma boundary gives the bulk rotational flow of tritium ions projected onto the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$, evaluated at the last closed flux surface where the confined plasma meets the scrape-off layer. This boundary value constrains the outer edge of the radial tritium rotation profile and reflects the balance between momentum injection, viscous transport across the pedestal, and ion-neutral friction at the plasma edge.

The defining relation is the projection of the tritium ion fluid velocity vector $\mathbf{v}_T$ onto $\hat{\phi}$ at the last closed flux surface:

$$
v_{\phi,T}^{\rm b} = \mathbf{v}_T \cdot \hat{\phi}\Big|_{\rm LCFS}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height.

The toroidal ion velocity at the boundary is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), inferring the flow from Doppler shifts of charge-exchange emission lines in the steep-gradient edge region. For tritium-containing plasmas, measurements carry additional constraints due to the radioactive nature of the fuel species. Edge toroidal ion velocities in tokamak plasmas range from ~1 km/s in L-mode to ~100 km/s in strongly heated H-mode discharges. Comparing this quantity with [toroidal tritium velocity at the pedestal] and [toroidal tritium velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) characterizes the full radial rotation profile; [toroidal helium-3 velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) provides the analogous boundary quantity for the helium-3 species.

The toroidal tungsten velocity at the H-mode pedestal top is the density-weighted mean of the toroidal fluid velocities of tungsten impurity ions over their ionization states. It is evaluated at the core-side shoulder of the edge transport barrier in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining charge-state average is

$$
V_{\phi,\mathrm{W}} = \frac{\sum_q n_q v_{\phi,q}}{\sum_q n_q}
$$

where $V_{\phi,\mathrm{W}}$ is the tungsten toroidal velocity, $n_q$ is the number density of tungsten ions in charge state $q$, and $v_{\phi,q}$ is their toroidal velocity component.

The average is density-weighted over tungsten ion charge states, not a sum of velocities and not a flux-surface average. It therefore differs from the [toroidal flux-surface-averaged tungsten velocity at the plasma boundary]; [toroidal carbon velocity at the pedestal top](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_pedestal_top) is the analogous species-specific quantity.

Sign convention: Positive when the tungsten velocity component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

Total ion density at the plasma boundary is the local number density of all positively charged ion populations at the separatrix, the last closed flux surface separating confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. It is the charge-state-summed specialization of [ion density at the plasma boundary].

The total ion density is defined by

$$
n_i^{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_s \sum_{Z\geq 1} n_{s,Z}
$$

where $n_{s,Z}$ is the number density of ion species $s$ in charge state $Z$, and the sums include every charged ion species and charge state present at the boundary.

Neutral particles are excluded, and each ion contributes one particle regardless of its charge. The corresponding surface average is [flux-surface-averaged total ion density at the plasma boundary], which averages this local quantity over the separatrix.

Number density of tritium ions at the plasma boundary is the local, intensive particle count per physical volume for the tritium-ion population evaluated on the last closed magnetic flux surface. The plasma boundary is the limiting closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off-layer region.

The local tritium-ion number density is the zeroth velocity moment of the tritium-ion distribution function at a boundary point:

$$
n_\mathrm{T}(\mathbf{x}_b,t) = \int f_\mathrm{T}(\mathbf{x}_b,\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $n_\mathrm{T}$ is the tritium-ion number density, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a point on the last closed magnetic flux surface, $t$ is time, $\mathbf{v}$ is tritium-ion velocity, $f_\mathrm{T}$ is the tritium-ion phase-space distribution function, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

This quantity applies specifically to ionized tritium and excludes neutral tritium, deuterium, protium, electrons, impurity ions, and total ion density. It is a local boundary value, with no averaging over the boundary surface or over a volume; for tritium, the relevant positive ion population is singly ionized tritium, so no aggregation over multiple positive ionization stages is applied.

It is the tritium-specific instance of [density at the plasma boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). The related [flux-surface-averaged tritium density at the plasma boundary] instead represents the average of tritium-ion density over the same last closed magnetic flux surface, while [hydrogen density at the plasma boundary](name:hydrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [deuterium density at the plasma boundary](name:deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary) refer to different hydrogen-isotope ion populations.

Vorticity due to diamagnetic drift is the signed field-parallel scalar component of the curl of the diamagnetic-drift contribution to plasma velocity. It represents local rotation of the pressure-gradient-driven cross-field drift about the local magnetic-field direction.

The scalar component is defined by projecting the curl of the diamagnetic-drift velocity onto the local magnetic-field direction:

$$
\omega_{\mathrm{dia}} = \hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \left(\nabla \times \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia}}\right)
$$

where $\omega_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is vorticity due to diamagnetic drift, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the local magnetic-field unit vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the [bulk plasma velocity due to diamagnetic drift], and $\nabla \times$ denotes the spatial curl.

The scope is local plasma-fluid vorticity at a point in the plasma region where the diamagnetic-drift velocity is defined. The aggregation convention is unaveraged: no volume integral, flux-surface average, time average, or species/charge-state sum is included by this name.

It is not the magnitude of vorticity and must retain the sign of the field-parallel projection. It is not total vorticity; it excludes rotational contributions from electric-field drift, parallel flow, neutral flow, imposed rotation, or turbulence unless those contributions are part of the diamagnetic-drift velocity.

It is obtained from [bulk plasma velocity due to diamagnetic drift] by taking the curl and retaining the field-parallel component. In a decomposition of [parallel vorticity](name:parallel_vorticity) by flow mechanism, this quantity is the diamagnetic-drift term; other drift or flow terms are separate contributions.

Sign convention: Positive when $\nabla \times \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ has a component in the direction of the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

The parallel diamagnetic current density is the projection of the total [diamagnetic current density] onto the local magnetic-field direction. It arises from the magnetic-field–pressure-gradient drift current and represents the signed field-aligned component of [current density due to diamagnetic drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

The projection is defined by:

$$
j_{\mathrm{dia},\parallel} = \hat{\mathbf{b}}\cdot\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{dia},\parallel}$ is the parallel diamagnetic current density, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/B$ is the unit vector in the local magnetic-field direction, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $B=|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic-field magnitude, and $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the [current density due to diamagnetic drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

This quantity applies to the total included edge-plasma current density carried by all included charge carriers; it is not species- or charge-state-resolved unless those qualifiers are part of the standard name. It is a signed component, not the scalar magnitude [diamagnetic current density], and not a perpendicular component with respect to the magnetic-field direction.

It is distinct from signed cylindrical projections such as [radial diamagnetic current density](name:radial_diamagnetic_current_density), [vertical diamagnetic current density](name:vertical_diamagnetic_current_density), and [toroidal diamagnetic current density]. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, radial, toroidal, and vertical projections are along $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$ respectively; the parallel projection is along $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, not along any fixed cylindrical basis vector.

The same resolved contribution is denoted by [parallel current density due to diamagnetic drift](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) when expressed as a contribution to [current density](name:current_density). For the ideal isotropic scalar-pressure relation $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}=\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p/B^2$, where $p$ is total scalar plasma pressure and $\nabla p$ is its spatial gradient, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$ and therefore $j_{\mathrm{dia},\parallel}=0$; this is distinct from return-current contributions such as [Pfirsch-Schlüter current density](name:pfirsch_schlueter_current_density).

The parallel diamagnetic current density is the projection of the total [diamagnetic current density](name:diamagnetic_current_density) onto the local magnetic-field direction. It arises from the magnetic-field–pressure-gradient drift current and represents the signed field-aligned component of [current density due to diamagnetic drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

The projection is defined by:

$$

$$

The poloidal heat-viscosity current density is the poloidal component of the electric-current contribution generated when heat-viscosity terms in a collisional magnetized-plasma fluid closure drive net charge transport. It is the projection of the [heat-viscosity current density vector](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) onto the local poloidal direction in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

The component is defined by the projection of the parent vector onto the poloidal unit tangent:

$$
j_{\mathrm{hv},\theta} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{hv},\theta}$ is the poloidal heat-viscosity current density, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}}$ is the [heat-viscosity current density vector](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the unit tangent in the direction of increasing $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$.

This quantity applies to the net electric current density in the collisional magnetized edge-plasma fluid regime represented by heat-viscosity terms. It is local and signed, and its aggregation is the net charge-flow sum over species already contained in $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}}$, rather than a species-resolved component or a scalar magnitude.

It is distinct from the [radial component](name:radial_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) along $\hat{R}$, the [vertical component](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) along $\hat{Z}$, and the [toroidal component](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) along $\hat{\phi}$ of the same vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is also distinct from the [parallel component](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) projected along the local magnetic-field direction and from the [diamagnetic component](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) projected perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the poloidal-flux gradient; [current density due to collisions] denotes the separate contribution from inter-species collisional friction.

Sign convention: Positive when the heat-viscosity-driven net charge flow has a positive projection along the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

The poloidal current density due to perpendicular viscosity is the poloidal projection of the current-density contribution generated by the divergence of the perpendicular viscous stress tensor in a magnetized plasma. It represents the component tangent to a magnetic flux surface in the poloidal plane.

$$
J_{\pi_\perp,\theta}=\mathbf{J}_{\pi_\perp}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_\theta=\frac{\left[\mathbf{B}\times(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\pi}_\perp)\right]\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_\theta}{B^2}
$$

Here $\mathbf{J}_{\pi_\perp}$ is the perpendicular-viscosity current-density contribution, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, $B=|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude, $\boldsymbol{\pi}_\perp$ is the perpendicular viscous stress tensor, and $\hat{\mathbf e}_\theta$ is the unit tangent toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. The component is resolved in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This component is one projection of [current density due to perpendicular viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and is distinct from the toroidal projection [toroidal current density due to perpendicular viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity). It is also the perpendicular-viscosity contribution to [poloidal current density due to viscosity], which includes other viscous mechanisms.

Sign convention: Positive when the current-density projection points toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

Poloidal electron diffusivity is an effective scalar transport coefficient for diffusive electron-particle transport along the poloidal direction of flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

The constitutive relation is

$$
\Gamma_{e,\theta}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{e,\theta}\,\nabla_\theta n_e
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\theta}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the poloidal component of the diffusive electron particle-flux vector, $D_{e,\theta}$ is the poloidal electron diffusivity, $\nabla_\theta n_e$ is the metric-scaled electron-density gradient along increasing poloidal angle $\theta$, and $n_e$ is electron number density. The associated flux component is positive toward increasing $\theta$.

This is the poloidal projection of the anisotropic transport represented by [electron diffusivity]. It describes diffusive transport only and excludes convective fluxes, particle sources, and sinks; [poloidal particle diffusivity] is the corresponding species-independent quantity.

Poloidal ion energy diffusivity is the effective transport coefficient for local diffusive smoothing of ion thermal-energy density in the poloidal direction. The poloidal direction is the tangent to increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed radial flux label $\rho$ and toroidal angle $\phi$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. It represents the Fickian part of ion energy transport, distinct from convective transport and explicit energy sources or sinks.

The defining closure relates the physical diffusive ion thermal-energy flux component along the poloidal tangent to the metric poloidal gradient of ion thermal-energy density:

$$
q_{\theta,E,i}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -\chi_{\theta,E,i}\,\nabla_\theta w_i = -\chi_{\theta,E,i}\,\frac{1}{h_\theta}\left(\frac{\partial w_i}{\partial\theta}\right)_{\rho,\phi}
$$

where $q_{\theta,E,i}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive ion thermal-energy flux component in the direction of increasing $\theta$, $\chi_{\theta,E,i}$ is poloidal ion energy diffusivity, $w_i$ is ion thermal-energy density, $\nabla_\theta w_i$ is the metric poloidal gradient, and $h_\theta=|\partial\mathbf{x}/\partial\theta|_{\rho,\phi}$ is the poloidal metric scale factor for the position vector $\mathbf{x}(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. The minus sign specifies that positive $\chi_{\theta,E,i}$ gives down-gradient transport along poloidal arclength.

For an unresolved ion population, $w_i$ and $q_{\theta,E,i}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ denote quantities summed over the included ion species and charge states before the effective coefficient is applied; the coefficient is not the arithmetic sum of charge-state diffusivities. Charge-state-resolved quantities such as [poloidal ion charge-state energy diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_energy_diffusivity) retain that resolution. This quantity is the poloidal directional form of [ion energy diffusivity](name:ion_energy_diffusivity) and is distinct from field-aligned [parallel ion energy diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_energy_diffusivity), from [poloidal ion diffusivity] for particle transport, and from [poloidal ion momentum diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_momentum_diffusivity) for momentum transport.

The poloidal ion momentum diffusivity $D_{\mathrm{pol}}^i$ is the effective diffusion coefficient characterizing down-gradient redistribution of the poloidal component of momentum within the total ion population summed over all charge states.

The poloidal diffusive ion momentum flux density satisfies:

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{mom},i}^{\mathrm{pol}} = -n_i m_i D_{\mathrm{pol}}^i \nabla_{\mathrm{pol}} v_i
$$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{mom},i}^{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal component of the diffusive ion momentum flux density, $n_i$ is the total ion number density summed over charge states, $m_i$ is the ion mass associated with that population, $v_i$ is the poloidal component of the mean ion fluid velocity, and $\nabla_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the directional gradient along the poloidal transport direction. The negative sign specifies down-gradient diffusion.

This quantity applies to effective ion momentum transport in the edge plasma and represents one scalar diffusivity for the poloidal direction. It aggregates the total ion population over all charge states, does not resolve individual charge states, and excludes convective momentum transport and particle or energy diffusion.

The poloidal coefficient is a directional specialization of the parent [ion momentum diffusivity], which represents the corresponding effective ion-momentum diffusivity without this poloidal specialization. It is the poloidal-direction counterpart of [parallel ion momentum diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_momentum_diffusivity); the latter describes field-aligned transport while retaining the same total-ion, charge-state-summed scope. It is distinct from [parallel ion charge-state momentum diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity), which resolves momentum transport by charge state.

Poloidal total current density is the projection of [total current density] onto the local poloidal direction. It retains the net conventional current from ohmic, bootstrap, and externally driven mechanisms, aggregated over all resolved species and charge states.

The component is defined by

$$
J_{\theta,\mathrm{total}} = \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{total}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{total}}$ is the total current-density vector and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}$ is the unit tangent in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed flux label $\rho$ and toroidal angle $\phi$ in the flux coordinate $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

This total aggregate is distinct from [poloidal current density], which does not specify the total aggregation. It is the poloidal counterpart of [radial total current density](name:radial_total_current_density), whose projection is normal to magnetic flux surfaces.

Radial electron convection velocity is the effective advective velocity component for electron particle transport in the radial direction of a flux coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. It is a transport coefficient rather than necessarily the microscopic electron fluid velocity, representing directed electron particle transport after diffusive density-gradient transport is separated.

The radial electron particle flux is decomposed into diffusive and convective contributions:

$$
\Gamma_{e,\rho} = -D_{e,\rho}\frac{1}{h_\rho}\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial \rho} + n_e v_{e,\rho}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\rho}$ is the radial electron particle flux, $D_{e,\rho}$ is the radial electron particle diffusivity, $n_e$ is electron number density, $v_{e,\rho}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial electron convection velocity, $\rho$ is the radial flux coordinate, and $h_\rho$ converts variation in $\rho$ into physical distance. This component specializes the effective [electron convection velocity] and complements the [poloidal electron convection velocity](name:poloidal_electron_convection_velocity); its species contrast is the [radial ion convection velocity](name:radial_ion_particle_convection_velocity).

Sign convention: Positive when electron particle convection is directed toward increasing radial flux coordinate $\rho$.

Radial total current density $J_R$ is the component of the aggregated [total current density] vector resolved along the geometric major-radius direction. It represents net conventional charge transport in the cylindrical radial direction and is not the full current-density vector.

The radial projection is defined by:

$$
J_R = \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{tot}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}
$$

where $J_R$ is radial total current density, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the aggregated total current-density vector, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to edge-plasma charge transport at a spatial point and aggregates the charged species, charge states, and current-generation mechanisms included in the total current density. Its aggregation convention is algebraic summation of scalar contributions after projection onto the radial basis, so oppositely directed contributions cancel. It excludes displacement-current density and is distinct from electric current through a specified surface.

The radial direction is the geometric major-radius direction, not the normal to a magnetic flux surface. Accordingly, this quantity is distinct from [poloidal total current density](name:poloidal_total_current_density), [toroidal total current density](name:toroidal_total_current_density), and the mechanism-specific [radial current density due to anomalous transport](name:radial_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport); the latter includes only the anomalous-transport contribution rather than the total aggregate.

Sign convention: Positive when the aggregated conventional current-density vector has a component toward increasing major radius $R$.

Thermal plasma pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure of thermal electrons and ions, the scalar part of the kinetic pressure tensor in a fluid or magnetohydrodynamic description. It represents equilibrium mechanical stress from the included thermal populations and is not a perturbation amplitude.

The combined thermal pressure is defined by

$$
p_{\mathrm{th}} = p_e + \sum_i p_i
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal plasma pressure, $p_e$ is the thermal electron pressure, $p_i$ is the pressure of represented thermal ion species and charge states, and $i$ indexes those ion contributions.

This quantity applies to equilibrium isotropic thermal electron and ion populations, with the ion contribution summed over the represented ion species and charge states. It excludes fast-particle, neutral, magnetic, dynamic ram, anisotropic-tensor, and first-order perturbed pressure contributions; it is neither normalized nor volume integrated.

[Thermal ion pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) is the ion-only component of this quantity, while [thermal neutral pressure](name:thermal_neutral_pressure) describes a separate neutral contribution. The sum over all represented equilibrium kinetic populations, including contributions beyond the thermal electron and ion populations, is [total plasma pressure](name:total_plasma_pressure); this quantity is the thermal electron-and-ion specialization of [plasma pressure].

Thermal plasma pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure of thermal electrons and ions, the scalar part of the kinetic pressure tensor in a fluid or magnetohydrodynamic description. It represents equilibrium mechanical stress from the included thermal populations and is not a perturbation amplitude.

The combined thermal pressure is defined by

$$
p_{\mathrm{th}} = p_e + \sum_i p_i
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal plasma pressure, $p_e$ is the thermal electron pressure, $p_i$ is the pressure of represented thermal ion species and charge states, and $i$ indexes those ion contributions.

This quantity applies to equilibrium isotropic thermal electron and ion populations, with the ion contribution summed over the represented ion species and charge states. It excludes fast-particle, neutral, magnetic, dynamic ram, anisotropic-tensor, and first-order perturbed pressure contributions; it is neither normalized nor volume integrated.

[Thermal ion pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) is the ion-only component of this quantity, while [thermal neutral pressure](name:thermal_neutral_pressure) describes a separate neutral contribution. The sum over all represented equilibrium kinetic populations, including contributions beyond the thermal electron and ion populations, is [total plasma pressure](name:total_plasma_pressure); this quantity is the thermal electron-and-ion specialization of plasma pressure.

Vertical total current density is the component of the aggregated current-density vector [total current density] resolved along the vertical direction. It combines ohmic, bootstrap, and externally driven contributions over all included plasma species and charge states, distinguishing it from the generic [vertical current density].

The defining projection is:

$$
J_{\mathrm{v,total}} = \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{total}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $J_{\mathrm{v,total}}$ is the vertical total current density, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{total}}$ is the aggregated conventional current-density vector, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector. The projection is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Sign convention: Positive when conventional current has a component in the $+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ direction, corresponding to increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

The perpendicular wave-vector magnitude is the non-negative length of the part of a local electromagnetic wave vector transverse to the equilibrium magnetic field. It characterizes cross-field phase variation and is the scalar magnitude associated with the [perpendicular wave vector].

For wave vector $\mathbf{k}$ and magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, the perpendicular magnitude is defined by

$$
k_\perp = \left|\mathbf{k} - (\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}})\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right|
$$

where $k_\perp$ and $\mathbf{k}$ have units of inverse length, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is tangent to the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. The quantity excludes the wave-vector component parallel to the magnetic field and is non-negative by definition.

The electron plasma frequency is the natural electrostatic oscillation frequency of the local free-electron population at the measurement position. It is a plasma property, not the carrier frequency of a diagnostic source.

For the cold-electron response, the frequency is defined by

$$
f_{pe} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{n_e e^2}{\varepsilon_0 m_e}}
$$

where $f_{pe}$ is the electron plasma frequency, $n_e$ is the local free-electron number density, $e$ is the elementary charge, $\varepsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity, and $m_e$ is the electron mass.

This quantity is the local cutoff scale for ordinary-mode electromagnetic-wave propagation. It differs from the externally selected [diagnostic antenna frequency](name:frequency_of_diagnostic_antenna), while serving as the physical component of [frequency at measurement position].

Radial wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the signed projection of the local wave vector carried by a beam-tracing ray or beam onto the major-radius direction. The radial direction is the $\hat{R}$ basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The component is defined by projecting the local wave vector:

$$
k_R = \mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{R}
$$

where $k_R$ is the radial wave-vector component, $\mathbf{k}$ is the local [wave vector of the beam-tracing beam], and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector toward increasing $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the beam-tracing beam itself at a specified point along its path; no average, integral, or summation over the path or beam cross-section is implied. It is the cylindrical radial component only, not the radial position coordinate, not a direction unit-vector component, and not a flux-surface-normal or magnetic-field-perpendicular projection.

It is one component of the cylindrical decomposition $\mathbf{k}=k_R\hat{R}+k_\phi\hat{\phi}+k_Z\hat{Z}$, where $k_\phi$ is the [toroidal wave-vector component](name:toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), $k_Z$ is the [vertical wave-vector component](name:vertical_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), and $\hat{\phi}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are the toroidal and vertical basis directions of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Its normalized counterpart is the [radial refractive-index component], $N_R = c k_R/\omega$, where $N_R$ is the radial refractive-index component, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\omega$ is the angular frequency of the wave.

Sign convention: Positive when the local wave vector has a component in the $+\hat{R}$ direction, toward increasing major radius $R$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The perpendicular refractive index $N_\perp$ is the magnitude of the component of the refractive-index vector projected onto the plane perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field direction. It is the field-normal part of the dimensionless wave-propagation vector used to describe electromagnetic waves in a magnetized plasma.

The defining relation is:

$$
N_\perp = \left|\mathbf{N} - (\mathbf{N}\cdot\hat{b})\hat{b}\right|, \qquad \mathbf{N}=\frac{\mathbf{k}}{k_0}, \qquad k_0=\frac{\omega}{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{N}$ is the refractive-index vector, $\mathbf{k}$ is the local wave vector, $k_0$ is the vacuum wave number, $\omega$ is angular frequency, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field.

This scalar is the nonnegative magnitude of the perpendicular projection, not a signed projection along a chosen transverse basis direction. Together with the [parallel refractive index](name:parallel_refractive_index) $N_\parallel=\mathbf{N}\cdot\hat{b}$, it satisfies $N_\perp^2+N_\parallel^2=|\mathbf{N}|^2$; the corresponding unnormalized quantity is the [perpendicular wave-vector magnitude].
documents.after:

Toroidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the signed toroidal direction cosine of the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point. It is the projection of the local unit wave vector onto the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The normalized toroidal component is defined by

$$
k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\phi}}{\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert} = \frac{k_\phi}{\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert}
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$, $k_\phi=\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the [toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), and $\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert$ is the wave-vector magnitude.

This is a launch-point quantity, not an integral or average over a beam path. It is distinct from the [normalized toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:normalized_toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), which denotes the same toroidal direction cosine evaluated along a traced beam rather than specifically at launch. For real nonzero $\mathbf{k}$ it satisfies $-1 \leq k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}} \leq 1$; together with the [radial normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and the [vertical normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:vertical_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), the cylindrical direction cosines obey $k_{R,\mathrm{norm}}^2+k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}}^2+k_{Z,\mathrm{norm}}^2=1$. The [poloidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam] is instead a related projection in the meridional plane spanned by $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$.

Sign convention: Positive when the projection of $\mathbf{k}$ onto $\hat{\phi}$ is along the local $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The twist period is the repeat arclength along the sensing-fiber centerline for the effective birefringent-axis orientation to return to the same state.

Let $s$ denote arclength along the fiber centerline and $Q(s)$ denote the specified effective birefringent-axis state. The twist period $L_{\rm tw}$ is defined by

$$
Q(s + L_{\rm tw}) = Q(s)
$$

where $L_{\rm tw}$ is the smallest positive repeat arclength.

This is the twist-specific member of the [fiber optic current sensor period]. It describes spatial repetition of the optical anisotropy, not the total fiber arclength, the [initial twist phase](name:initial_spun_twist_phase_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor), or the [polarization beat length].

The vertical wave-vector component is the signed projection of an electromagnetic wave’s spatial phase-gradient vector onto the vertical direction at the launch point of an electron-cyclotron beam. It specifies the local propagation phase variation along the vertical coordinate.

The defining relation is

$$
k_Z = \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{Z} = \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial Z}
$$

where $k_Z$ is the vertical wave-vector component, $\mathbf{k}$ is the full electromagnetic wave vector, $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector, $\Phi$ is the spatial phase, and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate. The coordinate frame is the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$ and $\hat{R} \times \hat{\phi} = \hat{Z}$.

This quantity applies to one electron-cyclotron beam at its launch point. It is a local vector component, with no summation over beams, ray segments, or modes, and it is not a path-integrated or averaged quantity.

It is distinct from the [vertical wave electric field](name:vertical_wave_electric_field), which is a field projection rather than a wave-vector component. Unlike the [normalized wave vector], it retains the signed vertical component of the wave vector rather than a dimensionless rescaling of the full vector.

The corresponding toroidal projection is represented by the [toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam); together, such projections describe directional components of electromagnetic-wave phase propagation.

Sign convention: Positive when the wave-vector projection points toward increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Voltage of a reflectometer antenna is the peak amplitude of a narrow-band microwave voltage associated with a reflectometer antenna terminal or specified electrical reference plane. It is a calibrated voltage amplitude, meaning the value is referred to that terminal or reference plane after applying the gain, attenuation, and reference-plane convention that define the reported electrical amplitude.

For a narrow-band waveform represented by the complex voltage phasor $\tilde V(t)$ through $v(t)=\Re\{\tilde V(t)e^{-i\omega_0 t}\}$, the antenna voltage is defined by:

$$
V_\mathrm{ant}(t)=|\tilde V(t)|
$$

where $v(t)$ is the real microwave voltage waveform in volts, $\tilde V(t)$ is the slowly varying complex voltage phasor in volts at the reference plane, $\omega_0$ is the carrier angular frequency in radians per second, and $V_\mathrm{ant}(t)$ is the reported peak voltage amplitude in volts. For a pure sinusoid, the corresponding root-mean-square voltage is $V_\mathrm{ant}/\sqrt{2}$; this standard name denotes the peak amplitude.

As a generic reflectometer-antenna terminal amplitude, this quantity can include launched-wave leakage, plasma-reflected or scattered components, antenna coupling, standing-wave effects, and receiver-chain response unless a component has been separated by definition. It is the reflectometer-specific counterpart of [voltage of a diagnostic antenna](name:voltage_of_diagnostic_antenna) and is broader than [reflected voltage of a reflectometer antenna], which denotes only the reflected-wave component; it is not a reflection coefficient, cutoff position, or plasma density.

Initial power of a beam-tracing beam is the electromagnetic wave power carried by a single coherent beam at the start of its traced trajectory. It is the total power assigned to that beam before propagation and energy transfer to plasma particles.

The single-beam power balance relates the initial power to residual and absorbed power:

$$
P_0 = P_{mathrm{res}} + P_{mathrm{abs}}
$$

where $P_0$ is the initial power defined here, $P_{\mathrm{res}}$ is the residual [power of a beam-tracing beam] at the trajectory endpoint, and $P_{\mathrm{abs}}$ is the total [absorbed power of a beam-tracing beam](name:absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam) transferred to plasma particles along the same trajectory.

This quantity applies to one coherent beam and aggregates the electromagnetic wave power across all plasma-interaction channels before any such transfer occurs. It is distinct from residual endpoint power, which remains in the beam after propagation, and from absorbed power, which is transferred to the plasma; species-resolved quantities such as [electron absorbed power of a beam-tracing beam](name:electron_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam) describe components of the latter.

Temperature-equivalent radiation energy scale of electron-cyclotron emission, evaluated at the magnetic axis. The magnetic axis is the degenerate innermost magnetic surface of the equilibrium, the locus in the poloidal cross-section where the gradient of the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) vanishes; evaluation at this locus does not imply that the radiative temperature has an extremum there.

The blackbody-equivalent radiation energy scale is defined by matching the radiation field's specific intensity to the Planck spectral intensity:

$$
I_\nu = \frac{2 h \nu^3}{c^2}\left[\exp\!\left(\frac{h\nu}{T_\mathrm{rad}}\right)-1\right]^{-1}
$$

where $I_\nu$ is the radiation specific intensity, $\nu$ is the radiation frequency, $h$ is the Planck constant, $c$ is the speed of light, and $T_\mathrm{rad}$ is the [radiative temperature].

This quantity is restricted to the radiation field associated with electron-cyclotron emission at the magnetic-axis locus. For layer-resolved electron-cyclotron emission, the axis value is the radiative temperature of the resonance layer whose effective emission location is closest to the magnetic axis; the aggregation convention is nearest-layer selection, not a spatial average over neighboring layers. Ordinary-mode and extraordinary-mode electron-cyclotron emission are polarization-specific variants; the unqualified quantity does not select a polarization mode and is not a sum or mean over modes.

It is the radiation-field member of [temperature at the magnetic axis](name:temperature_at_magnetic_axis) and the magnetic-axis counterpart of [radiative temperature]. It must not be identified with the local kinetic [electron temperature at the magnetic axis](name:electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) except in the limiting case of optically thick thermal emission, where the brightness temperature approaches the electron thermal energy scale.

This quantity is the signed imaginary quadrature component of the parallel electromagnetic wave electric-field phasor. It retains phase information and is not the field amplitude or magnitude.

$$
\tilde E_\parallel = \tilde{\mathbf E}\cdot\hat{\mathbf b} = E_{\parallel,R}+iE_{\parallel,I},\qquad E_{\parallel,I}=\operatorname{Im}(\tilde E_\parallel)
$$

Here $\tilde{\mathbf E}$ is the complex wave electric-field phasor, $\hat{\mathbf b}$ is the unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field, and $E_{\parallel,R}$ and $E_{\parallel,I}$ are its real and imaginary quadrature components. The imaginary component, together with the [parallel wave electric field](name:parallel_wave_electric_field), specifies the complex parallel field; its algebraic sign follows the selected temporal phasor convention. It is distinct from the [parallel wave electric field amplitude].

Sign convention: Positive when the imaginary quadrature electric-field component points along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction.

Vacuum wavelength of a wave beam is the spatial period of its electromagnetic phase in vacuum, assigned to the beam’s carrier radiation. It characterizes the beam itself rather than a spectral transition or an instrument-response feature.

The vacuum wavelength $\lambda_0$ is related to the beam’s temporal frequency $f$ by:

$$
\lambda_0 = \frac{c}{f}
$$

where $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum and $f$ is the temporal oscillation frequency of the electromagnetic wave.

This quantity applies to a probing electromagnetic wave beam and describes its vacuum propagation property, independent of plasma-induced changes in phase velocity. It is assigned to the beam as a whole and is not a sum, average, or integral over beams, paths, channels, or spectral components. It excludes the in-medium wavelength and wavelengths associated with filters, detector pixels, or spectral transitions.

This beam-specific specialization of [vacuum electromagnetic wavelength] supplies the wavelength used to characterize the beam’s propagation and its interaction with plasma. For a vacuum plane wave, the magnitude of its [wave vector] satisfies the equivalent relation $|\mathbf{k}| = 2\pi/\lambda_0$, where $\mathbf{k}$ is the vacuum wave vector.

Electric current carried by a plasma current-carrying filament element is the signed toroidal current assigned to one discrete element in an axisymmetric filamentary representation of the distributed plasma current. It represents that element's contribution to the plasma current rather than a geometric property of the element.

For filament element $k$, the current is the cross-sectional integral of the toroidal plasma current density over that element:

$$
I_k = \int_{A_k} j_\phi \, dA
$$

where $I_k$ is the electric current carried by plasma filament element $k$, $A_k$ is the [area of the plasma filament element] in the poloidal cross-section, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the plasma current density in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and $dA$ is a differential area element of the poloidal cross-section.

The scope is one plasma current-carrying filament element, with no aggregation over multiple elements. It applies only to plasma-current filaments in the axisymmetric representation and excludes currents in coils, passive conductors, and other non-plasma structures. It is an integrated current, not a current density and not a geometric descriptor; the element geometry is described separately by [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament), [height](name:height_of_plasma_filament), and area.

The represented [plasma current](name:plasma_current) of a collection of plasma current-carrying filament elements is the algebraic sum of their signed filament currents.

Sign convention: Positive when the current of the plasma filament element flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; this is counter-clockwise when viewed from the positive $Z$ direction.

Elongation is the shape ratio of an individual nested magnetic flux surface, describing how extended its poloidal cross-section is vertically relative to horizontally.

For a given flux surface, the elongation is defined by

$$
\kappa = \frac{a_v}{a_h}
$$

where $\kappa$ is the elongation, $a_v$ is the vertical semi-axis of the poloidal cross-section, and $a_h$ is its horizontal semi-axis.

The quantity applies separately to each nested magnetic flux surface and is a shape ratio rather than an integrated, summed, or averaged quantity. It is not restricted to the outermost surface; the distinct [elongation of the plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) refers specifically to the last closed plasma boundary.

The [radial derivative of elongation of a flux surface] describes the change of $\kappa$ across nested surfaces, whereas this quantity gives the elongation at one surface.

This quantity is the full vertical dimension of the rectangular cross-section associated with one discrete plasma current-carrying filament. It is a geometric extent, not the filament current or its current density.

The height $H$ is defined by the difference between the upper and lower vertical coordinates:

H = Z_{\mathrm{upper}} - Z_{\mathrm{lower}}

where $Z_{\mathrm{upper}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{lower}}$ are the upper and lower coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $Z$ denoting vertical height and $\hat{Z}$ the vertical basis direction.

This quantity applies only to the vertical dimension of the rectangular filament cross-section. The horizontal full width is defined separately by [plasma filament width](name:plasma_filament_width), while the in-plane thickness is defined by [thickness of plasma filament].

Radial coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point is the $R$ coordinate, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, of a specified point on a plasma-boundary or separatrix contour where $R$ is locally stationary with respect to $Z$. In this frame, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The coordinate is defined by the stationary-radius condition on the specified contour:

$$
R_{\mathrm{dR/dZ=0}} = R(P_0), \qquad \left.\frac{dR}{dZ}\right|_{C,P_0} = 0
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{dR/dZ=0}}$ is the radial coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point, $P_0$ is the specified dR/dZ zero point, $C$ is the plasma-boundary or separatrix contour on which $P_0$ lies, $R(P_0)$ is the major-radius coordinate of $P_0$, $Z$ is the vertical-height coordinate, and $dR/dZ$ is the derivative of the contour coordinate $R$ with respect to $Z$ along $C$.

The scope is a single specified geometric point on the contour; the value is not an average over the contour, over toroidal angle $\phi$, or over all stationary points. If several points on the contour satisfy $dR/dZ=0$, the definition does not by itself impose an inboard, outboard, upper, or lower selection rule; each specified zero point has its own radial-coordinate value.

This quantity is only the cylindrical $R$ coordinate of the point, not a flux-surface-normal displacement or a flux-label coordinate. Together with the [vertical coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point], it locates the point in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ cross-section at fixed $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is distinct from the [radial coordinate of an X-point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point), which locates a magnetic null on a separatrix rather than a radial extremum of a boundary or separatrix contour.

Thickness of a plasma filament is the full transverse extent of a rectangular (thick-line) filament cross-section, measured in the local plane of the element along the direction normal to the filament's central segment. The central segment lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and the local tangential-normal basis is defined within that plane: the tangential direction follows the central segment while the normal direction is the in-plane perpendicular. It is a full side length, not a half-width.

For a rectangular filament cross-section, the cross-sectional area is the product of the two full local side lengths:

$$
A_\mathrm{fil} = L_\mathrm{tan}\, t
$$

where $A_\mathrm{fil}$ is the filament cross-sectional area in $\mathrm{m}^2$, $L_\mathrm{tan}$ is the [tangential length](name:thickness_of_plasma_filament) in $\mathrm{m}$, and $t$ is the thickness in $\mathrm{m}$. When the local tangential and normal directions align with the cylindrical axes, the thickness coincides with either the width (radial $R$-direction extent) or the [height](name:height_of_plasma_filament) (vertical $Z$-direction extent) of the same rectangular cross-section.

In equilibrium filament descriptions, the thickness is set by the chosen local geometric representation of a discrete current-carrying plasma element. For a thick-line element it is specified directly as the rectangle side perpendicular to the central segment.

The value is a non-negative geometric length governed by the spatial resolution and local size of the filament representation. No universal device-independent numerical range applies; it should be interpreted relative to the associated tangential length and to neighboring filament spacing.

The toroidal angle identifies the azimuthal location of a point on the control surface about the machine symmetry axis. It is the geometrical coordinate defined for [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle), with the control-surface locus providing the points to which it applies.

For a point with Cartesian coordinates $x$ and $y$ in the right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, the angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame is defined by:

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x) \pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $R$ is the major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and the zero of $\phi$ follows the facility-defined reference direction. The angle is periodic, so values differing by an integer multiple of $2\pi$ represent the same toroidal direction; it is distinct from the [vertical coordinate of the control surface].

Sign convention: Positive when $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

The reference point and its associated direction specify the gap geometry; this coordinate is not the clearance distance, which is represented by [gap at plasma boundary].
