Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. For this flux-surface-averaged quantity, that distance is averaged over each nested magnetic flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The flux-surface average of major radius is defined by

$$
\langle R\rangle_\psi = \frac{\oint_\psi R\,dl/B_p}{\oint_\psi dl/B_p}
$$

where $\langle R\rangle_\psi$ is the averaged major-radius coordinate, $\psi$ is the magnetic-flux label identifying the surface, $l$ is poloidal arc length along that surface, and $B_p$ is the magnitude of the poloidal magnetic field. The contour integral extends around the complete poloidal intersection of the nested magnetic flux surface.

This quantity applies to a complete magnetic flux surface and aggregates the local [major radius] using the flux-surface weighting defined by the inverse poloidal-field magnitude. It is therefore distinct from pointwise major radius and contains no point-specific or localized evaluation.

The quantity is the flux-surface-averaged counterpart of [major radius]. It must not be confused with [flux-surface-averaged inverse of major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), which averages the reciprocal $1/R$ rather than averaging $R$ itself; consequently, it is not generally the reciprocal of that neighboring average.

The minimum safety factor is the signed field-line winding number evaluated on the nested closed magnetic flux surface where the magnitude of the safety factor is smallest. It represents the extremal value of the safety-factor function within the confined closed-surface domain.

The minimizing value is defined by

$$
q_{\min} = q(\rho_\ast), \qquad \rho_\ast \in \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0 \leq \rho \leq 1} |q(\rho)|
$$

where $q(\rho)$ is the signed [safety factor](name:safety_factor) on the flux surface labeled by $\rho$, $\rho_\ast$ is the label of a surface at which the magnitude $|q(\rho)|$ is minimized, and $q_{\min}$ is the signed value evaluated there. The label $\rho$ is a monotonic flux-surface coordinate whose endpoints denote the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface. In flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The extremum is taken over all nested closed magnetic flux surfaces and is neither a flux-surface average nor a sum. The location-defining quantity is separate: [poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor] identifies the corresponding surface, while this quantity reports only the signed safety factor. It is also distinct from a safety factor evaluated at a prescribed locus, such as the magnetic axis.

Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal angle advance of a magnetic field line is in the direction of increasing $\phi$ as the poloidal angle $\theta$ increases.

Inner radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the inner circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the boundary between the hollow central region and the conducting annular region.

For the inner circular boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the inner radius $a_\mathrm{inner}$ is the distance from the filament cross-section center $(R_c, Z_c)$ to any point $(R, Z)$ on that boundary:

$$
a_\mathrm{inner} = \sqrt{(R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, $(R_c, Z_c)$ is the center of the annular cross-section, and $(R, Z)$ is a point on the inner circular boundary.

This quantity applies to the hollow-disk annular representation of a discrete plasma current-carrying filament and denotes the smaller of its two concentric boundary radii. The current-carrying cross-section occupies the region outside $a_\mathrm{inner}$ and inside $a_\mathrm{outer}$, where $a_\mathrm{outer}$ is the [outer radius of the plasma filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament), with $0 \le a_\mathrm{inner} \le a_\mathrm{outer}$.

Together with the [outer radius of the plasma filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament), this quantity determines the [width of the plasma filament] as the radial thickness of the annulus and the [area of the plasma filament] as the area of the current-carrying annular region. It excludes the outer boundary radius itself, the annular width or area, the [height of the plasma filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament), the curvature radius of a noncircular contour segment, and the major radius of a filament centerline about the toroidal symmetry axis.

Outer radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the outer circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the external boundary of the conducting annular region; material outside this boundary is not part of that annular filament cross-section.

For the outer circular boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the outer radius $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the distance from the filament cross-section center $(R_c, Z_c)$ to any point $(R, Z)$ on that boundary:

$$

where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, $(R_c, Z_c)$ is the center of the annular cross-section, and $(R, Z)$ lies on the outer circular boundary.

Toroidal total current density is the net conventional electric-charge flux density at a point, resolved along the geometric toroidal direction. It is an aggregate signed component rather than the full current-density vector.

The toroidal component is defined by algebraically summing the toroidal projections of all included current-density contributions:

$$
J_{\phi,\mathrm{tot}}(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_k J_{k,\phi}(\mathbf{x},t), \qquad J_{k,\phi}(\mathbf{x},t) = \mathbf{J}_k(\mathbf{x},t) \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $J_{\phi,\mathrm{tot}}$ is the toroidal total current density, $J_{k,\phi}$ is the toroidal scalar contribution from contribution $k$, $\mathbf{J}_k$ is its current-density vector, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the toroidal unit vector, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $t$ is time, and $k$ indexes the included charged-species, charge-state, or current-generation contributions.

This quantity applies to conventional charge transport at plasma points, including the edge-plasma region, over all charged species, charge states, and current-generation mechanisms included in the aggregate. Contributions are combined by algebraic summation, so opposite signed toroidal contributions cancel. It excludes displacement-current density and is distinct from an electric current through a specified surface, a species-resolved or mechanism-resolved contribution, and the full [current density](name:current_density) vector.

The [total current density] provides the corresponding aggregate before toroidal projection. The [poloidal total current density](name:poloidal_total_current_density) applies the same aggregation convention to the local poloidal direction, while this quantity selects the toroidal component. The projection uses the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal component of conventional current density points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

Area of a Rogowski coil is the effective cross-sectional area linked by one sensing turn of a closed Rogowski winding. It is a scalar geometry factor of the winding, not the signed current threaded by the coil or the measured coil voltage.

In the ideal uniformly wound limit, the area appears as the non-negative sensitivity factor in the linear constitutive relation between coil voltage and enclosed-current time derivative:

$$
V_R(t) = \sigma \mu_0 n A \frac{d I_\mathrm{enc}}{dt}
$$

where $A$ is the Rogowski-coil area, $n$ is the winding turn density along the closed winding path, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $I_\mathrm{enc}$ is the signed [Rogowski-coil current](name:current_of_rogowski_coil) threaded by the coil, $V_R$ is the [Rogowski-coil voltage], and $\sigma$ is the sign set by winding orientation and terminal polarity.

The effective area may represent a calibrated equivalent for a real winding with finite pitch or nonuniform cross-section, but it remains a per-turn area factor. It is in the same geometric-coil-area family as [area of a poloidal magnetic field probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and [area of a toroidal magnetic field probe](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe); multiplying by turn density, turn number, or path length gives related sensitivity factors, not this quantity.

The signed turn count of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the number of conductor turns linked by the probe aperture, including the orientation imposed by the winding sense and the chosen terminal polarity. Its magnitude multiplies the magnetic flux coupled into the coil, while its sign records whether the coil's signed area normal corresponds to the positive or negative $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The electromagnetic calibration follows the flux-linkage form of Faraday's law:

$$
V = -\frac{d\Lambda}{dt}, \qquad \Lambda = N\Phi_+ = N\int_{S_+} \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}_+ \simeq N A B_\phi
$$

where $V$ is the open-circuit [terminal voltage](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) in volts, $\Lambda$ is the flux linkage in webers, $N$ is this signed turn count, $\Phi_+$ is the flux through a reference turn, and $d\mathbf{S}_+$ is the vector area element in square meters with normal chosen along increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The approximation uses the effective [probe area](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) $A$ in m$^2$ and a locally uniform toroidal magnetic-field component $B_\phi$ in tesla.

The magnitude of $N$ is assigned from winding records and checked by magnetic calibration with a known time-varying $B_\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The sign is determined from the documented terminal polarity and the right-hand rule for the coil winding; calibration verifies it by comparing the measured terminal-voltage polarity with that predicted by Faraday's law. The [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) specifies the sensitive-axis orientation, and the [probe length] characterizes finite spatial sampling rather than multiplying the flux pickup factor $N A$.

Typical magnitudes are 1-10 turns for high-bandwidth probes and 10-500 turns for higher-sensitivity or low-noise coils. Larger magnitude increases induced voltage for a given $dB_\phi/dt$ but generally increases winding resistance, self-inductance, and capacitance, so the selected count reflects a trade-off between sensitivity and frequency response.

Sign convention: Positive when the winding and terminal polarity define a signed area normal pointing in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Terminal voltage at a poloidal magnetic-field probe is the signed coil-terminal electromotive force associated with the probe winding that senses the local poloidal magnetic field. The sensed field component lies in the $R$-$Z$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and is projected along the probe sensitive-axis normal.

For a probe with algebraic turn count $N$ and geometric per-turn area $A$, Faraday's law relates the terminal voltage to the local poloidal field component $B_p$ as:

$$
V = -N A \frac{dB_p}{dt}
$$

where $V$ is the terminal voltage at the coil terminals, $B_p$ is the local poloidal magnetic-field component along the positive sensitive-axis normal, $N$ is the algebraic turn count including winding direction, $A$ is the [area of poloidal magnetic-field probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), and $t$ is time.

The quantity applies to one poloidal-field probe coil and is not aggregated over multiple probes. Its locus is specified by the [major radius of poloidal magnetic-field probe], [toroidal angle of poloidal magnetic-field probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), and [poloidal angle of poloidal magnetic-field probe]; these position quantities identify where the local field component is sampled and are not themselves voltages.

This quantity is distinct from the derived local poloidal magnetic field. It is the poloidal-field-probe counterpart of [voltage of toroidal magnetic-field probe](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), for a coil oriented to sense the toroidal field, and is distinct from [voltage of flux loop](name:voltage_of_flux_loop), which corresponds to a loop enclosing magnetic flux rather than a local magnetic-field probe winding.

Sign convention: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux threading the coil in the direction of the probe's positive sensitive-axis normal is decreasing with time.

The alpha angle is the signed orientation of the designated alpha-side edge of an iron core segment in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It identifies the alpha-side orientation and is independent of the edge length.

For an oriented alpha-side vector with signed radial and vertical components $\Delta R$ and $\Delta Z$, the angle is defined by

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}(\Delta Z,\Delta R)
$$

where $\alpha$ is the alpha angle, $\Delta R$ is the component along the outward major-radius direction, and $\Delta Z$ is the component along the vertical direction. This quantity is the alpha-side specialization of the general [iron core segment orientation angle], not a length or cross-sectional dimension.

Sign convention: Positive when the oriented alpha-side vector is inclined from the outward $+R$ direction toward increasing $Z$.

Fast neutron number flux is the incident crossing rate of the fast-neutron population per unit area on the inboard-facing surface of a non-axisymmetric correction coil. It is the fast-neutron component of [neutron flux of correction coil].

The differential number flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{fast}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{fast}}}{dA\,dt}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the number of fast neutrons incident on surface area $A$ and $t$ is time; $A$ is measured in m$^2$ and $t$ in s.

The inboard-facing surface is the side directed toward decreasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This quantity includes only incident fast-neutron crossings and excludes outgoing crossings and the energy-integrated neutron flux.

Force of a poloidal-field coil is a signed scalar electromagnetic load on an individual poloidal-field coil. It is the Lorentz-force resultant selected by a force-combination matrix from the coil's radial and vertical force components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The force-combination definition is

$$
F_{c\ell} = C_{\ell R} F_{R,c} + C_{\ell Z} F_{Z,c}
$$

where $F_{c\ell}$ is this force for coil $c$ and force-combination row $\ell$, $C_{\ell R}$ and $C_{\ell Z}$ are the radial and vertical coefficients of the [force-combination matrix], $F_{R,c}$ is the [radial force of a poloidal-field coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), and $F_{Z,c}$ is the [vertical force of a poloidal-field coil](name:vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil).

The scope is one poloidal-field coil and one force-combination row; no summation over multiple coils is implied. This quantity is distinct from the radial and vertical component forces themselves, and it is not a magnetic field, current, torque, or structural stress.

The [minimum force of a poloidal-field coil](name:minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [maximum force of a poloidal-field coil](name:maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) are lower and upper bounds on this same force-combination scalar.

Sign convention: Positive when $C_{\ell R}F_{R,c}+C_{\ell Z}F_{Z,c}>0$ after taking $F_{R,c}$ positive outward toward increasing $R$ and $F_{Z,c}$ positive upward toward increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Inner radius of a correction coil is the non-negative distance from the center of an annular non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor or winding-pack cross-section to its inner circular boundary. It defines the bore size of the annular material region.

This quantity applies only to correction-coil cross-sections whose geometry is annular. It is a local cross-sectional geometric distance for the conductor or winding pack, not an aggregation over multiple coils or turns.

It is distinct from the correction-coil centerline position, from any major-radius coordinate of the coil in space, from the outer cross-sectional radius, and from the material cross-sectional area. It describes the inner hole boundary, not the amount of conductor material.

For an annular correction-coil cross-section, this inner radius complements the corresponding [correction-coil radius] in specifying the radial bounds of the annulus. The [area of a correction coil](name:area_of_correction_coil) is a related cross-sectional quantity, but its definition is geometry-dependent and is not generally determined by this inner radius alone.

L_\alpha = \sqrt{(R_2-R_1)^2+(Z_2-Z_1)^2}
$$

where $R_i$ are major-radius coordinates and $Z_i$ are vertical coordinates, both in meters, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The toroidal coordinate is fixed for this poloidal cross-sectional length. The quantity is a magnitude and is therefore non-negative.

Major length of a poloidal field coil is the non-negative Euclidean length of the edge of an oblique coil cross-section that is inclined by the alpha angle from the major-radius direction. The edge is defined in a constant-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

With $L_\alpha$ denoting this major length and $\Delta\boldsymbol{x}_\alpha$ denoting the endpoint-to-endpoint displacement vector of the alpha-inclined edge in that cross-section, the defining relation is:

$$
L_\alpha = \left\lVert \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_\alpha \right\rVert \ge 0
$$

where the norm is the Euclidean norm in the constant-$\phi$ section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The scope is an active poloidal field coil or coil element whose conductor cross-section is represented by an oblique parallelogram in a constant-$\phi$ section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It is a single side length of that cross-section; no toroidal path length, conductor centerline length, cross-sectional averaging, summation over elements, or integration over the coil is implied. This quantity is not a signed radial or vertical projection, not the alpha angle, and not a rectangular radial width or vertical height.

The edge orientation is set by the [alpha angle of the poloidal field coil]; $L_\alpha$ supplies only the corresponding edge magnitude. In a parallelogram oblique cross-section, the [area of the poloidal field coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil) satisfies $A = L_\alpha L_\beta |\sin(\beta-\alpha)|$, where $A$ is that cross-sectional area, $\alpha$ is the alpha angle, $L_\beta$ is the length of the other parallelogram side, and $\beta$ is that side's angle measured from the same major-radius direction.

Radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative geometry radius that defines an axis-centered boundary or a circular-arc boundary of the segment. The relevant cross-section is the plane spanned by $R$ and $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height. The reference is the toroidal symmetry axis only for boundary geometry specified about that axis; when an explicit arc center is specified in the poloidal cross-section, that center is the reference.

The defining distance is selected by the reference geometry:

$$
r = \begin{cases}
R_b, & \text{for boundary geometry referenced to the toroidal symmetry axis}, \\
\sqrt{(R_b - R_c)^2 + (Z_b - Z_c)^2}, & \text{for boundary geometry referenced to an explicit arc center}.
\end{cases}
$$

where $r$ is the radius, $(R_b, Z_b)$ is the boundary point, and $(R_c, Z_c)$ is the explicit circular-arc center; $r$, $R_b$, $Z_b$, $R_c$, and $Z_c$ are expressed in meters. In the axis-referenced case, $R_b$ is the shortest distance from the boundary point to the toroidal symmetry axis.

This quantity is a boundary-geometry radius, not the [radial coordinate of an iron-core segment], which is the $R$ coordinate of a point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is distinct from the [outer radius of an iron-core segment](name:outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment), which is the outermost axis-referenced radial extent of the segment; a local or specified radius of an iron-core segment need not be that maximum. The radius alone does not specify the boundary point, arc endpoints, angular sweep, or traversal orientation.

The inner radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative major-radius distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the inner boundary of an annular iron region. It is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an annular cross-section, the inner radius $R_{\rm in}$ is the radial location of the inner boundary, and it is smaller than the corresponding outer radius $R_{\rm out}$:

$$
0 \le R_{\rm in} < R_{\rm out}
$$

The quantity specifies the hollow-bore boundary and radial extent, not the position along the toroidal direction, vertical height, boundary thickness, or local curvature of an arc. Unlike the curvature radius represented by [radius of an iron-core segment], it is a radial boundary dimension. Together with the [outer radius of an iron-core segment](name:outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment), it defines the annular radial interval.

Radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative geometry radius that defines the outer boundary of an annular iron-core region. This member specializes [radius of an iron-core segment] to the outermost boundary measured from the toroidal symmetry axis. The relevant cross-section is the plane spanned by $R$ and $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height.

The outer radius is the maximum major-radius coordinate on the cross-sectional boundary:

$$
r_{\rm out} = \max_{(R,Z)\in\partial A} R
$$

where $r_{\rm out}$ is the outer radius, $A$ is the iron-core cross-sectional region, and $\partial A$ is its boundary; $R$, $Z$, and $r_{\rm out}$ are expressed in meters.

For annular geometry, the outer radius together with the [inner radius of an iron-core segment](name:inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment) determines the radial thickness through $r_{\rm out}-r_{\rm in}$. It is an axis-referenced outer extent, not the radius of a local circular arc about an explicit off-axis center or the full rectangular extent described by the [width of an iron-core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment).

The inner radius is the smaller of the two radial dimensions characterizing the annular conductor cross-section of a poloidal field coil, measured from the center of the annulus to its inner conducting boundary in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It specifies the radius of the conductor bore of the annular cross-section.

For an annular conductor cross-section, the area associated with the inner and outer radii is

$$
A = \pi\left(r_o^2 - r_i^2\right)
$$

where $A$ is the [area of the poloidal field coil cross-section](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil), $r_i$ is the inner radius, $r_o$ is the [outer radius of the poloidal field coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil), and $\pi$ is the circle constant.

The scope is the circular-annulus geometry of a single poloidal-field-coil conductor cross-section; if a coil is represented by multiple conductor elements, the definition applies separately to each element and is not a sum or average over the coil. This quantity is distinct from the outer radius, from any circular-arc curvature radius used to approximate a coil contour, and from a centerline radius about the machine symmetry axis.

Together with the [major-radius coordinate], the [vertical coordinate](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), and the outer radius, $r_i$ specifies the annulus geometry in the poloidal plane. The analogous inner-radius quantity for a correction coil is [inner radius of correction coil](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil).

The resistance of a non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor is the proportionality between its steady conventional current and the associated ohmic voltage drop. It describes dissipation in the conductor rather than inductive or other reactive voltage contributions.

For a uniform conductor, the resistance is defined by

$$
R = \rho \frac{L}{A}
$$

where $R$ is resistance in ohms, $\rho$ is electrical resistivity in ohm-meters, $L$ is the effective conductor length in meters, and $A$ is the cross-sectional area in square meters. The terminal relation is $V = IR$, where $V$ is the ohmic voltage drop and $I$ is the current; the corresponding resistive power is $P = I^2R$. The current is the [current of the correction coil], and the conductor area is represented by the [area of the correction coil](name:area_of_correction_coil).

Saturated permeability of a ferritic element is the absolute scalar permeability of an identified ferritic element, evaluated on the high-field branch of its nonlinear magnetization curve where the magnetization has passed the knee and approached its saturation value. It quantifies the residual differential response of magnetic flux density to changes in magnetic field strength on that branch, and assumes an isotropic (or isotropized) material response so that a single scalar characterizes the element.

It is defined as the tangent slope of the flux-density versus field-strength characteristic evaluated on the saturated branch:

$$
\mu_\mathrm{sat} = \left.\frac{dB}{dH}\right|_\mathrm{saturated}
$$

where $B$ is the magnetic flux density in tesla, $H$ is the magnetic field strength in ampere per meter, and the derivative is taken at field strengths large enough that the incremental magnetization has become small. In the idealized limit of a truly constant saturation magnetization the collinear relation $B = \mu_0 (H + M_\mathrm{sat})$ gives a limiting tangent slope of $\mu_0$; the saturated permeability is the finite high-field branch value, which for real ferritic steels remains somewhat larger than $\mu_0$ because the magnetization still varies weakly.

This quantity is a branch-specific specialization of the general field-dependent [permeability of a ferritic element]. It is distinct from the [initial permeability], which is the tangent slope evaluated near zero field, from a secant permeability defined as the ratio $B/H$, and from the [relative permeability], which is a dimensionless ratio normalized by the vacuum permeability $\mu_0$.

The toroidal angle of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross section is the angular coordinate of a conductor-contour point measured relative to a designated reference point on that cross section. It is the toroidal component of the point location in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For contour point $i$, the relative toroidal angle is defined as the difference between the point and reference toroidal coordinates:

$$
\phi_{\mathrm{rel},i} = \phi_i - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\phi_i$ is the toroidal coordinate of the contour point, $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the toroidal coordinate of the reference point, and $\phi_{\mathrm{rel},i}$ is expressed in radians. Because toroidal angle is periodic, values that differ by $2\pi n$, with integer $n$, represent the same toroidal direction; the physical definition does not impose a device-independent wrapping interval.

In practice, this coordinate is computed from the engineered conductor geometry by evaluating the toroidal coordinate of each contour point and subtracting the reference-point toroidal coordinate. Together with the radial coordinate major_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil and vertical height [height_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil), it locates the contour point in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The corresponding generic conductor quantity is [toroidal_angle_of_conductor_cross_section](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_field_coil).

Typical numerical values are design-specific and depend on the chosen reference point and conductor cross-section geometry. The relevant universal scale is the angular periodicity $2\pi$ rad, so the values should be interpreted as relative toroidal coordinates rather than as absolute toroidal positions of the coil.

Sign convention: Positive when the contour point is displaced from the reference point in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the signed vertical coordinate of the geometric center of one rectangular conductor cross-section. It locates the rectangle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \\phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a rectangle with upper and lower vertical boundary coordinates, the geometric-center coordinate is

$$
Z_c = \\frac{Z_{\\mathrm{top}} + Z_{\\mathrm{bottom}}}{2}
$$

where $Z_c$ is the vertical coordinate of the rectangle center, and $Z_{\\mathrm{top}}$ and $Z_{\\mathrm{bottom}}$ are the vertical coordinates of its upper and lower boundaries.

The quantity applies to a single rectangular conductor cross-section, including a rectangular representation of an axisymmetric magnetic component. It is not summed or averaged over multiple conductors, cross-sections, or the conductor's longitudinal extent, and it is distinct from the rectangle's full vertical extent or area. For coil conductor elements, its geometric-center meaning is closely related to [vertical centroid of coil conductor element]; unlike [vertical coordinate of passive structure], it is tied specifically to the center of a rectangular cross-section rather than to a generic structure reference point.

The vertical outline of a conductor cross-section is the $Z$ coordinate of a point on the conductor boundary, commonly the start point of a circular-arc segment in a piecewise-circular contour. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters measured from the machine midplane.

A boundary point in a meridional cross-section can be identified by its major-radius and vertical coordinates:

$$
p_i = (R_i, Z_i)
$$

where $p_i$ is the outline point, $R_i$ is the corresponding major-radius coordinate, and this quantity is $Z_i$. For a circular-arc outline, the point coordinates alone specify only the arc start point; the arc radius, curvature or sweep information, and ordering of neighboring points are also required to define the local boundary segment.

This quantity is obtained from conductor engineering geometry, magnetic-field-system design models, or geometry reconstruction of the cross-section contour. It is used together with the corresponding [major-radius outline] and [arc radius] to build the conductor boundary used in field and structural calculations.

Typical local outline offsets are 0.01-0.5 m for many coil conductors, while absolute vertical coordinates of conductors and passive magnetic structures commonly span -10-10 m in medium-sized devices and may reach -20-20 m in larger devices.

Sign convention: Positive when the outline point lies above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

where $p_i$ is the outline point, $R_i$ is the corresponding major-radius coordinate, and this quantity is $Z_i$. For a circular-arc outline, the point coordinates alone specify only the arc start point; the arc radius, curvature or sweep information, and ordering of neighboring points are also required to define the local boundary segment.

This quantity is obtained from conductor engineering geometry, magnetic-field-system design models, or geometry reconstruction of the cross-section contour. It is used together with the corresponding major-radius outline and arc radius to build the conductor boundary used in field and structural calculations.

Typical local outline offsets are 0.01-0.5 m for many coil conductors, while absolute vertical coordinates of conductors and passive magnetic structures commonly span -10-10 m in medium-sized devices and may reach -20-20 m in larger devices.

Sign convention: Positive when the outline point lies above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Critical momentum due to avalanche is the scalar electron momentum threshold that separates electrons slowed by collisional drag from electrons accelerated by the parallel electric field into runaway avalanche multiplication. It is a local electron momentum magnitude and does not encode the sign of field-aligned motion.

The defining balance is between the electric force magnitude and the collisional slowing-down force at the threshold momentum:

$$
e\,|E_\parallel| = F_\mathrm{drag}\!\left(p_{c,\mathrm{av}}\right)
$$

where $p_{c,\mathrm{av}}$ is the critical momentum due to avalanche, $e$ is the elementary charge in coulombs, $E_\parallel$ is the electric-field component parallel to the magnetic field in volts per meter, and $F_\mathrm{drag}(p)$ is the magnitude of the collisional drag force on an electron with momentum magnitude $p$ in newtons.

A finite threshold requires an accelerating field strong enough for the force-balance equation to have a solution; in the usual Coulomb-drag limit this corresponds to $|E_\parallel|$ exceeding the [critical electric field](name:critical_electric_field). This quantity is the threshold itself, not [momentum due to avalanche] or an avalanche growth rate, and it differs from [volume-averaged runaway-electron critical momentum due to avalanche](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_critical_momentum_due_to_avalanche), which is a volume average of the same local threshold.

This quantity is the electrostatic potential of a plasma or plasma-facing electrical boundary relative to a chosen electrical reference. It represents electric potential energy per unit positive test charge and is defined only up to an additive reference value.

The electrostatic contribution to the electric field is defined by

$$
\mathbf{E}_{\rm es} = -\nabla \Phi
$$

where $\Phi$ is the [electrostatic potential](name:electrostatic_potential), $\mathbf{E}_{\rm es}$ is the electrostatic part of the [electric field](name:electric_field), and $\nabla$ is the spatial-gradient operator.

The quantity has no mandatory locus or aggregation. It may represent a local value in the core, edge, or scrape-off-layer plasma, a mean over a magnetic flux surface, or a value associated with a plasma-facing wall or electrically isolated probe. Local and boundary realizations are not averaged; a flux-surface realization is averaged over the specified magnetic flux surface. It is not intrinsically species-resolved.

This general quantity does not by itself impose the zero-net-current condition that defines the [floating electrostatic potential](name:floating_electrostatic_potential), nor does it imply a wall voltage or an applied bias. Real, imaginary, and amplitude forms are representation-specific components or measures of a potential representation rather than additional electrostatic mechanisms, as illustrated by the [real electrostatic-potential component](name:electrostatic_potential_real_part).

The gradient relation connects spatial variation of the potential to the electrostatic electric field; in particular, radial variation of a flux-surface-averaged potential determines the corresponding electrostatic contribution to the radial electric field. Only potential differences and gradients are independent of the chosen electrical reference.

Sign convention: Positive when a positive test charge has greater electrostatic potential energy at the evaluated location than at the chosen electrical reference.

documents.before:
Per-toroidal-mode growth rate is the exponential rate associated with one linear magnetohydrodynamic eigenmode at a specified toroidal mode number. It characterizes the temporal change of that eigenmode's amplitude, separating unstable growth from damping for the same toroidal harmonic.

For a linear perturbation represented by a toroidal Fourier eigenmode, the defining convention is

$$
\delta q_n(R,Z,\phi,t) = \tilde{q}_n(R,Z)\exp[i n\phi - i\omega_n t], \qquad \gamma_n = \operatorname{Im}(\omega_n)
$$

where $\delta q_n$ is a perturbation of an MHD field quantity, $\tilde{q}_n$ is its eigenfunction, $n$ is the integer toroidal mode number, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $t$ is time, $i$ is the imaginary unit, $\omega_n$ is the complex [mode frequency] of the eigenmode, and $\gamma_n$ is the per-toroidal-mode growth rate.

The scope is a single eigenmode within a single toroidal harmonic; there is no summation, averaging, maximization, or aggregation over toroidal mode numbers or over distinct eigenbranches. This quantity applies to the linear perturbation amplitude and excludes nonlinear saturation, mode-coupling effects, and spectrum-wide instability measures.

This quantity is distinct from [mode frequency] as an oscillation-rate quantity and from [per-toroidal-mode perturbed energy] as an energy-like quadratic measure of the same toroidal harmonic. For fixed eigenfunction normalization in the linear regime, a modal amplitude scales as $\exp(\gamma_n t)$ and a quadratic perturbation measure scales as $\exp(2\gamma_n t)$.

Sign convention: Positive when the mode amplitude increases exponentially in time.

The imaginary component of the complex first-order plasma-temperature eigenfunction for a single toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD. It is the quadrature component relative to the real component under the selected Fourier phase convention.

The defining decomposition is:

$$
\delta T = \delta T_R + i\,\delta T_I
$$

where $\delta T$ is the complex temperature amplitude, $\delta T_R$ is its real component, $\delta T_I$ is the imaginary component represented by this quantity, and $i$ is the imaginary unit.

Together with the [real component of the perturbed plasma temperature](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part), this quantity reconstructs the complex [perturbed plasma temperature]. In the perturbation $T=T_0+\delta T e^{i(n\phi-\omega t)}$, $T_0$ is the equilibrium temperature, $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $\omega$ is the complex eigenfrequency, and $t$ is time. Its value depends on the selected Fourier phase origin and does not by itself represent the complete physical temperature perturbation.

The quantity is the real, in-phase component of the first-order plasma-temperature perturbation associated with one toroidal Fourier harmonic. It is a component of the complex eigenfunction represented by [perturbed plasma temperature].

The in-phase component is defined from the complex perturbation amplitude by

$$
\delta T_{\mathrm{R}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\delta T\right)
$$

where $\delta T_{\mathrm{R}}$ is the real temperature-perturbation component and $\delta T$ is the full complex first-order temperature eigenfunction. It is not the equilibrium temperature or the complete complex perturbation.

This quantity is the discrete mode label that identifies the poloidal periodicity of a linear magnetohydrodynamic perturbation through its phase dependence. It is a poloidal harmonic index, not a spatial wavevector, physical displacement, radial branch index, or complete linear-MHD mode label.

For a single Fourier harmonic, the poloidal dependence is represented by

$$
\tilde{f}_m(\theta) = \hat{f}_m \exp(i m \theta)
$$

where $\tilde{f}_m$ is the selected poloidal harmonic of the perturbed physical quantity $f$, $\hat{f}_m$ is its complex amplitude, $m$ is the poloidal mode number, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle measured from a specified reference point, and $i$ is the imaginary unit.

This quantity applies to the poloidal structure of a linear MHD perturbation and, when a periodic antenna surface-current distribution is decomposed, identifies each corresponding harmonic. The poloidal angle is defined relative to the reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It denotes an individual Fourier label, not a sum or average over poloidal harmonics.

It does not specify the radial branch, toroidal periodicity, perturbation amplitude, or phase, and it carries no intrinsic dominant-harmonic or lower-of-two-harmonics selection. The sign of $m$ follows the chosen Fourier phase convention; reversing the sign in the exponential reverses the reported harmonic index.

Within the [perturbed linear-MHD mode-number parent], this quantity supplies the poloidal component of the mode labeling. Together with the [toroidal MHD mode number](name:toroidal_mhd_mode_number), it identifies the angular helical periodicity, while the broader [MHD mode-number vector](name:mhd_mode_number) also includes radial-branch information.

Radial mode number is a dimensionless integer branch index that specifies the radial branch of a linear MHD perturbation. It identifies radial structure rather than periodicity in either angular direction.

The radial branch index is defined by

$$
n_r = N_{\mathrm{nodes}}[\xi(\rho)]
$$

where $n_r$ is the radial mode number, $\xi(\rho)$ is the radial eigenfunction, $N_{\mathrm{nodes}}$ counts its interior zeros, and $\rho$ is the radial coordinate within the flux-coordinate set $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$; the count is taken between the magnetic axis and the plasma boundary.

The radial mode number is one component of the [mode number], distinct from the angular harmonics represented by the [poloidal mode number](name:poloidal_mode_number) and [toroidal MHD mode number](name:toroidal_mhd_mode_number).

Vorticity is the curl of the plasma bulk velocity field and represents the local rotational content of the single-fluid plasma flow. For solid-body rotation it is twice the angular-velocity vector of a fluid element.

The vorticity field $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ is defined by the curl of the plasma bulk velocity field:

$$
\boldsymbol{\omega} = \nabla \times \mathbf{v}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ is the vorticity field, $\mathbf{v}$ is the [plasma bulk velocity], and $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator with right-handed orientation.

The scope is the local magnetohydrodynamic plasma bulk-flow field at a point in the plasma. The bare name carries no surface, volume, time, species, or charge-state aggregation. It is not vorticity magnitude, flow shear, strain rate, divergence, or magnetic-field-line twist.

The unqualified quantity is the parent for scalar directional projections of the same curl. [Radial vorticity](name:radial_vorticity), [toroidal vorticity](name:toroidal_vorticity), and [vertical vorticity](name:vertical_vorticity) are projections onto $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, respectively; [parallel vorticity](name:parallel_vorticity) is the projection along the local magnetic-field direction. The bare name does not designate a poloidal projection.

Sign convention: Positive when $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ has a positive projection on the stated scalar direction: $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, or the local magnetic-field direction for a field-aligned projection.

Related quantities: [poloidal_vorticity](name:poloidal_vorticity).

The imaginary part of the complex radial vacuum magnetic-field perturbation, $\delta B_R^{\rm im}$, is the quadrature component of the first-order linearized magnetic-field perturbation projected along $+\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, in the current-free vacuum region surrounding the plasma. In linear MHD stability analysis, perturbed fields are cast as complex Fourier harmonics in the toroidal angle $\phi$; the imaginary part encodes the phase of the eigenmode relative to the normalization reference, together with the [real part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part).

In the vacuum region, $\delta\mathbf{B}$ satisfies $\nabla \times \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$ and $\nabla \cdot \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$. The complex radial component decomposes as:

$$
\delta\tilde{B}_R^{\rm vac} = \delta B_R^{\rm re} + i\,\delta B_R^{\rm im}
$$

where $\delta B_R^{\rm re}$ is the [real part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and $\delta B_R^{\rm im}$ is this imaginary part. The perturbation amplitude is $|\delta\tilde{B}_R^{\rm vac}| = \sqrt{(\delta B_R^{\rm re})^2 + (\delta B_R^{\rm im})^2}$ and the phase is $\theta = \mathrm{atan2}(\delta B_R^{\rm im},\,\delta B_R^{\rm re})$.

This quantity is computed by linear MHD stability codes for a specified toroidal mode number $n$. Matching conditions at the plasma-vacuum interface link it to its plasma-region counterpart, [the radial plasma imaginary part]. Alongside [the toroidal vacuum imaginary component](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part), it characterizes the helical spatial structure of the perturbed vacuum field. As with all linear eigenfunctions, the partition between real and imaginary parts depends on the phase normalization convention applied to the eigenmode.

Radial perturbed plasma magnetic field real part is the real part of the cylindrical radial component of a complex first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation for a selected toroidal Fourier harmonic. The radial direction is the $+\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ basis direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining component is

$$
\delta B_{R,n}^{\mathrm{re}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\widetilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_n \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right)
$$

where $\delta B_{R,n}^{\mathrm{re}}$ is this real component, $\widetilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_n$ is the complex first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation for toroidal Fourier mode number $n$, $\operatorname{Re}$ takes the real part, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial basis vector.

Together with [radial perturbed plasma magnetic field imaginary part], it determines the complex [radial perturbed plasma magnetic field](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field); changing the chosen complex phase of the harmonic rotates the real and imaginary parts without changing the represented perturbation. It is the radial component counterpart of [toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic field](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field) and is distinct from a flux-surface-normal projection, which would use a unit normal to a specified flux coordinate rather than $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$.

Sign convention: Positive when the in-phase radial perturbation component points in the $+\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ direction of increasing major radius $R$.

The quantity is the real, in-phase component of the complex first-order plasma mass-density perturbation eigenfunction associated with one toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD stability theory. The complete complex quantity is [perturbed plasma mass density].

The real component is defined by

$$
\widetilde{\rho}_{n,\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\widetilde{\rho}_n(\mathbf{x})\right]
$$

where $\widetilde{\rho}_n$ is the complex first-order mass-density eigenfunction, $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode number, and $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position. The decomposition is relative to the phase convention of the complex eigenfunction.

This quantity excludes the imaginary quadrature component and must not be interpreted as the magnitude of the complex perturbation. Its meaning parallels the real component of the corresponding temperature eigenfunction, [perturbed plasma temperature real part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part).

where $\widetilde{\rho}_n$ is the complex first-order mass-density eigenfunction, $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode number, and $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position. The decomposition is relative to the phase convention of the complex eigenfunction.

This quantity excludes the imaginary quadrature component and must not be interpreted as the magnitude of the complex perturbation. Its meaning parallels the real component of the corresponding temperature eigenfunction, [perturbed plasma temperature real part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part).

Total toroidal runaway-electron current is the net electric current contributed by the runaway-electron population through a poloidal cross-section. It is a global population contribution, distinct from the total plasma current and from local current density.

$$
I_{\mathrm{RE},\phi} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{pol}}} \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{RE}} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\,dS = \int_{S_{\mathrm{pol}}} j_{\mathrm{RE},\phi}\,dS
$$

Here $I_{\mathrm{RE},\phi}$ is the total current, $S_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is a poloidal cross-sectional surface, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the [runaway electron current density] in A m$^{-2}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the toroidal unit vector, and $dS$ is the surface element in m$^2$. The projection is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Sign convention: Positive when the runaway-electron current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The vertical component $A_Z$ is the signed projection of the gage-dependent [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential) $\mathbf{A}$ onto the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It retains the component aligned with increasing vertical height while preserving the gage dependence of $\mathbf{A}$.

The defining projection is:

$$
A_Z = \mathbf{A} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $A_Z$ is the vertical component of the magnetic vector potential, $\mathbf{A}$ is the [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential), and $\hat{Z}$ is the unit vector toward increasing vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is a pointwise cylindrical component of the full vector field in the physical region under consideration; no species, charge-state, flux-surface, or volume aggregation is implied. It is distinct from the vertical position coordinate $Z$, from the magnitude of $\mathbf{A}$, from the [parallel projection](name:parallel_magnetic_vector_potential), and from the [poloidal projection](name:poloidal_magnetic_vector_potential).

Together with the [radial component](name:radial_magnetic_vector_potential) and [toroidal component], $A_Z$ forms the cylindrical decomposition of $\mathbf{A}$. The curl of the complete vector potential gives the magnetic induction, so spatial variation of $A_Z$ contributes through that curl relation, but $A_Z$ alone does not define a magnetic-induction component. The [vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) denotes the external-source contribution only and is not implied by this unqualified component.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic vector potential has a component in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction, the direction of increasing vertical height $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The area of a Langmuir probe is the total geometric surface area of the probe collector, representing its full physical size as a fixed hardware property independent of local plasma conditions or magnetic-field geometry. It is the parent area concept from which two operationally distinct sub-areas are derived: the [wetted area](name:wetted_area_of_langmuir_probe), which captures only the portion of the collector surface directly exposed to plasma, and the [effective collection area](name:effective_area_of_langmuir_probe), which is the projection onto the plane perpendicular to the local magnetic field that governs ion collection in a magnetized sheath.

For probes oriented at a grazing angle to the magnetic field — quantified by the [field-aligned incident angle] — the effective collection area can be substantially smaller than the total geometric area. Conflating the two when normalizing the [ion saturation current] to obtain the [ion saturation current density] introduces systematic errors in the inferred plasma density and particle flux at the probe surface.

Probe areas are treated as fixed diagnostic geometry parameters, determined from engineering drawings or direct measurement of the fabricated collector prior to installation.

The effective area of a Langmuir probe is the plasma-facing collector surface area projected onto the plane perpendicular to the local magnetic-field direction. It represents the area governing particle collection when the sheath is magnetized.

$$
A_{\mathrm{eff}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{w}}} \left|\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}\right|\,dA
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective collection area, $S_{\mathrm{w}}$ is the plasma-exposed collector surface, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local outward unit normal, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the local magnetic-field unit vector, and $dA$ is an element of collector surface area. The absolute dot product gives the geometrical projection factor.

Unlike the total [area of a Langmuir probe], this quantity accounts for magnetic-field orientation; unlike the [wetted area of a Langmuir probe](name:wetted_area_of_langmuir_probe), it is not the unprojected plasma-exposed surface area.

Neutral pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel is the calibrated neutral-gas pressure equivalent assigned to one mass-discriminated channel of a mass spectrometer. The channel denotes a response in mass-to-charge space after ionization, so the quantity is a pressure equivalent for neutrals that can contribute to that channel, not a pressure of the detected ions.

This quantity is neutral in scope: it excludes charged-particle plasma pressure, electron pressure, and any pressure contribution not represented as neutral gas before ionization. It is the neutral-specific counterpart of [pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel].

A channel value need not be the thermodynamic partial pressure of a single species, because fragmentation, isotopologues, charge states of produced ions, and isobaric species can overlap in the same mass-to-charge channel. Summing channel values represents [total neutral pressure](name:total_neutral_pressure) only when the calibrated channels are non-overlapping, span the neutral mixture being represented, and treat cross-sensitivities consistently.

This quantity is the temporal standard deviation of the total ion-carried charge-current density after projection onto the local magnetic-field direction at the specified plasma-facing probe. Ion contributions from all included species and charge states are summed with their signed charge weighting before the fluctuation statistic is evaluated. It is the parallel specialization of [fluctuating ion current density].

With $t$ denoting time in seconds, the defining relation is:

$$
\sigma_{j_i,\parallel}=\left\langle\left[j_{i,\parallel}(t)-\left\langle j_{i,\parallel}\right\rangle_t\right]^2\right\rangle_t^{1/2},\qquad j_{i,\parallel}(t)=\mathbf{j}_i(t)\cdot\hat{\mathbf b}(t),\qquad \hat{\mathbf b}(t)=\frac{\mathbf{B}(t)}{|\mathbf{B}(t)|}
$$

Here $\mathbf{j}_i$ is the aggregated ion current-density vector in A m$^{-2}$, $\hat{\mathbf b}$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic field in tesla, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ denotes the temporal average.

The aggregation and projection precede the standard-deviation operation; this is not a sum of separately calculated species fluctuations. Unlike [fluctuating saturated ion current density](name:fluctuating_saturated_ion_current_density), it represents the total ion current rather than only the ion-saturation current component. The result is nonnegative even when the underlying parallel current changes sign.

Thermal power at a plant-component port is the rate of heat energy transferred from the component into the coolant circuit. It is the thermal component of [power of a plant component port].

The defining relation is

$$
P_\mathrm{th} = \dot{m}\left(h_\mathrm{out}-h_\mathrm{in}\right)
$$

where $P_\mathrm{th}$ is thermal power, $\dot{m}$ is coolant mass flow rate in kg s$^{-1}$, and $h_\mathrm{in}$ and $h_\mathrm{out}$ are the coolant specific enthalpies at the inlet and outlet in J kg$^{-1}$, respectively.

Positive values mean that the coolant gains enthalpy along the flow path and therefore removes heat from the plant component. This quantity excludes electrical, radiative, and other non-coolant-mediated power transfers.

This is the path-length average of lithium ion number density, summed over all ionization stages from Li$^+$ through fully stripped Li$^{3+}$, along a specified chord through the plasma.

The chord average is defined by

$$
\langle n_{Li} \rangle_L = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_{Li}(s)\,ds
$$

where $n_{Li}(s)$ is the local lithium ion number density in m$^{-3}$, $s$ is path length in meters along the chord, and $L$ is the total chord length in meters.

This quantity weights each path-length element equally and excludes neutral lithium. It differs from the [flux-surface-averaged lithium density at the plasma boundary], which averages over a separatrix, and from [volume-averaged lithium density](name:volume_averaged_lithium_density), which averages over confined plasma volume.

This quantity is the incident fusion-neutron number flux on the neutron-sensitive active surface of the detector. It is the surface-crossing flux, not the neutron production rate or the registered detection-event rate described by [rate of neutron detector]. The parent quantity [flux of neutron detector] expresses the same surface-transport concept.

The defining relation is

$$
\Phi_n = \frac{dN_n}{dA\,dt}
$$

where $\Phi_n$ is the incident neutron number flux, $N_n$ is the number of neutrons crossing the active surface, $A$ is active surface area, and $t$ is time. The surface is the neutron-sensitive area characterized by [area of neutron detector]; passive housing, shielding, supports, and electronics are excluded. Registered event rates additionally depend on detector response and efficiency.

The solid angle is the geometric measure of the aperture’s apparent extent from a neutron emission point. It is nonnegative and depends only on the aperture geometry, its orientation, and the source-point location; detector efficiency and converter response are excluded.

For a point source, the solid angle is defined by

$$
\Omega = \int_A \frac{\cos\theta}{r^2}\,dA
$$

where $A$ is the aperture surface, $r$ is the distance from the source point to an aperture element, and $\theta$ is the angle between the aperture normal and the line from the source point to that element. For a finite source region, the quantity denotes the specified volume average of this point-source solid angle; it does not imply weighting by the neutron emission profile. The geometric aperture dimensions described by [area of neutron detector] and [radius of neutron detector](name:radius_of_neutron_detector) can determine the acceptance but do not include detector efficiency, which is a separate quantity described by [efficiency of neutron detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_neutron_detector).

This quantity is the thermodynamic temperature of the neutron detector assembly or neutron-conversion material, characterizing its thermal state rather than the detector's electrical response or neutron-counting behavior.

The temperature is defined thermodynamically by

$$
\frac{1}{T}=\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\right)_{V,N}
$$

where $T$ is thermodynamic temperature, $S$ is entropy, $U$ is internal energy, $V$ is volume, and $N$ is the amount of material or particle number held fixed in the derivative. The quantity applies to the specified detector or converter material and is distinct from the local material temperature at a [sensor attachment point]. It is not the neutron-energy threshold represented by [energy of a neutron detector].

The vertical coordinate $Z$ specifies the position of a neutron detector along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height measured from the geometric midplane.

Together with the [major-radius coordinate], this quantity fully locates the detector in the poloidal cross-section, determining the chord geometry through the plasma and the emission region sampled. The transverse aperture dimensions are separately characterized by [width_of_neutron_detector](name:width_of_neutron_detector) and [height_of_neutron_detector](name:height_of_neutron_detector).

The coordinate is established from engineering survey data or design drawings of the diagnostic port geometry and enters the line-of-sight integrals used in neutron emission tomography and absolute neutron yield calibration. The same vertical-coordinate convention is applied to [vertical_coordinate_of_bolometer](name:vertical_coordinate_of_bolometer) and [vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector), ensuring geometric consistency across diagnostic systems. Typical $Z$ values range from approximately $-2$ m to $+2$ m in medium-sized tokamaks, depending on machine height and port allocation.

Sign convention: Positive when the detector is located above the geometric midplane in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The commanded bias voltage is the electrical potential difference specified for energizing a neutron-detector module between its bias terminal and return or reference terminal. It is a setpoint, distinct from the instantaneous detector waveform represented by [voltage of neutron detector].

$$
V_{\mathrm{bias,set}} = \phi_{\mathrm{bias}} - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{bias,set}}$ is the commanded bias voltage, and $\phi_{\mathrm{bias}}$ and $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ are the electrical potentials of the bias and return/reference terminals, respectively, expressed in volts.

The quantity specifies the intended applied potential and excludes the measured supply output, detector signal amplitude, pulse waveform, and derived neutron count rate. Its setpoint meaning distinguishes it from the detector bias voltage represented by [voltage of mass spectrometer](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer) and the spectrometer supply command [requested voltage of spectrometer](name:requested_voltage_of_spectrometer_channel).

Sign convention: Positive when the bias terminal is at higher electrical potential than the return or reference terminal.

Wave-beam energy is the pulse-integrated cycle-averaged electromagnetic energy transported by a coherent wave beam through a specified oriented transverse surface at a specified position along its propagation path. Cycle averaging is over the carrier oscillation; the pulse envelope time dependence is retained until integration over the pulse interval.

The defining relation to wave-beam power is:

$$
E_\mathrm{beam}(s) = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} P_\mathrm{beam}(s,t)\,dt
$$

where $E_\mathrm{beam}(s)$ has unit $\mathrm{J}$, $P_\mathrm{beam}(s,t)$ is [wave-beam power] through the same oriented surface and has unit $\mathrm{W}$, $t$, $t_1$, and $t_2$ have unit $\mathrm{s}$ and bound the pulse interval, and $s$ labels position along the beam centerline and has unit $\mathrm{m}$.

This quantity is distinct from [wave-beam power], which is an energy-flow rate rather than its pulse integral. It also differs from [power of beam-tracing beam](name:power_of_beam_tracing_beam), which denotes residual power at the endpoint of a traced beam trajectory rather than the general pulse-integrated energy through an arbitrary beam cross-section.

Vacuum electromagnetic wavelength is the spatial period of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum and the spectral coordinate associated with a transition or optical response. It may characterize a propagating beam, an unshifted spectral line, or a selected point in an instrument response.

$$
\lambda_0 = \frac{c}{\nu_0} = \frac{2\pi}{\lvert \mathbf{k}_0 \rvert}
$$

where $\lambda_0$ is vacuum wavelength, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum in m s$^{-1}$, $\nu_0$ is temporal frequency in s$^{-1}$, and $\mathbf{k}_0$ is the vacuum wave vector in m$^{-1}$. Line-averaged effective ionic charge characterizes the charge composition of a plasma mixture through the average of its local effective charge along a prescribed line of sight.

The line average is defined by

$$
\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{1}{L} \int_{0}^{L} Z_{\mathrm{eff}}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the line-averaged effective ionic charge, $L$ is the total path length through the plasma, $\ell$ is distance along the line of sight, and $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}(\ell)$ is the local effective charge at position $\ell$.

This quantity applies to the complete included ion mixture along the line of sight. At each position, the ionic contribution is summed over all represented ion species and charge states, while the line aggregation is a uniform average over physical path length.

The local integrand is the [effective charge](name:effective_charge), defined from the second ionic charge moment divided by free-electron density. This quantity is distinct from a local effective charge at a single position and from the [volume-averaged effective charge](name:volume_averaged_effective_charge), which uses volume weighting rather than line-of-sight path-length weighting; it also differs from the [flux-surface-averaged effective charge at the plasma boundary], which averages over a boundary surface.

Time-integrated equivalent-electron inventory of helium-4 atoms delivered by gas injection after plasma breakdown is the cumulative amount of helium-4 added through gas-injection fueling, counted with atomic number $Z=2$ so each atom contributes two equivalent electrons. The accumulation starts at plasma breakdown and includes only helium-4 gas injected after that time.

The accumulated equivalent-electron count is defined from the equivalent-electron injection rate, or equivalently from the neutral helium-4 atom injection rate:

$$
N_{\mathrm{He4,eq}}(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{He4,eq}}(t')\,dt' = 2\int_{t_0}^{t} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{He4,atom}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{He4,eq}}$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count (dimensionless), $t$ and $t_0$ are times in seconds, $t_0$ is the plasma-breakdown time, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{He4,eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron gas-injection rate in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{He4,atom}}$ is the corresponding neutral helium-4 atom injection rate in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The factor of 2 is the helium atomic number and must not be applied again when the integrated rate is already expressed as an equivalent-electron rate.

This quantity is distinct from an instantaneous [helium-4 source rate due to gas injection](name:helium_4_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection). It has the same post-breakdown equivalent-electron counting convention as [helium-4 count due to gas injection]; the explicit accumulated name denotes the time integral over the gas-injection history rather than a rate or an atomic-particle count.

Cumulative number of krypton atoms injected into the machine since plasma breakdown, expressed as 36 equivalent electrons for each krypton atom, is the post-breakdown time integral of the krypton atom influx into the machine with a fixed species multiplier. The multiplier is the krypton atomic number used as an equivalent-electron counting convention.

The accumulated count at time $t$ is defined by

$$
N_{\mathrm{Kr,acc}}(t) = Z_{\mathrm{Kr}} \int_{t_{\mathrm{bd}}}^{t} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{Kr}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{Kr,acc}}$ is the accumulated krypton count, $Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}=36$ is the krypton atomic-number multiplier, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the krypton atom injection rate into the machine, $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the plasma-breakdown time, $t$ is the evaluation time, and $t'$ is the integration time.

The scope is krypton introduced after plasma breakdown; it excludes krypton present before breakdown, non-krypton species, instantaneous injection rate, and any plasma number density. The species population is not charge-state resolved; if charge-state labels are used, krypton contributions are summed over all charge states before applying the fixed multiplier.

The equivalent-electron convention means this quantity equals 36 times the unweighted accumulated krypton atom count. It follows the same post-breakdown accumulated-species convention as [accumulated neon count](name:accumulated_neon_count), [accumulated ammonia count](name:accumulated_ammonia_count), and [accumulated helium-3 count due to gas injection]. The factor 36 is a counting convention and does not specify the ionization state of the injected krypton.

This quantity includes only argon introduced before breakdown and excludes wall recycling, neutral-beam or pellet fueling, later gas injection, and retained or ionized inventory. It is the argon-specific component of [prefill count](name:prefill_count) and follows the isotope-resolved convention used for tritium prefill count.

The quantity is the local thermodynamic pressure of the coolant or working fluid at a component-port interface, with perfect vacuum as the zero-pressure reference. Static pressure is the isotropic mechanical stress of the fluid and excludes kinetic-energy contributions associated with bulk flow.

$$
\boldsymbol{\sigma}=-p_{\mathrm{abs}}\mathbf{I}
$$

The value represents local pressure at the port, not stagnation pressure, pressure drop, or pressure difference. Maximum gas flow is the upper reliable operating limit of the pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It represents the aggregate gas stream rather than a particular molecular species, charge state, mass flow, or particle-number rate.

The defining pressure-volume throughput at the upper delivery limit is

$$
Q_g^{\max} = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g^{\max}$ is the maximum gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is the gas pressure at the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to gas delivered through a gas injection valve for fueling, impurity seeding, or disruption mitigation. The maximum qualifier denotes a reliable upper delivery limit for the aggregate gas stream, not a species-resolved flow, mass-flow rate, or particle-number rate.

The quantity is the upper-bound member of the [gas flow] family: gas flow denotes the same pressure-volume throughput without an upper-limit restriction, while [minimum gas flow](name:minimum_gas_flow) denotes its lower reliable operating limit.

Instantaneous injection rate of carbon-13-labeled methane into the plasma vessel is the rate at which neutral $^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4$ enters the plasma vessel, counted using the equivalent-electron convention. Each neutral carbon-13-labeled methane molecule contributes 10 equivalent electrons.

The constitutive relation between the equivalent-electron source rate and the molecular injection rate is:

$$
\dot{S}_{^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4} = 10\,\dot{N}_{^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4}
$$

where $\dot{S}_{^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4}$ is the carbon-13-labeled methane source rate, $\dot{N}_{^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4}$ is the molecule-counted injection rate of neutral carbon-13-labeled methane, and $^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4$ denotes methane with carbon-13 as the carbon isotope.

This quantity applies only to neutral carbon-13-labeled methane crossing into the plasma vessel by gas injection, aggregated over the relevant injection locations as an instantaneous total. It excludes unlabeled methane, other hydrocarbons, gas remaining upstream of the vessel, and accumulated injected amount.

It is distinguished from a molecule-counted [methane source rate](name:methane_source_rate) by the equivalent-electron counting convention: the present quantity is 10 times the corresponding molecule-counted rate for the same carbon-13-labeled methane population. When the corresponding accumulated count is used, this source rate is the time derivative of the [accumulated methane carbon-13 count due to gas injection] under the same equivalent-electron convention.

Sign convention: Positive when carbon-13-labeled methane enters the plasma vessel.

Minimum gas flow is the lower reliable operating limit of the pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It identifies the smallest controllable value of the aggregate gas stream throughput, rather than a molecular-species flow or particle-number rate.

The pressure-volume throughput represented by this quantity is defined as

$$
Q_g = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g$ is gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is gas pressure at the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the aggregate gas stream delivered through an injection system across a defined flow boundary. The stream is not restricted to a particular molecular species or charge state, and this quantity is distinct from mass flow and particle-number rate. Its defining distinction is the lower reliable operating bound, rather than an unrestricted instantaneous throughput.

The [gas flow] quantity defines the same pressure-volume throughput without imposing a lower-limit condition; minimum gas flow is its lower reliable operating bound. Conversely, [maximum gas flow](name:maximum_gas_flow) is the upper reliable operating bound, so the two quantities delimit the controllable range rather than represent different throughput definitions.

Normalized atomic count of a pellet is the total inventory of atomic nuclei associated with one pellet after division by a fixed reference atomic inventory. Molecules, compounds, and mixtures are converted to their constituent atoms before summation, regardless of molecular bonding, phase, or species.

For constituent entity types indexed by $i$, the normalized atomic inventory is defined by

$$
N_{\mathrm{atom,n}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{atom}}}{N_{\mathrm{ref}}} = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{ref}}}\sum_i a_i N_i
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{atom,n}}$ is the normalized atomic count, $N_{\mathrm{atom}}$ is the physical atomic inventory, $N_{\mathrm{ref}}=10^{20}$ is the fixed reference atomic inventory, $N_i$ is the number of entities of type $i$, and $a_i$ is the number of atomic nuclei in each entity; molecular multiplicity is represented by [molecular atomic multiplicity].

This quantity is the scaled counterpart of [atomic count of pellet](name:atomic_count_of_pellet), which is unnormalized, and remains an atomic inventory rather than a separately counted molecule inventory in [count of pellet](name:count_of_pellet). Layer-restricted values, such as [core atomic count of pellet](name:core_atomic_count_of_pellet) and [outer atomic count of pellet](name:outer_atomic_count_of_pellet), partition the same atomic inventory, while normalized atomic count applies only the reference scaling; it is not a fraction or probability.

This quantity is the real electrical power consumed by one plant subsystem at its electrical boundary. It represents the subsystem's contribution to auxiliary electrical load, distinct from plant-wide aggregation and net electrical balance quantities.

$$
P_{\rm sub} = \left\langle v(t)i(t) \right\rangle_t
$$

where $P_{\rm sub}$ is the boundary real power, $v(t)$ is the instantaneous terminal voltage, $i(t)$ is the instantaneous current directed into the subsystem, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ denotes averaging over the relevant operating interval. For multiple terminals, the boundary power is the algebraic sum of the terminal power contributions. Positive power denotes consumption by the subsystem; exported or generated power is not included as consumed load. The quantity is distinct from [absorbed power of a plant system], [total power of a plant system], and [net power of a plant system].

Real electrical power is the rate of electrical-energy transfer or accounting associated with a plant system at its electrical boundary. It excludes reactive power and other non-electrical energy flows.

The instantaneous power is defined by

$$
P = \frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

where $E$ is the electrical energy associated with the accounting boundary and $t$ is time.

The accounting convention is fixed by the specialized quantity. [Absorbed power of a plant system] represents one-way incoming electrical load, [net power of a plant system] represents generation minus internal consumption and is positive for net export, and [total power of a plant system] is the sum of the loads of all included systems. These forms are distinct applications of the same plant-boundary electrical-power concept.

Net power of a plant system is the real electrical power balance of one plant system, with generation counted positively and internal consumption counted negatively. It is the generated-minus-consumed counterpart to the load-oriented [power of a plant system](name:power_of_plant_system), rather than thermal, apparent, reactive, or accumulated energy.

For a consistently defined system boundary, the net power is defined as

$$
P_\mathrm{net} = P_\mathrm{generated} - P_\mathrm{consumed} = -P_\mathrm{system}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{net}$ is this plant-system quantity, $P_\mathrm{generated}$ is real electrical power generated within the boundary, $P_\mathrm{consumed}$ is real electrical power consumed within the boundary, and $P_\mathrm{system}$ is [power of a plant system](name:power_of_plant_system) using the load-positive convention. Internal transfers between included subsystems cancel. The quantity is the negative of [net absorbed power of a plant system] when both use the same boundary and scope; positive values denote net electrical export from the system boundary.
