The helium-3 source rate due to gas injection characterizes the instantaneous rate at which neutral helium-3 is admitted to the plasma vessel by gas-injection hardware, expressed as an equivalent-electron count rate. Each helium-3 atom contributes two equivalent-electron counts because helium has atomic number $Z_{\mathrm{He}} = 2$.

The defining relation is:

$$
\dot{S}_{^{3}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{gas}} = Z_{\mathrm{He}}\,\dot{N}_{^{3}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{gas}} = 2\,\dot{N}_{^{3}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{gas}}
$$

This quantity is isotope-specific: it applies only to neutral helium-3 gas admitted through gas injection and is aggregated over all gas-injection paths feeding the plasma vessel. This quantity is the instantaneous particle supply from active injection systems, expressed on an equivalent-electron basis when multiple injected species are combined. It represents the electron inventory that the supplied material can contribute after ionization.

The equivalent-electron source rate is defined by

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}}(t)=\sum_s Z_s\dot{N}_s(t)
$$

The thermal efficiency of a plant system is the dimensionless ratio of gross useful electrical power produced to total thermal power supplied to the heat-conversion system over the same accounting interval. It is a specific conversion metric within the broader [efficiency of a plant system](name:efficiency_of_plant_system) concept.

The defining relation is:

$$
\eta_{\mathrm{th}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{gross}}}{P_{\mathrm{th,in}}} = 1 - \frac{P_{\mathrm{th,out}}}{P_{\mathrm{th,in}}}
$$

where $\eta_{\mathrm{th}}$ is thermal efficiency, $P_{\mathrm{gross}}$ is gross useful electrical power, $P_{\mathrm{th,in}}$ is total thermal power entering the conversion cycle as represented by [total thermal power at inlet], and $P_{\mathrm{th,out}}$ is rejected thermal power represented by [total thermal power at outlet](name:total_thermal_power_at_outlet).

Thermal efficiency accounts for thermal-to-electric conversion and excludes subtraction of internal electrical consumption from gross output. That recirculating-power accounting distinguishes it from [net efficiency of a plant system](name:net_efficiency_of_plant_system).

Thermal power at inlet is the recoverable heat-input rate entering a power-conversion cycle at its heat-input boundary before thermal-to-electric conversion. This member is the cycle-level total, summed over all inlet streams and heat-input contributions feeding the cycle, rather than the rate of a single stream or port.

The total inlet heat-input rate is the sum over the heat-input boundary contributions:

$$
P_\mathrm{th,in} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_\mathrm{in}} \dot{Q}_{\mathrm{th,in},i}
$$

where $\mathcal{I}_\mathrm{in}$ is the set of heat-input boundary contributions, $\dot{Q}_{\mathrm{th,in},i}$ is the recoverable thermal power delivered by contribution $i$ into the cycle in watts, and $P_\mathrm{th,in}$ is the aggregate inlet thermal power in watts. Each per-port contribution corresponds to a [thermal power of plant component port](name:thermal_power_of_plant_component_port) evaluated at an inlet port, and the single-stream counterpart is [thermal power at inlet].

This quantity excludes [total thermal power at outlet](name:total_thermal_power_at_outlet), which is the heat rejected from the cycle, and excludes net electrical output. Over the same balance boundary, [thermal efficiency of plant system](name:thermal_efficiency_of_plant_system) relates these quantities through $\eta_\mathrm{th} = (P_\mathrm{th,in} - P_\mathrm{th,out})/P_\mathrm{th,in}$, where $P_\mathrm{th,out}$ is the rejected thermal power.

Sign convention: Positive when net heat flows into the power-conversion cycle across the heat-input boundary.

Signed vertical ($Z$) coordinate of a pellet path point is the $Z$ coordinate of a point on the pellet injection trajectory in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$. In this frame $R$ is major radius from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle) increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height relative to the equatorial plane.

The scoped path point is the second point in a two-point geometric definition of the pellet injection trajectory; the paired first point defines the same trajectory together with it. The quantity applies to the position of that geometric path point only; it is not an average along the path, an aggregate over pellets or fragments, or a time-of-flight coordinate.

The coordinate is one component of the point position, not the full position vector. The full point position is specified by this coordinate together with the [radial coordinate at the pellet path point] and the [toroidal coordinate at the pellet path point](name:toroidal_coordinate_at_pellet_path_point); it does not specify pellet velocity, travel direction, mass, fragmentation, or ablation.

Sign convention: Positive when the pellet path point lies above the equatorial plane in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

Argon density at a limiter is the local number density of argon ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface. The evaluation point is on the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance, and neutral argon atoms are excluded.

The charge-state-summed density is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar}}(\mathbf{r}_L)=\sum_{q>0} n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}(\mathbf{r}_L)
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}$ are number densities in m$^{-3}$, $q$ is the positive argon ionization state, and $\mathbf{r}_L$ is the limiter-side position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This is the argon-specific member of [density at a limiter](name:density_at_limiter). It counts argon ions rather than the electrons represented by [electron density at a limiter](name:electron_density_at_limiter), and is local rather than the flux-surface average represented by [flux-surface-averaged argon density at the plasma boundary].

Electron density at a limiter is the local number density of electrons in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface. The evaluation point is on the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance.

$$
n_e(\mathbf{r}_L)=\frac{dN_e}{dV}
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density in m$^{-3}$, $N_e$ is the number of electrons, $V$ is volume in m$^3$, and $\mathbf{r}_L$ is the limiter-side evaluation position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

Unlike [ion density at a limiter], this quantity counts electrons only and includes neither ions nor neutral atoms. It is the electron-specific member of [density at a limiter](name:density_at_limiter) and is distinct from [electron density at the plasma boundary](name:electron_density_at_plasma_boundary), which uses a different evaluation locus.

This quantity is the local kinetic temperature of the electron population at the plasma-wall interface on the plasma-facing side of a limiter, where open scrape-off-layer field lines terminate. It is the electron-specific member of [temperature at limiter].

For an isotropic electron population, its temperature expressed in energy units is defined by

$$
T_e = \frac{2}{3}\langle E_{\mathrm{kin},e} \rangle
$$

where $T_e$ is the electron kinetic temperature and $\langle E_{\mathrm{kin},e} \rangle$ is the mean random kinetic energy per electron.

The quantity refers to electrons on the plasma-facing side of the limiter interface and does not denote the temperature of the limiter material. It is distinct from the density-weighted population average [average temperature at limiter], which combines the relevant plasma populations.

Incident radiative energy flux density is the incoming photon power crossing a plasma-facing material surface, resolved per unit surface area. It is the incident component of [flux at wall due to radiation], not the net energy deposited in the material.

For an incident radiation field, the flux is defined by

$$
q_{\mathrm{rad}}^{\mathrm{inc}} = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{in}}} I_{\mathrm{rad}}(\hat{\mathbf{s}})\,[-\hat{\mathbf{s}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}] \, d\Omega
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the frequency-integrated radiance, $\hat{\mathbf{s}}$ is the photon propagation direction, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the outward surface normal, $\Omega_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the set of directions propagating toward the surface, and $d\Omega$ is solid angle. The quantity excludes energy removed by absorption, redirected by reflection, or returned by surface re-emission; those effects are not part of the incident flux itself.

The ion component of the local plasma temperature at a limiter is the density-weighted mean kinetic temperature of all positive ion species and charge states on the plasma-facing side of the limiter. It is the ion-specific component of [average temperature at the limiter].

$$
T_{i,\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{\sum_s \sum_q n_{s,q} T_{s,q}}{\sum_s \sum_q n_{s,q}}
$$

where $s$ indexes ion species, $q$ indexes their positive charge states, $n_{s,q}$ is the corresponding ion number density, and $T_{s,q}$ is its kinetic temperature. The denominator is the [total ion density at the limiter](name:total_ion_density_at_limiter).

This quantity includes all ion species and charge states in the local plasma population and excludes electrons, neutral particles, and the solid limiter material. It is distinct from [temperature at the limiter], which may denote a specified population or a different population aggregation.

Ion energy flux at the wall due to recombination quantifies the rate at which recombination-associated energy from incident plasma ions leaves a plasma-facing surface per unit area. It is the ion-associated component summed over incident-ion species and charge states, not the incident plasma energy flux or energy deposited in the wall material.

The aggregate is defined from charge-state-resolved components by:

$$
Q_{\mathrm{rec,ion}}(\mathbf{x}_w) = \sum_{s,q} Q_{\mathrm{rec},s,q}(\mathbf{x}_w)
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_w$ is the wall location, $s$ identifies an incident-ion species, $q$ identifies its charge state, and $Q_{\mathrm{rec},s,q}$ is the corresponding [ion charge-state energy flux at the wall due to recombination](name:ion_charge_state_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination). The sum includes all represented incident-ion species and charge states.

As a component of [energy flux at the wall due to recombination](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination), this quantity retains only the ion-associated energy channel. Unlike [particle flux at the wall due to recombination], it weights the outgoing recombination contribution by carried energy; it is distinct from incident [ion kinetic energy flux at the wall](name:ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall).

This quantity is the ion-resolved component of the incident kinetic-energy flux at a plasma-facing wall. It contributes to the parent [kinetic energy flux at wall] and includes all incident ion species and charge states, but excludes electron, neutral-particle, radiative, and electromagnetic contributions.

For an outward wall normal $\hat{n}$ directed from the material into the plasma, the flux is defined by

$$
q_{i}^{\mathrm{kin}} = \sum_s \int_{\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{n}<0} \frac{1}{2}m_s |\mathbf{v}|^2 (-\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{n}) f_s(\mathbf{v})\,d^3\mathbf{v}
$$

where $s$ indexes ion species and charge states, $m_s$ is the ion mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $f_s$ is the incident velocity distribution. The minus sign converts the inward particle velocity into a positive arrival flux; the resulting quantity is non-negative.

Lithium density at a limiter is the local number density of lithium ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface. The evaluation point is on the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance.

$$
n_{\mathrm{Li}}(\mathbf{r}_L)=\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Li}}}{dV}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Li}}$ is the lithium-ion number density in m$^{-3}$, $N_{\mathrm{Li}}$ is the counted number of lithium ions, $V$ is volume in m$^3$, and $\mathbf{r}_L$ is the evaluation position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in m, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in m.

The quantity is summed over all positive lithium ionization states and excludes neutral lithium atoms. It is the lithium-specific specialization of [density at a limiter](name:density_at_limiter) and differs from the broader [ion density at a limiter], which does not select lithium.

This quantity is the geometric area contributed by one specified optically active surface of an optical element. It is a component of the total [area of the optical element], not the projected clear-aperture area.

The component area is defined by

$$
A_c = \int_{\mathcal{S}_c} dA
$$

where $\mathcal{S}_c$ is the specified physical material surface and $dA$ is its differential surface-area element. The surface may be curved or planar. Inactive material regions and projected-area representations are excluded; when the active surfaces form a disjoint partition, their component areas sum to the total optical-element area.

Surface emissivity is the effectiveness of a material surface in emitting thermal electromagnetic radiation relative to an ideal blackbody at the same temperature. It is a material property of the emitting surface and is distinct from the emitted energy flux described by [energy flux due to surface emission](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission).

The effective emissivity is defined by

$$
\varepsilon = \frac{M_{\mathrm{emit}}(T_s)}{M_{\mathrm{bb}}(T_s)}
$$

where $M_{\mathrm{emit}}$ is the surface thermal radiative exitance, $M_{\mathrm{bb}}$ is the blackbody exitance, and $T_s$ is the surface temperature. The ratio applies to the specified spectral band and angular averaging; it is not a wavelength- and direction-resolved emissivity. Incident radiation and geometric surface area, such as [optical-element area], are excluded.

Plasma-ion recombination power at the wall is the rate at which recombination energy from incident plasma ions is deposited in plasma-facing wall material. It is the ion-channel contribution to the total wall heat load from recombination.

The contribution is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}}^{\mathrm{plasma}} = \sum_s \int_A \Gamma_s^{\mathrm{ion}} E_{\mathrm{rec},s}\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $s$ indexes the contributing plasma-ion species and charge states, $\Gamma_s^{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the incident particle flux, $E_{\mathrm{rec},s}$ is the recombination energy deposited per event, and $A$ is the total plasma-facing wall area.

This quantity excludes surface recombination of incident neutral particles into molecules, represented by [neutral recombination power at the wall]. Together, the two channels form [total recombination power at the wall], which is distinct from volumetric [power due to recombination](name:power_due_to_recombination).

Visible-camera brightness is the photon radiance of a radiation field along a specified viewing direction after integration over a visible wavelength interval or passband. It is normalized to projected collecting area, observation time, and accepted solid angle, and counts photons rather than radiant energy.

The band-integrated photon radiance is defined by integrating the spectral photon radiance over the visible passband:

$$
B_\mathrm{vis} = \int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} L_\lambda^{(\gamma)}(\lambda)\, d\lambda
$$

where $B_\mathrm{vis}$ is the visible-camera brightness, $L_\lambda^{(\gamma)}(\lambda)$ is the spectral photon radiance at wavelength $\lambda$, and $[\lambda_1,\lambda_2]$ is the wavelength interval defining the visible passband.

The quantity is non-negative because spectral photon radiance is non-negative over the passband. It is distinct from [spectral radiance], which retains wavelength dependence, and from [radiance at spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line), which refers to an individual spectral line or narrow line interval; it also differs from energy radiance because photons are counted without weighting by photon energy.

A visible-camera radiometric factor converts a consistently corrected detector signal into band-integrated photon radiance. It represents the combined response of the optical throughput, detector sensitivity, pixel etendue, and exposure treatment rather than the radiance itself.

The defining conversion is

$$
L_{\mathrm{vis}} = C_{\mathrm{vis}} S_{\mathrm{corr}}
$$

where $L_{\mathrm{vis}}$ is the [visible-camera brightness](name:brightness_of_visible_camera), $C_{\mathrm{vis}}$ is this visible-camera factor, and $S_{\mathrm{corr}}$ is the corrected detector signal. The spectral dependence is integrated over the relevant visible passband. Unlike the resulting brightness, the factor is a calibration coefficient and must be applied to the corrected signal; it is the camera-specific component of the parent [factor of visible camera].

The signed local radius of curvature characterizes how an optical-element surface bends in a specified tangent direction at a surface point. It is a surface-shape property, distinct from the aperture size represented by [radius of optical element](name:radius_of_optical_element).

For unit tangent direction $\hat{t}$, the radius is defined by the reciprocal of the signed normal curvature:

$$
R_c(\hat{t}) = \frac{1}{\kappa_n(\hat{t})}
$$

where $R_c$ is the signed radius of curvature and $\kappa_n(\hat{t})$ is the signed normal curvature in direction $\hat{t}$. A spherical surface has equal directional curvatures, whereas cylindrical and toroidal surfaces can have direction-dependent curvature. The radius of a spectral image surface is a distinct quantity described by [spectral surface curvature of optical element].

Sign convention: Positive when the center of curvature lies on the designated positive side of the surface normal.

Efficiency of a spectrometer channel is a bounded dimensionless fraction, between zero and one, of photons already within the channel's geometrical and spectral acceptance that reach the active detector area after propagation through the channel optical path. It characterizes the channel efficiency after acceptance, not the acceptance itself.

The channel efficiency is defined by the ratio of photon rates for the same accepted spectral interval:

$$
\eta_\mathrm{ch} = \frac{\dot{N}_\mathrm{det}}{\dot{N}_\mathrm{acc}}
$$

where $\dot{N}_\mathrm{det}$ is the photon rate arriving at the active detector area and $\dot{N}_\mathrm{acc}$ is the photon rate within the channel acceptance before optical-path losses. Both rates are expressed in the same units, for example photons per second for an interval-integrated rate or photons per second per meter for a wavelength-resolved rate.

This quantity is distinct from [spectral etendue of a spectrometer channel](name:spectral_etendue_of_spectrometer_channel), which defines the accepted geometrical and spectral phase-space extent rather than a loss probability. It excludes [detector quantum efficiency], detector gain, and electronic registration probability after photons reach the active detector area. Component filter properties such as [absorptivity of a filter] and [transmissivity of a filter] describe individual optical elements; they may contribute to, but are not synonyms for, the aggregate spectrometer-channel efficiency.

The deuterium-deuterium neutron emissivity $\varepsilon_{DD}$ is the local number of neutrons produced per unit volume per unit time from D-D fusion reactions. Only the neutron-emitting D-D branch contributes, so this quantity is the local source of prompt fusion neutrons from deuterium-deuterium reactions that produce a neutron.

For identical deuterium reactants, the branch emissivity is given by:

$$
\varepsilon_{DD} = \frac{1}{2} n_D^2 \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DD,n}
$$

where $\varepsilon_{DD}$ is the deuterium-deuterium neutron emissivity, $n_D$ is the local deuterium reactant number density, $\sigma$ is the fusion cross-section for the neutron-emitting D-D branch, $v$ is the relative speed of the deuterium reactants, and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DD,n}$ is the velocity average of $\sigma v$ over the local reactant distributions. The factor $1/2$ avoids double-counting unordered pairs of identical deuterium reactants.

The scope is the D-D reaction channel at a plasma location, aggregated over all deuterium reactant charge states and kinetic populations that contribute to the local neutron-emitting D-D branch unless a component-resolved quantity is specified. It excludes the proton-emitting D-D branch, subsequent D-T neutron production involving tritium born from D-D reactions, and the [deuterium-tritium neutron emissivity due to fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion). The reaction-pair label deuterium_deuterium denotes two deuterium reactants; it is not a charge-state-resolved fuel-state quantity.

Integrating $\varepsilon_{DD}$ over a plasma volume gives the D-D contribution to the global [neutron flux] for the same reactant population, and weighting that contribution by the branch neutron energy gives its contribution to [total neutron power]. When reactant populations are resolved, the corresponding global neutron production can be decomposed into [thermal neutron flux](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion), [beam-thermal neutron flux], and [beam-beam neutron flux] contributions; those are population decompositions of the volume-integrated source, not separate definitions of the local D-D emissivity. Together with [deuterium-tritium neutron emissivity due to fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), this quantity is a reaction-channel-specific member of [neutron emissivity due to fusion].

The integration duration is the elapsed time between the start and end of the photon-accumulation interval for a spectrometer channel. It defines the temporal window contributing to one spectral measurement and is distinct from the channel's spectral response, including its [effective spectral width](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel).

It is defined by

$$
\Delta t = t_{\mathrm{end}} - t_{\mathrm{start}}
$$

where $\Delta t$ is the integration duration, and $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and $t_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the times at which photon accumulation begins and ends. The accumulated signal is determined by the time integral of the [incident spectral flux] over this interval.

Extent of a detector pixel is the nonnegative linear size of one pixel footprint along a specified in-plane axis of the right-handed local detector frame $(\hat{t}_1,\hat{t}_2,\hat{n})$, where $\hat{t}_1$ and $\hat{t}_2$ are the first and second local tangential directions in the detector plane and $\hat{n}$ is the detector-plane normal. The footprint is the area assigned to that pixel for geometric mapping or active collection, independent of the optical point-spread function.

For a coordinate $s_a$ along the selected local tangential axis, the extent is the separation of the footprint boundaries:

$$
r_a = s_{a,+} - s_{a,-}
$$

where $a$ is either $1$ or $2$ and selects the axis $\hat{t}_a$, $r_a$ is the detector-pixel extent in meters, $s_{a,-}$ and $s_{a,+}$ are the lower and upper footprint-boundary coordinates in meters along $\hat{t}_a$, and $s_{a,+} \ge s_{a,-}$. Consequently $r_a \ge 0$.

This quantity is a footprint-edge separation, not the detector-pixel center location, the center-to-center pitch, the optical point-spread width, or the spacing or inactive gap between neighboring pixels. The detector-pixel center location is described by separate coordinate quantities, such as [horizontal coordinate of detector pixel] and [vertical coordinate of detector pixel](name:vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel). The extent equals the pitch along the same selected axis only when adjacent pixel footprints tile the detector plane contiguously with negligible inactive gap; this condition is independent of whether the footprint is square or non-square.

Hard X-ray brightness is the photon radiance received from a viewing direction by a channel. It represents photon arrival rate with the photon-energy dependence integrated over the selected hard X-ray band.

The band-integrated photon radiance is defined by

$$
B_{\mathrm{HX}} = \frac{dN_\gamma}{dt\,dA_{\mathrm{proj}}\,d\Omega}
$$

where $B_{\mathrm{HX}}$ is the hard X-ray brightness, $N_\gamma$ is the number of received photons in the selected energy band, $t$ is time, $A_{\mathrm{proj}}$ is projected collecting area, and $\Omega$ is accepted solid angle.

This quantity applies to hard X-ray photons received by a channel and is evaluated separately for each selected energy band. Its aggregation convention is integration over photon energy within that band while retaining normalization by projected area and solid angle. It is a received radiometric quantity, not a local volumetric source term, and it counts photons rather than their deposited or carried energy.

The local production counterpart is [hard X-ray emissivity], which describes photon generation per unit volume and solid angle before propagation to the channel. Integrating this brightness over the collecting geometry represented by the [etendue of a hard X-ray detector](name:etendue_of_hard_xray_detector) gives the received photon rate under the corresponding angular and area acceptance. Unlike [incident soft X-ray radiance](name:incident_soft_xray_radiance), which is energy-weighted, this quantity is photon-count radiance; photon registration probability is a separate detector property described by [spectral efficiency of a hard X-ray detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector).

The neutron kinetic energy is the translational energy carried by one neutron produced in a fusion reaction. It characterizes the energy distribution of emitted neutrons rather than their total production rate or transported power.

$$
E_n = \frac{1}{2}m_n v_n^2
$$

where $E_n$ is the neutron kinetic energy, $m_n$ is the neutron mass, and $v_n$ is the neutron speed; the result is converted from joules to eV. The quantity applies to individual fusion-born neutrons and may vary with reaction channel and emission conditions. The corresponding integrated production rate is [neutron flux], while its local source distribution is described by [emissivity due to fusion].

Normalized count at detector pixel is the detector-pixel count divided by a positive count-equivalent reference from the same acquisition frame. The reference is a relative scale for that frame and must be common to the detector pixels whose normalized values are compared.

The defining ratio for detector pixel $p$ is

$$
C_\mathrm{norm}(p) = \frac{C(p)}{C_\mathrm{ref}}, \qquad C_\mathrm{ref} > 0
$$

where $C_\mathrm{norm}(p)$ is the normalized count, $C(p)$ is the [count at detector pixel], and $C_\mathrm{ref}$ is the positive count-equivalent reference for the same acquisition frame.

The same definition applies to count rates or exposure-normalized count-equivalent signals only when $C(p)$ and $C_\mathrm{ref}$ use identical time or exposure normalization. The quantity is a relative normalization; it does not specify whether $C_\mathrm{ref}$ is a total-frame, peak, mean, or externally specified reference count, and it is distinct from an absolute calibration factor.

The D-D fusion power density is the local rate at which deuterium-deuterium thermonuclear reactions $D + D \rightarrow {}^3\mathrm{He} + n$ and $D + D \rightarrow T + p$ release energy per unit plasma volume. It includes both the neutron-producing branch and the proton-producing branch, so it represents branch-summed D-D fusion energy release rather than only neutron-branch energy.

For a thermal deuterium population, the branch-summed power density is

$$
P_{\mathrm{DD}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2} n_D(\mathbf{x})^2 \left[\langle\sigma v\rangle_n Q_n + \langle\sigma v\rangle_p Q_p\right]
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium ion number density in m$^{-3}$, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_n$ and $\langle\sigma v\rangle_p$ are the thermonuclear rate coefficients in m$^3$ s$^{-1}$ for the helium-3-neutron and tritium-proton branches, $Q_n$ and $Q_p$ are the corresponding branch energies in joules, and the factor $1/2$ avoids double counting identical deuteron pairs. The branch Q-values are $Q_n = 3.27\,\mathrm{MeV}$ for $D + D \rightarrow {}^3\mathrm{He} + n$ and $Q_p = 4.03\,\mathrm{MeV}$ for $D + D \rightarrow T + p$; equal branch probabilities give a branch-weighted $Q_{\mathrm{DD}} \simeq 3.65\,\mathrm{MeV}$ per D-D reaction, to be converted to joules in the equation.

The displayed expression is the thermal-thermal specialization of the definition. For beam-thermal, beam-beam, or otherwise non-Maxwellian deuteron populations, $P_{\mathrm{DD}}$ is still the branch-summed local energy-release rate, with each branch reaction-rate density multiplied by its branch energy rather than using Maxwellian rate coefficients. This quantity is the D-D channel instance of [fusion power density](name:power_density_due_to_fusion); it includes neutron and charged-particle product energy and is distinct from [fusion neutron emissivity], from deposited heating of fusion products, and from [D-T fusion power density](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion).
documents.after:

The reference wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the vacuum wavelength corresponding to the maximum of that channel’s spectral instrument function. It is the peak-position specialization of [wavelength of a spectrometer channel], not the wavelength of a plasma emission line or an independently selected calibration reference.

The reference wavelength is defined by

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}} = \underset{\lambda}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\; \mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ch}}(\lambda)
$$

where $\lambda$ is vacuum wavelength and $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ch}}(\lambda)$ is the spectral instrument function of the channel as a function of wavelength. The value identifies the response maximum; the response spread is described separately by quantities such as [spectral width of a spectrometer channel].

Spectral absorptivity of a filter is the fraction of incident photons at a specified wavelength that are absorbed within the filter material. It describes absorption alone, rather than transmission, reflection, scattering, or detector registration.

The spectral absorptivity is defined by

$$
\alpha(\lambda) = \frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{abs}}(\lambda)}{\Phi_{\mathrm{inc}}(\lambda)}
$$

where $\alpha(\lambda)$ is the absorptivity, $\Phi_{\mathrm{abs}}(\lambda)$ is the absorbed spectral photon-flux density, $\Phi_{\mathrm{inc}}(\lambda)$ is the incident spectral photon-flux density, and $\lambda$ is photon wavelength measured in meters; the two flux densities have units of photons per square meter per second per meter. The value lies between zero and one wherever the incident flux is nonzero.

The broadband [absorptivity of a filter] is the incident-flux-weighted average of $\alpha(\lambda)$. This quantity is distinct from [spectral efficiency of a filter](name:spectral_efficiency_of_filter), which includes the probability that an incident photon produces a registered detection event.

This quantity is the wavelength-specific component of the [calibration factor of a spectrometer]. It converts a dark-corrected photon count rate from one channel into absolute photon spectral radiance density at that channel's wavelength.

For channel wavelength $\lambda_c$, the calibrated spectral radiance density is defined by

$$
L_\lambda(\lambda_c) = C(\lambda_c) S(\lambda_c)
$$

where $L_\lambda$ is photon spectral radiance density, $C(\lambda_c)$ is this calibration factor, and $S(\lambda_c)$ is the dark-corrected count rate in s$^{-1}$. The wavelength $\lambda_c$ is the channel value defined by [wavelength of spectrometer channel]. The coefficient includes the channel's wavelength-dependent optical throughput, detector response, etendue, and effective spectral-width normalization; its spectral response is related to the [effective spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel).

The wavelength-resolved filter efficiency is the conditional probability that a photon arriving at the filter input with wavelength $\lambda$ produces a registered detection event. It includes the wavelength-dependent transmission and conversion losses of the filter, optical path, detector, and readout chain, and is distinct from material absorptivity alone.

$$
\eta_{\mathrm{filter}}(\lambda)=P(\mathrm{registered\ detection}\mid\mathrm{photon\ incident\ at\ wavelength\ }\lambda)
$$

Here, $\lambda$ is the photon wavelength and $P$ denotes a conditional probability. The parent [efficiency of filter] is the incident-spectrum-weighted average of this response, with weighting supplied by the [incident spectral flux] over the relevant wavelength range. Consequently, this quantity is dimensionless and bounded from 0 to 1.

This quantity is the phase refractive index of the optical-element material resolved as a function of wavelength. It describes how the material changes electromagnetic phase propagation relative to vacuum.

For vacuum wavelength $\lambda$, the refractive index is defined by

$$
n(\lambda) = \frac{c}{v_p(\lambda)}
$$

where $n(\lambda)$ is the dimensionless refractive index, $c$ is the vacuum speed of light, $v_p(\lambda)$ is the material phase velocity, and $\lambda$ is the vacuum wavelength; $c$ and $v_p$ are measured in m s$^{-1}$ and $\lambda$ in m.

The wavelength dependence represents material dispersion and distinguishes this quantity from the wavelength-independent abstraction [refractive index of the optical element]. It describes phase propagation only and does not represent absorptive loss or a complex extinction component. The wavelength coordinate is the spectral axis defined by [spectral wavelength of optical element](name:spectral_wavelength_of_optical_element).

The filter-window surface area is the geometric area of the actual material surface associated with a radiation filter and participating in interception or transmission of incoming radiation. It is the window-specific component of the parent [filter area].

The area is defined by integrating the surface-area element over the filter-window surface:

$$
A_w = \int_{S_w} dS
$$

where $A_w$ is the filter-window area, $S_w$ is the actual window surface, and $dS$ is an infinitesimal surface-area element.

This quantity includes curvature of the material surface and excludes a planar projected aperture area or areas belonging to other filter components.

Filter thickness is the geometric separation of the two opposing surfaces of one filter window, measured locally along the material normal. It represents the material thickness itself rather than a photon path length through the window.

For corresponding points on the opposing surfaces, the local thickness is defined by

$$
d = \left| (\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \right|
$$

where $d$ is the filter thickness, $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ are the position vectors of the corresponding surface points, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local unit normal to the filter surface.

This quantity applies to the material of a single filter window used for X-ray spectral selection, including soft-X-ray, hard-X-ray, and crystal-spectrometer filter windows. It is not a sum over multiple windows, diagnostic channels, or detector elements, and it is distinct from the longer oblique photon path through the material.

For homogeneous material at normal incidence, thickness enters the attenuation relation $T(E) = \exp[-\mu(E)d]$, where $T(E)$ is photon transmission at energy $E$, $E$ is photon energy, and $\mu(E)$ is the material attenuation coefficient. Thus, thickness is a geometric input to [spectral absorptivity of the filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter), whereas [filter width] describes the wavelength span of the transmitted passband rather than the material dimension.

The red-side cutoff is the long-wavelength boundary of a visible-camera detector channel’s spectral sensitivity band. It identifies the upper endpoint of the characteristic wavelength range represented by [wavelength of camera].

For a band with short-wavelength boundary $\lambda_{\rm blue}$ and long-wavelength boundary $\lambda_{\rm red}$, the sensitivity interval is represented by

\Lambda_{\rm camera} = [\lambda_{\rm blue},\lambda_{\rm red}]
$$

where $\Lambda_{\rm camera}$ is the defined vacuum-wavelength sensitivity interval and both boundary wavelengths are measured in m.

This quantity is a band edge, not a central wavelength or bandwidth. Photons with vacuum wavelength greater than $\lambda_{\rm red}$ lie beyond the defined detector response interval.

This quantity is the volume-integrated neutron count rate from fusion reactions between two nonthermal fast fuel ions generated by neutral beam injection. It includes only neutron-producing reaction branches and aggregates the represented isotope channels. It is the neutron-count component of [beam-beam fusion flux], distinct from beam-thermal and thermonuclear neutron production.

$$
\dot{N}_{n}^{\mathrm{bb}} = \sum_{(a,b)\in\mathcal{C}} \int_{V} \nu_{ab}^{(n)}(\mathbf{r})\,R_{ab}^{\mathrm{bb}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

Here $\dot{N}_{n}^{\mathrm{bb}}$ is the total neutron count rate, $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of included fast-ion reaction channels, $a$ and $b$ label the fast-ion fuel species, $R_{ab}^{\mathrm{bb}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local beam-beam reaction rate density, $\nu_{ab}^{(n)}$ is the neutron multiplicity of the reaction branch, $V$ is the active plasma volume, and $\mathbf{r}$ is position. Channel-specific entries such as [deuterium-deuterium neutron flux due to beam-beam fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_beam_beam_fusion) and [deuterium-tritium neutron flux due to beam-beam fusion] resolve the aggregate by fuel channel.

Neutron flux due to beam-thermal fusion is the global neutron emission rate from fusion reactions in which fast ions originating from injected neutral beams react with thermal plasma ions. It is integrated over the plasma volume and summed over all neutron-emitting beam-thermal reaction channels.

For resolved fast-ion and thermal-ion velocity distributions, the channel-summed neutron emission rate is defined by:

$$
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{BT}} = \sum_{(a,b)\in \mathcal{C}_n} \int_V \int \int f_a^{\mathrm{beam}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{v}_a) f_b^{\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{v}_b) \sigma_{ab}(v_{\mathrm{rel}}) v_{\mathrm{rel}} Y_{ab}(v_{\mathrm{rel}}) \, d^3v_a \, d^3v_b \, dV
$$

where $\Phi_n^{\mathrm{BT}}$ is the beam-thermal neutron emission rate, $V$ is the plasma volume over which the reactions are counted, $\mathcal{C}_n$ is the set of ordered neutron-emitting beam-thermal reaction pairs, $a$ labels the fast beam-ion isotope, $b$ labels the thermal target isotope, $f_a^{\mathrm{beam}}$ and $f_b^{\mathrm{th}}$ are velocity-space density distributions normalized so that velocity integration gives the corresponding number density, $\sigma_{ab}$ is the fusion cross-section, $v_{\mathrm{rel}}=|\mathbf{v}_a-\mathbf{v}_b|$ is the relative speed, and $Y_{ab}$ is the neutron yield per reaction.

This quantity is the neutron-yield-weighted sum of channel-resolved beam-thermal fusion rates, including [deuterium-deuterium beam-thermal neutron flux] and [deuterium-tritium beam-thermal neutron flux] when those channels are present. It excludes thermal-thermal fusion, beam-beam fusion, and non-fusion neutron sources. It counts emitted neutrons rather than reaction events, so neutron-branching fractions and neutron multiplicities are included in $Y_{ab}$.

Neutron flux due to beam-thermal fusion is the global neutron emission rate from fusion reactions in which fast ions originating from injected neutral beams react with thermal plasma ions. It is integrated over the plasma volume and summed over all neutron-emitting beam-thermal reaction channels.

For resolved fast-ion and thermal-ion velocity distributions, the channel-summed neutron emission rate is defined by:

$$
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{BT}} = \sum_{(a,b)\in \mathcal{C}_n} \int_V \int \int f_a^{\mathrm{beam}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{v}_a) f_b^{\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{v}_b) \sigma_{ab}(v_{\mathrm{rel}}) v_{\mathrm{rel}} Y_{ab}(v_{\mathrm{rel}}) \, d^3v_a \, d^3v_b \, dV
$$

where $\Phi_n^{\mathrm{BT}}$ is the beam-thermal neutron emission rate, $V$ is the plasma volume over which the reactions are counted, $\mathcal{C}_n$ is the set of ordered neutron-emitting beam-thermal reaction pairs, $a$ labels the fast beam-ion isotope, $b$ labels the thermal target isotope, $f_a^{\mathrm{beam}}$ and $f_b^{\mathrm{th}}$ are velocity-space density distributions normalized so that velocity integration gives the corresponding number density, $\sigma_{ab}$ is the fusion cross-section, $v_{\mathrm{rel}}=|\mathbf{v}_a-\mathbf{v}_b|$ is the relative speed, and $Y_{ab}$ is the neutron yield per reaction.

This quantity is the neutron-yield-weighted sum of channel-resolved beam-thermal fusion rates, including deuterium-deuterium beam-thermal neutron flux and deuterium-tritium beam-thermal neutron flux when those channels are present. It excludes thermal-thermal fusion, beam-beam fusion, and non-fusion neutron sources. It counts emitted neutrons rather than reaction events, so neutron-branching fractions and neutron multiplicities are included in $Y_{ab}$.

Power density due to radiation is the local volumetric rate at which plasma energy is converted into emitted electromagnetic radiation. It is the non-negative magnitude of radiative energy loss from the emitting plasma volume.

The radiated power density is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{rad}} = \frac{\mathrm{d}P_{\mathrm{emit}}}{\mathrm{d}V}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{emit}}$ is the emitted electromagnetic power and $V$ is the emitting volume. This quantity represents radiative emission rather than the signed source term in the plasma energy balance; radiation contributes negatively to that balance. It is a volumetric quantity and is distinct from the incident surface flux represented by [flux at wall due to radiation]. The broader [power density](name:power_density) includes radiative and non-radiative source or loss mechanisms.

The Bragg-crystal aperture radius is the transverse geometric extent of the circular active diffracting surface, measured from its center to its circumferential edge. It describes aperture size rather than the curvature of the crystal substrate.

For a boundary point of the aperture, the radius is defined by

$$
r_{\mathrm{ap}} = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{edge}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{center}} \right\rVert
$$

where $r_{\mathrm{ap}}$ is the aperture radius, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{edge}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{center}}$ are position vectors in the aperture plane, with $r_{\mathrm{ap}}$ expressed in meters.

For an ideal circular aperture, this distance is the same for every boundary point. It is analogous to the [radius of a diagnostic aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture), but must not be confused with the [toroidal curvature of the Bragg crystal] or its [vertical curvature](name:vertical_curvature_of_bragg_crystal).

The wavelength associated with a detector pixel is the vacuum spectral coordinate of incoming photons whose Bragg-dispersed rays reach that pixel.

The pixel-specific wavelength follows Bragg's law:

$$
\lambda_{\rm pix}=2d\sin\theta_{\rm pix}
$$

where $\lambda_{\rm pix}$ is the vacuum wavelength assigned to the incoming photons at the pixel, $d$ is the crystal lattice-plane spacing, and $\theta_{\rm pix}$ is the Bragg angle for rays reaching that pixel.

This quantity is a per-pixel spectral assignment for an X-ray crystal spectrometer. It primarily varies along the dispersive detector direction and also varies along the perpendicular detector-face direction because the constant-wavelength surfaces have elliptical curvature. It is not a single wavelength averaged over the detector face or over a wavelength band, and it does not denote the crystal's wavelength independently of a pixel.

It is a detector-pixel specialization of [vacuum electromagnetic wavelength]. Unlike [energy_of_detector_pixel](name:energy_of_detector_pixel), which uses photon energy as the spectral coordinate, this quantity uses wavelength for the same pixel-specific incoming-photon assignment.

Lower wavelength of a filter is the vacuum-wavelength spectral coordinate that identifies the short-wavelength boundary of a diagnostic filter's transmitted spectral band. It marks the high-photon-energy edge of the interval selected by the filter transmission response.

For a lower-bound characteristic associated with temporal frequency $\nu_\mathrm{lower}$, the vacuum wavelength is defined by:

$$
\lambda_\mathrm{lower} = \frac{c}{\nu_\mathrm{lower}}
$$

where $\lambda_\mathrm{lower}$ is the lower filter-boundary vacuum wavelength, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\nu_\mathrm{lower}$ is the temporal frequency corresponding to that boundary.

This quantity applies to the transmitted spectral band of the filter and is a single lower-edge value, not a wavelength average, an integrated spectral quantity, or the complete transmission function. It is distinct from a spectral-line rest wavelength and from a wavelength defined inside a material medium.

As the lower-bound member of [wavelength of a filter](name:wavelength_of_filter), it identifies one characteristic point of the filter response. Together with the [upper wavelength of a filter](name:upper_wavelength_of_filter), it defines the passband span represented by the [width of a filter].

It is a property of the filter transmission response, rather than the rest-frame wavelength of a spectral line or the wavelength inside a material medium.

\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}} = \frac{c}{\nu_{\mathrm{low}}}

The first-wall area is the geometric measure of the material surface exposed toward the plasma and forming the innermost plasma-facing boundary. It includes installed wall armor and bare vessel surface where no armor is present, but excludes backing structures and surfaces that are not plasma-facing.

$$
A_{\mathrm{FW}} = \int_{\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{FW}}} \mathrm{d}A
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{FW}}$ is the total first-wall area, $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{FW}}$ is the plasma-facing first-wall surface, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is an elemental surface area. This surface measure is distinct from the enclosed [volume of the first wall](name:volume_of_first_wall) and provides the geometric basis for integrating areal loads such as [energy flux at the wall].

Coolant pressure at a cooling-circuit inlet is the absolute static thermodynamic pressure of the coolant where it enters a hydraulically defined cooling circuit or component. It denotes the scalar upstream boundary pressure of the coolant and excludes gage pressure, dynamic pressure, and stagnation pressure.

For the same hydraulic flow path, the associated static pressure drop is related to this inlet pressure by:

$$
p_{\mathrm{coolant,in}} = p_{\mathrm{coolant,out}} + \Delta p_{\mathrm{coolant}}
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{coolant,in}}$ is this inlet absolute static coolant pressure in pascals, $p_{\mathrm{coolant,out}}$ is the corresponding outlet absolute static coolant pressure in pascals, and $\Delta p_{\mathrm{coolant}}$ is the total static pressure drop in pascals, defined positive when the outlet static pressure is lower than the inlet static pressure.

This quantity is the coolant-specific specialization of [pressure at a cooling-circuit inlet]: when the working fluid is coolant, both names denote the same inlet absolute static pressure. It is also the cooling-circuit-inlet value of [coolant pressure](name:coolant_pressure), and it is distinct from pressure loss, pump head, and mechanical stress in the surrounding structure.

Coolant thermal power of a single breeder blanket module is the net rate at which heat leaves the module through its coolant circuits. It aggregates the thermal energy carried by every coolant branch serving that module, regardless of whether the heat originated from nuclear deposition or absorbed incident radiation.

The defining branch balance is

$$
P_{\mathrm{cool}} = \sum_b \dot{m}_b\left(h_{b,\mathrm{out}} - h_{b,\mathrm{in}}\right)
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{cool}}$ is the coolant-transferred power, $b$ indexes coolant branches, $\dot{m}_b$ is the mass flow rate in branch $b$, and $h_{b,\mathrm{in}}$ and $h_{b,\mathrm{out}}$ are its inlet and outlet specific enthalpies. The quantity is the coolant-transferred component of [thermal power of a breeder blanket module], distinct from source-specific quantities such as [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) and [absorbed radiated power of a breeder blanket module](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

Nuclear heating power of the breeder blanket is the total rate at which neutron and photon interactions deposit energy as heat throughout all included blanket materials. It is the blanket-wide nuclear component of [heating power of the breeder blanket].

The defining relation is

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{BB}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nuclear heating power density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{r}$ is position within the blanket, $dV$ is differential volume in m$^3$, and $V_{\mathrm{BB}}$ is the union of the included blanket-module and constituent-material volumes.

The integral includes energy deposited by neutron scattering, neutron capture, and photon interactions, including secondary gamma absorption, without double-counting overlapping material descriptions. It excludes power carried by neutrons or photons crossing into the blanket before deposition and separate plasma-facing surface loads. Module- and layer-restricted integrals are represented by [nuclear heating power of the breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) and [nuclear heating power of the breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer), respectively.

It is the nuclear component of [heating power of a breeder-blanket layer], rather than the local volumetric quantity [nuclear power density of a breeder-blanket layer](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer).

Electrical resistivity is the material property that determines the electric field required to sustain conduction in a mobile plasma-facing component unit. It governs induced-current and eddy-current response within that unit.

For an isotropic material, the local constitutive relation is

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho\,\mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric-field vector, $\rho$ is the electrical resistivity, and $\mathbf{J}$ is the conventional current-density vector.

This quantity applies to the material of one mobile plasma-facing component unit and is not summed over multiple units or converted into a lumped resistance. It is a local material property, distinct from the effective resistivity of a broader [passive conducting structure] or [wall material](name:resistivity_of_wall_material). When geometry is included, it contributes to a lumped [passive-loop resistance](name:resistance_of_passive_loop), which also depends on current-path length and cross-sectional geometry.

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho\mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric-field vector, $\mathbf{J}$ is the local conventional current-density vector, and $\rho$ is the isotropic electrical resistivity.

This quantity applies to one vacuum-vessel unit, whether represented as an annular unit or a discrete block element. It is a local material property and is not summed or otherwise aggregated over multiple vessel units; the value may be used for eddy-current and halo-current response during transient electromagnetic events.

It is distinct from the lumped [resistance of a vacuum vessel](name:resistance_of_vacuum_vessel), which additionally depends on the conducting geometry and current path. It is the vacuum-vessel-specific form of [resistivity of passive structure] and is related to the broader [resistivity of wall material](name:resistivity_of_wall_material) by its restriction to vacuum-vessel material.

Electrical resistivity is the local bulk material property that opposes electric current in the wall and converts electromagnetic energy into heat. It applies to the wall material at each physical location, with values allowed to vary between material locations.

For an isotropic local response, resistivity is defined by

$$
\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}) = \rho(\mathbf{r})\,\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{r})
$$

where $\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local electric-field vector, $\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local conventional current-density vector, $\rho(\mathbf{r})$ is the local electrical resistivity, and $\mathbf{r}$ denotes physical position in the wall.

This quantity is a local bulk material property, not a wall-wide average, a lumped current-path resistance, or an interface or contact resistance. It is therefore distinct from the lumped [resistance of a vacuum vessel](name:resistance_of_vacuum_vessel) and [resistance of a passive structure], which also depend on conductor geometry and current-path length.

The local irreversible heating density is $p_{\rm ohm}=\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}$, where $p_{\rm ohm}$ is ohmic power density; integrating this density over the wall material gives the [power at the wall due to ohmic dissipation](name:power_at_wall_due_to_ohmic_dissipation).

Lower thickness of a breeder blanket module is the geometric thickness of the cap that closes the module at its lower end. The reference surfaces are the lower exterior boundary of the cap and the interface where the lower cap joins the main module body. It is distinct from the overall [thickness of a breeder blanket module] and the corresponding [upper thickness of a breeder blanket module](name:upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module).

The lower-cap thickness is the normal projection of the separation between the reference surfaces:

$$
t_{\mathrm{lower}} = \left|\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}$ are corresponding points on the lower exterior boundary and cap-to-body interface, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local unit normal directed through the cap, and $t_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is the lower-cap thickness. The quantity is a non-negative geometric magnitude; it is not a signed vertical coordinate or displacement and excludes the thicknesses of internal breeder, coolant, or shielding layers.

Volumetric fraction of a breeder blanket layer is the part-to-whole volume ratio for one specified constituent material, phase, void region, coolant region, or gas region within a breeder blanket layer. It describes the layer composition used for homogenized material properties over the same geometric region.

For constituent $i$, the fraction is defined by:

$$
f_i = \frac{V_i}{V_\mathrm{layer}}
$$

where $f_i$ is the volumetric fraction, $V_i$ is the volume of constituent $i$ in cubic meters, and $V_\mathrm{layer}$ is the total bulk volume of the same breeder blanket layer in cubic meters over the homogenization region.

The numerator and denominator must refer to the same layer region. For an exhaustive non-overlapping partition of that region, $0 \le f_i \le 1$ and $\sum_i f_i = 1$; separately represented voids, coolant, or gas regions are included as their own constituents. This quantity is distinct from mass fraction, atomic fraction, porosity, and selected-solid packing factor, and its layer denominator differs from the whole-blanket volume described by [volume of breeder blanket].

Co-passing fast-particle pressure is the scalar trace pressure carried by suprathermal particles on co-passing guiding-center orbits. It is the co-passing-orbit contribution to [fast-particle pressure], complementary to the field-aligned [parallel co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and transverse [perpendicular co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure).

The flux-surface-averaged pressure is defined by the co-passing-particle second velocity moment:

$$
P_{\mathrm{co,fast}}(\psi) = \left\langle \frac{1}{3}\sum_s m_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co},s}(\mathbf{x})} v^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v \right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $\psi$ labels the magnetic flux surface, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes its flux-surface average, $s$ labels fast-particle species, $m_s$ is particle mass, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is particle speed, $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the distribution function, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{co},s}$ contains only co-passing guiding-center orbits. The factor one-third gives the scalar trace; with the same orbit selection, $P_{\mathrm{co,fast}}=(P_{\parallel,\mathrm{co,fast}}+2P_{\perp,\mathrm{co,fast}})/3$. [Counter-passing fast-particle pressure](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and [trapped fast-particle pressure](name:trapped_fast_particle_pressure) populations are excluded.
documents.after:

The quantity is the net toroidal electric current carried by the plasma as a result of non-inductive current-drive mechanisms. It excludes current produced by the transformer-induced electric field and includes the algebraic sum of the included non-inductive contributions. The plasma-specific realization is [plasma current due to non-inductive current drive](name:current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive).

The current is defined by the flux of non-inductive current density through a poloidal cross-section:

$$
I_{\mathrm{NI}} = \int_{S_p} \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{NI}} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{NI}}$ is the non-inductive current, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{NI}}$ is the corresponding electric-current density, and $d\mathbf{S}$ is the oriented area element of the poloidal cross-section. Contributions such as [current due to electron-cyclotron current drive](name:current_due_to_electron_cyclotron_current_drive) and [current due to ion-cyclotron current drive](name:current_due_to_ion_cyclotron_current_drive) are instances of this quantity, whereas [plasma current due to ohmic induction] is excluded.

Sign convention: Positive when the net current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Particle number density of beryllium ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the beryllium-ion population at that flux-surface location. Beryllium has atomic number $Z = 4$; unless a charge state is specified separately, this quantity is the elemental beryllium ion density, summed over all beryllium ion charge states and excluding neutral beryllium atoms. The internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where locally reduced cross-field turbulent transport can sustain steep density gradients.

The charge-state aggregation is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be,ITB}} = \sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{ITB}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be,ITB}}$ is the beryllium ion number density on the internal-transport-barrier flux surface, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the number density of beryllium charge state $q$ on the same flux surface, and $q$ runs over positive beryllium ion charge states. The lower limit excludes neutral beryllium.

This is an unweighted particle density, not the charge-weighted impurity charge density or the electron density contributed by beryllium. It is a species-specific instance of [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and differs from [ion density at the internal transport barrier], which may represent a broader ion population.

This quantity is the net energy-transfer rate to a specified plasma particle population from a specified source or sink, integrated over the confined plasma volume. It may represent either deposition into the population or removal from it.

$$
P_{\mathrm{dep}} = \int_V p_{\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the integrated power, $p_{\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local net power-transfer density at position $\mathbf{x}$, and $V$ is the integration volume. A positive value denotes net energy gain by the population, while a negative value denotes net energy loss. The [electron deposited power](name:electron_deposited_power) quantity is the electron-population instance of this general definition; collisional contributions are represented by [power due to collisions](name:power_due_to_collisions) or, for a fast-particle channel, [particle power due to collisions].

This quantity is the plasma stored energy associated with the total pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field. It includes thermal and fast-particle populations and excludes electromagnetic-field energy and bulk-flow kinetic energy.

The diamagnetic stored energy is defined by

$$
W_{\mathrm{dia}} = \frac{3}{2}\int_V p_\perp\,dV
$$

where $W_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic stored energy, $p_\perp$ is the total plasma pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic-field direction, and $V$ is the plasma volume over which the energy is evaluated.

This quantity is distinct from [thermal plasma energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), which excludes fast-particle contributions, and from [total plasma energy], whose pressure scope is defined by the corresponding total internal-energy convention. Its time rate of change is represented by [tendency of diamagnetic energy].

Particle number density of electrons evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the electron population at that flux-surface location. Electrons are counted directly as mobile negative charge carriers; no ion charge-state aggregation is involved.

The number density is defined by

$$
n_e = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N_e}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density in m$^{-3}$, $\Delta N_e$ is the dimensionless number of electrons in the volume element, and $\Delta V$ is the volume element in m$^{3}$.

This is the electron-specific member of [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier). It is distinct from [ion density at the internal transport barrier], which counts ions rather than electrons; in a quasineutral plasma the electron density is related to ion charge densities at the same flux surface by charge balance. The internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep density gradients.

Electron diffusion coefficient is the direction-unspecified scalar Fickian transport coefficient for electron particle diffusion. It denotes the coefficient multiplying the local electron number-density gradient in the diffusive part of electron particle transport.

The defining Fick relation is:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{e,\mathrm{diff}} = -D_e \nabla n_e
$$

where $D_e$ is the electron diffusion coefficient, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{e,\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive contribution to the electron particle flux, and $n_e$ is the [electron number density]. The minus sign states that, for positive scalar diffusivity, the diffusive flux is directed down the electron density gradient.

This quantity applies to the electron population and is local to the transport description; no volume, flux-surface, or time averaging convention is included in the name. It is a scalar coefficient whose direction is unspecified, so any projection of the flux-gradient relation onto a named direction is a different quantity.

It is distinct from [effective electron diffusivity](name:effective_electron_diffusivity), which denotes an effective or equivalent transport coefficient rather than only the Fickian density-gradient coefficient. Electron diffusion coefficient is the direction-unspecified scalar Fickian transport coefficient for electron particle diffusion. It denotes the coefficient multiplying the local electron number-density gradient in the diffusive part of electron particle transport.

The defining Fick relation is:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{e,\mathrm{diff}} = -D_e \nabla n_e
$$

where $D_e$ is the electron diffusion coefficient, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{e,\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive contribution to the electron particle flux, and $n_e$ is the [electron number density](name:electron_number_density). The minus sign states that, for positive scalar diffusivity, the diffusive flux is directed down the electron density gradient.

This quantity applies to the electron population and is local to the transport description; no volume, flux-surface, or time averaging convention is included in the name. It is a scalar coefficient whose direction is unspecified, so any projection of the flux-gradient relation onto a named direction is a different quantity.

It is distinct from [effective electron diffusivity](name:effective_electron_diffusivity), which denotes an effective or equivalent transport coefficient rather than only the Fickian density-gradient coefficient. It is also distinct from [radial effective electron diffusivity](name:radial_effective_electron_diffusivity), which selects the $\hat{R}$ projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, from [parallel electron diffusivity](name:parallel_electron_diffusivity), which is along the magnetic-field direction, and from [poloidal electron diffusivity](name:poloidal_electron_diffusivity), which is direction-resolved in the poloidal direction.

Kinetic temperature at an internal transport barrier is the energy-equivalent measure of random motion for the electron population on the barrier’s assigned flux surface. It is the electron-specific member of the temperature family.

For an isotropic electron population, the defining relation is:

$$
T_e = \frac{2}{3}\langle E_e\rangle
$$

where $T_e$ is the electron kinetic temperature and $\langle E_e\rangle$ is the mean random kinetic energy per electron. The quantity applies only to electrons and is distinct from the ion-population [average temperature at an internal transport barrier]. It is a local value on the assigned core flux surface, not an integral across the barrier; the population-unspecified parent is [temperature at an internal transport barrier].

Energy confinement time is the characteristic timescale on which the confined plasma loses its stored thermal energy through net outward energy transport and other thermal-energy loss channels. The stored energy is the volume-integrated quantity defined by [thermal plasma energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), not a particle confinement time or the duration of plasma confinement.

$$
\tau_E = \frac{W_{\mathrm{th}}}{P_{\mathrm{loss}}}
$$

where $\tau_E$ is the energy confinement time, $W_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the stored thermal energy in J, and $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ is the net power loss from that thermal-energy reservoir in W. In a stationary power balance, $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ equals the net heating power deposited in the plasma. It is distinct from [plasma confinement time], which denotes the elapsed duration of confinement rather than an energy-loss timescale.

The electron energy convection velocity is the effective advection coefficient $V_{E,e}$ that parameterizes the convective, non-diffusive component of electron thermal-energy transport. It is distinct from the bulk plasma fluid velocity and represents the coefficient associated with drift and pinch contributions.

The convective electron-energy flux in a selected transport direction is defined by:

$$
Q_{\mathrm{conv},e} = \tfrac{3}{2} n_e T_e V_{E,e}
$$

where $Q_{\mathrm{conv},e}$ is the convective electron-energy flux, $n_e$ is the electron number density, $T_e$ is the electron temperature expressed as an energy, and $V_{E,e}$ is the electron energy convection velocity.

This is the electron-specific member of the [energy convection velocity] family and does not impose a radial or field-parallel projection. Its field-aligned specialization is [parallel_electron_energy_convection_velocity](name:parallel_electron_energy_convection_velocity); it is distinct from [radial_electron_convection_velocity](name:radial_electron_convection_velocity), which describes particle rather than energy transport.

Kinetic energy density is the local kinetic energy carried by a specified particle population per unit volume. It represents translational kinetic energy, including directed, random, nonthermal, or relativistic contributions when they are present in the population.

For the included species or internal states, the kinetic energy density is defined by

$$
w_{\mathrm{kin}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \int f_a(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p})\,E_{\mathrm{kin},a}(\mathbf{p})\,d^3p
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of included species or internal states, $f_a$ is the phase-space number-density distribution for member $a$, $\mathbf{p}$ is particle momentum, $E_{\mathrm{kin},a}$ is its kinetic energy excluding rest-mass energy, and $d^3p$ is the momentum-space volume element.

The quantity is local to the plasma domain, including edge regions, and aggregates contributions over exactly the species and internal states included in the defined population. It is not a volume-integrated energy and does not imply inclusion of other particle populations. Rest-mass, potential, radiation, and electromagnetic-field energies are excluded.

The [runaway electron energy density](name:runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density) is the instance restricted to runaway electrons, while [ion kinetic energy density](name:ion_kinetic_energy_density) applies the same definition to the ion population. A volume-integrated quantity such as [plasma energy] requires integration over volume and aggregation of the relevant confined electron and ion populations, so it is distinct from this local density.

Energy flux is the signed component of energy flux density normal to an oriented surface, for energy carried by a specified particle, neutral, plasma, wave, radiation, or field reservoir. It gives the rate per unit area at which that reservoir crosses the surface, including convective, conductive, collisional, radiative, wave, or field transport channels only when those channels are part of the stated reservoir definition.

For an oriented surface with chosen unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, the scalar energy flux $F_E$ is the normal projection of the corresponding energy-flux-density vector $\mathbf{q}_E$:

$$
F_E = \mathbf{q}_E \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_E$ is the vector density of energy transport for the selected reservoir and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ defines the positive normal direction.

Energy flux is a parent quantity for more specific transport channels. [Heat flux](name:heat_flux) is the thermal-energy specialization; [neutral energy flux](name:neutral_energy_flux) and [internal-state energy flux] restrict the carried energy reservoir; [flux due to radiation] denotes the radiative channel. The scalar flux is distinct from an energy density, a volumetric source or sink, and from any carrier velocity because it already combines transported energy content with the normal transport rate.

Sign convention: Positive when the energy-flux-density vector has a component in the direction of the chosen unit normal to the oriented surface.

Electron energy flux is the signed component of electron energy-flux density normal to an oriented surface. It gives the rate at which energy carried by the electron population crosses the surface per unit area, including convective and conductive contributions when those channels are in scope.

For an oriented surface with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, the electron energy flux $F_{E,e}$ is defined by

$$
F_{E,e} = \mathbf{q}_{E,e} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_{E,e}$ is the electron energy-flux-density vector and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ defines the positive crossing direction.

This quantity applies to the electron population crossing the chosen oriented surface and represents the electron contribution only. It is the electron-population form of [energy flux], not a total plasma energy flux, not an electromagnetic Poynting flux, and not a sum over ion species, ion charge states, or neutral species.

When conductive and convective channels are both in scope, this scalar is the net surface-normal contribution of those electron energy-transport channels. It is distinct from [parallel electron energy flux](name:parallel_electron_energy_flux), which projects electron energy-flux density along the magnetic-field direction, from [poloidal electron energy flux](name:poloidal_electron_energy_flux), which is the poloidal component, and from [radial electron energy flux](name:radial_electron_energy_flux), which is the $\hat{R}$ component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. [Energy convection velocity] characterizes convective energy transport rather than the energy flux itself.

Sign convention: Positive when the electron energy-flux density has a component in the direction of the chosen unit normal to the oriented surface.

This quantity is the local production rate of fast electrons generated by Compton scattering of high-energy gamma-ray photons from free plasma electrons. Only recoiling electrons that enter the defined fast-electron population are included; losses and subsequent evolution are excluded.

The rate is defined by

$$
S_{\rm fast}^{\rm C} = \left.\frac{\partial n_{\rm fast}}{\partial t}\right|_{\rm Compton,\ production}
$$

where $S_{\rm fast}^{\rm C}$ is the source rate, $n_{\rm fast}$ is the number density of fast electrons, and $t$ is time. It is the fast-electron component of the [electron source rate due to Compton scattering], whereas [runaway electron source rate due to Compton scattering](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering) includes only electrons classified as runaway. The quantity is a source term, not a net rate after subtracting losses.

Volume-integrated kinetic-energy loss rate from the confined fast-ion population due to charge exchange is the rate at which electron-transfer reactions with neutral particles remove kinetic energy from confined fast ions. The removed energy is not Coulomb energy transfer to plasma particles; it is a loss from the confined fast-ion energy content.

The volume integral is taken over the corresponding local loss-rate density:

$$
P_{\mathrm{CX},f} = \int_V p_{\mathrm{CX},f}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{CX},f}$ is the fast-ion power due to charge exchange, $p_{\mathrm{CX},f}(\mathbf{x})$ is the [fast-ion power density due to charge exchange], $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $V$ is the region over which the confined fast-ion population is defined. Locally, $p_{\mathrm{CX},f}$ is the charge-exchange event-rate density weighted by the kinetic energy removed from the confined fast-ion population per event, summed over all included fast-ion species and charge states.

This quantity excludes Coulomb collisional energy transfer, ionization losses not involving charge exchange, prompt orbit loss, power that was never absorbed into the fast-ion population, and charge-exchange loss assigned solely to thermal ions. It is the fast-ion component of [ion power due to charge exchange] and contributes to the broader [power due to charge exchange]; in a fast-ion energy balance written with positive gains, this loss magnitude enters as a sink.

Co-passing fast-particle collisional power density is the local rate at which Coulomb collisions change the kinetic-energy density of fast particles on co-passing guiding-center orbits. It is one orbit-class contribution to the complete [fast-particle collisional power density](name:fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions), including energy exchange with all included charged collision partners.

The orbit-class aggregation is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = P_{\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{coll}} + P_{\mathrm{counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}} + P_{\mathrm{trapped}}^{\mathrm{coll}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the complete fast-particle collisional power density, $P_{\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is this co-passing contribution, and the other terms are the [counter-passing fast-particle collisional power density](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions) and [trapped fast-particle collisional power density]. Positive values denote net kinetic-energy gain by the co-passing population; negative values denote net loss.

Counter-passing fast-particle collisional power density is the local rate at which Coulomb collisions change the kinetic-energy density of fast particles on counter-passing guiding-center orbits. Counter-passing orbits are passing trajectories whose parallel transit is opposite to the reference co-passing direction; this quantity is the collisional source or sink for that orbit class, not its stored kinetic-energy density.

For fast species $a$, the counter-passing contribution is the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator restricted to counter-passing phase space:

$$
P_{\mathrm{counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{a\in\mathrm{fast}} \sum_b \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}} \frac{1}{2} m_a v^2 C_{ab}[f_a,f_b](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the counter-passing fast-particle collisional power density at position $\mathbf{x}$, $m_a$ is the mass of fast species $a$, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed, $C_{ab}$ is the Coulomb collision operator giving the collisional time derivative of the fast-species distribution $f_a$ due to charged partner species $b$, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}$ is the counter-passing region of velocity or guiding-center phase space.

Together with [co-passing fast-particle collisional power density](name:co_passing_fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions) and [trapped fast-particle collisional power density], it forms the orbit-class decomposition of [fast-particle collisional power density](name:fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions): $P_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = P_{\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{coll}} + P_{\mathrm{counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}} + P_{\mathrm{trapped}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$. The partner sum includes only the charged collision partners represented in the collisional model; a partner-resolved quantity would use the corresponding single partner contribution.

Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the kinetic-energy density of the counter-passing fast-particle population.
