Particle number density of helium-3 ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the helium-3-ion population at that flux-surface location. Helium-3 (${}^3\mathrm{He}$, mass number $A = 3$, atomic number $Z = 2$) has a nucleus with two protons and one neutron; at species level this quantity includes singly ionized ${}^3\mathrm{He}^{+}$ and fully ionized ${}^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}$ and excludes neutral ${}^3\mathrm{He}$ atoms.

The charge-state-summed particle number density is defined by

$$
n_{{}^3\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ITB}} = \left.\lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N_{{}^3\mathrm{He}^{+}} + \Delta N_{{}^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}}}{\Delta V}\right|_{\mathrm{ITB}}
$$

where $n_{{}^3\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the helium-3 ion number density at the internal-transport-barrier reference flux surface, $\Delta N_{{}^3\mathrm{He}^{+}}$ and $\Delta N_{{}^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}}$ are the counted singly ionized and fully ionized helium-3 ions in the volume element $\Delta V$, and the vertical bar denotes evaluation at that assigned flux surface.

This is a particle number density, not a charge-weighted density; both ionization stages contribute one counted ion per particle. It is the internal-transport-barrier evaluation of [helium-3 density](name:helium_3_density) and the helium-3-specific member of [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier), distinct from broader ion aggregates such as [ion density at the internal transport barrier] and from isotope counterparts such as [helium-4 density at the internal transport barrier](name:helium_4_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep density gradients.

The global particle confinement time of thermalized helium-4 ash is the characteristic retention timescale for fully ionized helium-4 ions in the confined plasma. It describes particle loss from the total confined inventory, rather than the confinement of thermal energy or the survival of the plasma as a whole.

For source-free decay, the confinement time is defined by

$$
\frac{dN_{\mathrm{He}}}{dt}=-\frac{N_{\mathrm{He}}}{\tau_{\mathrm{p,He}}}, \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{p,He}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{He}}}{\Gamma_{\mathrm{He,loss}}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{He}}$ is the total confined helium-4 ion inventory, $t$ is time, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{He,loss}}$ is the corresponding outward particle-loss rate. The definition assumes loss proportional to inventory and excludes helium sources during the decay interval. It is distinct from [energy confinement time] and [plasma confinement time].

The global particle confinement time of thermalized helium-4 ash is the characteristic retention timescale for fully ionized helium-4 ions in the confined plasma. It describes particle loss from the total confined inventory, rather than the confinement of thermal energy or the survival of the plasma as a whole.

For source-free decay, the confinement time is defined by

$$
\frac{dN_{\mathrm{He}}}{dt}=-\frac{N_{\mathrm{He}}}{\tau_{\mathrm{p,He}}}, \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{p,He}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{He}}}{\Gamma_{\mathrm{He,loss}}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{He}}$ is the total confined helium-4 ion inventory, $t$ is time, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{He,loss}}$ is the corresponding outward particle-loss rate. The definition assumes loss proportional to inventory and excludes helium sources during the decay interval. It is distinct from [energy confinement time](name:energy_confinement_time) and plasma confinement time.

Particle number density of hydrogen ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the hydrogen-ion population at that flux-surface location. Here hydrogen denotes protium, $^1\mathrm{H}$, with mass number $A = 1$, distinct from deuterium and tritium fuel isotopes.

The species-level hydrogen density is the charge-state sum

$$
n_\mathrm{H} = \sum_{q=1}^{Z_\mathrm{H}} n_{\mathrm{H}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{H}$ is the hydrogen-ion number density, $n_{\mathrm{H}^{q+}}$ is the density of protium ions with charge state $q$, and $Z_\mathrm{H}=1$ is the hydrogen atomic number. The neutral population $q=0$ is excluded.

This quantity is the hydrogen isotope instance of [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and an ion-species contribution to [ion density at the internal transport barrier], without charge weighting. The ion atomic number $Z_n$ is the number of protons in the nucleus of the ion species, an intrinsic nuclear property that is independent of ionization state and uniquely identifies the element. In fusion-relevant plasmas, common values include $Z_n = 1$ for hydrogen isotopes (deuterium, tritium), $Z_n = 2$ for helium, $Z_n = 6$ for carbon, $Z_n = 18$ for argon, and $Z_n = 74$ for tungsten.

The maximum realizable ionization charge for a fully stripped ion equals $Z_n$, making it the natural upper bound for ion_charge. The effective plasma charge $Z_\mathrm{eff} = \sum_i n_i Z_i^2 / n_e$, where $n_i$ is the number density of ion species $i$, $Z_i$ is its ionization charge state, and $n_e$ is the electron density, depends directly on $Z_n$ for fully ionized impurities.

As a fixed nuclear property, $Z_n$ is an invariant input to plasma transport modeling rather than a plasma-measurable quantity. Unlike ion_charge, which reflects the realized ionization state and varies with local temperature and density, $Z_n$ is immutable for a given element. The companion quantity [ion_atomic_mass](name:ion_atomic_mass) provides the nuclear mass, while [atomic_number](name:ion_atomic_number) covers the same concept without restricting to the ion population.

Sign convention: Positive for all physical ion species, as $Z_n$ counts nuclear proton number and is never negative.

This quantity is the arithmetic mean of the kinetic temperatures of all charged ion species on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier. It retains the locus and population scope of [average temperature at an internal transport barrier].

$$
T_{i,\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{1}{N_i}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{C}} T_{i,s}
$$

where $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of included charged ion species, $N_i$ is the number of species in that set, and $T_{i,s}$ is the kinetic temperature of species $s$. For each species, $T_{i,s}$ is the density-weighted mean over its charge-state temperatures, using $T_{i,s}=\sum_Z n_{s,Z}T_{s,Z}/\sum_Z n_{s,Z}$, where $n_{s,Z}$ is the number density of charge state $Z$ and $T_{s,Z}$ is its [ion charge-state temperature](name:ion_charge_state_temperature). Charge-state weighting is therefore applied within each species, but distinct ion species are averaged equally; electrons and neutral species are excluded.

Ion charge-state diffusivity is the effective Fickian particle diffusivity for ions in a specified ionization state, without specifying a spatial projection. It is the scalar transport coefficient that relates the diffusive particle flux component of that charge state to the negative directional gradient of its number density.

For a chosen projection direction $\hat{\mathbf{e}}$, the defining Fickian relation is:

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{s,e} = -D_s\,\nabla_e n_s
$$

where $\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{s,e}$ is the projected diffusive particle flux density of charge state $s$, $D_s$ is this diffusivity, $n_s$ is the number density of charge state $s$, and $\nabla_e n_s = \hat{\mathbf{e}}\cdot\nabla n_s$ is the directional derivative of that number density. A positive flux component is directed along $+\hat{\mathbf{e}}$; the minus sign makes a positive diffusivity drive diffusive flux opposite to the projected density gradient.

This quantity is charge-state-resolved: it applies to a single ionization state rather than to the density-weighted mean over all charge states represented by [ion diffusivity]. It is the same physical coefficient as [ion charge-state diffusion coefficient](name:ion_charge_state_diffusion_coefficient) when that name is used for the same Fickian closure. Directionally specified counterparts include [radial ion charge-state diffusivity](name:radial_ion_charge_state_diffusivity) and [parallel ion charge-state diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_diffusivity); convective or pinch transport, particle sources and sinks, and energy or momentum transport coefficients are separate quantities.

Ion energy diffusivity is the effective transport coefficient for local diffusive smoothing of ion thermal-energy density. It represents the Fickian part of ion energy transport, distinct from convective transport and explicit energy sources or sinks.

The defining closure relates the diffusive ion thermal-energy flux to the energy-density gradient:

$$
\mathbf{q}_{E,i} = -\chi_{E,i}\nabla w_i
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_{E,i}$ is the diffusive ion thermal-energy flux, $\chi_{E,i}$ is ion energy diffusivity, and $w_i$ is ion thermal-energy density. The minus sign specifies down-gradient transport. For an unresolved ion mixture, $w_i$ and the associated flux are summed over the included ion species and charge states; species-resolved quantities such as [ion charge-state energy diffusivity] retain that resolution. Directional forms include [poloidal ion energy diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_energy_diffusivity) and [parallel ion energy diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_energy_diffusivity), while [energy diffusivity] provides the broader constituent-independent concept.

Ion energy flux is the signed component of ion energy-flux density normal to an oriented surface. It gives the rate at which energy carried by a specified ion population crosses the surface per unit area, including convective, conductive, or other channels only when they belong to the stated ion-energy reservoir.

For an oriented surface with chosen unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, the scalar ion energy flux $F_{E,i}$ is the normal projection of the ion energy-flux-density vector $\mathbf{q}_{E,i}$:

$$
F_{E,i} = \mathbf{q}_{E,i} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_{E,i}$ is the vector density of energy transport for the selected ion population and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ defines the positive normal direction.

Ion energy flux is a species- and charge-state-resolved or aggregated specialization of [energy flux]. [Total ion energy flux](name:total_ion_energy_flux) aggregates all ion species and charge states, while [parallel ion energy flux](name:parallel_ion_energy_flux) uses the local magnetic-field direction for its projection. The quantity is distinct from ion energy density, a volumetric energy source or sink, and ion velocity.

Sign convention: Positive when the ion energy-flux-density vector has a component in the direction of the chosen unit normal to the oriented surface.

Total-ion diamagnetic-drift momentum source density is the local rate per unit volume at which pressure-gradient-driven ion drift transport changes [toroidal_ion_momentum](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_source). It is an internal transport contribution, not an externally applied torque, and the sum includes all ion species and charge states. The toroidal component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Written as a conservative transport contribution, the source density is the negative divergence of the diamagnetic flux of ion toroidal angular momentum:

$$
S_{\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}} = -\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{L_\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}} = -\nabla \cdot \sum_{a\in\mathrm{ions}} \left(m_a n_a R v_{\phi,a}\right)\mathbf{v}_{D,a}
$$

where $S_{\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is in kg.m^-1.s^-2, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{L_\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the [ion diamagnetic momentum flux] in kg.s^-2, $\nabla\cdot$ is the spatial divergence operator with components in m^-1, and $a$ indexes ion species and charge states. Here $m_a$ is ion mass in kg, $n_a$ is ion number density in m^-3, $R$ is major radius in meters in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $v_{\phi,a}$ is toroidal fluid velocity in m.s^-1, and $\mathbf{v}_{D,a}$ is diamagnetic drift velocity in m.s^-1 generated by the perpendicular ion pressure gradient.

In practice the term is computed by combining equilibrium geometry, ion pressure-gradient estimates, species composition, and toroidal-flow information to construct the charge-state-resolved diamagnetic momentum fluxes and then taking their divergence. It is usually inferred from momentum-balance and transport analyzes rather than measured directly; charge-state-resolved contributions correspond to ion_state_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift, and the total plasma contribution is momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift. The related neutral contribution, when included in the same source decomposition, is neutral_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift.

Typical absolute magnitudes are order $10^{-4}$-$10^1$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 in weak-gradient core regions and $10^1$-$10^4$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 locally in pedestal, edge, or scrape-off-layer regions with short pressure-gradient scale lengths. The value can change sign with the direction of toroidal flow, pressure-gradient orientation, magnetic geometry, and spatial convergence or divergence of the diamagnetic momentum flux.

Sign convention: Positive when convergence of the ion diamagnetic-drift momentum flux increases total-ion toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

Ion charge state pressure characterizes the kinetic pressure associated with ions occupying a single ionization state, resolving the multi-species plasma composition down to the charge-state level. Depending on the physical population under consideration, this quantity may represent the [thermal component](name:thermal_ion_state_pressure) arising from Maxwellian random motion and excluded from non-thermal contributions, the fast suprathermal component from an energetic ion distribution, or the [total pressure](name:total_ion_state_pressure) combining both thermal and non-thermal contributions.

For the Maxwellian thermal component, the defining relation is:

$$
p_s = n_s k_B T_s
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ions in charge state $s$ and $T_s$ is the ion temperature of that charge state expressed in energy units; the fast-particle contribution adds the non-thermal pressure from energetic ions resolved as the second velocity moment of the suprathermal distribution.

The charge-state pressure appears in charge-state-resolved momentum and energy balance equations within multi-fluid and kinetic transport models. Radial structure is encoded by [the first radial derivative] with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, and by [the second radial derivative] giving the local radial profile curvature. The underlying thermal kinetic energy is captured by [ion_charge_state_temperature](name:ion_charge_state_temperature), while the aggregate thermal pressure summed over charge states is given by [thermal_ion_pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure).

Sign convention: Positive when the ion charge state exerts kinetic pressure on surrounding fluid elements, consistent with the non-negative definiteness of the pressure tensor as the second moment of the velocity distribution.

The upper-bound charge number specifies the highest ionization state included in an ion charge-state bundle, where the ionization charge $Z$ counts the number of electrons removed from the neutral atom. In multi-fluid plasma models, consecutive ionization states of the same ion species are often grouped into bundles to reduce computational expense; this quantity gives the ceiling $Z_\mathrm{max}$ of the charge range $[Z_\mathrm{min}, Z_\mathrm{max}]$ spanned by the bundle.

When a bundle encloses only a single charge state, $Z_\mathrm{max}$ equals the corresponding [lower-bound charge]. For multi-state bundles the interval width $Z_\mathrm{max} - Z_\mathrm{min} \geq 1$, and the [concentration-weighted average charge] or [mean charge] provides a representative effective charge for transport and source-term calculations.

Charge-state values are non-negative integers bounded above by the nuclear charge number $Z_n$ of the species: for hydrogen $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 1$, for carbon $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 6$, and for heavy impurities such as tungsten $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 74$. The bundle definition is set at model initialization and does not vary with plasma conditions at a given time step.

Sign convention: Positive when the ion carries net positive charge, corresponding to the removal of one or more electrons from the neutral atom.

Particle number density of krypton ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the krypton-ion population at that flux-surface location. The [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) is the parent quantity for this krypton-specific population.

The number density is defined by

$$
n = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n$ is number density, $N$ is the number of particles, and $V$ is volume. The quantity sums all ionized krypton charge states and excludes neutral krypton atoms. It is therefore an elemental ion density, analogous to the [ion density at the internal transport barrier], rather than a density for one specified charge state. The internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where locally reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep impurity-density gradients.

This quantity is the effective coefficient describing the advective, non-diffusive transport of momentum for a selected population, momentum component, and transport direction. It is a transport closure quantity, not the population’s actual bulk flow velocity.

For each selected momentum component and transport direction, the convective momentum flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{P,\mathrm{conv}} = V_{\mathrm{conv}} P
$$

where $\Gamma_{P,\mathrm{conv}}$ is the corresponding convective momentum flux, $V_{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the momentum convection velocity, and $P$ is the corresponding momentum density. The definition applies componentwise when momentum or transport direction is resolved.

The population may be total plasma, ions aggregated over charge states, a specified ion charge state, or neutral matter. Examples include [ion momentum convection velocity](name:ion_momentum_convection_velocity), [ion charge-state momentum convection velocity](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_convection_velocity), [neutral momentum convection velocity](name:neutral_momentum_convection_velocity), and [parallel momentum convection velocity]. Distinct attributed contributions, such as [diamagnetic momentum convection velocity](name:diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity), need not be projections of one physical bulk-flow vector.

Sign convention: Positive when the associated convective momentum flux is in the chosen positive transport direction for positive transported momentum density.

Distinct attributed contributions, such as [diamagnetic momentum convection velocity](name:diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity), need not be projections of one physical bulk-flow vector.

Sign convention: Positive when the associated convective momentum flux is in the chosen positive transport direction for positive transported momentum density.

This quantity is the effective coefficient describing the diamagnetic contribution to advective, non-diffusive transport of momentum for a selected population, momentum component, and transport direction. It is a transport-closure quantity, not the population’s actual bulk flow velocity.

Momentum diffusivity for an ion state is the transport coefficient appearing in the diffusive closure of the ion-state-resolved momentum equation, quantifying how collisional, neoclassical, turbulent, and charge-exchange processes redistribute the momentum of the selected ion population. This scalar quantity denotes a single diagonal or otherwise specified transport projection, rather than the full anisotropic momentum-diffusion operator.

For selected ion state $a$ and component $\alpha$, the scalar Fick's-law closure is

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{m,a,\alpha} = -D^{(m)}_{a,\alpha}\frac{\partial (m_a n_a u_{a,\alpha})}{\partial \ell_\alpha}
$$

where $a$ labels the ion state, $\alpha$ labels the selected component, $\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{m,a,\alpha}$ is the diffusive flux density of the $\alpha$-directed momentum, $D^{(m)}_{a,\alpha}$ is the ion-state momentum diffusivity, $m_a$ is the ion mass, $n_a$ is the ion-state number density, $u_{a,\alpha}$ is the flow velocity component, and $\ell_\alpha$ is distance along the selected transport direction. The product $m_a n_a u_{a,\alpha}$ is the local directed momentum density, and the minus sign makes a nonnegative diffusive coefficient oppose its local gradient.

This name is the ion-state-resolved scalar specialization of [momentum diffusivity](name:momentum_diffusivity). It differs from [ion momentum diffusivity], which is the effective coefficient in a closure for total ion momentum flux and total ion momentum density after those extensive fields are summed over all ion states; it should not be interpreted as an unqualified sum of state-resolved coefficients. When the ion-state label is an ionization state, it is the scalar state-resolved counterpart of [ion-charge-state momentum diffusivity](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity). Ion charge state momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift is the signed cylindrical-$R$ flux density of toroidal linear momentum carried by one specified charge state of an ion species and associated with its pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic drift. The transported momentum is the $\hat{\phi}$ component and the flux direction is $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The diamagnetic contribution is defined as the product of the charge-state toroidal momentum density and the cylindrical-$R$ component of the same charge state's diamagnetic drift velocity:

$$
\Pi_{R\phi,\alpha}^{\mathrm{dia}} = m_i n_\alpha u_{\phi,\alpha} v_{R,\alpha}^{\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $\Pi_{R\phi,\alpha}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is this momentum flux, the first tensor index $R$ denotes the flux direction, the second tensor index $\phi$ denotes the toroidal momentum component, $\alpha$ labels the ion charge state, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_\alpha$ is the charge-state number density, $u_{\phi,\alpha}$ is the toroidal flow velocity of that charge state, and $v_{R,\alpha}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the [radial ion charge state velocity due to diamagnetic drift](name:radial_ion_charge_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

This quantity is local in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame; it is not a flux-surface average, a flux-surface integral, or a flux-surface-normal projection. It is charge-state resolved and excludes contributions to the same $R\phi$ momentum-flux component from non-diamagnetic transport mechanisms. The [radial ion momentum flux at flux surface due to diamagnetic drift] is tied to a magnetic-flux-surface locus, while [toroidal ion charge state velocity due to diamagnetic drift](name:toroidal_ion_charge_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [perpendicular ion charge state velocity due to diamagnetic drift](name:perpendicular_ion_charge_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) are velocity components rather than momentum fluxes; perpendicular is relative to the magnetic-field direction.

Sign convention: Positive when toroidal linear momentum associated with motion in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ is transported toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

Neutral diffusion coefficient is the scalar Fickian diffusion coefficient for neutral-particle transport. It characterizes local diffusion of neutral particles by relating the diffusive neutral particle-flux vector to the neutral particle density gradient without selecting a transport direction.

The defining Fickian relation for the scalar closure is

$$
\mathbf{\Gamma}_{n,\mathrm{diff}} = -D_n \nabla n_n
$$

where $D_n$ is the neutral diffusion coefficient, $\mathbf{\Gamma}_{n,\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive neutral particle-flux vector, $n_n$ is the neutral particle number density, and $\nabla n_n$ is its spatial gradient. The minus sign denotes diffusive transport down the neutral-density gradient.

The quantity applies to neutral particles in edge-plasma transport and to the state-unspecified neutral population described by $n_n$; when multiple neutral internal states are combined, $D_n$ is the effective coefficient multiplying the combined density gradient, not a sum of internal-state coefficients. It excludes tensor diffusivity, advective neutral flow, particle sources or sinks, and coefficients resolved for a specified neutral internal state.

Directional siblings apply the same Fickian concept after a direction is selected: [radial neutral diffusion coefficient](name:radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient) is for transport in the $\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, and [poloidal neutral diffusion coefficient] is for transport in the poloidal direction in the plane spanned by the $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ unit vectors. [Poloidal neutral internal-state diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_internal_state_diffusion_coefficient) is narrower because it is both poloidal and resolved for a specified neutral internal state; it is not a charge-state counterpart.

Neutral energy flux is the signed component of energy-flux density carried by neutral atoms and molecules normal to an oriented surface. It gives the rate at which the neutral energy reservoir crosses unit area, summed over neutral species and internal states.

For an oriented surface with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, the neutral energy flux $F_{E,\mathrm{n}}$ is defined by

$$
F_{E,\mathrm{n}} = \mathbf{q}_{E,\mathrm{n}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_{E,\mathrm{n}}$ is the neutral energy-flux-density vector and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ defines the positive surface-normal direction.

This quantity is the neutral specialization of [energy flux]. It includes the energy carried by neutral particle transport, including translational and internal-state contributions when present; [neutral particle flux](name:neutral_particle_flux) counts particle transport without weighting by carried energy. Directional projections are represented by [radial neutral energy flux](name:radial_neutral_energy_flux), [poloidal neutral energy flux](name:poloidal_neutral_species_energy_flux), and [parallel neutral energy flux](name:parallel_neutral_energy_flux), while [neutral internal-state energy flux](name:neutral_internal_state_energy_flux) restricts the reservoir to a specified internal state.

Sign convention: Positive when the neutral energy-flux-density vector has a component in the direction of the chosen unit normal to the oriented surface.

The neutral-state diffusion coefficient characterizes irreversible particle transport of neutral atoms or molecules occupying a specified internal state — electronic, vibrational, or charge-resolved — through the edge plasma, where neutral recycling, plasma fueling, and impurity sourcing drive steep density gradients.

The diffusive flux of neutrals in state $s$ obeys the Fick-law constitutive relation:

$$
\mathbf{J}_{n,s} = -D_{n,s} \, \nabla n_{n,s}
$$

where $n_{n,s}$ is the number density of neutrals in state $s$ and $D_{n,s}$ is the state-resolved diffusion coefficient.

This quantity is the direction-agnostic parent of its directional projections: the [poloidal neutral-state diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient) governs transport along the poloidal direction, and the [poloidal neutral diffusion coefficient] provides an analogous coefficient aggregated over all neutral states. In edge-plasma fluid and kinetic models, $D_{n,s}$ is evaluated on unstructured geometry grids covering the scrape-off layer and divertor region; values are obtained from neutral Monte Carlo transport calculations or prescribed as free parameters in reduced fluid formulations.

Neutral-state temperature is the translational kinetic temperature of neutral atoms or molecules conditional on occupancy of a specified internal state $s$, such as an electronic, vibrational, or rotational excitation. It characterizes the random kinetic energy of that state-resolved neutral population and is distinct from the internal excitation energy of the state. When state populations are equilibrated it approaches the state-averaged [neutral_temperature](name:neutral_state_temperature), but in weakly collisional or radiating plasmas different states can have different temperatures.

The scalar temperature is defined by the second central moment of the state-resolved velocity distribution:

$$
T_{n,s} = \frac{m_n}{3 e}\left\langle \left|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{n,s}\right|^2 \right\rangle_s
$$

where $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass, $e$ is the elementary charge used to express the result in eV, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $\mathbf{u}_{n,s}$ is the bulk velocity of neutrals in state $s$, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_s$ denotes an average over that state's velocity distribution. For an isotropic scalar closure, the related [thermal_neutral_state_pressure](name:thermal_neutral_state_pressure) satisfies $p_{n,s}=n_{n,s} e T_{n,s}$ when $T_{n,s}$ is in eV.

Neutral-state temperature is inferred from diagnostics that are sensitive to the velocity distribution of a selected state, especially Doppler broadening of atomic emission lines or molecular bands, and from neutral particle energy spectra when state selectivity is available. It is also computed in state-resolved neutral transport or collisional-radiative models from the velocity-space moment of each state population, including effects of wall recycling, charge exchange, dissociation, excitation, ionization, and recombination.

Typical values for cold wall-recycled ground-state atoms or molecules are 0.01-1 eV. Excited atomic or molecular populations in edge and divertor plasmas are commonly 1-20 eV, while charge-exchange neutrals connected to hotter plasma regions can reach 10-1000 eV depending on the parent ion temperature and collisional history.

This quantity is the trapped-electron neoclassical collisionality parameter, measuring electron pitch-angle scattering relative to the characteristic bounce motion of trapped particles. It distinguishes the geometry-scaled regime from the parent [electron collisionality].

The parameter is defined by

$$
\nu_e^* = \frac{\nu_e q R}{\epsilon^{3/2} v_{te}}
$$

where $\nu_e$ is the electron pitch-angle-scattering frequency, $q$ is the safety factor, $R$ is the major radius, $\epsilon$ is the inverse aspect ratio, and $v_{te}$ is the electron thermal speed. The denominator represents the trapped-electron bounce-frequency scaling, including the inverse-aspect-ratio dependence.

This quantity is a geometry-normalized collisionality measure, not a collision frequency or a transport coefficient. Its localized pedestal-top counterpart is [normalized electron collisionality at the pedestal top].

This quantity is the field-aligned, flux-surface-averaged current-density contribution produced by non-inductive current-drive processes. It includes bootstrap and externally driven contributions represented by the [non-inductive current-density parent].

It is defined by

$$
J_{parallel}^{\mathrm{NI}} = \left\langle \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{NI}} \cdot \mathbf{b} \right\rangle_{\psi}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = \frac{\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{NI}}$ is the non-inductive current-density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $\mathbf{b}$ is its unit direction, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes averaging over a magnetic flux surface labeled by $\psi$.

The aggregate excludes current driven by an inductive electric field. Mechanism-specific quantities such as [parallel current density due to anomalous transport](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport) resolve particular contributions rather than replacing this total non-inductive component.

Sign convention: Positive when the non-inductive current density points along the local magnetic-field vector.

Parallel electron diffusivity is an effective transport coefficient for diffusive electron-particle transport along the local magnetic-field direction in a magnetized plasma.

The constitutive relation is

$$
\Gamma_{e,\parallel}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{e,\parallel}\,\nabla_{\parallel} n_e
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\parallel}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the parallel component of the diffusive electron particle-flux vector, $D_{e,\parallel}$ is the parallel electron diffusivity, $\nabla_{\parallel} n_e$ is the derivative of electron number density along the local magnetic-field direction, and $n_e$ is electron number density. The subscript $e$ denotes electrons and the subscript $\parallel$ denotes the field-aligned projection.

This quantity applies specifically to electron particle transport and represents the parallel diffusive contribution, with no aggregation over other plasma species. It excludes convective particle fluxes, particle sources, and particle sinks, and it is distinct from the electron density gradient and from the resulting particle flux.

It is the parallel directional component of the transport represented by [electron particle diffusivity]. The corresponding poloidal directional coefficient is [poloidal electron diffusivity](name:poloidal_electron_diffusivity), while [effective electron diffusivity](name:effective_electron_diffusivity) describes the same effective directional transport-coefficient family without selecting this parallel direction.

Parallel electron energy diffusivity is the scalar local transport coefficient for field-aligned diffusive smoothing of electron thermal-energy density. It represents only the Fickian, down-gradient contribution to electron energy transport along the magnetic field.

The defining closure for the field-aligned diffusive electron thermal-energy flux is:

$$
q_{E,e,\parallel}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -\chi_{E,e,\parallel}\,\partial_\parallel w_e
$$

where $q_{E,e,\parallel}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the field-aligned diffusive electron thermal-energy flux, $\chi_{E,e,\parallel}$ is this diffusivity, $w_e$ is electron thermal-energy density, and $\partial_\parallel = \hat{\mathbf b}\cdot\nabla$ is differentiation along the magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf b}$.

This directional specialization of [electron energy diffusivity] excludes convective transport, explicitly nonlocal transport, and energy sources or sinks. It is distinct from [parallel electron diffusivity](name:parallel_electron_diffusivity), which describes particle transport, and from [poloidal electron energy diffusivity](name:poloidal_electron_energy_diffusivity), which describes the poloidal direction. It is not a temperature-gradient heat-transport coefficient unless the density and heat-capacity factors relating temperature and energy-density gradients are included.

Parallel electron energy diffusivity is the scalar local transport coefficient for field-aligned diffusive smoothing of electron thermal-energy density. It represents only the Fickian, down-gradient contribution to electron energy transport along the magnetic field.

The defining closure for the field-aligned diffusive electron thermal-energy flux is:

$$
q_{E,e,\parallel}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -\chi_{E,e,\parallel}\,\partial_\parallel w_e
$$

where $q_{E,e,\parallel}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the field-aligned diffusive electron thermal-energy flux, $\chi_{E,e,\parallel}$ is this diffusivity, $w_e$ is electron thermal-energy density, and $\partial_\parallel = \hat{\mathbf b}\cdot\nabla$ is differentiation along the magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf b}$.

This directional specialization of electron energy diffusivity excludes convective transport, explicitly nonlocal transport, and energy sources or sinks. It is distinct from [parallel electron diffusivity](name:parallel_electron_diffusivity), which describes particle transport, and from [poloidal electron energy diffusivity](name:poloidal_electron_energy_diffusivity), which describes the poloidal direction. It is not a temperature-gradient heat-transport coefficient unless the density and heat-capacity factors relating temperature and energy-density gradients are included.

Parallel fast-particle pressure is the field-aligned component of the kinetic pressure tensor carried by suprathermal particles. It is the all-orbit contribution to [fast-particle pressure], complementary to the transverse [perpendicular fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure).

The flux-surface-averaged pressure is defined by the parallel second velocity moment:

$$
P_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}(\psi)=\left\langle \sum_s m_s\int v_\parallel^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v\right\rangle_\psi
$$

where $\psi$ labels the magnetic flux surface, $\langle\cdot\rangle_\psi$ denotes its flux-surface average, $s$ labels fast-particle species, $m_s$ is particle mass, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is velocity, $v_\parallel=\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{b}$ is velocity along the magnetic-field unit vector $\mathbf{b}$, and $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the distribution function.

All guiding-center orbit classes are included, including co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped particles. The associated scalar trace satisfies $P_{\mathrm{fast}}=(P_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}+2P_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}})/3$; an orbit-restricted counterpart is [parallel co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure).

Parallel ion energy flux is the signed component of ion energy-flux density along the local magnetic-field direction. It gives the rate at which energy carried by a specified ion population crosses a surface whose chosen unit normal is the local magnetic-field direction, including convective, conductive, or other channels only when they belong to the stated ion-energy reservoir.

For local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, the scalar parallel ion energy flux $F_{E,i,\parallel}$ is the projection of the ion energy-flux-density vector $\mathbf{q}_{E,i}$ onto $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$:

$$
F_{E,i,\parallel} = \mathbf{q}_{E,i} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_{E,i}$ is the vector density of energy transport for the selected ion population and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of the local [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field) $\mathbf{B}$.

Parallel ion energy flux applies where the local magnetic-field direction is defined and the selected ion-energy reservoir is specified. For an ion species identified without a charge state, it is summed over all charge states of that species; the charge-state-resolved counterpart is [parallel ion charge-state energy flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_energy_flux). [Total ion energy flux](name:total_ion_energy_flux) aggregates all ion species and charge states.

Parallel ion energy flux is a field-aligned specialization of [ion energy flux](name:ion_energy_flux) and a species-scoped specialization of [energy flux]. Sign convention: Positive when $\mathbf{q}_{E,i}$ has a component in the direction of the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

The parallel ion momentum convection velocity is the parallel effective velocity that advects the parallel component of ion momentum density for a specified ion species. The parallel direction follows the local magnetic-field direction, so the velocity direction and transported momentum component coincide. Because this is an intensive coefficient for a species-level quantity, it is represented as the density-weighted mean over all charge states unless a charge-state-resolved quantity is named.

For the parallel ion-momentum component, the advective contribution to its field-aligned flux is

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{conv}}_{p_{i,\parallel},\parallel} = p_{i,\parallel} V^{\mathrm{conv}}_{i,M,\parallel}
$$

where $i$ identifies the ion species, $p_{i,\parallel}$ is its parallel momentum density, $\Gamma^{\mathrm{conv}}_{p_{i,\parallel},\parallel}$ is the field-aligned component of the non-diffusive convective flux, and $V^{\mathrm{conv}}_{i,M,\parallel}$ is this velocity. The parent [ion momentum convection velocity](name:ion_momentum_convection_velocity) gives the same closure without selecting the parallel projection. The [parallel ion charge state momentum convection velocity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_convection_velocity) resolves one ionization state, whereas [parallel ion velocity] is the bulk-flow velocity rather than this transport coefficient.

Sign convention: Positive when $V^{\mathrm{conv}}_{i,M,\parallel}$ points along the local magnetic-field direction.

The parallel ion momentum diffusivity $D_{\\parallel}^i$ is the effective diffusion coefficient characterizing down-gradient redistribution of the field-aligned component of momentum within the total ion population summed over all charge states.

The diffusive parallel ion momentum flux density satisfies:

$$
\\Gamma_{\\mathrm{mom},\\parallel} = -\\rho_i D_{\\parallel}^i \\nabla_{\\parallel} v_{i,\\parallel}
$$

where $\\Gamma_{\\mathrm{mom},\\parallel}$ is the diffusive flux density of parallel ion momentum, $\\rho_i$ is the total ion mass density, $v_{i,\\parallel}$ is the mean parallel ion velocity, and $\\nabla_{\\parallel}$ is the derivative along the local magnetic-field direction.

This quantity applies to the effective parallel transport coefficient for the aggregate ion population, with ion charge states summed, and excludes charge-state-resolved coefficients such as [parallel ion charge-state momentum diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity). It describes the field-aligned component and is not the full momentum-diffusivity tensor or a cross-field component.

It is the parallel component-resolved specialization of [ion momentum diffusivity]. The corresponding poloidal component is [poloidal ion momentum diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_momentum_diffusivity), which characterizes redistribution along the poloidal direction rather than along the magnetic field.

Parallel runaway electron current density $J_{\rm RE,\parallel}$ characterizes the field-aligned conventional charge transport carried by the runaway-electron population, a suprathermal electron population extending beyond the collisional drag limit. It is the field-aligned projection of [runaway electron current density].

The parallel current density is the first velocity moment of the runaway-electron distribution projected onto the magnetic-field direction:

$$
J_{\rm RE,\parallel}(\mathbf{x}) = q_e \int_{\mathcal{R}} (\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}) f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $q_e$ is the electron charge, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic-field unit vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $f_e$ is the runaway-electron phase-space number density, $\mathcal{R}$ is the velocity-space subset classified as beyond the collisional drag limit, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

The integration includes only the runaway-electron population and excludes current carried by non-runaway populations. It therefore differs from [co-passing fast current density], which is selected by an orbit class rather than the runaway criterion. The related [runaway electron density](name:runaway_electron_density) describes the carrier abundance rather than its charge transport.

Sign convention: Positive when the conventional runaway-electron current points along $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, with the magnetic field expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the plasma-volume average of the local field-aligned conventional current density carried only by runaway electrons. It selects the magnetic-field-parallel contribution of the runaway-electron current before applying the same volume averaging represented by [volume-averaged runaway-electron current density].

$$
\left\langle j_{\parallel,\mathrm{RE}} \right\rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{RE}}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the local conventional current-density vector of the runaway-electron population, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the local unit vector in the magnetic-field direction, $V_p$ is the selected plasma volume, and $dV$ is its volume element. Contributions from thermal electrons, ions, and non-runaway populations are excluded. Because this is conventional current, its direction is opposite to the motion of negatively charged runaway electrons.

Sign convention: Positive when the local conventional runaway-electron current component points along the local magnetic-field direction.

Number density of particles of a given species is the local count of particles of that species per physical volume. It is the zeroth velocity-space moment of the species distribution function and includes all thermal, suprathermal, and non-Maxwellian populations represented for that species.

The density $n_s$ of species $s$ is defined by integrating the species distribution function over velocity space:

$$
n_s(\mathbf{x}, t) = \int f_s(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}, t)\, d^3\mathbf{v}
$$

where $n_s$ is the particle density of species $s$, $f_s$ is the distribution function of species $s$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $t$ is time, and $d^3\mathbf{v}$ is the velocity-space volume element.

The quantity applies to one specified particle species. For a species with multiple charge states, this species-level density is summed over all charge states of that species; it is not a charge-state-resolved density. It includes both thermal and non-thermal particle populations and is not restricted to a Maxwellian component, a fast-particle component, or a particular guiding-center orbit class.

This quantity is distinct from charge density, mass density, pressure, and any density weighted by energy, charge, or mass. It is also distinct from a density summed over different species: summing the corresponding species densities gives [total particle density], and summing over electron, ion, and neutral particle populations gives [total electron-ion-neutral particle number density]. A flux-surface-averaged value, when explicitly specified, is the flux-surface average of this same per-species density rather than a different velocity-space moment.

This quantity is the directed transport velocity of runaway electrons across magnetic flux surfaces, isolated from the field-aligned component of the [runaway-electron convection velocity].

The perpendicular component is defined by

$$
v_{\perp}^{\rm RE} = \mathbf{v}_{\rm RE} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\psi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\rm RE}$ is the effective runaway-electron convection-velocity vector and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\psi}$ is the outward unit normal to nested magnetic flux surfaces. This convective quantity describes directed cross-field transport and excludes diffusive spreading, which is characterized by the [perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity). It contributes to the [perpendicular runaway-electron particle flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux) together with the runaway-electron density.

Sign convention: Positive when runaway-electron convection is directed outward from the magnetic axis toward increasing flux label.

Poloidal ion state energy flux is the component of the ion energy-flux density vector tangent to the poloidal direction for a specified ion species and ionization charge state. The poloidal direction lies in the $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and follows increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in a chosen flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. This signed scalar represents the net power carried by that charge-state population across unit area normal to the local poloidal direction.

The component is defined by projecting the ion-state energy-flux density vector onto the local poloidal unit vector:

$$
q_{\theta,i,z} = \mathbf{q}_{i,z} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $q_{\theta,i,z}$ is the poloidal ion-state energy flux in W m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{q}_{i,z}$ is the total energy-flux density vector for ion species $i$ and ionization charge state $z$ in W m$^{-2}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $\theta$.

It is computed from kinetic moments or fluid energy-balance models for the selected ion state, including the modeled transport of thermal and flow energy. It is closely related to the corresponding [poloidal ion state velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity), [poloidal ion state particle flux](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_particle_flux), [poloidal ion state momentum flux](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_flux), and transport-coefficient quantities such as the [poloidal ion state momentum diffusion coefficient]. Radial, toroidal, and field-aligned projections are represented by [radial ion state energy flux](name:radial_ion_state_energy_flux), [toroidal ion state energy flux], and [parallel ion state energy flux].

Typical absolute magnitudes are highly device-, region-, and model-dependent. Local transport calculations often span about $10^2$-$10^7$ W m$^{-2}$, with values near zero where poloidal transport is weak and larger values in steep-gradient edge, scrape-off-layer, or divertor regions.

Sign convention: Positive when energy flows in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

It is closely related to the corresponding [poloidal ion state velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity), [poloidal ion state particle flux](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_particle_flux), [poloidal ion state momentum flux](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_flux), and transport-coefficient quantities such as the poloidal ion state momentum diffusion coefficient. Radial, toroidal, and field-aligned projections are represented by [radial ion state energy flux](name:radial_ion_state_energy_flux), toroidal ion state energy flux, and parallel ion state energy flux.

Typical absolute magnitudes are highly device-, region-, and model-dependent. Local transport calculations often span about $10^2$-$10^7$ W m$^{-2}$, with values near zero where poloidal transport is weak and larger values in steep-gradient edge, scrape-off-layer, or divertor regions.

Sign convention: Positive when energy flows in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

Poloidal neutral state convection velocity is the state-resolved advective speed that multiplies the density of one neutral atomic or molecular state in the poloidal particle flux. It describes directed transport along the poloidal coordinate $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, separate from radial transport and from the species-summed [poloidal neutral species convection velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_convection_velocity). The corresponding energy-transport quantity is [poloidal neutral state energy convection velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity).

The convective contribution to the poloidal particle flux density is defined by:

$$
\Gamma_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_a\,v_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $a$ labels the specified neutral state, $\Gamma_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective poloidal particle flux density in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $n_a$ is the neutral-state number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $v_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the poloidal convection velocity in $\mathrm{m.s}^{-1}$.

In transport modeling, this velocity is usually an effective coefficient inferred from the ratio of poloidal advective particle flux to state density after separating diffusive, source, and sink contributions. It may be constrained by neutral density, emission, and particle-balance measurements, or computed from kinetic or fluid neutral-transport closures; it should not be interpreted automatically as the ballistic speed of individual neutral particles.

Representative modeled magnitudes are strongly regime- and closure-dependent. Values may be close to 0 m.s^-1 where poloidal neutral advection is weak, while effective coefficients of order 1-100 m.s^-1 are common scales used to characterize modest poloidal redistribution; larger local values should be checked against the defining flux-to-density ratio rather than treated as universal typical behavior.

Sign convention: Positive when $v_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$ in the flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

Poloidal neutral-state momentum flux is the $\theta$-$\theta$ projection of the state-resolved momentum-flux tensor for neutral particles, giving the flux of poloidal linear momentum across a surface whose oriented normal is poloidal. The state qualifier restricts the population to neutrals in a specified atomic, molecular, charge, or excitation state, and $\theta$ is the poloidal angle in a chosen flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ is the flux label and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

The defining projection of the state-resolved [neutral-state momentum-flux tensor] is:

$$
\Pi_{\theta\theta}^{(s)} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}^{(s)} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $\Pi_{\theta\theta}^{(s)}$ is this poloidal neutral-state momentum flux for state $s$, $s$ identifies the internal neutral state, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the local unit vector in the direction of increasing $\theta$, and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{(s)}$ is the state-resolved momentum-flux tensor. For the convective-plus-pressure contribution, the same component is $m_s n_s v_{s,\theta}^2 + p_s$, where $m_s$ is the particle mass of state $s$, $n_s$ is the number density of state $s$, $v_{s,\theta}$ is the poloidal component of the mean neutral velocity for state $s$, and $p_s$ is the scalar pressure of state $s$.

This scalar component applies locally wherever state $s$ exists and a neutral momentum balance is defined. Its aggregation convention is state-resolved: no sum over atomic, molecular, charge, or excitation states and no spatial averaging is included. Summing $\Pi_{\theta\theta}^{(s)}$ over the neutral states included in an aggregate population gives [poloidal neutral momentum flux](name:poloidal_neutral_momentum_flux); without that sum the state-resolved and aggregate quantities are not identical.

This quantity is the poloidal-poloidal tensor component, not the flux-surface-normal transport of poloidal momentum $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\rho \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}^{(s)} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$, where $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\rho$ points toward increasing flux label $\rho$; that cross projection is a different tensor component. It is also distinct from [radial neutral-state momentum flux](name:radial_neutral_state_momentum_flux), [vertical neutral-state momentum flux](name:vertical_neutral_state_momentum_flux), and [parallel neutral-state momentum flux](name:parallel_neutral_internal_state_momentum_flux): radial and vertical refer to the $R$ and $Z$ directions in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, while parallel refers to the local magnetic-field direction.

Sign convention: Positive when positive-$\theta$ linear momentum is transported across a surface whose oriented normal points in the positive $\theta$ direction of the chosen flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

Power density is the net rate at which energy is transferred to or from a designated recipient per unit volume. The recipient may be a plasma population, energy channel, orbit class, radiation field, or material region, as defined by the applicable energy balance.

For a differential volume, the volumetric power density is defined by

$$
p_E = \frac{dE}{dt\,dV}
$$

where $E$ is the energy transferred to the designated recipient, $t$ is time, and $V$ is volume. A flux-surface, spatial, or population average may be applied while retaining the underlying per-volume meaning.

Positive values denote net energy gain by the designated recipient; negative values denote net energy loss. Heating, collisional exchange, radiation, nuclear deposition, particle interactions, and transport-model source or sink terms may contribute according to the qualified balance. [ion charge-state power density](name:ion_charge_state_power_density) specializes the recipient, while [radiated power density](name:radiated_power_density) specializes the transfer channel and [power density of limiter tile] specializes a material region.

Co-passing power density is the flux-surface-averaged rate at which kinetic energy is transferred to or from the co-passing orbit population per unit physical volume. Co-passing particles are passing particles that circulate continuously in the co-current direction.

For a flux surface labeled by poloidal magnetic flux $psi$, it is defined as

$$
p_{E,\mathrm{co}}(\psi)=\left\langle\frac{dE_{\mathrm{co}}}{dt\,dV}\right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{co}}$ is the kinetic energy of the co-passing population, $t$ is time, $V$ is physical volume, and the angle brackets denote a flux-surface average. Positive values denote net energy gain by this population; negative values denote net energy loss. Wave-particle interactions, collisions, and particle sources may contribute. The related [counter-passing power density](name:counter_passing_power_density) applies the same energy-transfer definition to the oppositely circulating orbit class, while [power density] is the unqualified parent quantity.

Counter-passing power density is the flux-surface-averaged rate at which energy is transferred to or from the counter-passing orbit population per unit physical volume. It is the orbit-class specialization of [power density]; counter-passing particles are passing particles that circulate opposite to the plasma-current direction, distinct from [co-passing power density](name:co_passing_power_density) and [trapped power density](name:trapped_power_density).

For the underlying local energy balance, volumetric power density is defined by

$$
p_{\mathrm{cp}} = \frac{dE_{\mathrm{cp}}}{dt\,dV}
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the energy transferred to the counter-passing population, $t$ is time, and $V$ is physical volume. The flux-surface average is applied to this local rate while retaining its per-volume meaning.

Positive values denote net energy gain by the counter-passing population; negative values denote net energy loss. Wave-particle interactions, collisions, and particle sources contribute when they are included in the counter-passing energy balance.

Electron power density is the net rate at which energy is transferred to or from the electron population per unit volume. It is the scalar source term for the electron recipient in an electron energy transport equation, including only the source and sink terms assigned to electrons in that balance.

For a differential volume, the electron power density is defined by

$$
p_e = \frac{dE_e}{dt\,dV}
$$

where $p_e$ is the electron power density, $E_e$ is the signed energy transfer to the electron population through the included electron energy source and sink channels, $t$ is time, and $V$ is physical volume.

The scope is the electron population in the specified plasma region, with contributions from applicable heating, collisional energy exchange, ionization, recombination, radiation loss, and other electron energy-transfer processes when those terms are assigned to the electron balance. The aggregation convention is a net local source term over the included electron channels; it is not an individual process contribution, a diagnostic-specific estimate, a flux-surface average, or a total stored electron energy.

Electron power density specializes [power density] to the electron recipient. It excludes source terms whose recipient is another population, such as [ion power density](name:ion_power_density) or [neutral power density](name:neutral_power_density), even when the same interaction exchanges energy between populations; it is also distinct from [radiated power density], which represents energy emitted as radiation rather than the net source assigned to the electron recipient.

The volume integral of $p_e$ over a specified plasma region gives [electron power](name:electron_power) for the same electron energy balance. When recipient-resolved source terms are defined for the same region and channel set, their aggregate contributes to [net plasma power density].

Sign convention: Positive when the included balance terms increase the energy of the electron population.

Neutral internal-state power density is the net rate at which energy is transferred to or from a specified neutral species state per unit volume. It is the state-resolved source term in that state's energy balance.

For a differential volume, the volumetric power density is defined by

$$

Counter-passing fast-electron collisional power density is the local rate of change of kinetic energy density of the counter-passing component of the fast-electron distribution caused by Coulomb collisions with other plasma species. It is the counter-passing orbit-class contribution to the fast-electron collisional energy balance. The counter-passing component consists of passing guiding-center states whose bounce-averaged toroidal angular motion is opposite to the plasma-current circulation; the toroidal angle is $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity is the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator over the counter-passing part of fast-electron phase space:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{fast,counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_s \int \chi_{\mathrm{counter}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, \frac{1}{2} m_e v^2\, C_{es}[f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}, f_s](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where the sum is over collision partners $s$, $\chi_{\mathrm{counter}}$ is the phase-space indicator equal to one on counter-passing fast-electron guiding-center states and zero elsewhere, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed, $f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is normalized so that $\int f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}\,d^3v$ gives the local fast-electron density, $f_s$ is the distribution of species $s$, and $C_{es}$ is the Coulomb collision operator giving the collisional time derivative of $f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ due to species $s$. The counter-passing restriction is applied by $\chi_{\mathrm{counter}}$; it does not redefine the collision partners. For relativistic fast electrons, the kinetic-energy weight is replaced by the appropriate relativistic kinetic energy.

The orbit-class partition is non-overlapping: [co-passing], counter-passing, and [trapped](name:trapped_fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions) components sum to [fast-electron collisional power density] when the same collision operator and phase-space partition are used. This quantity excludes collisional energy exchange assigned to the thermal-electron population.

Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the counter-passing fast-electron component.

The neutral-beam shine-through power is the energy carried per unit time by injected neutral particles that cross the plasma without ionization or another stopping interaction and leave through the far plasma boundary. It includes only the outgoing neutral energy that is not deposited in the plasma.

The defining outward energy-flux integral is:

$$
P_{\mathrm{st}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{far}}} \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{E,n} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{st}}$ is the shine-through power, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{E,n}$ is the energy-flux vector carried by the exiting neutral particles, $A_{\mathrm{far}}$ is the far plasma-boundary surface, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is its outward unit normal. It is excluded from the [power absorbed by the plasma from a neutral beam injector].

The radial heat-viscosity current density is the radial component of the electric-current contribution generated when heat-viscosity terms in a collisional magnetized-plasma fluid closure drive net charge transport. It is the projection of the [heat-viscosity current density](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) vector onto $\hat{R}$, the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The radial component $j_{\mathrm{hv},R}$ is defined by projecting the heat-viscosity current-density vector onto the cylindrical radial basis vector:

$$
j_{\mathrm{hv},R} = \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{hv} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{hv},R}$ is the radial heat-viscosity current density, $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{hv}$ is the [heat-viscosity current density](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) vector, and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the plasma current-density contribution produced by heat-viscosity terms and represents the species-summed net charge flow associated with that mechanism. It is a cylindrical radial projection, not a flux-surface-normal component, not a scalar derivative with respect to a flux label, and not the full vector current density.

It is one geometric component of the parent [heat-viscosity current density](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity); the [toroidal](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) and [vertical](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) components are projections of the same parent vector along other directions in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The [poloidal](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), [parallel](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), and [diamagnetic](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) heat-viscosity current densities use different physically defined directions, while [radial current density due to parallel viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) and [current density due to collisions] denote distinct driving mechanisms.

Sign convention: Positive when the net heat-viscosity-driven charge flow points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

It is one geometric component of the parent [heat-viscosity current density](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity); the [toroidal](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) and [vertical](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) components are projections of the same parent vector along other directions in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The [poloidal](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), [parallel](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), and [diamagnetic](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) heat-viscosity current densities use different physically defined directions, while [radial current density due to parallel viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) and current density due to collisions denote distinct driving mechanisms.

Sign convention: Positive when the net heat-viscosity-driven charge flow points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Radial electron energy flux is the directed flux of electron thermal energy and enthalpy per unit area along the increasing-major-radius direction. It is the radial projection of the net [electron energy flux](name:electron_energy_flux), including conductive and convective contributions.

The radial component is defined by

$$
q_{e,R} = \mathbf{q}_e \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_e$ is the net electron energy flux density, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major radius, and $q_{e,R}$ is its radial component.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, this quantity uses the geometric radial direction and is distinct from the flux-surface-normal [radial total thermal electron energy flux]. The complementary [poloidal electron energy flux](name:poloidal_electron_energy_flux) resolves the same electron energy-flux vector along the poloidal direction.

Sign convention: Positive when the electron energy flux points toward increasing major radius $R$.

Radial neutral-state momentum flux is the radial-radial projection of the momentum-flux density tensor for neutral particles occupying one specified atomic, molecular, charge, or excitation state. It represents transport of radial linear momentum across a surface normal to the major-radius direction.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the convective-plus-pressure contribution for state $s$ is:

$$
\Pi_{RR}^{(s)} = m_s n_s v_{s,R}^{\,2} + p_s
$$

where $\Pi_{RR}^{(s)}$ is the radial-radial momentum-flux component, $s$ identifies the specified neutral state, $m_s$ is the particle mass of that state, $n_s$ is its number density, $v_{s,R}$ is its mean velocity component along the radial unit vector $\hat{R}$, and $p_s$ is its scalar pressure. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\hat{R}$ is the radial unit vector.

The quantity applies locally to all neutral particles in the specified state and includes their convective and pressure contributions, with no aggregation over other neutral atomic, molecular, charge, or excitation states. It is a directional component rather than the complete momentum-flux tensor or the full [neutral-state momentum flux] vector.

It excludes momentum carried by other neutral states and is distinct from particle flux, energy flux, and momentum source density. The radial component is the major-radius-directed counterpart of [poloidal neutral-state momentum flux](name:poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_flux). When the relevant neutral states are combined, their radial contributions form the aggregate [radial neutral momentum flux](name:radial_neutral_momentum_flux).

Sign convention: Positive when the radial momentum flux is directed toward increasing major radius $R$ through a surface whose oriented normal is $\hat{R}$.

The runaway-electron critical electric field is the threshold magnitude of the parallel electric field separating collisional braking from sustained electron acceleration.

In force-balance terms, the threshold is defined by

$$
e E_c = F_{\mathrm{drag,max}}
$$

where $E_c$ is the critical electric-field magnitude, $e$ is the elementary-charge magnitude, and $F_{\mathrm{drag,max}}$ is the maximum collisional drag force opposing electron acceleration.

This quantity applies to the collisional background-electron population at a specified plasma location. It is a local threshold, not a sum over electron populations or spatial regions and not a volume-averaged value. It is distinct from the Dreicer field, which is the bulk-electron reference field for spontaneous runaway generation.

As the runaway-electron-specific realization of the broader [critical electric field], it provides the threshold used to interpret the [runaway-electron source rate due to Dreicer](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer).

The safety factor at the internal transport barrier is the signed helical winding of magnetic field lines on the flux surface designated as the barrier. It counts toroidal turns per poloidal circuit at that specific locus.

The defining flux-increment relation is:

$$
q_{\mathrm{ITB}} = \left.\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{d\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}}\right|_{\mathrm{ITB}}
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the safety factor evaluated on the internal-transport-barrier flux surface, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is toroidal magnetic flux, $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is poloidal magnetic flux, and the subscript $\mathrm{ITB}$ denotes evaluation on that designated surface.

This quantity applies only to the flux surface associated with the internal transport barrier. It is a single flux-surface value, with no averaging or aggregation over neighboring surfaces, plasma volume, or other regions implied.

It is distinct from safety-factor values evaluated at other loci, such as the [safety factor at the pedestal top], and it does not represent a general radial profile or a value at the magnetic axis or plasma boundary.

The [safety factor](name:safety_factor) is the corresponding locus-independent flux-surface quantity; this name specializes it by fixing the evaluation surface. The [rotational transform](name:rotational_transform) uses the reciprocal field-line winding convention, counting poloidal turns per toroidal circuit.

Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal and poloidal flux increments have the same sign, taking $\phi$ as the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $Z$ the vertical height, and the positive poloidal circuit defined by increasing $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$.

Thermal-electron collisional power density is the net local volumetric energy exchange received by the bulk thermal electron population from Coulomb collisions with fast or otherwise non-Maxwellian particle populations.

The quantity is defined by

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_a \sum_o Q_{e,\mathrm{th}\leftarrow a,o}^{\mathrm{coll}}
$$

where $P_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the thermal-electron collisional power density in W m$^{-3}$, $Q_{e,\mathrm{th}\leftarrow a,o}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional energy-transfer rate per unit volume from source population $a$ in orbit class $o$, and the sums include the specified fast populations and orbit classes.

This is the thermal-target component of [electron collisional power density], resolved over classes such as co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped populations. Its volume integral gives [thermal-electron collisional power](name:thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions), while [trapped thermal-electron collisional power density](name:trapped_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions) is one orbit-resolved instance.

Sign convention: Positive when the bulk thermal electron population gains energy from the collision partners.

This quantity is the net Coulomb-collisional energy-transfer rate into the bulk thermal-electron population from fast non-Maxwellian particles. It is the thermal-electron component of [electron power due to collisions], including the represented trapped and passing orbit classes.

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \int_V p_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the volume-integrated power, $p_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local [thermal-electron collisional power density](name:thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions), $V$ is the integration volume, and $\mathbf{x}$ is position. The quantity includes energy received by thermal electrons and excludes the corresponding donor-side energy change represented by [fast-particle collisional power](name:fast_particle_power_due_to_collisions). Positive values denote net heating of the bulk thermal-electron population.

This quantity is the thermal-particle component of [particle power density due to thermalization]: the local rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from a fast or suprathermal population to the specified thermal population.

$$
q_{\mathrm{th}}=\left.\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{th}}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{Coulomb\ thermalization}}
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the transferred power density, in W m$^{-3}$, and $u_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal population's kinetic-energy density. The derivative includes only energy exchange attributable to collisional relaxation toward thermal equilibrium; it excludes direct injection, wave heating, radiation, and other non-thermalization sources. Positive values represent net energy gain by the thermal population.

Thermal plasma energy $W_{th}$ is the internal kinetic energy of the thermal electron and ion populations within the confined plasma. It excludes fast-particle energy and electromagnetic-field energy.

For scalar isotropic thermal pressure, it is defined by

$$
W_{th} = \frac{3}{2} \int_V p_{th}\,dV
$$

where $p_{th}$ is the sum of the thermal electron and ion pressures and $V$ is the confined plasma volume. It is the thermal contribution to [plasma energy].
