Toroidal component of electric current density carried by co-passing fast particles is the $\hat{\phi}$ component, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with $R$ major radius, $\phi$ toroidal angle, $Z$ vertical height, and $\hat{\phi}$ the direction of increasing $\phi$, of the electric current density due directly to fast nonthermal charged particles on co-passing untrapped guiding-center orbits. A co-passing orbit is an untrapped guiding-center orbit whose toroidal circulation is in the co-current direction, the direction of the plasma current.

The kinetic definition at position $\mathbf{r}$ is:

$$
J_{\phi,\mathrm{fast,co}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_s q_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}} v_\phi\, f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $J_{\phi,\mathrm{fast,co}}$ denotes this toroidal co-passing fast current-density component, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, $s$ labels fast-particle species, $q_s$ is the signed electric charge of species $s$, $v_\phi$ is the signed toroidal velocity component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-particle velocity-space distribution for species $s$, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $d^3v$ is the differential volume element in velocity space, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing region of velocity space.

Only the direct current carried by fast particles within $\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}$ is included. Thermal-electron and thermal-ion compensating return currents caused by momentum exchange with fast particles are excluded, as are counter-passing fast particles, trapped fast particles, and unrelated bulk-plasma current. The aggregation is a sum over the represented fast-particle species and over the co-passing velocity-space region; it is not a sum over thermal return-current carriers.

This scalar is the toroidal component of [co-passing fast current density](name:co_passing_fast_current_density). It is distinct from [toroidal co-passing current density](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_current_density), which includes associated electron and thermal-ion return-current terms. The complementary orbit-class components are [toroidal counter-passing fast current density](name:toroidal_counter_passing_fast_current_density) and [toroidal trapped fast current density](name:toroidal_trapped_fast_current_density); their sum with this component gives [toroidal fast-particle current density](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_fast_ion) after applying the same spatial aggregation. A flux-surface-averaged value is the magnetic-flux-surface average of this same direct fast-particle toroidal component and does not change the included particle population.

Sign convention: Positive when the co-passing fast-particle current density flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The toroidal fast-electron collisional torque density is the net rate at which Coulomb scattering transfers toroidal angular momentum per unit volume to the suprathermal electron population. It is the toroidal specialization of [fast-electron torque density due to collisions].

With respect to the toroidal symmetry axis, it is defined from the toroidal collisional force density by

Toroidal fast-ion state torque density due to collisions is the Coulomb-collisional source of mechanical toroidal angular momentum for fast ions in a specified charge state, expressed per unit plasma volume. It is summed over all fast-ion orbit topologies and is associated with the $\phi$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The local kinetic form is the toroidal angular-momentum moment of the collisional operator:

$$
\mathcal{T}_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{(q)} = R\,m_q \int v_\phi \left[\sum_b C_{qb}(f_q, f_b)\right] \, d^3v
$$

where $\mathcal{T}_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{(q)}$ is this torque density for charge state $q$ in N m$^{-2}$, $R$ is major radius in m, $m_q$ is the fast-ion mass in kg, $v_\phi$ is the particle velocity component in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction in m s$^{-1}$, $f_q$ and $f_b$ are fast-ion and background distribution functions normalized to number density with units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, $C_{qb}$ is the Coulomb collision operator for interactions with background population $b$ with units of $f_q$ per second, and $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The integral without $R$ is a toroidal force density in N m$^{-3}$; multiplying by $R$ gives torque per unit volume in N m$^{-2}$.

In practice the quantity is computed by applying Fokker-Planck, Monte Carlo, orbit-following, or transport collision operators to the fast-ion distribution and then taking the toroidal velocity moment for the selected charge state. Experimental analyzes infer it indirectly from fast-ion distribution modeling and toroidal momentum balance, constrained by diagnostics such as neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, gamma-ray emission, charge exchange, or collective scattering. Conceptually, it is the toroidal component of fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions; summing over charge states gives [toroidal_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions), volume integration gives [toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions), and the trapped-orbit contribution is [toroidal_trapped_fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical core magnitudes in beam-heated tokamak plasmas are $10^{-2}$-$10$ N m$^{-2}$. Strongly localized slowing-down or pitch-angle-scattering regions can approach $10$-$100$ N m$^{-2}$, while weak fast-ion populations or outer-plasma regions may be below $10^{-3}$ N m$^{-2}$.

Sign convention: Positive when the collisional torque accelerates the fast-ion charge-state population in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Toroidal fast-particle torque due to collisions is the volume-integrated toroidal torque exerted on the fast, non-thermal particle population by Coulomb collisions with the thermal background plasma. It is the component of collisional angular-momentum transfer about the symmetry axis associated with increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The aggregate torque is defined as the plasma-volume integral of the toroidal collisional force density weighted by the major radius:

$$
T_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \int_V R \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} f_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow j}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $T_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the toroidal fast-particle torque due to collisions, $V$ is the plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, $\mathcal{B}$ is the set of thermal-background collision partners, and $f_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow j}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the toroidal component of the collisional force density exerted on fast, non-thermal particles by partner $j$.

The set $\mathcal{B}$ contains thermal electrons and every thermal ion species and every charge state of each thermal ion species; the ion part is charge-state-summed. This quantity is the aggregate over those collision partners, not an electron-only or charge-state-resolved contribution; the [thermal-electron collision contribution] and the [thermal-ion charge-state collision contribution](name:toroidal_fast_ion_charge_state_torque_due_to_collisions) sum to it when defined over the same volume and fast-particle population. The equal-and-opposite collisional angular-momentum transfer to the thermal background is represented by the [thermal-electron](name:toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions) and [thermal-ion](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_due_to_collisions) reaction channels.

Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb collisions exert a net toroidal force on fast, non-thermal particles in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

T_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \int_V R \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} f_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow j}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $T_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the toroidal fast-particle torque due to collisions, $V$ is the plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, $\mathcal{B}$ is the set of thermal-background collision partners, and $f_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow j}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the toroidal component of the collisional force density exerted on fast, non-thermal particles by partner $j$.

The set $\mathcal{B}$ contains thermal electrons and every thermal ion species and every charge state of each thermal ion species; the ion part is charge-state-summed. This quantity is the aggregate over those collision partners, not an electron-only or charge-state-resolved contribution; the thermal-electron collision contribution and the [thermal-ion charge-state collision contribution](name:toroidal_fast_ion_charge_state_torque_due_to_collisions) sum to it when defined over the same volume and fast-particle population. The equal-and-opposite collisional angular-momentum transfer to the thermal background is represented by the [thermal-electron](name:toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions) and [thermal-ion](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_due_to_collisions) reaction channels.

Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb collisions exert a net toroidal force on fast, non-thermal particles in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Toroidal ion charge-state momentum diffusivity is the scalar kinematic transport coefficient governing diffusive toroidal-arc transport of toroidal momentum carried by ions in a specified ionization state. The toroidal direction is the $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes directional redistribution of toroidal momentum for that charge state through an effective local Fick's-law closure.

For local toroidal arc coordinate $x_\phi$ increasing with $\phi$, the diffusive momentum flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{m,\phi}^{(q)} = -D_{m,\phi}^{(q)} \frac{\partial\left(\rho_q u_\phi^{(q)}\right)}{\partial x_\phi}
$$

where $\Gamma_{m,\phi}^{(q)}$ is the diffusive flux of toroidal momentum carried by charge state $q$, positive in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$; $D_{m,\phi}^{(q)}$ is this diffusivity; $\rho_q$ is the mass density of the specified ion charge state; $u_\phi^{(q)}$ is its toroidal flow-velocity component; and $x_\phi$ is the local toroidal arc coordinate. The leading minus sign specifies down-gradient diffusion of toroidal momentum density.

The quantity is the toroidal directional member of [ion charge-state momentum diffusivity](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity); the matched charge-state-resolved directional members are [parallel ion charge-state momentum diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity), [poloidal ion charge-state momentum diffusivity], [radial ion charge-state momentum diffusivity](name:radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity), and [vertical ion charge-state momentum diffusivity](name:vertical_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity). It is resolved for one ionization state rather than being a density-weighted charge-state aggregate as in [ion momentum diffusivity], and it is a component-specific instance of [momentum diffusivity](name:momentum_diffusivity). It excludes advective momentum flux, external torque density, and off-diagonal tensor couplings.

The toroidal ion rotation frequency is the angular rate of an ion species’ charge-state-averaged bulk rotational motion about the toroidal symmetry axis. It is the toroidal component of [ion rotation frequency].

The frequency is defined from the toroidal bulk velocity as

$$
\Omega_{\phi,i} = \frac{V_{\phi,i}}{R}
$$

where $\Omega_{\phi,i}$ is the toroidal ion rotation frequency, $V_{\phi,i}$ is the toroidal component of the species’ charge-state-averaged bulk velocity, and $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The average is density-weighted over all ionic charge states.

This quantity describes fluid rotational motion rather than charged-particle gyrocenter orbit motion. It is distinct from the charge-state-resolved [toroidal ion charge-state rotation frequency](name:toroidal_ion_charge_state_rotation_frequency).

Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal bulk velocity points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

Toroidal ion torque is the net rate at which explicit momentum sources change the toroidal angular momentum of the total ion population. It is the toroidal component of [ion torque], with contributions summed over all ion species and charge states.

The defining volume integral is

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{ion}} = \int_V R\,\mathcal{S}_{\phi,\mathrm{ion}}\,dV
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{ion}}$ is the toroidal ion torque, $R$ is major radius in m, $\mathcal{S}_{\phi,\mathrm{ion}}$ is the toroidal component of the explicit ion momentum-source density in kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-2}$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, and $V$ is the plasma volume in m$^3$. The quantity is the volume-integrated counterpart of local torque densities such as [toroidal ion charge-state torque density](name:toroidal_ion_charge_state_torque_density) and excludes momentum transport unless represented as an explicit source.

Sign convention: Positive when the explicit sources increase ion angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The toroidal ion torque density is the local rate at which external processes change the angular momentum of the combined ion population about the symmetry axis. It is the toroidal component of the parent [ion torque density], summed over ion species and charge states; internal ion–ion exchanges cancel in this aggregate.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, it is defined from the net external ion force density by

$$
\tau_{\phi,i} = R f_{\phi,i} = R\,\mathbf{f}_i \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,i}$ is the toroidal ion torque density, $R$ is major radius in m, $\mathbf{f}_i$ is the external force density on the combined ion population in N m$^{-3}$, $f_{\phi,i}$ is its toroidal component, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle. Unlike the broader [toroidal torque density](name:toroidal_torque_density), this quantity is restricted to the ion population.

Sign convention: Positive when the external torque increases ion angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

First local tangential coordinate of a point on the closed outline of an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror is the signed scalar projection of the point displacement from the mirror-local origin onto the mirror's first local tangential axis. The mirror-local orthonormal triad $(\hat{\mathbf t}_1, \hat{\mathbf t}_2, \hat{\mathbf n})$ has $\hat{\mathbf t}_1$ and $\hat{\mathbf t}_2$ tangent to the mirror outline plane and $\hat{\mathbf n}$ as the plasma-facing normal. The first local tangential axis $\hat{\mathbf t}_1$ is the more horizontally directed in-plane tangent, oriented toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The coordinate is defined by the Euclidean projection of the outline-point position relative to the mirror-local origin onto the first local tangential unit vector:

$$
\xi_1 = (\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf t}_1
$$

where $\xi_1$ is the first local tangential coordinate of the mirror outline point, $\mathbf r$ is the position vector of the outline point, $\mathbf r_0$ is the mirror-local origin, and $\hat{\mathbf t}_1$ is the first local tangential unit vector.

This coordinate is paired with the [second local tangential coordinate of the electron-cyclotron launcher mirror](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror), which uses $\hat{\mathbf t}_2$ in the same mirror-local tangential plane. The second local tangential direction is fixed by $\hat{\mathbf t}_2 = \hat{\mathbf n} \times \hat{\mathbf t}_1$, so $\hat{\mathbf t}_1 \times \hat{\mathbf t}_2 = \hat{\mathbf n}$. This local coordinate is distinct from locating the mirror in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame through quantities such as the [radial centroid of the electron-cyclotron launcher mirror] and the [vertical coordinate of the electron-cyclotron launcher mirror](name:vertical_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror).

Sign convention: Positive when the displacement from the mirror-local origin to the outline point has a component in the direction of $\hat{\mathbf t}_1$.

Toroidal component, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, of the krypton ion bulk-flow velocity at the magnetic axis is the charge-state-aggregated krypton velocity projected along $\hat{\phi}$. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and the magnetic axis is the innermost closed-flux-surface locus where the gradient of [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) vanishes.

The charge-state-aggregated toroidal velocity at this locus is defined by projecting the density-weighted krypton velocity onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Kr},0} =
\left.
\left(
\frac{\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}\,\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}}{\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}}
\right)
\right|_{\mathrm{axis}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $q$ indexes krypton ionization charge states, $n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}$ is the number density of charge state $q$, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}$ is its bulk-flow velocity, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, and the subscript $0$ denotes evaluation at the magnetic axis.

This is an intensive species velocity: krypton charge-state velocities are combined as a density-weighted mean over all ionization states, not as a sum. It is distinct from [flux-surface-averaged toroidal krypton velocity at the plasma boundary] and from local toroidal krypton velocities at the [internal transport barrier](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [pedestal top](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_pedestal_top).

Sign convention: Positive when the krypton velocity component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Toroidal neutral torque density is the local source of plasma angular momentum about the machine symmetry axis produced by momentum exchange with neutral particles. It is aggregated over all neutral internal states and is distinct from the state-resolved quantity [toroidal neutral internal-state torque density](name:toroidal_neutral_internal_state_torque_density).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, it is defined by

$$
\tau_{\phi,n}(R,\phi,Z) = R\sum_s \mathcal{R}_{\phi,n,s}(R,\phi,Z)
$$

where $R$ is major radius in m, $s$ indexes neutral internal states, and $\mathcal{R}_{\phi,n,s}$ is the toroidal component of the momentum-exchange force density from state $s$. The sum gives the neutral contribution to the parent [neutral torque density].

Sign convention: Positive when neutral momentum exchange increases plasma angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

Toroidal component of the oxygen ion bulk velocity at an internal transport barrier is the component of the oxygen bulk-flow velocity along the toroidal basis direction at the radial location of the internal transport barrier. The toroidal direction is $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For species-level oxygen, the velocity is the density-weighted mean over all oxygen charge states:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{O}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}}) = \frac{\sum_q n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}})\,\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}})\cdot\hat{\phi}}{\sum_q n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}})}
$$

where $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the radial location of the internal transport barrier, $q$ indexes oxygen charge states, $n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}}$ is the number density of oxygen charge state $q$, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}}$ is its bulk velocity, and $\hat{\phi}$ points toward increasing toroidal angle.

This quantity is a local toroidal component at the internal-transport-barrier locus, not a flux-surface average or a boundary value. This quantity is the total toroidal linear momentum carried by electrons and all ion species within the volume enclosed by a closed magnetic flux surface as that surface approaches the magnetic axis. It is a linear-momentum projection, not toroidal angular momentum.

$$
P_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}} = \lim_{\psi\to\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}} \int_{V(\psi)} \sum_s m_s n_s v_{s,\phi}\,dV
$$

Here $P_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the limiting toroidal momentum, $\psi$ is a flux-surface label, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is its magnetic-axis value, $V(\psi)$ is the enclosed volume, $m_s$ is the mass of species $s$, $n_s$ is its number density, $v_{s,\phi}$ is its toroidal velocity component, and $dV$ is the volume element. The sum includes electrons and ions and excludes neutral species. Its aggregation and projection match [toroidal total plasma momentum](name:toroidal_total_plasma_momentum), while the corresponding boundary quantity is [toroidal total plasma momentum at plasma boundary].

Sign convention: Positive when the net enclosed momentum points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the flux-surface-averaged toroidal component of torque density transferred to a specified particle population by the magnetic Lorentz force associated with its current contribution. The toroidal direction is \(\hat{\phi}\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame, where \(R\) is major radius, \(\phi\) is toroidal angle, and \(Z\) is vertical height.

Toroidal component of the local collisional angular-momentum transfer density to trapped thermal electrons is the volume density of toroidal angular momentum delivered to that receiving population by Coulomb collisions. The trapped qualifier identifies thermal electrons whose guiding-center orbits are trapped; it does not restrict the collision partner.

The torque density is the major-radius lever arm multiplying the toroidal collisional force-density moment of the trapped thermal-electron distribution:

$$
\tau_{\phi,e,\mathrm{th,tr}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = R(\mathbf{x})\,m_e \int v_\phi\, C_{e,\mathrm{th,tr}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{v};\mathbf{x})\, d^3v
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,e,\mathrm{th,tr}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is this torque density, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $R$ is major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $m_e$ is electron mass, $v_\phi$ is the velocity component along $\hat{\phi}$, and $C_{e,\mathrm{th,tr}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collision-operator contribution to the evolution of the trapped thermal-electron distribution.

This quantity includes collisional momentum exchange with all collision partners. The electron-electron partner contribution is [toroidal trapped thermal electron torque density due to Coulomb collisions with electrons]; together with the co-passing and counter-passing thermal-electron orbit-class contributions it forms the orbit-class decomposition of [toroidal thermal electron torque density due to collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions). It is distinct from the corresponding ion charge-state quantity [toroidal trapped thermal ion charge state torque density due to collisions](name:toroidal_trapped_thermal_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

Second local tangential coordinate of a hard X-ray detector is the signed scalar coordinate of a detector outline vertex along the detector-local second tangential direction. It is defined in the right-handed object-local Cartesian basis $(\hat{\mathbf e}_1, \hat{\mathbf e}_2, \hat{\mathbf e}_3)$, where $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ is the first local tangential unit vector, $\hat{\mathbf e}_3$ is the detector-local normal unit vector, and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2 = \hat{\mathbf e}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf e}_1$.

The coordinate $q_2$ of a vertex at position $\mathbf r$ is the signed projection of its displacement from the detector-local origin:

$$
q_2 = (\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf e}_2
$$

where $\mathbf r_0$ is the detector-local origin and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ is the second local tangential unit vector.

Only the component along $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ is included. The companion coordinate along $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ is the [first local tangential coordinate of a hard X-ray detector]; neither quantity is a radial, toroidal, or vertical component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Sign convention: Positive when the vertex displacement from the detector-local origin is toward $\hat{\mathbf e}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf e}_1$.

Volume-integrated net power transferred to the ion population by a specified plasma source or sink is the net rate at which that source term changes the energy of ions within the confined plasma. It is source-indexed and species-summed: one value corresponds to one specified source or sink term and aggregates over all ion species.

For a source or sink labeled $s$, the total ion power $P_{i,s}$ is defined by integrating the species-resolved local ion power density over the confined plasma volume:

$$
P_{i,s} = \sum_a \int_{V_c} q_{i,a}^{(s)}(\mathbf{x}) \, dV
$$

where $a$ indexes ion species, $q_{i,a}^{(s)}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local volumetric power density transferred by source term $s$ to ion species $a$ at position $\mathbf{x}$, $dV$ is the volume element, and $V_c$ is the confined plasma volume.

Energy transferred directly to electrons is excluded; the electron-channel counterpart is [electron deposited power](name:electron_deposited_power). Sink terms are retained with their sign, so the quantity is distinct from [total ion heating power](name:total_ion_heating_power), which includes only energy gain by ions. Summing $P_{i,s}$ over a complete set of source and sink terms gives the corresponding contribution to [ion power]; [deposited power] is the related source-resolved transferred-power concept without the all-ion population restriction.

Sign convention: Positive when the specified source term transfers net energy to the ion population.

The total ion pressure is the isotropic scalar pressure of the entire ion fluid at a given point in the plasma, combining the Maxwellian thermal bulk and suprathermal fast-ion contributions summed over all charge states of the species. It represents the physically complete ion kinetic pressure entering force-balance and energy-transport equations in multi-fluid and magnetohydrodynamic models.

The total ion pressure decomposes additively as:

$$
P_i = P_{i,\mathrm{th}} + P_{i,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $P_{i,\mathrm{th}}$ is the [thermal ion pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) from the Maxwellian bulk, satisfying $P_{i,\mathrm{th}} = n_i k_B T_i$ with $n_i$ the ion number density and $T_i$ the ion temperature, and $P_{i,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the suprathermal fast-ion contribution. The [total thermal ion pressure](name:total_thermal_ion_pressure) isolates the bulk-only term; the [total ion state pressure] provides per-charge-state resolution.

Together with [total electron pressure](name:total_electron_pressure), the total ion pressure contributes to the full plasma pressure $P = P_e + P_i$ appearing in the MHD force-balance $\nabla P = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$. Fast-ion contributions can become comparable to or exceed the thermal term during neutral beam injection or ion cyclotron resonance heating. The quantity is inferred by combining ion temperature and density profile diagnostics with energetic-particle measurements and fast-ion transport modeling.

Sign convention: Positive when the ion population has nonzero kinetic energy, which holds for all physical ion populations; scalar ion pressure is an intrinsically non-negative quantity.

The [total thermal ion pressure](name:total_thermal_ion_pressure) isolates the bulk-only term; the total ion state pressure provides per-charge-state resolution.

Together with [total electron pressure](name:total_electron_pressure), the total ion pressure contributes to the full plasma pressure $P = P_e + P_i$ appearing in the MHD force-balance $\nabla P = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$. Fast-ion contributions can become comparable to or exceed the thermal term during neutral beam injection or ion cyclotron resonance heating. The quantity is inferred by combining ion temperature and density profile diagnostics with energetic-particle measurements and fast-ion transport modeling.

Sign convention: Positive when the ion population has nonzero kinetic energy, which holds for all physical ion populations; scalar ion pressure is an intrinsically non-negative quantity.

Total neutral density is the local number density of electrically neutral atoms and molecules in the fully aggregated neutral population. It shares the unresolved population scope of [neutral density](name:neutral_density) and makes explicit that neutral species, kinetic-population, internal-state, and parent-ion-associated labels are summed out. It is a pointwise volumetric particle density, not a flux-surface-averaged or volume-averaged quantity unless an averaging operation is part of the named quantity.

The local total neutral density is defined by the total neutral particle count per volume element:

$$
n_0^{\mathrm{tot}} = \frac{dN_0^{\mathrm{tot}}}{dV} = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathcal{P}_0^{\mathrm{tot}}} n_\alpha
$$

where $n_0^{\mathrm{tot}}$ is total neutral density, $N_0^{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the number of neutral particles in the infinitesimal volume element $dV$, $\mathcal{P}_0^{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the set of non-overlapping neutral population classes included in the total, and $n_\alpha$ is the local density of class $\alpha$.

For this total name, $\mathcal{P}_0^{\mathrm{tot}}$ includes neutral atomic and molecular species, thermal and suprathermal kinetic populations, internal quantum states, and parent-ion-associated neutral states that are not retained as separate labels. For a non-overlapping partition into thermal, suprathermal, and parent-ion-associated components, the population-class sum recovers the sum of those component densities; [thermal neutral density](name:thermal_neutral_density) and [suprathermal neutral density](name:fast_neutral_density) retain the first two kinetic restrictions, while [ion neutral density] retains association with a specified parent ion species. The total excludes ions and electrons; [neutral internal-state density](name:neutral_internal_state_density) retains an internal-state label, and [volume-averaged neutral species density](name:volume_averaged_neutral_species_density) applies an averaging and species resolution not present in this pointwise total.

Total neutron power is the kinetic-energy loss rate carried away from the plasma by fusion-born neutrons. It is the branch-summed form of [neutron power], excluding energy transported by charged fusion products and energy deposited within the plasma.

$$
P_n^{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}_n} \dot{N}_r\,\langle E_{n,r}\rangle
$$

where $P_n^{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total neutron power, $\mathcal{R}_n$ is the set of neutron-producing fusion reaction branches, $\dot{N}_r$ is the neutron production rate for branch $r$, and $\langle E_{n,r}\rangle$ is the mean kinetic energy per emitted neutron in that branch. Neutrons are uncharged and therefore are not confined by the magnetic field; their carried-away energy is distinct from plasma-deposited charged-product power.

Trapped fast-electron collisional power density is the local volumetric energy exchange assigned to the trapped guiding-center component of the suprathermal, non-Maxwellian electron population during Coulomb collisions with electron collision partners.

For the electron-collision channel, the quantity is defined by

$$
P_{fe,t\leftarrow e}^{\mathrm{coll}} = Q_{fe,t\leftarrow e}^{\mathrm{coll}}
$$

where $P_{fe,t\leftarrow e}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the trapped fast-electron collisional power density, $Q_{fe,t\leftarrow e}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the energy-transfer rate from the electron collision-partner population to the trapped fast-electron target, $fe$ denotes the suprathermal fast-electron population, $t$ denotes its trapped orbit class, $e$ denotes the electron collision partner, and $\mathrm{coll}$ denotes the Coulomb-collision channel.

The quantity is restricted to the trapped orbit class and to collisions with electron partners. It is local and volumetric, with no aggregation over co-passing or counter-passing orbit classes and no aggregation over other collision-partner channels.

It excludes the collisional energy exchange assigned to the bulk thermal-electron target and to passing fast-electron orbit classes. It is distinct from [trapped fast-ion collisional power density](name:trapped_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions), which concerns a fast-ion target population.

This trapped, electron-partner contribution forms one component of [fast-electron collisional power density], whose aggregate combines the represented fast-electron orbit classes and collision-partner channels. The corresponding counter-passing quantity, [counter-passing fast-electron collisional power density](name:counter_passing_fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions), has the same collision-partner and target-population definition but resolves the counter-passing orbit class instead.

Sign convention: Positive when the trapped fast-electron population gains energy from the electron collision partners.

Trapped fast-particle pressure is the scalar trace pressure carried by suprathermal particles on trapped guiding-center orbits. It is the trapped-orbit contribution to [fast-particle pressure], complementary to the field-aligned [parallel trapped fast-particle pressure](name:parallel_trapped_fast_particle_pressure) and transverse [perpendicular trapped fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_trapped_fast_particle_pressure).

The flux-surface-averaged pressure is defined by the trapped-particle second velocity moment:

$$
P_{\mathrm{tr,fast}}(\psi) = \left\langle \frac{1}{3}\sum_s m_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{tr},s}(\mathbf{x})} v^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v \right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $\psi$ labels the magnetic flux surface, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes its flux-surface average, $s$ labels fast-particle species, $m_s$ is particle mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is particle speed in m s$^{-1}$, $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the distribution function, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{tr},s}$ contains only trapped guiding-center orbits. The factor one-third gives the scalar trace; with the same orbit selection, $P_{\mathrm{tr,fast}}=(P_{\parallel,\mathrm{tr,fast}}+2P_{\perp,\mathrm{tr,fast}})/3$. Co-passing and counter-passing populations are excluded.

Trapped power density is the flux-surface-averaged rate at which energy is transferred to or from the trapped orbit population per unit physical volume. It is the orbit-class specialization of [power density] for particles whose parallel motion reverses at magnetic mirror points, so their guiding-center orbits bounce rather than circulate toroidally.

For a magnetic flux surface, the flux-surface-averaged trapped power density is defined by

$$
p_{\mathrm{tr}} = \left\langle \frac{dE_{\mathrm{tr}}}{dt\,dV} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{fs}}
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{tr}}$ is the trapped power density, $E_{\mathrm{tr}}$ is the energy transferred to the trapped orbit population, $t$ is time, $V$ is physical volume, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{fs}}$ denotes a flux-surface average over that magnetic flux surface.

The scope is the trapped part of the particle distribution, with contributions from applicable heating and collisional energy-transfer processes. The aggregation convention is a net source term over those processes for the trapped orbit population on the flux surface; it is not a diagnostic-specific estimate, a point value before flux-surface averaging, or a total stored energy.

It excludes passing-orbit populations: [co-passing power density](name:co_passing_power_density) resolves particles circulating in the co-current direction, and [counter-passing power density](name:counter_passing_power_density) resolves particles circulating opposite to that direction. Together, trapped, co-passing, and counter-passing orbit-class power densities partition the orbit-resolved contribution to [net plasma power density] when defined for the same particle population and energy channels.

Sign convention: Positive when energy is transferred to the trapped orbit population.

Particle number density of tritium ions at the internal transport barrier is the local number density of tritium ions on the flux surface selected as the barrier reference location. The internal transport barrier is a confined-plasma region where effective cross-field transport is locally reduced, allowing steep density gradients to form and persist.

The local tritium-ion density $n_T$ at the ITB reference surface is the zeroth velocity moment of the charge-state-resolved distribution functions:

$$
n_T(\rho_\mathrm{ITB}) = \sum_Z \int f_{T,Z}(\mathbf{v}, \rho_\mathrm{ITB})\,d^3v
$$

where $Z$ labels tritium ion charge states, $f_{T,Z}$ is the corresponding velocity distribution, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$ identifies the ITB flux surface in coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. This quantity is summed over all tritium ion charge states and excludes neutral tritium. It is the tritium-specific counterpart of [ion density at the internal transport barrier] and contributes to the species-agnostic [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

Neutral-state velocity due to diamagnetic drift is a signed scalar component or projection of the particle-flow velocity assigned to a specified neutral atomic or molecular state and attributed to the diamagnetic, pressure-gradient part of transport. For an uncharged neutral state, it denotes an effective contribution in a modeled velocity decomposition rather than a direct single-particle Lorentz-force drift. This parent concept generalizes component refinements such as radial, toroidal, vertical, poloidal, and [field-parallel](name:parallel_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) projections.

For any requested component direction $\alpha$, the scalar component is the projection of the effective neutral-state diamagnetic velocity vector onto that direction:

$$
v_{a,\alpha}^{\mathrm{dia}} = \mathbf{e}_{\alpha} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{a}^{\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $a$ labels the neutral state, $\mathbf{v}_{a}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the effective diamagnetic velocity contribution for that state, and $\mathbf{e}_{\alpha}$ is the unit vector defining the selected component. Examples include $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, or $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; a unit vector tangent to increasing $\theta$ in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$; or $\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ for a field-parallel projection. The equation defines the scalar component and does not impose a particular closure for the effective neutral-state diamagnetic velocity vector.

In practice this quantity is computed within neutral transport, edge-fluid, or kinetic-fluid models from the model's decomposition of neutral-state velocity into transport contributions. It is not normally isolated by a direct diagnostic measurement; observations such as spectroscopy or neutral-particle measurements constrain the broader neutral-state transport model. The corresponding momentum contribution is [neutral-state momentum due to diamagnetic drift], while state-aggregated counterparts include [neutral velocity due to diamagnetic drift] and [neutral momentum due to diamagnetic drift].

No universal numerical range is implied by this quantity name. Magnitudes depend on the selected neutral state, pressure-gradient scale length, magnetic geometry, collisional coupling, and the component direction, so values should be interpreted together with the same model's other neutral-state velocity contributions. Charged-particle analogs include [ion-state diamagnetic velocity due to diamagnetic drift](name:ion_state_diamagnetic_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [ion-charge-state diamagnetic velocity due to diamagnetic drift](name:ion_charge_state_diamagnetic_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

Sign convention: Positive when the selected component or projection points along its named positive direction: $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame for radial, toroidal, or vertical components; increasing $\theta$ in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ for a poloidal component; or $\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ for a field-parallel projection.

Parallel neutral-state velocity due to diamagnetic drift is the signed field-aligned component of particle-flow velocity assigned to a specified neutral atomic or molecular state and attributed to the diamagnetic, pressure-gradient part of transport. For an uncharged neutral state, it is an effective contribution in a modeled velocity decomposition rather than a direct single-particle Lorentz-force drift.

The parallel component is the projection of the effective neutral-state diamagnetic velocity onto the local magnetic-field direction:

$$
v_{a,\parallel}^{\mathrm{dia}} = \mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{a}^{\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $v_{a,\parallel}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the parallel diamagnetic-drift velocity component of neutral state $a$, $\mathbf{v}_{a}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is that state's effective diamagnetic velocity vector, and $\mathbf{b}$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic-field vector.

This quantity applies locally to one specified neutral species and one specified atomic or molecular internal state. It retains that state identity and is not summed over neutral species or internal states; it also excludes the total neutral velocity and velocity contributions attributed to other transport mechanisms. The effective diamagnetic contribution is not a direct force-driven drift of the uncharged neutral particle.

This is the field-aligned specialization of [neutral-state velocity due to diamagnetic drift]. It is distinguished from the [poloidal neutral-state velocity due to diamagnetic drift](name:poloidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), which projects the same state-specific contribution onto the poloidal direction rather than along the magnetic field.

Sign convention: Positive when the effective neutral-state diamagnetic velocity points along the local magnetic-field vector.

The parallel neutral-state velocity due to the $E\times B$ drift is the scalar component, along the local magnetic-field direction, of the velocity contribution labeled as $E\times B$ drift for a selected neutral species state. The drift itself is species independent; the neutral-state label identifies the population to which this velocity contribution is assigned. A pure $E\times B$ drift is exactly perpendicular to the magnetic field, so its physical parallel projection vanishes.

For neutral-state label $n$, the defining projection is

$$
v_{\parallel,E\times B}^{(n)} = \hat{\mathbf{b}}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{E\times B}^{(n)} = \hat{\mathbf{b}}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}}{B^2} = 0
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field in V.m^-1, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $B=|\mathbf{B}|$, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/B$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the magnetic field, and the superscript $n$ labels the neutral species state rather than a power. The scalar $v_{\parallel,E\times B}^{(n)}$ has unit m.s^-1. The final equality follows from the vector identity $\mathbf{B}\cdot(\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B})=0$.

The quantity is normally computed from electric-field or electrostatic-potential estimates together with the local magnetic field, followed by projection along $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$. Nonzero values for this pure contribution are interpreted as numerical residuals, field-projection inconsistencies, or an explicitly documented model-decomposition convention, not as a physical drift along the magnetic field caused by magnetic geometry.

The expected physical value is 0 m.s^-1. In practical calculations, any nonzero residual should be small compared with the related [radial](name:radial_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift), [poloidal](name:poloidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift), and [toroidal](name:toroidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) components of [neutral-state velocity due to E cross B drift](name:neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift); no universal residual range is meaningful because it depends on the numerical and modeling procedure. The analogous ion quantity is [parallel ion-state velocity due to E cross B drift].

Sign convention: Positive when the component is directed along the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

In practical calculations, any nonzero residual should be small compared with the related [radial](name:radial_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift), [poloidal](name:poloidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift), and [toroidal](name:toroidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) components of [neutral-state velocity due to E cross B drift](name:neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift); no universal residual range is meaningful because it depends on the numerical and modeling procedure. The analogous ion quantity is parallel ion-state velocity due to E cross B drift.

Sign convention: Positive when the component is directed along the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

The volume-averaged neon density is the mean elemental neon number density over the plasma volume. It includes neutral neon and all neon ionization states, extending the local definition of [neon density] to a spatial average.

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Ne}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V}\int_V n_{\mathrm{Ne}}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $V$ is the plasma volume, $dV$ is a volume element, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, and $n_{\mathrm{Ne}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local neon number density summed over all ionization states. The volume integral represents the total neon inventory divided by the plasma volume. This quantity provides the numerator in the [neon abundance ratio](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_neon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density), which additionally normalizes it to the volume-averaged electron density.

The radial diamagnetic current density is the projection of the total [diamagnetic current density] onto the local radial direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It arises from the differential ion and electron guiding-center drifts produced by a pressure gradient in a magnetized plasma.

The radial component is defined by projecting the diamagnetic current-density vector:

$$
j_R = \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} \cdot \hat{R} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p}{B^2}\right) \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $j_R$ and $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia}$ are current densities, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $p$ is the total scalar plasma pressure, $B=|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic-field magnitude, and $\hat{R}$ is the radial unit vector. The quantity is the radial projection only; it excludes non-diamagnetic current contributions and differs from the [vertical diamagnetic current density](name:vertical_diamagnetic_current_density) through its projection axis. The radial direction is the increasing-major-radius direction, not generally the normal to a magnetic flux surface.

Sign convention: Positive when $j_R$ points in the $+R$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The ion energy diffusion coefficient $D_{i,E}$ quantifies gradient-driven diffusive transport of thermal energy carried by the ion population, providing the Fick's-law proportionality between the density-normalized diffusive ion heat flux and the local ion temperature gradient. It is the ion-population specialization of the general [energy diffusion coefficient](name:energy_diffusion_coefficient) and is distinct from convective or $E \times B$ contributions to the total ion heat flux. As an intensive species-level coefficient, the total-ion value is the density-weighted mean over all ion species and charge states; [ion charge-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:ion_charge_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient) denotes the corresponding coefficient for a specified ion charge state.

The defining Fickian relation for the diffusive ion thermal-energy flux $\mathbf{Q}_{i,\mathrm{diff}}$ is:

$$
\mathbf{Q}_{i,\mathrm{diff}} = - n_i D_{i,E} \nabla T_i
$$

where $\mathbf{Q}_{i,\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive ion thermal-energy flux, $n_i$ is the total ion number density, $D_{i,E}$ is the ion energy diffusion coefficient, $T_i$ is the total-ion temperature expressed as thermal energy per ion, and $\nabla T_i$ is its spatial gradient. For ion species and charge-state components indexed by $a$, $n_i = \sum_a n_a$, $T_i = \sum_a n_a T_a / n_i$, and the intensive aggregation convention for component coefficients $D_{a,E}$ is $D_{i,E} = \sum_a n_a D_{a,E}/n_i$. The leading minus sign encodes down-gradient Fickian diffusion: for positive $D_{i,E}$, the diffusive flux points opposite to $\nabla T_i$.

This name is direction-agnostic. [Radial ion energy diffusion coefficient] denotes the cylindrical $\hat{R}$ projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and [poloidal ion energy diffusion coefficient] denotes the projection tangent to the poloidal direction in the $(R, Z)$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is distinct from [energy diffusivity], which uses a thermal-energy-density gradient rather than the ion-temperature gradient, and from effective diffusivity names that combine diffusive and convective heat transport.

The ion-state energy diffusion coefficient is the charge-state-resolved Fickian transport coefficient relating the diffusive thermal energy flux for a specific ion population to the local temperature gradient. It is the ion-charge-state-specific instance of [energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:energy_diffusion_coefficient), enabling separate treatment of individual ionization stages of impurity species and main fuel ions rather than aggregating over all charge states.

For a given charge state $s$, the diffusive energy flux $\vec{q}_{E,s}$ satisfies:

$$
\vec{q}_{E,s} = -D_{E,s} \nabla T_s
$$

where $D_{E,s}$ is the energy diffusion coefficient for that charge state and $T_s$ is the corresponding ion temperature.

This quantity is the parent over direction-projected components: cross-field transport across flux surfaces (radial), edge-plasma diffusion in the poloidal direction as represented by the [poloidal ion-state energy diffusion coefficient], and field-aligned conduction along magnetic field lines. In magnetized fusion plasmas the transport is strongly anisotropic: cross-field values in the edge plasma span 0.1–10 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, while field-aligned values exceed these by several orders of magnitude. The charge-state resolution distinguishes this coefficient from aggregate formulations such as radial_total_energy_diffusion_coefficient, which combines contributions across all charge states.

Magnetic shear at an internal transport barrier is the local magnetic shear evaluated on the flux surface identified as the internal-transport-barrier location. It characterizes the radial variation of field-line pitch through the safety factor at that locus.

The defining relation is

$$
s_{\mathrm{ITB}} = \left.\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}{q}\frac{d q}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}\right|_{\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}=\rho_{\mathrm{tor,ITB}}}
$$

where $s_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the magnetic shear at the internal transport barrier, $q$ is the [safety factor](name:safety_factor), $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the [normalized toroidal flux radius] used as an outward flux-surface radial coordinate, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,ITB}}$ is the value of that coordinate at the internal-transport-barrier location.

The scope is the local value at the internal-transport-barrier flux surface in a magnetically confined plasma. It is not an average over the barrier width, not the position or width of the barrier, and not the [magnetic shear at the pedestal top] or another named flux-surface locus. Its aggregation convention is a single flux-surface evaluation with no averaging over neighboring flux surfaces.

This quantity is a locus-specific specialization of [magnetic shear at a flux surface](name:magnetic_shear_at_flux_surface): it uses the same normalized logarithmic safety-factor derivative, with the flux-surface label fixed to the internal-transport-barrier location. The derivative is local in $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$, so the quantity represents the local radial slope of $q$ rather than an integral measure across the barrier.

Sign convention: Positive when the safety-factor gradient with respect to increasing outward $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ has the same sign as the safety factor at the internal transport barrier.

The neutral energy diffusion coefficient $D_{n,E}$ quantifies gradient-driven diffusive transport of thermal energy carried by the neutral particle population, providing the Fick's-law proportionality between the density-normalized diffusive neutral heat flux and the local neutral temperature gradient. It is the neutral-population specialization of the [energy diffusion coefficient](name:energy_diffusion_coefficient) and is distinct from convective or other non-diffusive contributions to the total neutral heat flux.

The defining relation for the density-normalized diffusive neutral heat flux $\mathbf{q}_{n,\mathrm{diff}}$ is:

$$
\mathbf{q}_{n,\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{n,E}\,\nabla T_n
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_{n,\mathrm{diff}}$ is the density-normalized diffusive heat flux carried by neutral particles, $D_{n,E}$ is the neutral energy diffusion coefficient, and $T_n$ is the [neutral temperature](name:neutral_temperature). The minus sign denotes transport down the local neutral temperature gradient.

This quantity applies to the aggregated neutral particle population, not to electrons, ions, or ion charge states. When neutral internal states are resolved, the aggregate coefficient is the density-weighted mean over those internal states; it is not a sum and it is not a neutral charge-state quantity. As a direction-agnostic scalar parent, it does not select the cylindrical radial component along $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame or the poloidal component in an $(R,Z)$ cross-section of that frame.

The [neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient) is the state-resolved counterpart for a specified neutral internal state, while [radial neutral energy diffusion coefficient] and [poloidal neutral energy diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient) are directional component specializations of this parent. Direction-agnostic charged-particle analogs are the [electron energy diffusion coefficient](name:electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient) and the [ion energy diffusion coefficient](name:ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient). The [energy effective diffusivity] is separate because it folds diffusive and convective effects into an effective transport parameter.

Vertical component of the Pfirsch-Schlueter neoclassical current density is the signed projection of the local [Pfirsch-Schlueter current density](name:pfirsch_schlueter_current_density) vector onto the $+\hat{Z}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the vertical contribution to the neoclassical return current that restores current continuity when the pressure-gradient [diamagnetic current density] has finite divergence in toroidal magnetic geometry. The underlying vector is a contribution to [current density](name:current_density) and is predominantly aligned with the magnetic field before this scalar projection is taken.

The component is defined by the vector projection:

$$
J_{\mathrm{PS},Z} = \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{PS}}\cdot\hat{Z}
$$

where $J_{\mathrm{PS},Z}$ is the vertical Pfirsch-Schlueter current density, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{PS}}$ is the [Pfirsch-Schlueter current density](name:pfirsch_schlueter_current_density), and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is a component of the Pfirsch-Schlueter return current, not the [diamagnetic current density] whose divergence it closes, and it excludes bootstrap, Ohmic, and externally driven current-density contributions. It is distinct from the cylindrical co-projections [radial Pfirsch-Schlueter current density](name:radial_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density) and [toroidal Pfirsch-Schlueter current density](name:toroidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density), and from the [poloidal Pfirsch-Schlueter current density](name:poloidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density) and [parallel Pfirsch-Schlueter current density](name:parallel_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density). The token `vertical` denotes projection along $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; it is not a flux-surface-normal projection.

Sign convention: Positive when the Pfirsch-Schlueter current-density vector has a component in the direction of increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Thermal neutral pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure of the thermal neutral-particle population. It is the isotropic part of the central second velocity moment about the mean thermal-neutral flow and includes neutral internal states unless pressure is explicitly resolved by state.

For the thermal neutral distribution function $f_{n,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})$, the pressure tensor and scalar pressure are defined by:

$$
\mathbf{P}_{n,\mathrm{th}} = m_n \int (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{n,\mathrm{th}})(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{n,\mathrm{th}}) f_{n,\mathrm{th}}\,d^3v,\qquad p_{n,\mathrm{th}} = \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{P}_{n,\mathrm{th}}
$$

where $m_n$ is neutral particle mass in kg, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{u}_{n,\mathrm{th}}$ are particle and mean-flow velocities in m s$^{-1}$, and $\operatorname{tr}$ denotes the tensor trace.

Unlike [neutral pressure], this quantity excludes the suprathermal contribution represented by [fast neutral pressure](name:fast_neutral_pressure). A selected internal-state contribution is represented by [thermal neutral internal-state pressure](name:thermal_neutral_internal_state_pressure), while [total neutral pressure](name:total_neutral_pressure) includes both thermal and fast populations.

The partial time derivative $\partial\psi/\partial t$ of the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) $\psi$ quantifies how rapidly the flux profile changes at each flux-surface label as the plasma current profile evolves. It is the central time-advance term in the poloidal flux diffusion equation, governing the resistive-timescale evolution of the current density and safety-factor profile. Because $\psi$ depends on the chosen radial flux coordinate, the partial time derivative is strictly defined only with that coordinate held fixed; the sibling [time_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_constant_toroidal_flux](name:time_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux) makes this explicit by constraining differentiation to constant toroidal flux $\Phi$.

By Faraday's law, $\partial\psi/\partial t$ equals the negative circulation of the toroidal electric field around the corresponding flux contour:

$$
\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t} = -\oint_C \mathbf{E}\cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell}
$$

where $C$ is the closed toroidal circuit at flux-surface label $r$ and $d\boldsymbol{\ell}$ is oriented in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. In resistive MHD, this loop electromotive force is balanced by the parallel resistive response and non-inductive current-drive source terms, yielding the parabolic flux diffusion equation that self-consistently evolves the current profile alongside the [radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux).

This quantity is computed numerically within transport solvers by finite-differencing $\psi$ between successive time steps at fixed grid points in the chosen radial coordinate. Typical magnitudes range from $\sim 10^{-3}$ V during quasi-steady operation to $\sim 1$ V during current ramp-up phases.

Sign convention: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ increases with time at the given flux-surface label.

The partial time derivative $\partial\psi/\partial t$ of the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) $\psi$ quantifies how rapidly the flux profile changes at each flux-surface label as the plasma current profile evolves. It is the central time-advance term in the poloidal flux diffusion equation, governing the resistive-timescale evolution of the current density and safety-factor profile. Because $\psi$ depends on the chosen radial flux coordinate, the partial time derivative is strictly defined only with that coordinate held fixed; the sibling time_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_constant_toroidal_flux makes this explicit by constraining differentiation to constant toroidal flux $\Phi$.

By Faraday's law, $\partial\psi/\partial t$ equals the negative circulation of the toroidal electric field around the corresponding flux contour:

$$
\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t} = -\oint_C \mathbf{E}\cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell}
$$

where $C$ is the closed toroidal circuit at flux-surface label $r$ and $d\boldsymbol{\ell}$ is oriented in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. In resistive MHD, this loop electromotive force is balanced by the parallel resistive response and non-inductive current-drive source terms, yielding the parabolic flux diffusion equation that self-consistently evolves the current profile alongside the [radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux).

This quantity is computed numerically within transport solvers by finite-differencing $\psi$ between successive time steps at fixed grid points in the chosen radial coordinate. Typical magnitudes range from $\sim 10^{-3}$ V during quasi-steady operation to $\sim 1$ V during current ramp-up phases.

Sign convention: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ increases with time at the given flux-surface label.

Number density of free electrons per physical volume for the complete local electron population is the local continuum count density of electrons not bound to atoms, molecules, or ions, including both thermal and fast nonthermal contributions.

The complete local electron density is defined by:

$$
n_e^{\mathrm{total}} = n_e^{\mathrm{thermal}} + n_e^{\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $n_e^{\mathrm{total}}$ is the complete local free-electron number density, $n_e^{\mathrm{thermal}}$ is the density of the local thermal electron population represented by [thermal electron density](name:thermal_electron_density), and $n_e^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the density of the local fast, nonthermal electron population represented by [fast electron density](name:fast_electron_density).

This quantity applies locally to the full free-electron population and is aggregated over its thermal and fast components. It excludes electrons bound in atoms, molecules, or ions, and it is not restricted to either population component. It is also distinct from [line-averaged electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density) and [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), which apply spatial averaging rather than a local evaluation.

As the complete-population form of [electron density](name:electron_density), it includes both thermal and nonthermal contributions. Integrating this local quantity over a specified plasma volume gives [volume-integrated total electron density], whereas the component names retain only one electron population.

Total neutral pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure of the complete neutral-particle population. It combines thermal and fast neutral populations and includes all unresolved internal quantum states, rather than selecting one population or state.

For the total neutral distribution function $f_n(mathbf{x},mathbf{v})$, the pressure tensor and scalar pressure are defined by:

$$
\mathbf{P}_n = m_n \int (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_n)(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_n) f_n(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v,\qquad p_n = \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{P}_n
$$

where $m_n$ is neutral particle mass, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $n_n=\int f_n\,d^3v$ is total neutral number density, and $\mathbf{u}_n=n_n^{-1}\int\mathbf{v}f_n\,d^3v$ is the total mean neutral flow velocity. Thus, the central moment includes both random motion and relative streaming between included populations. It is the aggregate counterpart of [neutral pressure], whereas [thermal neutral pressure](name:thermal_neutral_pressure) excludes the fast population and [neutral internal state pressure](name:neutral_internal_state_pressure) selects a specified internal state.

Volume-averaged effective ionic charge is the effective charge of the complete ion mixture after spatially averaging the local charge-weighted ionic charge moment over the confined plasma volume.

The defining relation is

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff},V} = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} Z_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{eff},V}$ is the volume-averaged effective charge, $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local [effective charge](name:effective_charge), $V_p$ is the confined plasma volume, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, and $dV$ is the volume element.

The average applies to the complete included ion mixture at every position, with ionic contributions summed over all represented species and charge states. It covers the confined plasma volume and is not restricted to one species, one charge state, one region, or one flux surface; it is distinct from an ordinary ion charge average.

This quantity is the volume-averaged counterpart of [effective charge](name:effective_charge). It differs from [flux-surface-averaged effective charge at the plasma boundary], which averages the local effective charge over a boundary surface, and from [volume-averaged ion charge](name:volume_averaged_ion_charge), which represents an ordinary ion charge number rather than the second charge moment normalized by free-electron density.

This is the volume average of lithium ion number density, summed over all ionization stages from Li+ through fully stripped Li3+, throughout the confined plasma. Neutral lithium is excluded. The quantity provides a global measure of lithium impurity content rather than a local or boundary value.

The volume average is defined as

$$
\overline{n}_{Li} = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} n_{Li}\,dV
$$

where $n_{Li}$ is the local lithium-ion number density, $V_p$ is the confined plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface, and $dV$ is the physical volume element. Unlike the boundary value [flux-surface-averaged lithium density at the plasma boundary], this quantity averages over the full confined volume. Its electron-normalized counterpart is the [ratio of volume-averaged lithium density to volume-averaged electron density].

Volume-averaged tungsten-ion density is the spatial mean of the local charge-state-summed density [tungsten-ion density] over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. It includes all positive tungsten ionization states and excludes neutral tungsten.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{W}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}}\int_{V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}} n_{\mathrm{W}}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{W}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local tungsten-ion density, $V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is the enclosed plasma volume, $\mathbf{r}$ denotes position, and $dV$ is the volume element. The local density is the sum of the densities of all tungsten charge states from W$^{1+}$ through W$^{74+}$.

This quantity is distinct from the boundary [flux-surface-averaged tungsten density] and from the impurity-abundance [ratio of volume-averaged tungsten density to volume-averaged electron density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_tungsten_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density), which is normalized to electron density.

The electron temperature at the outboard midplane is the local energy-equivalent kinetic temperature of the bulk electron population at the low-field-side equatorial intersection of a chosen magnetic flux surface. It is the electron-specific component of [temperature at outboard midplane].

For an isotropic electron velocity distribution, the energy-equivalent temperature is defined by

$$
T_e = \frac{2}{3}\left\langle E_{e,\mathrm{rand}} \right\rangle
$$

where $T_e$ is the electron temperature, and $\left\langle E_{e,\mathrm{rand}} \right\rangle$ is the mean random kinetic energy per electron, with both expressed on the same energy scale.

This quantity is local to the outboard-midplane intersection and is not a field-line average, flux-surface average, or value at the plasma boundary.

This collisionality measures the strength of interspecies collisional relaxation relative to collisionless motion along magnetic-field trajectories.

$$
\nu_{ab}^{*} = \frac{\nu_{ab}}{\omega_{\mathrm{char}}}
$$

where $\nu_{ab}$ is the collision frequency between species $a$ and $b$, and $\omega_{\mathrm{char}}$ is the relevant characteristic streaming, transit, or bounce angular frequency; both quantities have reciprocal-time units.

The denominator must be interpreted according to the selected orbit or motion class, so this quantity is distinct from the collision frequency itself. It generalizes the population-specific [electron collisionality] and complements [collisionality at the pedestal top] when the characteristic frequency is evaluated there.

Normalized gyrocenter perturbed density is the species-resolved zeroth velocity-space moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution divided by a positive reference density. It is the before-finite-Larmor-radius [gyrocenter density] fluctuation response; the normalization removes the scale of the reference density while preserving perturbation amplitude and phase.

For magnetic moment $\mu = m_s v_\perp^2/(2B)$, the normalized moment is defined by:

$$
\widehat{n}_{gc,s} = \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{ref},s}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{\infty} \delta f_{gc,s}(v_\parallel,\mu)\,\frac{2\pi B}{m_s}\,d\mu\,dv_\parallel
$$

where $\widehat{n}_{gc,s}$ is the normalized gyrocenter perturbed density for species $s$, $n_{\mathrm{ref},s}$ is the positive reference number density for that species, $\delta f_{gc,s}$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution with respect to ordinary velocity-space volume, $B$ is the local magnetic-field magnitude, $m_s$ is the species mass, $v_\parallel$ is velocity parallel to the magnetic field, $v_\perp$ is speed perpendicular to the magnetic field, and $\mu$ is magnetic moment. The factor $2\pi B/m_s$ is the gyroangle-integrated velocity-space Jacobian for this definition of $\mu$.

For a species represented by multiple charge states, the perturbed gyrocenter-density numerator and the reference density are charge-state-summed before the ratio is formed. This quantity excludes any Bessel-function or finite-Larmor-radius weighting inside the velocity-space integral; that weighted moment is the [normalized gyrocenter gyroaveraged density]. The dimensional numerator of the ratio is the unnormalized gyrocenter-density perturbation; the related [perturbed gyrocenter density] denotes a dimensionless gyrocenter-density perturbation in the same family. The [normalized gyrocenter perturbed pressure] is the corresponding perturbed pressure moment. For complex perturbation amplitudes, the integral is taken over the complex amplitude; the arbitrary overall mode phase is external to the definition.

Sign convention: Positive when, for a real perturbation amplitude, the velocity-space integral of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution gives an excess gyrocenter density relative to the positive reference density.

This quantity is the normalized form of [particle charge] for a particle species. It preserves the sign of the physical charge and expresses its magnitude relative to a common positive reference charge.

The normalized charge is defined by

$$
q_{\rm n} = \frac{q}{q_{\rm ref}}
$$

where $q$ is the species' physical electric charge and $q_{\rm ref}$ is the strictly positive reference charge, both expressed in the same charge units.

The result is dimensionless and is used as the charge-coupling coefficient in normalized electromagnetic and electrostatic equations. Its sign distinguishes positive and negative charge, while its magnitude gives the charge relative to the selected reference.

This quantity is the normalized magnetic-flutter contribution to turbulent radial particle transport caused by fluctuations of the perturbed parallel vector potential. It isolates this electromagnetic channel from other contributions to the total turbulent particle flux.

$$
\widehat{\Gamma}_{r,A_\parallel}=\frac{\Gamma_{r,A_\parallel}}{\Gamma_{\rm GB}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{r,A_\parallel}$ is the radial particle-flux contribution attributed to the perturbed parallel vector potential, and $\Gamma_{\rm GB}$ is the positive reference gyro-Bohm particle-flux scale. The normalized result is dimensionless and corresponds to the related unnormalized [particle-flux contribution].

It excludes particle transport produced by electrostatic fluctuations, collisional processes, or other electromagnetic perturbation channels unless they are included in the defined parent contribution.

Sign convention: Positive when the net particle transport is outward, toward increasing distance from the magnetic axis.

This quantity expresses the inertial mass of one particle of a specified species relative to a strictly positive reference mass. It is the normalized counterpart of [particle mass], rather than an independent mass or mass density.

The normalized particle mass is defined by

$$
\bar{m}_s = \frac{m_s}{m_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass of species $s$ and $m_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the positive reference mass used by the normalization. The result preserves the relative inertial ordering of species while removing the mass scale from normalized equations of motion.

The reference mass must be kept fixed when comparing normalized masses; changing it rescales all such ratios by the same factor. This quantity excludes mass associated with a population or volume and does not represent a mass density.

Normalized perturbed electrostatic potential amplitude is the modulus of the complex normalized electrostatic-potential perturbation eigenfunction for a gyrokinetic mode. It represents the phase-independent strength of the electrostatic potential component of the mode and excludes the arbitrary complex phase of the eigenfunction.

For a complex [normalized perturbed electrostatic potential] eigenfunction $\delta\hat{\phi}$, the amplitude $A_{\phi_N}$ is defined by its complex modulus:

$$
A_{\phi_N} = |\delta\hat{\phi}| = \sqrt{\left(\operatorname{Re}\delta\hat{\phi}\right)^2 + \left(\operatorname{Im}\delta\hat{\phi}\right)^2}
$$

where $\operatorname{Re}\delta\hat{\phi}$ and $\operatorname{Im}\delta\hat{\phi}$ are the real and imaginary parts of the same normalized eigenfunction, and $A_{\phi_N}$ is the corresponding dimensionless amplitude.

This quantity is not the complex eigenfunction itself and contains no phase information. Its value is non-negative and depends on the normalization chosen for $\delta\hat{\phi}$, so it denotes relative mode structure within that normalization rather than an independently fixed absolute scale.

This quantity is the parallel component of the normalized gyrocenter current-density perturbation. It represents the charge-weighted first moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution along the local magnetic-field direction and is the field-aligned component of [normalized gyrocenter perturbed current density].

$$
J_{parallel,g}^{(s)} = \frac{q_s}{J_{\rm ref}} \int v_\parallel\,\delta g_s\,d^3v
$$

where $q_s$ is the charge of species $s$, $v_\parallel$ is its velocity along the local magnetic field, $\delta g_s$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element, and $J_{\rm ref}$ is the reference current-density scale. The underlying unnormalized moment is the corresponding [perturbed gyrocenter current density]. For a linear eigenmode, the quantity may be complex, with its phase defined by the eigenmode convention.

Sign convention: Positive when the perturbed gyrocenter current density points along the local magnetic field.

Parallel normalized particle perturbed current density is the normalized parallel-current-density moment of the perturbed particle distribution for one kinetic species in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode. It represents the species contribution to the perturbed current projected along the equilibrium magnetic field in the particle frame.

The normalized moment is defined by the particle-frame parallel current-density moment divided by its reference normalization:

$$
\hat{j}^{\,p}_{\parallel s} = \frac{\int q_s v_\parallel \delta f^{\,p}_s(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v}{j_\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\hat{j}^{\,p}_{\parallel s}$ is the parallel normalized particle perturbed current density for species $s$, $q_s$ is the charge of that species, $v_\parallel$ is the particle velocity component along the equilibrium magnetic field, $\delta f^{\,p}_s$ is the perturbed particle distribution function, $d^3v$ denotes integration over particle velocity space, and $j_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference current-density scale for the normalized moment.
