This quantity is the dimensionless finite-Larmor-radius contribution to the parallel perturbed current-density moment of a gyrocenter distribution. It is the Bessel-weighted component associated with the first-order gyroaveraging response and refines the full [parallel normalized perturbed current density].

A defining normalized moment is

$$
\mathcal{J}_{\parallel,\mathrm{FLR}}^{(1)} = \frac{1}{j_{\mathrm{ref}}} \sum_s q_s \int d^3v\, v_\parallel J_1(k_\perp\rho_s)\,\delta f_s
$$

where $q_s$ is the charge of species $s$ in C, $v_\parallel$ is its velocity along the local magnetic field in m/s, $\delta f_s$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space measure, $J_1$ is the dimensionless first-order Bessel function, $k_\perp$ is the perpendicular wavenumber in m$^{-1}$, $\rho_s$ is the species gyroradius in m, and $j_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the positive reference current-density scale in A/m$^2$.

This component retains only the $J_1$-weighted finite-Larmor-radius contribution; it is not the complete parallel response or the unrestricted vector quantity [normalized gyrocenter perturbed current density].

Sign convention: Positive when the charge-weighted moment is directed along the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf b}$.

The parallel normalized perturbed magnetic field is the component of the magnetic-field perturbation aligned with the local equilibrium field, scaled by the equilibrium field magnitude. It describes compressional magnetic fluctuations rather than perturbations that only bend field lines.

$$
\delta \hat{B}_{\parallel} = \frac{\delta \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{b}_0}{B_0}
$$

where $\delta \mathbf{B}$ is the perturbed magnetic-field vector, $\mathbf{B}_0$ is the equilibrium magnetic field, $B_0 = |\mathbf{B}_0|$ is its magnitude, and $\mathbf{b}_0 = \mathbf{B}_0/B_0$ is the equilibrium field-line unit vector. This is the parallel projection of the [normalized perturbed magnetic field]. For a complex mode representation, taking the modulus yields the phase-independent [parallel normalized perturbed magnetic field amplitude](name:parallel_normalized_perturbed_magnetic_field_amplitude).

Sign convention: Positive when the perturbation has a component in the direction of the local equilibrium magnetic field.

The parallel normalized wave-vector component is the projection of a local fluctuation wave vector onto the magnetic-field direction, expressed relative to a reference gyroradius. It describes phase variation along field lines and is the field-aligned component of the [normalized wave vector].

It is defined by

$$
k_{\parallel}^{\mathrm{norm}} = \rho_{\mathrm{ref}} k_{\parallel} = \rho_{\mathrm{ref}}\,\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $k_{\parallel}$ is the parallel wave number in inverse meters, $\mathbf{k}$ is the local wave vector in inverse meters, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the local magnetic-field unit vector, and $\rho_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is a positive reference gyroradius in meters. The quantity is dimensionless; it excludes perpendicular wave-vector projections, which describe variation across the magnetic field.

Perpendicular normalized particle perturbed energy is the perpendicular member of the particle perturbed-energy moment family for a species in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode. Its velocity-space weight is the perpendicular speed squared multiplied by the total speed squared, and the reference normalization is the corresponding unperturbed total-speed-squared energy moment.

The quantity is defined as the ratio of the weighted perturbed moment to the unperturbed reference moment:

$$
M_{\perp E,s} = \frac{\displaystyle\int \tfrac{1}{2} m_s v_\perp^2 v^2\,\delta f_s(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v}{\displaystyle\int \tfrac{1}{2} m_s v^2\, v^2\, f_{0,s}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v}
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass of species $s$, $v_\perp$ is the particle speed perpendicular to the local magnetic-field direction, $v_\parallel$ is the particle speed parallel to the local magnetic-field direction, $v^2 = v_\parallel^2 + v_\perp^2$ is the total particle speed squared, $\delta f_s$ is the perturbed particle distribution of the eigenmode, $f_{0,s}$ is the unperturbed (equilibrium) particle distribution, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The denominator is the unperturbed total-speed-squared energy moment shared by the parent [normalized particle perturbed energy] and its parallel counterpart, so the parallel and perpendicular members are directly comparable.

This scalar is the perpendicular entry of the [normalized particle perturbed energy] decomposition and is paired with the [parallel normalized particle perturbed energy] evaluated with the same perturbed distribution and normalization. It is distinct from the [perpendicular normalized particle perturbed pressure](name:perpendicular_normalized_particle_perturbed_pressure), whose weight is the perpendicular speed squared alone: the energy moment retains the additional total-speed-squared factor. Because a linear eigenmode carries an arbitrary complex amplitude, only comparisons made under the same eigenmode amplitude and phase convention are physically meaningful.

Sign convention: Positive when the velocity-space integral of $\tfrac{1}{2} m_s v_\perp^2 v^2\,\delta f_s$ is positive under the chosen eigenmode phase convention.

Perpendicular normalized perturbed pressure is the dimensionless gyrotropic perpendicular pressure moment of a perturbed particle or gyrocenter distribution in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode, normalized to the species reference thermal pressure. It represents the part of the perturbed pressure tensor associated with kinetic energy perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic-field direction.

For species $s$, the normalized perpendicular moment is defined by

$$
\tilde{p}_{\perp,s} = \frac{1}{p_{\mathrm{ref},s}} \int \varepsilon_{\perp,s}\,\delta f_s\,d\Lambda_s
$$

where $\tilde{p}_{\perp,s}$ is the perpendicular normalized perturbed pressure, $p_{\mathrm{ref},s}$ is the species reference thermal pressure, $\varepsilon_{\perp,s}$ is the particle or gyrocenter kinetic energy associated with motion perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field, $\delta f_s$ is the perturbed distribution-function amplitude, and $d\Lambda_s$ is the local velocity-space or gyrocenter velocity-space measure for that distribution.

This quantity is the perpendicular member of the gyrotropic pressure-moment pair; the companion member is [parallel normalized perturbed pressure]. When formed from the same distribution and normalization, the scalar trace pressure perturbation [normalized perturbed pressure] is related by $\tilde{p}_s = (\tilde{p}_{\parallel,s} + 2\tilde{p}_{\perp,s})/3$. For complex linear eigenmodes this quantity is a complex amplitude whose overall phase follows the eigenmode normalization; relative phases, ratios, and magnitudes within the same normalization carry the invariant information.

Sign convention: Positive when the perpendicular pressure perturbation is an enhancement of the equilibrium perpendicular thermal pressure.

The radial derivative of flux surface elongation quantifies how the vertical-to-horizontal shape of nested toroidal magnetic surfaces changes as a function of radial position. The flux surface elongation $\kappa$ equals the ratio of the vertical to horizontal semi-axis of the poloidal cross-section, so its radial derivative captures the rate at which flux surfaces become more (or less) vertically elongated moving outward from the magnetic axis.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{d\kappa}{d\hat{r}}
$$

where $\kappa$ is the [elongation of the flux surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface) and $\hat{r}$ is the normalized minor radius running from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the plasma boundary. Both $\kappa$ and $\hat{r}$ are dimensionless, so the derivative is also dimensionless.

This derivative is a required geometric input to local gyrokinetic flux-tube simulations, entering the metric coefficients that govern field-line curvature and grad-$B$ drift terms within the flux-tube domain. It belongs to the broader family of radial flux surface shape coefficient derivatives that also includes the [radial derivative of flux surface shape coefficient](name:radial_derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface). In plasmas with significant edge shaping, this quantity grows in magnitude toward the separatrix, while remaining near zero for nearly circular flux surfaces where $\kappa \approx 1$ throughout the minor radius.

Sign convention: Positive when the elongation $\kappa$ increases with increasing normalized minor radius $\hat{r}$, corresponding to flux surfaces that become more vertically elongated toward the plasma boundary.

This quantity is the total energy contained in a selected electron population component throughout the plasma volume. The component may represent bulk thermal electrons or fast suprathermal electrons, as illustrated by [thermal electron energy](name:thermal_electron_energy) and [fast electron energy].

Its defining relation is

$$
W_{e,a} = \int_{V} u_{e,a}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $W_{e,a}$ is the integrated energy content of electron component $a$, $u_{e,a}(\mathbf{r})$ is its local energy density, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

The component definitions are mutually scoped: thermal electron energy excludes fast suprathermal electrons and non-electron populations, while fast electron energy excludes the bulk thermal electron contribution. The quantity is an energy content, not a power or an energy-transfer rate.

Net plasma power available for confinement losses is the part of [total plasma heating power] not used to change the [stored plasma energy]. It represents the global heating-loss balance term after transient accumulation or depletion of stored plasma energy has been separated out.

The defining global power-balance relation is:

$$
P_\mathrm{steady} = P_\mathrm{heat} - \frac{dW_\mathrm{p}}{dt}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{steady}$ is this quantity, $P_\mathrm{heat}$ is the [total plasma heating power], $W_\mathrm{p}$ is the [stored plasma energy], and $t$ is time.

This quantity is distinct from [total plasma heating power] because it subtracts the transient energy-storage term. In a closed global plasma energy balance it is the natural counterpart of the [total lost plasma power at the plasma boundary], which denotes outward power loss rather than the heating-minus-storage balance term.

Sign convention: Positive when the total plasma heating power exceeds the time rate of increase of stored plasma energy.

Ion current density $\mathbf{J}_i$ is the vector density of conventional electric charge flux carried by ions. It represents signed charge transport from all included ion species and charge states.

The kinetic definition is the charge-weighted first velocity moment of the ion distribution functions:

$$
\mathbf{J}_i(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_{s\in\mathrm{ions}} q_s \int \mathbf{v}\,f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v = \sum_{s\in\mathrm{ions}} q_s n_s \mathbf{u}_s
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $t$ is time, $s$ indexes ion species and charge states, $q_s$ is the charge of population $s$, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $f_s$ is its velocity-space distribution function, $n_s$ is its number density, and $\mathbf{u}_s$ is its mean velocity.

This quantity includes ion-carried charge flux and excludes electron-carried and displacement-current density. Its qualified instances may select a magnetic-field-aligned projection such as [parallel ion current density](name:parallel_ion_current_density), a temporal fluctuation measure such as [fluctuating ion current density], or an ion-saturation collection condition.

Sign convention: Positive when an ion-carried charge-flux component is aligned with the positive direction of its defining basis vector or oriented surface normal.

Signed component along the z axis of the unit vector defining an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror's translation direction or rotation axis at its home position is the scalar projection of that mirror direction vector onto the z-axis basis direction in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. The $\hat{z}$ basis direction is vertical.

For mirror direction unit vector $\mathbf{u}$, the component is defined by:

$$
u_z = \mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}, \qquad \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert = 1
$$

where $u_z$ is the z-axis component of the electron-cyclotron launcher mirror direction unit vector, $\mathbf{u}$ is the unit vector defining that mirror's translation direction or rotation axis at its home position, $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the positive z-axis basis vector in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame, and $\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert$ is the Euclidean norm of $\mathbf{u}$.

The quantity applies to an individual electron-cyclotron launcher mirror at its home position. It is a single Cartesian component of the movement direction or rotation axis, not an aggregate over launchers or mirrors and not an average over a range of mirror motion.

It is not a mirror position, displacement, the [vertical coordinate] of a point, or the [angle of the electron-cyclotron launcher mirror]. The corresponding [x-axis component](name:x_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and [y-axis component](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) complete the same home-position unit vector; with $u_x$ and $u_y$ denoting those linked components, the components satisfy $u_x^2 + u_y^2 + u_z^2 = 1$.

This quantity is the geometric radius of the circular collimating aperture or sensitive opening associated with an individual neutron detector. It defines the transverse boundary of the opening and its geometric acceptance, not the detector efficiency or energy response.

For a circular aperture, the radius is related to the full aperture diameter by

$$
r = \frac{D}{2}
$$

where $r$ is the aperture radius and $D$ is the full diameter of the [diagnostic aperture](name:diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture).

The quantity applies only to circular aperture geometry and represents one detector aperture; no plasma-population, charge-state, or detector-array aggregation is included. It excludes rectangular aperture dimensions, such as the [first local tangential width of the neutron detector](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_neutron_detector) and [second local tangential width of the neutron detector], as well as detector efficiency and energy-response parameters.

The aperture radius contributes to the geometric acceptance represented by the [neutron-detector solid angle](name:solid_angle_of_neutron_detector), but it is a physical aperture dimension rather than a solid angle or an efficiency.

This quantity is the signed, normalized term in turbulent energy flux produced by the perturbed parallel electromagnetic vector potential $\delta A_\parallel$. It isolates the energy transport associated with this electromagnetic field contribution rather than representing the total turbulent energy flux.

The field-attributed flux decomposition is represented by

$$
Q_{E,\mathrm{norm}} = Q_{E,\mathrm{norm}}^{(\phi)} + Q_{E,\mathrm{norm}}^{(A_\parallel)} + Q_{E,\mathrm{norm}}^{(\delta B_\parallel)}
$$

Y-axis component of the unit vector along the first measurement axis of a structural strain-rosette gage is the scalar projection of that oriented measurement-axis unit vector onto the $\hat{y}$ basis direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$. It is a direction cosine describing gage orientation, not a strain value.

The component is defined by the dot product:

$$
u_{1y} = \mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \hat{y}
$$

where $u_{1y}$ is this y-axis component, $\mathbf{u}_1$ is the unit vector along the first measurement axis of the structural strain-rosette gage, and $\hat{y}$ is the y basis vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.

Together with the corresponding [x-axis component] and [z-axis component], it specifies the full orientation of the first measurement axis and satisfies the unit-vector normalization $u_{1x}^2 + u_{1y}^2 + u_{1z}^2 = 1$. It is distinct from the [y-axis component of the unit vector along the second measurement axis].

Sign convention: Positive when the unit vector along the first measurement axis of the structural strain-rosette gage has a component in the $+\hat{y}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.

Toroidal magnetic field at a flux surface is the coefficient $B_\phi$ multiplying $\hat{\phi}$ in the cylindrical decomposition of the equilibrium magnetic-field vector at a point on a selected magnetic flux surface. The direction $\hat{\phi}$ belongs to the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis, where $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

The component is the signed scalar projection onto the toroidal basis vector:

$$
B_\phi(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\phi}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the point on the selected magnetic flux surface and $\mathbf{B}$ is the equilibrium magnetic-field vector.

This is the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ toroidal component, not the [poloidal magnetic field at a flux surface], [radial magnetic field at a flux surface], [vertical magnetic field at a flux surface], or [magnetic-field magnitude at a flux surface]. The surface locus is specified independently, for example by the [poloidal magnetic flux at a flux surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface); this quantity is not the flux label itself.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic-field vector component is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The parallel ion momentum diffusion coefficient is the parallel directional component of the [ion momentum diffusion coefficient](name:ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient) vector. It parameterizes down-gradient diffusion of bulk-ion momentum along the local magnetic-field direction, distinct from radial and poloidal transport components.

In a gradient-diffusion closure, its constitutive relation is:

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,\mathrm{mom}}=-\chi_{\parallel,\mathrm{mom}}\nabla_{\parallel}(m_i n_i v_{i,\parallel})
$$

where $\Gamma_{\parallel,\mathrm{mom}}$ is the diffusive parallel flux density of ion momentum, $\chi_{\parallel,\mathrm{mom}}$ is this coefficient, $\nabla_{\parallel}$ is the derivative along the local magnetic field, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_i$ is the ion number density, and $v_{i,\parallel}$ is the parallel bulk-ion flow velocity. The coefficient describes parallel momentum diffusion only; it is not the momentum flux itself and does not represent cross-field transport. The species-agnostic [parallel momentum diffusion coefficient](name:parallel_momentum_diffusion_coefficient) and the directionally distinct [toroidal ion momentum diffusion coefficient] define related but broader or differently projected quantities.

This quantity is the effective kinematic momentum diffusivity associated with the vertical component of plasma momentum. The vertical component is defined along $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a scalar down-gradient closure, the diffusive flux of vertical momentum is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\mathrm{diff}}_Z = -\rho D_Z \nabla u_Z
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\mathrm{diff}}_Z$ is the flux vector of vertical momentum, $\rho$ is mass density, $D_Z$ is this diffusivity, $u_Z$ is vertical velocity, and $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient. The minus sign specifies down-gradient transport.

The subscript $Z$ identifies the transported momentum component, not necessarily the direction in which the flux crosses a surface. This aggregate plasma quantity is distinct from the species-resolved [vertical ion momentum diffusivity] and [vertical neutral momentum diffusivity](name:vertical_neutral_momentum_diffusivity).

Parallel edge-plasma momentum diffusivity is the scalar kinematic transport coefficient that multiplies the field-aligned gradient of parallel flow in the diffusive closure for the field-aligned flux of total edge-plasma momentum. Here total edge-plasma momentum means ion-fluid momentum summed over ion species and charge states; electron inertial momentum is excluded.

The diffusive contribution to the field-aligned flux of parallel momentum is defined by

$$
J_{M_\parallel}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -\rho_i D_{M_\parallel,\parallel}^{\mathrm{edge}} \frac{\partial u_\parallel}{\partial s}
$$

where $J_{M_\parallel}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive flux of parallel momentum, $\rho_i$ is the ion mass density summed over ion species and charge states, $D_{M_\parallel,\parallel}^{\mathrm{edge}}$ is the parallel edge-plasma momentum diffusivity, $u_\parallel$ is the mass-density-weighted ion-fluid velocity component along the magnetic field, and $s$ is field-line arclength increasing along the magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$. The flux $J_{M_\parallel}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is positive along increasing $s$; for positive $D_{M_\parallel,\parallel}^{\mathrm{edge}}$, the minus sign gives down-gradient transport of $u_\parallel$.

This quantity is the edge-plasma scoped member of the field-aligned momentum-diffusivity family; [parallel momentum diffusivity](name:parallel_edge_plasma_momentum_diffusivity) denotes the corresponding coefficient without the edge-plasma qualifier. It is not the cross-field [radial plasma momentum diffusion coefficient](name:flux_surface_normal_plasma_momentum_diffusivity). It is the diffusive counterpart of convective parallel momentum transport, such as [parallel total momentum convection velocity](name:parallel_total_momentum_convection_velocity), [parallel ion momentum convection velocity](name:parallel_ion_momentum_convection_velocity), and [parallel ion state momentum convection velocity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_convection_velocity); those velocities multiply momentum itself rather than its field-aligned gradient. The corresponding dynamic coefficient in this closure is $\rho_i D_{M_\parallel,\parallel}^{\mathrm{edge}}$, while this quantity denotes the kinematic factor $D_{M_\parallel,\parallel}^{\mathrm{edge}}$.

Spectrometer-channel factor is the scalar inverse effective acceptance associated with one spectrometer channel. It represents the normalization from a quantity aggregated over the channel's sampled spatial region and accepted viewing directions to the corresponding density per solid angle.

The factor is defined from the effective spatial-and-angular acceptance of the channel:

$$
F_c = \left[\int_{\mathcal{V}_c}\int_{\Delta\Omega_c} W_c(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathbf{s}})\, d\Omega\, dV\right]^{-1}
$$

where $F_c$ is the spectrometer-channel factor for channel $c$, $\mathcal{V}_c$ is the sampled volume, $\Delta\Omega_c$ is the accepted [solid angle], $W_c(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathbf{s}})$ is the relative channel acceptance weighting at position $\mathbf{x}$ and viewing direction $\hat{\mathbf{s}}$, $dV$ is an infinitesimal volume element, and $d\Omega$ is an infinitesimal solid-angle element.

The scope is a single spectrometer channel and the aggregation is over the full spatial region and full accepted range of viewing directions represented by that channel. The population normalized by this factor is the set of signal contributors accepted by that same channel; the factor itself does not specify a particle species, charge state, wavelength interval, or spectral line.

This quantity is not the viewed volume, the solid angle, the étendue, detector gain, spectral response, detector efficiency, or a measured spectrum. For uniform acceptance it reduces to the reciprocal of the product of the sampled volume and accepted solid angle, and for nonuniform acceptance the integral gives the corresponding effective acceptance.

The radial particle convection velocity is the effective coefficient of the density-proportional, convective contribution to particle transport across magnetic flux surfaces. It is the radial component of [particle convection velocity] and does not select a particular electron, ion, or neutral species.

The convective radial particle flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_r^{\mathrm{conv}} = n\,v_r^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\Gamma_r^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective radial particle flux in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, $n$ is the particle number density in m$^{-3}$, and $v_r^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial convection velocity in m s$^{-1}$.

This quantity excludes density-gradient-driven diffusive transport. Species-resolved counterparts, such as [radial electron convection velocity](name:radial_electron_convection_velocity) and [radial ion convection velocity](name:radial_ion_particle_convection_velocity), specify the transported population explicitly.

Sign convention: Positive when convective particle transport is directed radially away from the magnetic axis.

Poloidal electron convection velocity is the effective advective velocity component for electron particle transport in the poloidal direction of a flux coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. It is a transport coefficient rather than necessarily the microscopic electron fluid velocity, representing directed electron particle transport after diffusive density-gradient transport is separated.

The poloidal electron particle flux is decomposed into diffusive and convective contributions:

$$
\Gamma_{e,\theta} = -D_{e,\theta}\frac{1}{h_\theta}\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial \theta} + n_e v_{e,\theta}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\theta}$ is the poloidal electron particle flux, $D_{e,\theta}$ is the poloidal electron particle diffusivity, $n_e$ is electron number density, $v_{e,\theta}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is this poloidal electron convection velocity, $\theta$ is the poloidal flux coordinate, and $h_\theta$ converts variation in $\theta$ into physical distance. This component specializes the [electron convection velocity] and differs from the [poloidal electron velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity), which represents electron-fluid motion rather than an effective transport coefficient. Its species-resolved contrast is the [poloidal ion charge-state convection velocity](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_convection_velocity).

Sign convention: Positive when electron particle convection is directed clockwise around the magnetic axis in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, viewed with the machine centerline on the left.

Poloidal electron convection velocity is the effective advective velocity component for electron particle transport in the poloidal direction of a flux coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. It is a transport coefficient rather than necessarily the microscopic electron fluid velocity, representing directed electron particle transport after diffusive density-gradient transport is separated.

The poloidal electron particle flux is decomposed into diffusive and convective contributions:

$$
\Gamma_{e,\theta} = -D_{e,\theta}\frac{1}{h_\theta}\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial \theta} + n_e v_{e,\theta}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\theta}$ is the poloidal electron particle flux, $D_{e,\theta}$ is the poloidal electron particle diffusivity, $n_e$ is electron number density, $v_{e,\theta}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is this poloidal electron convection velocity, $\theta$ is the poloidal flux coordinate, and $h_\theta$ converts variation in $\theta$ into physical distance. This component specializes the electron convection velocity and differs from the [poloidal electron velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity), which represents electron-fluid motion rather than an effective transport coefficient. Its species-resolved contrast is the [poloidal ion charge-state convection velocity](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_convection_velocity).

Sign convention: Positive when electron particle convection is directed clockwise around the magnetic axis in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, viewed with the machine centerline on the left.

The channel voltage is the electrical potential difference delivered by a spectrometer detector channel relative to its electronics reference. It represents the raw detector and front-end response associated with that channel, not calibrated radiance, irradiance, photon flux, or optical power.

$$
V_{\mathrm{ch}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{sig}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{ch}}$ is the channel voltage in V, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{sig}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ are the electrical potentials of the signal and reference terminals, respectively. The polarity follows this reference definition; positive voltage means that the signal-terminal potential exceeds the reference-terminal potential. Offset or dark-signal subtraction and radiometric calibration are excluded. The quantity provides the common physical context for [measured voltage of a spectrometer channel](name:measured_voltage_of_spectrometer_channel) and is distinct from the calibrated [calibration factor of a spectrometer].

Area-normalized radial component of the total momentum source density is the net rate of radial momentum transfer to the included plasma particle population expressed as a density with respect to an area measure. It is projected onto $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The species aggregation is defined by:

$$
S_{R,\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{I}} S_{R,s} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{I}} \mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{mom},s} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $S_{R,\mathrm{tot}}$ is this area-normalized radial total momentum source density, $\mathcal{I}$ is the set of particle species included in the total, $S_{R,s}$ is the area-normalized radial momentum source density for species $s$, $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{mom},s}$ is the species $s$ area-normalized [momentum source](name:momentum_source) vector, and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major radius.

The included-species set defines the total being taken, and the area measure defines the density basis. This is an area-normalized source density, not a volume-normalized [radial volumetric momentum source]. Pairwise momentum exchange between two members of $\mathcal{I}$ cancels in the species sum and is not a net total source; exchange with a species outside $\mathcal{I}$ or with an external momentum reservoir contributes only through its residual radial source on the included population. For an ion species represented through charge states, this extensive source density contribution is summed over all charge states before it enters the total; a charge-state-resolved component is represented by [radial ion charge-state momentum source].

Relative to the vector [momentum source](name:momentum_source), this name selects the $\hat{R}$ component after the species sum; relative to [radial total momentum](name:radial_total_momentum_source), it is the corresponding source-density term. It is distinct from subset quantities such as [radial neutral momentum source](name:radial_neutral_momentum_source) and from [radial plasma momentum flux], which denotes transport of radial momentum rather than local creation or removal.

Sign convention: Positive when the net total momentum source points in the $+\hat{R}$ direction, toward increasing major radius $R$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Product of current density and major radius is the scalar major-radius-weighted toroidal current density at a point. It combines the major radius with the $\hat{\phi}$ component of current density in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining relation is:

$$
K_\phi(R, \phi, Z) = R\,j_\phi(R, \phi, Z)
$$

where $K_\phi$ denotes the product of current density and major radius, $j_\phi$ is [toroidal current density], and $R$ is [major radius].

In axisymmetric MHD equilibrium, $Rj_\phi$ is the toroidal-current source term in the Grad-Shafranov balance for [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux): with $\Delta^* = R^2 \nabla \cdot (R^{-2}\nabla)$, $\Delta^*\psi = -\mu_0 Rj_\phi$, where $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux and $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability. With pressure $p(\psi)$ and [poloidal current function](name:poloidal_current_function) $F(\psi)=R B_\phi$, the same source satisfies $\mu_0 Rj_\phi = \mu_0 R^2 dp/d\psi + F dF/d\psi$, where $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component.

This quantity is a local density-radius product rather than the total toroidal current. Relations to enclosed current or flux arise only after integration with the appropriate geometric measure, which defines a distinct quantity.

Sign convention: Positive when $j_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the plasma-volume average of the local critical momentum threshold for avalanche-driven runaway-electron generation. It characterizes the boundary between collisional drag-dominated and net-accelerated electron dynamics.

The volume average is defined by

$$
p_{c,\mathrm{av}} = \frac{1}{V}\int_V p_c(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $p_{c,\mathrm{av}}$ is the averaged threshold, $V$ is the plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, and $p_c(\mathbf{r})$ is the local [critical momentum due to avalanche] at position $\mathbf{r}$.

This quantity is an unweighted volume average, not the momentum carried by the runaway-electron population and not a volume average of electron momentum. It is the spatially aggregated form of the local avalanche threshold and is distinct from the broader [momentum due to avalanche], which need not denote a critical threshold.

The normalized particle perturbed pressure is a gyrotropic vector quantity representing the pressure fluctuation of the physical particle population in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode, decomposed into components parallel and perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, each expressed dimensionlessly as a ratio to a reference thermal pressure $p_\mathrm{ref}$.

For species $s$, the parallel and perpendicular components are the second velocity-space moments of the perturbed particle distribution function $\delta f_s$:

$$
\hat{p}_{\parallel,s} = \frac{m_s}{p_\mathrm{ref}} \int v_\parallel^2 \, \delta f_s \, d^3v, \qquad \hat{p}_{\perp,s} = \frac{m_s}{2 \, p_\mathrm{ref}} \int v_\perp^2 \, \delta f_s \, d^3v
$$

where $m_s$ is the species mass, $v_\parallel$ and $v_\perp$ are velocities parallel and perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$, and $p_\mathrm{ref} = n_\mathrm{ref} T_\mathrm{ref}$ is evaluated at the outboard midplane.

Unlike the corresponding [gyroaveraged gyrocenter perturbed pressure], this quantity is built from the full particle distribution function, implicitly incorporating finite-Larmor-radius corrections through the particle-to-gyrocenter coordinate transformation. The isotropic scalar parent particle_perturbed_pressure is recovered as the trace average $\hat{p}_s = (\hat{p}_{\parallel,s} + 2\hat{p}_{\perp,s})/3$. The parallel_normalized_particle_perturbed_pressure and [perpendicular_normalized_particle_perturbed_pressure](name:perpendicular_normalized_particle_perturbed_pressure) components together encode the pressure anisotropy of the eigenmode, with the ratio $\hat{p}_{\parallel,s}/\hat{p}_{\perp,s}$ quantifying deviation from local thermodynamic equilibrium relevant to mirror-mode and fire-hose stability.

Dimensionless imaginary part of the complex linear gyrokinetic eigenmode frequency, divided by the positive reference angular frequency, is the normalized temporal growth rate of a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode at a specified wavevector perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field in the local flux-tube approximation. It identifies the exponential amplitude change of that eigenmode in linear gyrokinetic theory.

The defining normalization is

$$
\gamma_\mathrm{norm} = \frac{\operatorname{Im}\omega}{\omega_\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\omega$ is the complex eigenfrequency for time dependence $\exp(-i\omega t)$ and $\omega_\mathrm{ref}>0$ is the reference angular frequency used for the normalized eigenfrequency. When the reference angular frequency is written as $v_{\mathrm{th,ref}}/L_\mathrm{ref}$, this is equivalently $\gamma_\mathrm{norm}=\gamma L_\mathrm{ref}/v_{\mathrm{th,ref}}$, with $\gamma=\operatorname{Im}\omega$, $v_{\mathrm{th,ref}}$ the reference thermal speed, and $L_\mathrm{ref}$ the reference length scale.

This quantity is for one linear gyrokinetic eigenmode at one specified perpendicular wavevector, not for a spectrum-averaged rate, nonlinear turbulent growth, or finite-amplitude envelope evolution. It is the imaginary-part counterpart to the [normalized_frequency_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode](name:normalized_frequency_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode), which uses the real part of the same $\omega$; the eigenmode-specific scope distinguishes it from [normalized_growth_rate](name:normalized_linear_growth_rate_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode), which does not by itself require a linear gyrokinetic eigenvalue.

Sign convention: Positive when the eigenmode amplitude increases exponentially with time.

The ratio of hydrogen density to total hydrogenic density is the fractional contribution of protium, $^1\mathrm{H}$, to the combined population of the main hydrogenic isotopes. It is a dimensionless composition variable for mixtures containing protium, deuterium, and tritium.

The defining relation is:

$$
f_H = \frac{n_H}{n_H + n_D + n_T}
$$

where $f_H$ is the ratio, and $n_H$, $n_D$, and $n_T$ are the protium, deuterium, and tritium number densities in m$^{-3}$, evaluated for the same physical region and particle population. The denominator is the [hydrogenic density] when it is defined as the summed density of protium, deuterium, and tritium.

In practice this ratio is computed from isotope-resolved density estimates using consistent spatial, temporal, and charge-state definitions for all three isotope densities. It may be used together with the corresponding deuterium and tritium fractions to describe fuel composition; these three total-density fractions sum to one when only protium, deuterium, and tritium are included in the hydrogenic total.

The physically valid range is 0-1. A value of 0 means that no protium is present in the hydrogenic mixture, a value of 1 means that the hydrogenic mixture is entirely protium, and intermediate values indicate mixed-isotope composition. This quantity is related to, but distinct from, neutral-isotope ratios such as isotope_fraction, because its denominator is the total protium-deuterium-tritium density rather than a neutral-only or other-isotope reference.

The kinetic energy flux density at the plasma-facing wall surface carried by ions emitted outward via surface emission — the family of plasma–wall interaction processes, including physical sputtering, chemical sputtering, and ion backscattering, that return ionic species from the wall to the plasma. The `kinetic` qualifier restricts this to translational kinetic energy of the emitted ion velocity distribution, excluding potential energy stored in electronic excitation or residual ionization charge, which is captured separately by [energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination).

The emitted kinetic energy flux $\Phi_{\mathrm{kin,emit}}$ sums over all emitted ion species $s$:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{kin,emit}} = \sum_s \int_{v_n > 0} \tfrac{1}{2} m_s v^2 \, v_n \, f_{s,\mathrm{emit}}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_s$ is the ion mass of species $s$, $v = |\mathbf{v}|$ is the ion speed, $v_n > 0$ is the outward surface-normal velocity component at the wall, and $f_{s,\mathrm{emit}}(\mathbf{v})$ is the velocity distribution function of emitted ions.

In plasma–surface interaction modeling, this flux is evaluated by convolving incident plasma conditions with energy-resolved surface emission yields and backscattering coefficients from binary-collision approximation databases. It is the mechanism-attributed form of [ion_energy_flux_at_wall](name:ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission) and the emitted counterpart to [ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall](name:ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall), which captures the incident kinetic flux. Charge-state-resolved contributions are tracked by ion_state_energy_flux_at_wall, and the electron analog is [electron_energy_flux_at_wall](name:electron_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission).

Ratio of volume-averaged tritium density to volume-averaged electron density is the volume-averaged tritium number density divided by the volume-averaged electron number density. It expresses the tritium contribution to plasma composition relative to the electron population after both densities have been averaged over the same plasma volume.

The ratio is defined as:

$$
f_{T/e}^{V} = \frac{\langle n_T \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $f_{T/e}^{V}$ is this ratio, $\langle n_T \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged tritium density](name:volume_averaged_tritium_density), $\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), $n_T$ is the local [tritium density](name:tritium_density), $n_e$ is the local [electron density](name:electron_density), and $\langle q\rangle_V$ denotes $V^{-1}\int_V q\,dV$ for scalar field $q$ over the common plasma volume $V$.

The scope is the specified plasma volume and the particle populations contained in that volume. The tritium density is a species-level per-volume amount and is therefore summed over all tritium charge states before volume averaging. The definition contains no selection by the time of peak electron density or by any other operating condition.

This quantity is the ratio of volume averages, not the volume average of the local ratio $n_T/n_e$, and it is not normalized to the total hydrogenic-fuel density. It is the tritium-only counterpart of the [ratio of volume-averaged deuterium-tritium density to volume-averaged electron density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density), which uses the combined deuterium-plus-tritium numerator; it also differs from the local [ratio of tritium density to electron density].

Wave phase of an antenna strap is the phase angle of the oscillatory radio-frequency current phasor carried by that strap. It describes the strap-level excitation phase used in the antenna's toroidal phasing configuration.

The complex strap-current phasor may be represented as

$$
I_s = |I_s|e^{i\phi_s}
$$

where $I_s$ is the complex radio-frequency current phasor, $|I_s|$ is its current amplitude, and $\phi_s$ is the wave phase represented by this quantity. The phase is defined modulo $2\pi$ relative to a specified RF reference phase.

This quantity applies to one antenna strap and is not summed or averaged over multiple straps. It refers to the phase of the strap current, not the phase of a forward power-wave phasor, which is represented by [forward wave phase of an ion-cyclotron-heating antenna](name:forward_wave_phase_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna), or the phase associated with a complete antenna element.

The associated [wave current of antenna strap] provides the phasor whose phase is specified, while [wave current of antenna strap amplitude] determines its magnitude rather than its phase. Relative phases between straps determine the toroidal phasing of the antenna excitation and therefore influence the launched wave excitation spectrum. The phase-reference plane and any phase-unwrapping convention must be specified separately when comparing values.

Wave phase of an antenna strap is the phase angle of the oscillatory radio-frequency current phasor carried by that strap. It describes the strap-level excitation phase used in the antenna's toroidal phasing configuration.

The complex strap-current phasor may be represented as

$$
I_s = |I_s|e^{i\phi_s}
$$

where $I_s$ is the complex radio-frequency current phasor, $|I_s|$ is its current amplitude, and $\phi_s$ is the wave phase represented by this quantity. The phase is defined modulo $2\pi$ relative to a specified RF reference phase.

This quantity applies to one antenna strap and is not summed or averaged over multiple straps. It refers to the phase of the strap current, not the phase of a forward power-wave phasor, which is represented by [forward wave phase of an ion-cyclotron-heating antenna](name:forward_wave_phase_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna), or the phase associated with a complete antenna element.

The associated [wave current of antenna strap](name:wave_current_of_antenna_strap) provides the phasor whose phase is specified, while wave current of antenna strap amplitude determines its magnitude rather than its phase. Relative phases between straps determine the toroidal phasing of the antenna excitation and therefore influence the launched wave excitation spectrum. The phase-reference plane and any phase-unwrapping convention must be specified separately when comparing values.

actions.phrase: wave current of antenna strap amplitude

This quantity is the normalized total pressure moment of a perturbed physical-particle distribution associated with a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode. It combines the parallel and perpendicular pressure contributions while preserving their signed or complex perturbation amplitude.

The normalized pressure is defined by

$$
\widetilde{p}_{\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{\widetilde{p}_{\parallel} + \widetilde{p}_{\perp}}{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $\widetilde{p}_{\parallel}$ and $\widetilde{p}_{\perp}$ are the parallel and perpendicular perturbed particle pressure moments, and $p_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the positive reference pressure specified by the eigenmode normalization.

The numerator is an algebraic sum, not a magnitude or absolute value. Its component contributions are resolved by [parallel normalized particle perturbed pressure] and [perpendicular normalized particle perturbed pressure](name:perpendicular_normalized_particle_perturbed_pressure); it is distinct from the gyrocenter quantity [normalized gyrocenter perturbed pressure](name:normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure).

The perpendicular normalized particle perturbed pressure is a dimensionless complex eigenmode moment of the perturbed particle distribution function. It represents the fluctuation of thermal energy associated with random particle motion perpendicular to the background magnetic field and is the perpendicular component of the [normalized particle perturbed pressure](name:normalized_particle_perturbed_pressure).

For species $s$, it is defined by the perpendicular second velocity-space moment:

$$
\hat{p}_{\perp,s} = \frac{m_s}{2p_\mathrm{ref}} \int v_\perp^2\,\delta f_s\,d^3v
$$

where $m_s$ is the species mass, $v_\perp$ is the speed perpendicular to the background magnetic field, $\delta f_s$ is the perturbed particle distribution function, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element, and $p_\mathrm{ref}$ is a positive reference thermal pressure. The perpendicular and [parallel normalized particle perturbed pressure] components together describe the gyrotropic pressure perturbation.

Unlike the [perpendicular normalized gyrocenter perturbed pressure], this moment is formed from the physical particle distribution and includes finite-Larmor-radius effects associated with the particle-to-gyrocenter transformation.

Sign convention: Positive when the perpendicular pressure perturbation represents a local increase in perpendicular thermal energy relative to the equilibrium background.

The total particle count is the global normalization integral of the particle distribution function $f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v})$: it quantifies the total number of particles of the described species present in the plasma at a given instant, summed over all spatial positions within the plasma volume and all velocities in phase space. Being a pure count, it is dimensionless.

The quantity is defined by the phase-space integral

$$
N = \int_V \int f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v \, d^3x
$$

where $V$ is the plasma volume, $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector, and $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity. In marker-based kinetic simulations, $N$ reduces to the weighted sum over all simulation markers.

Monitoring $N$ over time provides a particle-conservation diagnostic in kinetic modeling: systematic drift from the initial value indicates numerical particle sources or losses. This quantity is closely related to [total_count](name:total_particle_count), which carries the same physical meaning with a less species-explicit name, and contrasts with [fast_count](name:total_fast_particle_count), which integrates only over the non-thermal sub-population of the distribution. The local spatial counterpart is total_particle_density, whose volume integral recovers $N$.

Poloidal electron beta at the low-field-side pedestal top is the ratio of local electron thermal pressure to the magnetic pressure computed from the local poloidal magnetic-field magnitude at the fitted core-side shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier. The low-field-side locus is the outboard-midplane point, equivalently the largest-major-radius point on that pedestal-top flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity is defined by the local pressure-to-field-pressure ratio at that point:

$$
\beta_{e,\mathrm{pol,LFS}} = \frac{p_{e,\mathrm{ped,LFS}}}{B_{\mathrm{pol,ped,LFS}}^2/(2\mu_0)} = \frac{2\mu_0 p_{e,\mathrm{ped,LFS}}}{B_{\mathrm{pol,ped,LFS}}^2}
$$

where $p_{e,\mathrm{ped,LFS}}$ is the local electron pressure at the low-field-side point of the pedestal-top surface, $B_{\mathrm{pol,ped,LFS}}$ is the local [poloidal magnetic-field magnitude] at the same point, and $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability.

This is a point-local low-field-side beta: both the electron pressure and the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude are evaluated at the same low-field-side pedestal-top point. It differs from [poloidal flux-surface-averaged electron beta at the pedestal top], which uses flux-surface averaging, from [poloidal electron beta at the high-field-side pedestal top](name:poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side), which uses the corresponding inboard point, and from [poloidal beta](name:poloidal_beta), which uses a global plasma-pressure convention rather than the local pedestal-top electron pressure.

The quantity is the local radius of curvature of the Bragg crystal's diffracting surface along its local vertical, or X2, tangent direction. It characterizes the crystal bending used for Bragg-diffraction focusing in a doubly curved geometry.

$$
R_v = \frac{1}{|\kappa_v|}
$$

where $R_v$ is the radius of curvature in m and $\kappa_v$ is the signed normal curvature in m$^{-1}$ along the local vertical tangent direction. A planar surface corresponds to zero curvature and an unbounded radius.

This quantity describes the diffracting surface, not the geometric aperture radius given by [radius of Bragg crystal](name:radius_of_bragg_crystal). Together with the [toroidal curvature of the Bragg crystal], it specifies the directional curvature scales of a doubly curved crystal.

Total electron deposited power is the volume-integrated rate at which a specified source or sink transfers energy to the electron population. It is a source-resolved global term in the electron energy balance and can represent either net heating or net cooling.

The volume-integrated deposited power is defined by integrating the electron power-deposition density over the confined plasma volume:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{dep}} = \int_V q_{e,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $q_{e,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local deposited power density assigned to electrons in W m^-3, $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position, and $V$ is the confined plasma volume.

In practice this quantity is computed from modeled or inferred source terms in the electron energy equation, using the part of each source or sink assigned to electrons. It is closely related to [electron_deposited_power](name:total_electron_deposited_power) as another integrated electron deposition quantity, and it contributes to broader energy-budget quantities such as [total_electron_power](name:total_electron_deposited_power), total_plasma_deposited_power, and total_plasma_particle_deposited_power.

Typical magnitudes are strongly source- and device-dependent. Weak source or sink terms may be in the 10^3-10^5 W range, while dominant electron-heating contributions in high-power plasmas are commonly in the 10^6-10^7 W range and can reach tens of megawatts in large devices or reactor scenarios.

Sign convention: Positive when the specified source term transfers energy to the electron population and negative when it removes energy from the electron population.

Radial width of a neoclassical tearing mode is the full cross-island extent of the associated magnetic island along the major-radius coordinate $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is evaluated across the island separatrix through the resonant rational surface and is a nonnegative full width, not a signed displacement of the island center.

The full-width convention is represented by the separation of the outer and inner separatrix crossings along $R$:

$$
w = R_\mathrm{out} - R_\mathrm{in}
$$

where $w$, $R_\mathrm{in}$, and $R_\mathrm{out}$ are lengths in meters, and $R_\mathrm{in}$ and $R_\mathrm{out}$ are the inner and outer separatrix crossing positions on the same island cross-section, ordered so that $R_\mathrm{out} \ge R_\mathrm{in}$.

This quantity uses a full-width convention; an island half-width is half of this value and is not the same quantity. The generic [mode width] uses the same full-island-width convention without the neoclassical-tearing-mode specialization, while [time derivative of mode width](name:radial_width_time_derivative_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode) denotes the temporal rate of change of the width. The position of the island center may be specified by the [toroidal flux coordinate of the neoclassical tearing mode center](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode_center).

Co-passing particles are those whose guiding-center parallel velocity component is aligned with the plasma current direction, a subset of non-trapped (passing) orbits. The total aggregation sums contributions from both the thermal bulk and any suprathermal (fast) minority populations, yielding the complete co-passing contribution to local number density. This orbit-class-resolved density is distinct from the full particle density, which also includes trapped and counter-passing orbit contributions.

The quantity is defined by integrating the complete particle distribution function over the co-passing partition of velocity space:

$$
n_\text{co} = \int_{\mathcal{D}_\text{co}} f(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f$ is the distribution function, $\mathbf{r}$ is the spatial position, $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity, and $\mathcal{D}_\text{co}$ restricts integration to orbits with $v_\parallel$ in the plasma-current direction.

This quantity is evaluated from kinetic or drift-kinetic models that resolve $f$ explicitly, available either as a flux-surface-averaged radial profile or as a full poloidal-plane distribution that reveals orbit-class density asymmetries.

Core values in deuterium plasmas lie in the $10^{19}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ range, with the co-passing fraction depending on collisionality and the trapped-particle fraction determined by local magnetic geometry.

The suprathermal subset alone is captured by [co_passing_fast_particle_density](name:co_passing_fast_particle_density), and the counter-directed analog is [counter_passing_density](name:total_counter_passing_particle_density). The corresponding pressure moment follows the same decomposition as total_co_passing_particle_pressure, and [co_passing_density](name:total_co_passing_particle_density) is a closely related name for the same aggregate quantity with less explicit notation.

Alpha parameter is the dimensionless normalized plasma pressure-gradient drive entering local ideal-MHD ballooning stability theory. It represents the destabilizing pressure-gradient contribution relative to magnetic-field-line bending and curvature in a local equilibrium description.

For a local minor radius $r$ increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, the ballooning normalization is:

$$
\alpha = -\frac{2\mu_0 q^2 R}{B_\phi^2}\frac{dp}{dr}
$$

where $p$ is the scalar plasma pressure entering the ideal-MHD equilibrium, $q$ is the safety factor, $R$ is major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component in that frame, and $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability.

The normalization makes $\alpha$ dimensionless. This quantity is the pressure-gradient drive itself, not a marginal-stability threshold; a critical alpha parameter is a threshold for the same drive, and [ratio of critical alpha parameter to alpha parameter at pedestal] is a distinct stability-margin quantity.

Sign convention: Positive when the plasma pressure decreases in the outward direction of the chosen local minor radius $r$ ($dp/dr < 0$).

Poloidal electron beta at the pedestal top high-field side is the ratio of electron kinetic pressure at the fitted core-side shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier to poloidal magnetic pressure evaluated on the high-field side. The electron pressure factor is [electron pressure at the pedestal top](name:electron_pressure_at_pedestal_top), and the high-field side is the smaller-major-radius side in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

It is defined by

$$
\beta_{p,e,\mathrm{ped,HFS}} = \frac{2\mu_0 p_{e,\mathrm{ped}}}{B_{p,\mathrm{ped,HFS}}^2}
$$

where $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space, $p_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ is the electron kinetic pressure at the pedestal top, and $B_{p,\mathrm{ped,HFS}}$ is the magnitude of the poloidal magnetic field at the high-field-side intersection of the pedestal-top flux surface. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, this poloidal magnitude is formed from the $R$ and $Z$ magnetic-field components and excludes the toroidal component $B_\phi$.

This quantity differs from [poloidal electron beta at the pedestal top low-field side](name:poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top_low_field_side) only by the point where the poloidal magnetic field is evaluated; both use the same pedestal-top electron kinetic pressure. Since the local poloidal field enters as a squared magnitude, this scalar does not depend on the direction of the poloidal magnetic field.

Magnetic shear at the plasma boundary is the flux-surface average of [magnetic shear] over the outermost closed flux surface — the separatrix bounding the confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.

Using the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ as the radial label ($\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = 1$ at the separatrix), the defining relation is

$$
s_{\mathrm{bdy}} = \left\langle \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}{q} \frac{dq}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{sep}}
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor and $\langle \cdot \rangle_{\mathrm{sep}}$ denotes the flux-surface average over the separatrix.

This boundary evaluation is distinct from interior counterparts such as magnetic_shear_at_pedestal_top and [magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis), which are evaluated on flux surfaces interior to the last closed flux surface.

Sign convention: Positive when $q^{-1}dq/d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is positive as $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases outward at the separatrix.

Accumulated impurity-radiation energy is the total energy carried away by photons produced through electron interactions with impurity ions over the disruption interval. It is a cumulative quantity, distinct from the instantaneous [impurity-radiation power].

$$
E_{\mathrm{imp}}(t_0,t_1)=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}P_{\mathrm{imp}}(t)\,dt
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{imp}}$ is the accumulated radiated energy, $P_{\mathrm{imp}}(t)$ is the total radiative power attributed to electron–impurity interactions in W, and $t$, $t_0$, and $t_1$ are times in s. The integration interval spans the defined disruption duration. The quantity includes the impurity-radiation channels represented in $P_{\mathrm{imp}}$ and excludes radiation not attributed to impurity interactions; it is therefore not equivalent to [total plasma radiated power](name:total_plasma_radiated_power).

In nonlinear gyrokinetic turbulence, the perturbed parallel electromagnetic vector potential $\delta A_\parallel$ drives magnetic-flutter fluctuations that displace gyrocenters along perturbed field lines and transport toroidal angular momentum across flux surfaces. This quantity represents the normalized toroidal momentum flux attributed to the $\delta A_\parallel$ contribution, restricted to the perpendicular velocity-space channel of the transported toroidal-momentum moment.

The wavevector-summed channel is defined by the normalized correlation between the $\delta A_\parallel$ magnetic-flutter flux-surface-normal velocity and the perpendicular toroidal-momentum moment:

$$
\widehat{\Pi}_{\phi,\perp}^{A_\parallel}
=
\frac{1}{\Pi_\mathrm{GB}}
\sum_s \sum_{\mathbf{k}}
\left\langle
\operatorname{Re}\!\left[
\int d^3v\,
m_s R v_{\phi,\perp,s}\,
\delta f_{s,\mathbf{k}}\,
\left(v_{\rho,A_\parallel,s,\mathbf{k}}^\mathrm{flut}\right)^*
\right]
\right\rangle_{FS}
$$

where $\widehat{\Pi}_{\phi,\perp}^{A_\parallel}$ is this normalized flux, $\Pi_\mathrm{GB}$ is the gyro-Bohm toroidal angular-momentum-flux reference scale, $s$ indexes all kinetic species, $\mathbf{k}$ indexes the retained turbulent wavevectors, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space integration measure, $m_s$ is the species particle mass, $R$ is major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $v_{\phi,\perp,s}$ is the toroidal projection of the velocity-space component perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field, $\delta f_{s,\mathbf{k}}$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution coefficient, $v_{\rho,A_\parallel,s,\mathbf{k}}^\mathrm{flut}$ is the flux-surface-normal magnetic-flutter velocity generated by $\delta A_{\parallel,\mathbf{k}}$ toward increasing flux-surface label $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{FS}$ denotes a flux-surface average. The reference scale is commonly $\Pi_\mathrm{GB}=n_{e,\mathrm{omp}}T_{e,\mathrm{omp}}R_\mathrm{ref}(\rho_\mathrm{ref}/a)^2$, where $n_{e,\mathrm{omp}}$ is the [electron density at the outboard midplane](name:electron_density_at_outboard_midplane), $T_{e,\mathrm{omp}}$ is the [electron temperature at the outboard midplane](name:electron_temperature_at_outboard_midplane), $R_\mathrm{ref}$ is a reference major radius, $\rho_\mathrm{ref}$ is a reference gyroradius, and $a$ is a reference minor-radius scale.

This quantity is the perpendicular velocity-space component of the [total $\delta A_\parallel$ momentum-flux channel](name:normalized_total_momentum_flux_due_to_perturbed_parallel_vector_potential) and complements the [parallel velocity-space channel]. It is distinct from the [perpendicular $\delta B_\parallel$ channel] and from electrostatic momentum-flux channels because the flux-surface-normal carrier is magnetic flutter from $\delta A_\parallel$. The corresponding $\delta A_\parallel$ energy-transport channel is [normalized energy flux due to the perturbed parallel vector potential](name:normalized_energy_flux_due_to_perturbed_parallel_vector_potential). For a rotating-frame decomposition, the toroidal velocity moment is taken relative to the mean toroidal flow; this frame choice does not change the electromagnetic field channel.

Sign convention: Positive when the $\delta A_\parallel$ magnetic-flutter contribution carries positive toroidal angular momentum, associated with motion in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, toward increasing flux-surface label $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

Toroidal neutral momentum convection velocity is the toroidal component of the effective velocity vector that advects neutral momentum in a transport closure for the aggregate neutral population. The toroidal component is the projection along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; toroidal modifies the velocity component, not the momentum component being transported. It is a convection coefficient and need not equal the [toroidal neutral velocity](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum_convection_velocity).

The projection defining this component is

$$
u_{\phi,\mathrm{mom}} = \mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{mom}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{mom}}$ is the [neutral momentum convection velocity](name:neutral_momentum_convection_velocity), $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $u_{\phi,\mathrm{mom}}$ is this quantity.

The unqualified neutral population denotes an aggregate over neutral species and internal states; resolved counterparts keep those populations separate. This coefficient belongs to the convective part of the neutral momentum flux and excludes diffusive, viscous, source, sink, and residual terms; it is not the [toroidal neutral momentum flux] itself.

Sign convention: Positive when $\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{mom}}$ has a component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of carbon introduced by gas injection during the plasma prefill phase, before plasma breakdown. It represents injected carbon atoms rather than an instantaneous injection rate.

The defining relation is

$$
N_{\mathrm{C,eq}} = Z_{\mathrm{C}}N_{\mathrm{C}} = 6N_{\mathrm{C}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{C,eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron count, $N_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the cumulative number of injected carbon atoms, and $Z_{\mathrm{C}}=6$ is the carbon atomic number. Both counts are dimensionless.

The prefill interval ends at plasma breakdown, so post-breakdown carbon delivery is represented separately by [accumulated carbon count due to gas injection]. The aggregation convention parallels [accumulated hydrogen prefill count](name:accumulated_hydrogen_prefill_count), with the atomic number providing the equivalent-electron weighting.

Accumulated total gas count at midplane due to gas injection is the cumulative unweighted count of neutral gas particles introduced by all gas-injection valves assigned to the equatorial-midplane valve group. It aggregates all injected species and all valves in that group; each gas particle contributes one count to the total inventory.

The accumulation over a specified time interval is the time integral of the unweighted total midplane gas-particle source rate:

$$
N_{\mathrm{gas,mid}}(t_1;t_0) = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{gas,mid}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{gas,mid}}$ is the accumulated dimensionless count, $t_0$ and $t_1$ are the interval endpoints in seconds, $t'$ is the integration time in seconds, and $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{gas,mid}}$ is the [total gas source rate at midplane due to gas injection](name:total_gas_source_rate_at_midplane_due_to_gas_injection) in particles per second, summed over all midplane gas-injection valves and all injected species.

For a post-breakdown accumulated inventory, $t_0$ is the plasma-breakdown time; for a prefill inventory, the interval is the pre-breakdown gas-fill interval. This quantity is the midplane contribution to the all-position [accumulated total particle count due to gas injection](name:accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection), not a per-valve count and not an equivalent-electron inventory. Species-specific inventories such as [accumulated neon count due to gas injection], [accumulated nitrogen count due to gas injection], and [accumulated carbon count due to gas injection] are separate components of the injected species inventory.

The net efficiency of a plant system is the dimensionless ratio of signed net electrical power exported outside the plant boundary to total internal electrical power consumed by plant systems over the same accounting interval. It is the net-electrical-gain specialization of [efficiency of a plant system](name:efficiency_of_plant_system), with recirculating electrical loads included in the net exported power balance.

The defining relation, including the corresponding net-power balance, is:

$$
\eta_{\mathrm{net,plant}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{net}}}{P_{\mathrm{cons}}}, \qquad
P_{\mathrm{net}} = P_{\mathrm{gen}} - P_{\mathrm{int}}, \qquad
P_{\mathrm{cons}} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{plant}}} P_{\mathrm{load},i}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ is the [net electrical power of the plant system] in W, $P_{\mathrm{cons}}$ is the positive total electrical consumption represented by [power of the plant system](name:power_of_plant_system) in W, $P_{\mathrm{gen}}$ is gross generated electrical power in W, $P_{\mathrm{int}}$ is the internal operational electrical consumption subtracted in the net-power balance in W, $P_{\mathrm{load},i}$ is the electrical consumption of included load $i$ in W, and $\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{plant}}$ is the set of electrically powered plant loads included in the accounting boundary.

The denominator $P_{\mathrm{cons}}$ is a gross positive consumption quantity, not the signed net exchange $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ and not the gross generated power $P_{\mathrm{gen}}$. It equals the internal-consumption term $P_{\mathrm{int}}$ only when the same loads, plant boundary, and interval define both the net-power balance and the denominator. Unlike [thermal efficiency of the plant system](name:thermal_efficiency_of_plant_system), this quantity relates net electrical export to internal electrical consumption rather than gross electrical output to thermal input.

Sign convention: Positive when signed net electrical power is exported from the plant system to an external electrical network or load.

The tendency of the rotation frequency of a neoclassical tearing mode is the instantaneous time derivative of the island angular rotation frequency. It is the signed angular acceleration or deceleration of the magnetic island associated with the mode.

For helical phase $\Phi$ and angular rotation frequency $\omega$ of the same island, the tendency $\dot{\omega}$ is defined by

$$
\dot{\omega} = \frac{d\omega}{dt} = \frac{d^2\Phi}{dt^2}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the [neoclassical tearing mode phase](name:neoclassical_tearing_mode_phase) measured in radians, $t$ is time measured in seconds, and $\omega$ is the [rotation frequency of the neoclassical tearing mode](name:rotation_frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode) measured in radians per second. Radians are dimensionless, so $\dot{\omega}$ has inverse-time-squared dimensionality.

This quantity is distinct from the rotation frequency itself and from the time evolution of island width. In island rotation dynamics it is related to the net toroidal torque acting on the island, including contributions represented by [toroidal plasma torque of neoclassical tearing mode]. A zero value of $\dot{\omega}$ indicates only locally steady rotation frequency; it is not by itself a mode-locking criterion, because locking concerns the rotation frequency and phase behavior over time.

Sign convention: Positive when the angular rotation frequency of the neoclassical tearing mode increases with time.
documents.after:

Nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket module is the rate of nuclear energy deposited within the material volume of one module by neutron interactions and the absorption of primary or secondary photons. It is an integrated deposition quantity, not incident radiation power or local power density.

The module-integrated power is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc,module}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{module}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{nuc,module}}$ is the integrated nuclear heating power, $V_{\mathrm{module}}$ is the module material volume, $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nuclear heating power density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{r}$ is position in the module in m, and $\mathrm{d}V$ is differential material volume in m$^{3}$.

The integration includes energy deposited in module materials by neutron and photon interactions. It excludes unde posited incident radiation, plasma-facing surface heat loads, and heat subsequently transferred to coolant. It is distinct from the local [nuclear power density of a breeder blanket module], the layer-resolved [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer), and the blanket-wide [nuclear heating power](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket).

This quantity is the incoming neutral-particle source rate produced by gas injection at the wall. It represents injected particles, not particles recycled from or incident on the wall.

The total rate is defined by

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{wall,gas}}(t)=\sum_i \dot{N}_i(t)
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{wall,gas}}$ is the total wall gas-injection particle source rate, and $\dot{N}_i$ is the injection rate for included particle species and gas-injection sources indexed by $i$. The aggregation uses particle counts on the selected species basis and does not apply charge-state or electron-equivalent weighting.

This incoming source is distinct from the [neutral particle flux at the wall], which describes particles arriving at the wall per unit area, and from the [total gas source rate at the midplane due to gas injection](name:total_gas_source_rate_at_midplane_due_to_gas_injection), which has a different injection locus.

The fast ion atomic number $Z_n$ is the number of protons in the nucleus of the energetic (non-thermal) ion species observed via Fast Ion Charge eXchange (FICX) spectroscopy. As an intrinsic nuclear property, $Z_n$ is invariant with respect to ionization state and unambiguously identifies the element: $Z_n = 1$ for hydrogen isotopes (deuterium, tritium), $Z_n = 2$ for helium (alpha particles), $Z_n = 6$ for carbon, and $Z_n = 74$ for tungsten.

This quantity is the fast-ion-population counterpart of ion_atomic_number, which gives the same nuclear property for a general ion species. It is physically distinct from [fast_ion_charge](name:fast_ion_atomic_number), which specifies the ionic charge state $Z_\text{ion}$ — the net charge arising from electron removal — and which can vary for the same element at different ionization conditions. Together with [fast_ion_mass](name:ion_atomic_mass), the atomic number fully characterizes the fast ion species entering the spectral interpretation of FICX emission.

In charge exchange diagnostics, the fast ion species is identified prior to line inversion; $Z_n$ is an integer-valued input parameter rather than a derived measurement, taking values from 1 (hydrogenic fast ions in D-T plasmas) to the atomic number of the heaviest injected impurity species.

Effective field-aligned convection velocity multiplying convective transport of total plasma momentum in the edge plasma is the scalar transport coefficient that relates the field-line-parallel convective flux of total parallel momentum density to that total parallel momentum density. It is defined for the total plasma momentum variable summed over the plasma species and charge states included in the total-momentum balance, and it is not necessarily the parallel bulk velocity of any single species.

The constitutive definition of the coefficient is:

$$
v_{\parallel,\mathrm{conv}} = \frac{\Gamma_{P_\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}}}{P_\parallel}
$$

where $\Gamma_{P_\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the field-line-parallel convective flux of total parallel momentum density, $P_\parallel$ is the total parallel momentum density, and $v_{\parallel,\mathrm{conv}}$ is this convection velocity. The density $P_\parallel$ may be written inline as $P_\parallel = \sum_a m_a n_a u_{a,\parallel}$, where $a$ indexes the included plasma species or charge states, $m_a$ is particle mass, $n_a$ is number density, and $u_{a,\parallel}$ is field-line-parallel velocity.

This quantity is an effective coefficient for the transported total momentum variable: it equals a center-of-mass parallel flow only when the closure uses that same flow to advect the summed momentum. Related effective-velocity coefficients for different transported variables include [parallel total ion energy convection velocity](name:parallel_total_ion_energy_convection_velocity), [parallel ion charge state convection velocity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_convection_velocity), and [parallel neutral internal state momentum convection velocity](name:parallel_neutral_internal_state_momentum_convection_velocity); the cross-field counterpart for total momentum transport is [radial effective momentum convection velocity].

Sign convention: Positive when the velocity is directed along the local magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

Effective field-aligned convection velocity multiplying convective transport of total plasma momentum in the edge plasma is the scalar transport coefficient that relates the field-line-parallel convective flux of total parallel momentum density to that total parallel momentum density. It is defined for the total plasma momentum variable summed over the plasma species and charge states included in the total-momentum balance, and it is not necessarily the parallel bulk velocity of any single species.

The constitutive definition of the coefficient is:

$$
v_{\parallel,\mathrm{conv}} = \frac{\Gamma_{P_\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}}}{P_\parallel}
$$

where $\Gamma_{P_\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the field-line-parallel convective flux of total parallel momentum density, $P_\parallel$ is the total parallel momentum density, and $v_{\parallel,\mathrm{conv}}$ is this convection velocity. The density $P_\parallel$ may be written inline as $P_\parallel = \sum_a m_a n_a u_{a,\parallel}$, where $a$ indexes the included plasma species or charge states, $m_a$ is particle mass, $n_a$ is number density, and $u_{a,\parallel}$ is field-line-parallel velocity.
