Signed local derivative of fitted electron pressure with respect to the normalized poloidal flux coordinate at the H-mode pedestal top is the local rate of change of the fitted electron-pressure function with the flux coordinate $\psi_N$ at the pedestal-top locus. It is not the derivative of the scalar [electron pressure at the H-mode pedestal top](name:electron_pressure_at_pedestal_top); that scalar is the pressure value at the same locus.

The derivative is defined by differentiating the fitted electron-pressure function with respect to $\psi_N$ and evaluating the result at the pedestal top:

$$
D_{p_e,\mathrm{ped\ top}} = \left.\frac{\partial p_e}{\partial \psi_N}\right|_{\mathrm{ped\ top}}
$$

where $D_{p_e,\mathrm{ped\ top}}$ is this quantity, $p_e$ is [electron pressure](name:electron_pressure), and $\psi_N$ is the normalized poloidal flux coordinate, with $\psi_N=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\psi_N=1$ at the plasma boundary.

This quantity is a local pedestal-top derivative. It excludes the steepest pressure-gradient value over a pedestal interval, represented by [gradient of electron pressure], and it is distinct from electron-density derivatives such as [derivative with respect to normalized poloidal flux coordinate of electron density at pedestal maximum](name:derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_density_at_pedestal_maximum).

Sign convention: Positive when electron pressure increases with increasing normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_N$ from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

Signed field-aligned convection velocity for transporting aggregate bulk-ion thermal energy in the parallel ion energy balance is the scalar coefficient multiplying bulk-ion thermal enthalpy density in the convective part of the parallel ion energy flux. It is defined along the local magnetic-field unit vector and describes the charge-state-aggregated bulk-ion population, not a single ion charge state.

The defining relation to the convective contribution to the parallel ion energy flux is

$$
q_{\parallel,i}^{\mathrm{conv}} = \frac{5}{2}\, n_i T_i\, v_{\parallel,\mathrm{heat}}^{i}
$$

where $q_{\parallel,i}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective contribution to the [parallel ion energy flux](name:parallel_ion_energy_flux), $n_i$ is the bulk-ion number density, $T_i$ is the bulk-ion temperature expressed as particle energy, and $v_{\parallel,\mathrm{heat}}^{i}$ is this velocity. The factor $5/2$ is the monatomic ideal-gas enthalpy convention.

This quantity is an effective heat-convection coefficient, not the total ion flow velocity, conductive heat flux, or total ion energy flux. As a species-level intensive quantity, it is the density-weighted mean of the corresponding charge-state-resolved ion heat-convection velocities over all ion charge states, with weights given by the charge-state number densities; the charge-state-resolved counterpart is [effective thermal ion charge-state energy velocity due to convection]. It is the parallel component of [ion heat convection velocity] and is distinct from [parallel total ion energy convection velocity](name:parallel_total_ion_energy_convection_velocity).

Sign convention: Positive when the convective contribution to the parallel ion energy flux is directed along the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

This quantity is the effective velocity associated with the convective part of the total ion-energy transport along magnetic field lines. It is a transport coefficient, not necessarily the bulk-flow velocity of any individual ion species.

The convective parallel energy flux is defined by

$$
F_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}} = v_{i,\parallel}^{E} E_{i,\mathrm{tot}}
$$

where $F_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the parallel convective ion-energy flux (W m$^{-2}$), $E_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total ion-energy density (J m$^{-3}$) summed over ion species, and $v_{i,\parallel}^{E}$ is this effective convection velocity. The quantity excludes nonconvective conductive, diffusive, and source terms. It is the field-aligned counterpart of [radial ion energy convection velocity] and is distinct from [parallel ion heat convection velocity](name:parallel_ion_heat_convection_velocity), which refers specifically to bulk ion thermal-energy advection.

Sign convention: Positive when the effective velocity points along the magnetic-field vector, with the magnetic field represented in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The stored thermal electron energy is the total kinetic energy of the thermal (Maxwellian) electron population integrated over the confined plasma volume. It is a global scalar that condenses the radial temperature and density profiles into a single measure of the electron energy inventory.

For a Maxwellian electron distribution the defining relation is:

$$
W_{e,\text{th}} = \frac{3}{2} \int p_{e,\text{th}} \, dV
$$

where $p_{e,\text{th}}$ is the local thermal electron pressure and the integral extends over the confined plasma volume. The factor $\tfrac{3}{2}$ reflects the three translational degrees of freedom of the electron gas.

The time derivative of $W_{e,\text{th}}$ equals the net power balance in the electron channel, directly linking this quantity to [total electron power](name:electron_deposited_power) via $dW_{e,\text{th}}/dt = P_e - P_{\text{loss},e}$. The integrand $p_{e,\text{th}}$ is a component of the total [thermal pressure] summed over all species.

In practice $W_{e,\text{th}}$ is inferred by integrating electron temperature and density profiles — measured by Thomson scattering and interferometry — over the equilibrium flux-surface volumes. Typical values range from a few kJ in small devices to several MJ in large tokamaks.

The reference phase is the angular offset assigned to the complex eigenfunction of a linear MHD perturbation with a specified toroidal harmonic. It fixes the mode’s phase origin and is not a spatial displacement or amplitude.

Using the complex-amplitude convention, the toroidal dependence of a perturbation quantity is written as:

$$
\widetilde{Q}(R,Z,\phi)=\widehat{Q}(R,Z)\exp\!\left[i\left(n\phi+\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}\right)\right]
$$

where $\widetilde{Q}$ is the complex perturbation, $\widehat{Q}$ is its complex amplitude, $n$ is the dimensionless integer toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference phase. $R$ and $Z$ are the major-radius and vertical coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The toroidal harmonic is identified by [mode number], while its phase is carried by quantities such as the [toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic field](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field).

The reference phase does not specify perturbation amplitude, growth rate, oscillation frequency, or temporal phase.

Sign convention: Positive when the complex mode phase advances in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

Total external heating power is the aggregate non-inductive power coupled to the plasma by auxiliary heating systems. It includes neutral-beam injection and electron-cyclotron, ion-cyclotron, and lower-hybrid systems, while excluding power associated with Ohmic induction.

The defining aggregate relation is

$$
P_{\mathrm{ext}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{aux}}} P_s
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the total external heating power, $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{aux}}$ is the set of included auxiliary heating systems, and $P_s$ is the power coupled to the plasma by auxiliary source $s$.

The quantity applies to the whole plasma and is summed over all included auxiliary sources rather than resolved by source, species, or spatial region. It represents external power input that may contribute to both plasma heating and non-inductive current drive; it is distinct from Ohmic heating and from generator power that is not coupled to the plasma. Source-specific contributions include [total power due to electron-cyclotron heating](name:total_power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating), [total power due to ion-cyclotron heating](name:total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating), and power absorbed from a [neutral-beam injector], whose aggregate forms contribute to the sum.

Instantaneous total rate at which neutral gas is introduced into the lower vacuum-vessel region by gas injection valves is the lower-region aggregate equivalent-electron source rate due to gas injection. It counts each injected neutral atom or molecule by the number of electrons associated with its neutral composition and sums over all injected species and all lower-region gas-injection valves.

The multi-species aggregate is defined by:

$$
\dot{N}_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{lower}} = \sum_{v \in \mathrm{lower}} \sum_m E_m\,\dot{N}_{v,m}
$$

where $\dot{N}_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{lower}}$ is this total lower gas source rate, $\dot{N}_{v,m}$ is the neutral gas injection rate of atomic or molecular species $m$ from lower-region valve $v$, and $E_m = \sum_a \nu_{a,m} Z_a$ is the equivalent-electron count for one neutral injected particle of species $m$, with $\nu_{a,m}$ the stoichiometric count of atom $a$ in species $m$ and $Z_a$ its atomic number.

This quantity is an injected source into the vacuum vessel and excludes pumping, wall recycling, ionization losses after entry, and gas introduced outside the lower region. Species-level quantities such as [neon source rate](name:neon_source_rate) and [propane source rate](name:propane_source_rate) are individual species contributions under the same equivalent-electron convention; [gas source rate of the vacuum vessel due to gas injection] is the vessel-level source quantity without the lower-region restriction.

Sign convention: Positive when neutral gas is introduced into the vacuum vessel through lower-region injection valves.

Deposited power at a divertor target due to halo current is the electrical work rate delivered to one divertor target by halo current crossing the plasma-facing target surface. Halo current is current in the edge or scrape-off-layer plasma that closes through conducting plasma-facing structures; this quantity selects only its contribution to current-driven target loading.

For a target surface with defined local current density and potential drop, the target-surface definition is:

$$
P_{\mathrm{halo},t} = \int_{A_t} j_{\mathrm{halo},n}^{\mathrm{in}}(\mathbf{r})\,\Delta\Phi_t(\mathbf{r})\,dA
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{halo},t}$ is this deposited power, $A_t$ is the portion of the plasma-facing target surface intercepted by halo current, $dA$ is a target-surface area element, $j_{\mathrm{halo},n}^{\mathrm{in}}$ is the conventional halo-current density projected on the local unit normal directed from the plasma into the target material, and $\Delta\Phi_t = \Phi_{\mathrm{plasma}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{target}}$ is the local plasma-to-target potential drop.

The surface integral of $j_{\mathrm{halo},n}^{\mathrm{in}}$ over $A_t$ is the halo-current contribution to [current at divertor target](name:current_at_divertor_target). This quantity excludes the conductive, convective, radiative, and neutral-particle target-power channels, and excludes current-driven target power not produced by halo current; together with other current-driven components it is part of [power at divertor target](name:power_at_divertor_target), while sums over divertor targets contribute to [power of divertor]. It is zero when no halo-current electrical work is deposited on the target; positive values denote net energy deposition on that target.

Sign convention: Positive when conventional halo current crosses from the plasma into the target along the plasma-to-material surface normal across a positive plasma-to-target potential drop.

Effective spectral width is the wavelength interval equivalent to the area of the spectrometer channel's normalized instrument-function response. It captures the integrated response of non-Gaussian line shapes and is distinct from the Gaussian standard-deviation measure named by [spectral width of a spectrometer channel].

$$
W_{\mathrm{eff}} = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{R(\lambda)}{R_{\max}}\,d\lambda
$$

where $R(\lambda)$ is the channel response to monochromatic radiation at wavelength $\lambda$, and $R_{\max}$ is its peak response. For a Gaussian response with standard deviation $\sigma$, the equivalent width is $W_{\mathrm{eff}} = \sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma$; therefore, this quantity is not numerically identical to the Gaussian spectral width.

The Bragg angle $\theta_B$ is the angle between the incident X-ray beam and the crystal lattice planes at which constructive interference produces wavelength-selective Bragg diffraction. It is the primary parameter governing the central wavelength of a measurement channel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer.

The selected X-ray wavelength $\lambda$ is determined by Bragg's law:

$$
n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta_B
$$

where $n$ is a positive integer diffraction order and $d$ is the crystal lattice plane spacing of the diffracting crystal. For a crystal with known $d$-spacing, $\theta_B$ uniquely determines the central wavelength of the spectral channel.

In X-ray crystal spectrometer systems used for fusion plasma diagnostics, the Bragg angle is established by the geometric orientation of the crystal relative to the plasma X-ray source and the detector. It is a key configuration parameter for selecting specific resonance lines used in impurity transport studies and ion temperature measurements via Doppler line-broadening analysis. Complementary crystal geometry parameters include the [radius of curvature of the diffracting surface in the toroidal direction] and the [aperture radius of the crystal](name:radius_of_bragg_crystal), while the physical transverse extent of the crystal along the first axis is given by [bragg_crystal_width](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_bragg_crystal).

This quantity is the normalized composition factor for target nuclei in the converter material of a neutron detector. It identifies the share of converter atoms belonging to the nuclear species that produces the intended neutron-induced detection reaction.

The target atomic fraction is defined by

$$
f_{\mathrm{target}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{target}}}{N_{\mathrm{all}}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{target}}$ is the number of target-species nuclei and $N_{\mathrm{all}}$ is the total number of atoms in the converter material. It is the nuclear-target realization of [target atomic fraction of a neutron detector converter], rather than a fraction based on converter volume, mass, or detector efficiency. The fraction is bounded between zero and one.

This quantity is the mean bulk-ion thermal temperature along an open magnetic field line through the scrape-off layer, between specified upstream and downstream locations. It represents the connected-field-line average rather than the local temperature at a single position.

The field-line average is defined by

$$
\overline{T}_i = \frac{1}{L_{\parallel}} \int_{s_u}^{s_d} T_i(s)\,ds
$$

where $T_i(s)$ is the local ion temperature, $s$ is arc length along the magnetic field line, $s_u$ and $s_d$ are the upstream and downstream endpoints, and $L_{\parallel}=s_d-s_u$ is the connection length. The result is distinct from the local [ion temperature at midplane] and does not denote a flux-surface average.

This quantity is the mean bulk-ion thermal temperature along an open magnetic field line through the scrape-off layer, between specified upstream and downstream locations. It represents the connected-field-line average rather than the local temperature at a single position.

The field-line average is defined by

$$
\overline{T}_i = \frac{1}{L_{\parallel}} \int_{s_u}^{s_d} T_i(s)\,ds
$$

where $T_i(s)$ is the local ion temperature, $s$ is arc length along the magnetic field line, $s_u$ and $s_d$ are the upstream and downstream endpoints, and $L_{\parallel}=s_d-s_u$ is the connection length. Gas source rate at midplane due to gas injection is the instantaneous total unweighted source rate of neutral gas particles injected by gas-injection valves assigned to the vessel equatorial midplane. It counts injected neutral gas particles themselves, not electron-equivalent particles, charge-weighted particles, or particles produced by later plasma or wall interactions.

For the set of midplane injection valves, the total rate is the sum of the individual unweighted valve particle throughputs:

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{mid}}^{\mathrm{gas\,inj}} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{mid}}} \dot{N}_k
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{mid}}^{\mathrm{gas\,inj}}$ is the gas source rate at midplane due to gas injection, $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{mid}}$ is the set of gas-injection valves assigned to the vessel equatorial midplane, and $\dot{N}_k$ is the unweighted neutral-particle throughput of valve $k$.

The total includes all gas-injection valves in the midplane group and excludes upper, lower, wall, recycling, pumping, ionization, and transport contributions. It is not additive with regional gas-source quantities that use an electron-equivalent or charge-weighted convention. Its time integral is the corresponding [accumulated total gas count at midplane due to gas injection].

Plasma energy deposition rate per unit area on the plasma-facing surface of the first wall is the local deposited-power density delivered from the plasma to first-wall material. It includes all relevant plasma-wall energy carriers unless a narrower carrier-specific or mechanism-specific quantity is named.

The first-wall flux is defined locally from the deposited power on the first-wall surface:

$$
q_\mathrm{fw}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{dP_{\mathrm{dep,fw}}}{dA}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $q_\mathrm{fw}$ is this local first-wall energy-deposition flux, $P_{\mathrm{dep,fw}}$ is the power deposited on the first wall, $A$ is first-wall plasma-facing surface area, and $\mathbf{x}$ is a point on that surface.

This quantity applies to the plasma-facing surface of the first wall and is local to a surface element. It is not the area-integrated first-wall deposited power, not a volume power density, and not a signed net energy flux away from the wall.

This is the parent first-wall surface quantity from which extrema are formed: [maximum first-wall flux] is obtained by taking the maximum of this local quantity over the first-wall surface. If carrier-specific or mechanism-specific deposited-power fluxes are defined, their complete sum gives this aggregate first-wall flux.

This quantity is the detected visible-bremsstrahlung count rate associated with one detector pixel. It represents photoelectron-equivalent detection events produced by the accepted bremsstrahlung continuum, not the local photon emissivity of the plasma.

The rate is defined from the accumulated bremsstrahlung count by

$$
r_{\mathrm{brem}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{brem}}}{dt}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{brem}}$ is the accumulated photoelectron-equivalent count, $t$ is elapsed time measured in seconds, and $r_{\mathrm{brem}}$ is the corresponding detection rate. The count is the accumulated quantity being differentiated; this name does not denote the derivative of an already defined rate.

The pixel-local detected rate is distinct from the plasma source quantity [bremsstrahlung spectral emissivity](name:spectral_bremsstrahlung_radiance), which describes photon emission per volume, spectral interval, and solid angle. It is analogous in detection semantics to the [photon-equivalent count rate] of a spectrometer channel.

Ratio of upper-bound plasma current to initial plasma current during a disruption is the higher-current threshold $X_2$ formed from the signed [plasma current](name:plasma_current) relative to its signed pre-disruption reference value. It identifies the earlier, higher-current crossing that bounds a custom linear plasma-current quench interval.

Let $t_2$ be the earlier crossing time selected for the upper endpoint of that interval. The threshold is defined by:

$$
X_2 = \frac{I_p(t_2)}{I_{p,0}}
$$

where $I_p(t_2)$ is the signed [plasma current](name:plasma_current) at the upper-endpoint crossing and $I_{p,0}$ is the signed pre-disruption reference [plasma current](name:plasma_current).

Together with the corresponding lower-bound threshold $X_1$, [ratio of lower-bound plasma current to initial plasma current during a disruption], the valid ordering for a decreasing-current interval is $0 < X_1 < X_2 \le 1$. The reference current must be nonzero, and the threshold applies to intervals in which the current at the crossings has the same sign as the pre-disruption reference current. The associated [linear plasma-current decay time during a disruption] uses $\tau_\mathrm{lin} = (t_2 - t_1)/(X_1 - X_2)$, where $t_1$ is the lower-threshold crossing time; for monotonic decay across the interval, $t_2 < t_1$ and the decay time is positive. This plasma-current threshold is distinct from analogous disruption-quench definitions for other current populations, such as the [linear runaway-electron decay time during a disruption].

The toroidal mode number is the integer Fourier harmonic that characterizes the toroidal periodicity of a linear magnetohydrodynamic perturbation. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a single toroidal harmonic, the perturbation varies as

$$
\delta X(\phi) = \widetilde{X}_{n_\phi}\exp(i n_\phi \phi)
$$

where $\delta X$ is the perturbed physical quantity, $\widetilde{X}_{n_\phi}$ is its complex Fourier amplitude, $n_\phi$ is the toroidal mode number, and $\phi$ is measured in radians. Periodicity after one toroidal circuit requires $n_\phi$ to be an integer.

The value $n_\phi=0$ denotes an axisymmetric perturbation; nonzero values denote non-axisymmetric structure. It is distinct from the [poloidal mode number](name:poloidal_mode_number), while the radial, poloidal, and toroidal indices together specify the modal branch represented by [mode number].

Sign convention: Positive when the Fourier phase advances as the toroidal angle $\phi$ increases.

The angular rotation frequency of a neoclassical tearing-mode magnetic island describes the instantaneous evolution of its helical phase. The phase identifies the island's orientation on the resonant flux surface, while its first derivative gives the rotation rate.

$$
\omega_{\mathrm{NTM}}(t) = \frac{d\phi_{\mathrm{NTM}}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $\omega_{\mathrm{NTM}}$ is the angular rotation frequency, $\phi_{\mathrm{NTM}}$ is the island's helical phase, and $t$ is time. The phase may advance or regress, so the frequency can have either sign. Its time derivative is the angular acceleration represented by [tendency of rotation frequency of a neoclassical tearing mode]. The phase itself is defined by [neoclassical tearing mode phase](name:neoclassical_tearing_mode_phase).

Flux-surface-averaged total plasma momentum in the toroidal direction at the plasma boundary is the flux-surface average, on the last closed magnetic flux surface, of the cumulative toroidal component of plasma linear momentum enclosed by that surface. The cumulative momentum includes electrons and all ion species and is treated as a flux-surface scalar before averaging.

The cumulative boundary value is defined by the enclosed-volume integral; writing the flux-surface average explicitly gives:

$$
P_{\phi,\mathrm{FSA}}^{\mathrm{b}}
=
\frac{\oint_{\psi=\psi_\mathrm{b}} P_\phi(\psi_\mathrm{b})\, dA/|\nabla\psi|}
     {\oint_{\psi=\psi_\mathrm{b}} dA/|\nabla\psi|}
=
\int_{V_\mathrm{b}} \sum_s m_s n_s(\mathbf{x})\, v_{\phi,s}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\phi,\mathrm{FSA}}^\mathrm{b}$ is this quantity, $P_\phi(\psi_\mathrm{b})$ is the [toroidal total plasma momentum](name:toroidal_total_plasma_momentum) associated with the boundary flux label, $\psi_\mathrm{b}$ is the boundary value of the [poloidal magnetic-flux label](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface), $dA/|\nabla\psi|$ is the flux-surface averaging measure normalized by the denominator, $V_\mathrm{b}$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface, $dV$ is the volume element, $s$ runs over electrons and all ion species, $m_s$ is species mass, $n_s$ is species number density, and $v_{\phi,s}=\mathbf{v}_s\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal velocity component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The product $m_s n_s v_{\phi,s}$ is the toroidal momentum density contribution of species $s$, so the flux-surface average is applied to the enclosed total $P_\phi(\psi_\mathrm{b})$, not directly to this local density.

This quantity is not a boundary-surface integral of local toroidal momentum density, not the flux-surface average of the local density $g_\phi=\sum_s m_s n_s v_{\phi,s}$ alone, and not a major-radius-weighted angular-momentum measure. It is the flux-surface-averaged representation of [toroidal total plasma momentum at the plasma boundary]; the analogous cumulative value at the pedestal top is [toroidal plasma momentum at the pedestal top](name:toroidal_plasma_momentum_at_pedestal_top).

Sign convention: Positive when the enclosed total toroidal momentum is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The parallel electric field at the plasma boundary is the signed projection of the local [electric field](name:electric_field) vector onto the local magnetic-field direction at the last closed flux surface. It is a point-local boundary value, distinct from the [parallel flux-surface-averaged electric field].

The defining projection is

$$
E_\parallel = \mathbf{E} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{E} \cdot \frac{\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $E_\parallel$ and $\mathbf{E}$ are the parallel component and electric-field vector in V m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic-field vector, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is its unit vector. All quantities are evaluated at the same boundary location.

The plasma boundary is the separatrix or last closed flux surface; no flux-surface or regional averaging is implied.

Sign convention: Positive when the electric field has a component in the direction of the local magnetic field.

Breakdown stray magnetic field magnitude is the scalar Euclidean magnitude of the stray magnetic-field vector at the plasma position during plasma initiation. It represents the local residual magnetic field at the breakdown location without retaining vector direction.

For a stray magnetic-field vector $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{stray}$ with components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the magnitude is defined by:

$$
B_\mathrm{stray} = |\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{stray}| = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_\phi^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are respectively the $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ components of the stray magnetic-field vector, and $B_\mathrm{stray}$ is the scalar magnitude.

This quantity is the breakdown-specific counterpart of [stray_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:breakdown_stray_magnetic_field_magnitude) and the scalar magnitude corresponding to breakdown_stray_magnetic_field. It differs from poloidal_breakdown_stray_magnetic_field_magnitude, which uses only the projection onto the $(\hat{R}, \hat{Z})$ poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; it also differs from directional component quantities because it contains no sign or orientation information.

It is the carbon-specific component of [source rate due to gas injection](name:source_rate_due_to_gas_injection).

Electron source rate at the pellet path due to pellet injection is the charge-weighted electron-equivalent production rate from ablation and ionization of pellet material at a specified position along the injected pellet trajectory. It counts the free-electron source associated with material reaching that path position, not the electron concentration of the surrounding plasma.

For trajectory coordinate $\ell$ and time $t$, the local rate is defined by the charge-weighted sum over ablated pellet constituents contributing at that same path position:

$$
S_e(\ell,t) = \sum_a Z_a^\mathrm{eff}(\ell,t)\,\dot{N}_a(\ell,t)
$$

where $S_e$ is the electron source rate at the pellet path due to pellet injection, $a$ indexes the pellet constituents or represented charge-state groups, $\dot{N}_a$ is the local production rate of constituent $a$ by ablation and ionization, and $Z_a^\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective number of free electrons contributed by one produced constituent. For a fully ionized atomic constituent, $Z_a^\mathrm{eff}$ reduces to its nuclear charge.

This is a path-position rate, not a source density per distance along the pellet trajectory or a volume-integrated source. The [electron source rate due to injection](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_injection) is obtained only after aggregating the appropriate local electron-equivalent contributions, while [electron density of pellet path] describes electron concentration along the same trajectory. The [accumulated particle count at pellet path due to pellet injection] is an unweighted cumulative particle count; it is not an electron-equivalent accumulated source unless the same charge weighting and time integration are applied.

The value is non-negative and is zero where injected pellet material at the considered path position does not produce free electrons.

The accumulated release at path distance $\ell$ is defined by

$$
N_{\mathrm{abl}}(\ell)=\int_{\ell_0}^{\ell}\frac{dN_{\mathrm{abl}}}{d\ell'}\,d\ell'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{abl}}$ is the dimensionless released-particle count, $\ell$ and $\ell'$ are distances along the pellet trajectory in m, $\ell_0$ is the trajectory entry position, and $dN_{\mathrm{abl}}/d\ell'$ is the local ablation release per unit path distance.

The count is nondecreasing along the trajectory when the ablation release rate is nonnegative. It represents deposited pellet material and is distinct from the initial pellet inventory given by [count of pellet].

where $N_{\mathrm{abl}}$ is the dimensionless released-particle count, $\ell$ and $\ell'$ are distances along the pellet trajectory in m, $\ell_0$ is the trajectory entry position, and $dN_{\mathrm{abl}}/d\ell'$ is the local ablation release per unit path distance.

The count is nondecreasing along the trajectory when the ablation release rate is nonnegative. It represents deposited pellet material and is distinct from the initial pellet inventory given by count of pellet.

The wetted area of a Langmuir probe is the portion of the collector's geometric surface directly exposed to plasma and available to receive particle current. It represents the plasma-contacting area rather than the full hardware extent described by [area of a Langmuir probe].

The wetted area is defined by integrating the surface element over the plasma-exposed collector surface:

$$
A_w = \int_{S_\mathrm{exp}} dS
$$

where $S_\mathrm{exp}$ is the plasma-exposed portion of the collector and $dS$ is its differential surface-area element. Surfaces shielded from direct plasma contact are excluded. This geometric contact area is distinct from the [effective area of a Langmuir probe](name:effective_area_of_langmuir_probe), which accounts for projection relative to the local magnetic field.

The total neutron source rate due to thermal fusion is the number of neutrons produced per unit time by the neutron-producing thermal deuterium-deuterium, deuterium-tritium, and tritium-tritium reaction branches between bulk ions with locally Maxwellian velocity distributions. It is the channel-summed member of [neutron source rate due to thermal fusion](name:neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion), equal to the sum of [deuterium-deuterium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion], [deuterium-tritium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion], and [tritium-tritium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion].

The channel-summed thermal neutron source rate is defined by

$$
S_{n,\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{th}} = \int_V \sum_{c \in \{DD,DT,TT\}} \nu_{n,c}\,\frac{n_{a_c} n_{b_c}}{1+\delta_{a_c b_c}}\,\langle\sigma v\rangle_c(T_{a_c},T_{b_c})\,dV
$$

where $S_{n,\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the total source rate, $V$ is the emitting plasma volume, $c$ labels a neutron-producing thermal fusion branch, $\nu_{n,c}$ is the neutron multiplicity of branch $c$, $a_c$ and $b_c$ are its reactant ion species, $n_{a_c}$ and $n_{b_c}$ are their local bulk number densities, $\delta_{a_c b_c}$ is one for identical reactants and zero otherwise, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_c$ is the Maxwellian-averaged reactivity, $T_{a_c}$ and $T_{b_c}$ are the local reactant temperatures, and $dV$ is a volume element. The denominator prevents double counting of identical reactant pairs.

Only reactions among locally Maxwellian bulk ions are included; beam-target, beam-beam, fusion-product, and other nonthermal fast-ion contributions are excluded. For deuterium-deuterium fusion, only the D(d,n)$^3\mathrm{He}$ neutron branch contributes; the D(d,p)T proton branch is not counted. For deuterium-deuterium and deuterium-tritium neutron branches $\nu_{n,c}=1$, while for tritium-tritium fusion $\nu_{n,c}=2$.

Molecular neutral species flow at an outlet is the pressure-volume throughput of one molecular neutral species removed across a pumping outlet. It is species-specific and uses the outlet partial pressure of that molecular neutral species rather than the [total neutral pressure](name:total_neutral_pressure).

The outlet throughput is defined by the product of the outlet species partial pressure and the effective pumping speed for that species:

$$
Q_{s,\mathrm{out}} = p_{s,\mathrm{out}} S_{s,\mathrm{out}}
$$

where $Q_{s,\mathrm{out}}$ is this molecular neutral species flow at the outlet, $p_{s,\mathrm{out}}$ is the outlet partial pressure of molecular neutral species $s$, and $S_{s,\mathrm{out}}$ is the effective pumping speed for species $s$ at the outlet.

This quantity is an outlet removal throughput, distinct from a gas source into the vessel such as [gas injection](name:total_lower_gas_source_rate_of_vacuum_vessel_due_to_gas_injection). It is the molecular, species-resolved outlet form of [neutral species flow](name:molecular_neutral_species_flow_at_outlet) and a species-specific specialization of [gas flow].

Sign convention: Positive when the molecular neutral species is removed through the outlet in the pumping direction away from the vessel.

The magnetic vector potential is a vector field whose spatial curl determines the associated magnetic field. A perturbation denotes the departure from an equilibrium vector potential and may be represented by a reference-scaled amplitude.

$$
\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}
$$

where $\mathbf{A}$ is the magnetic vector-potential field, $\mathbf{B}$ is its associated magnetic-field vector, and $\nabla \times$ is the spatial curl operator. The potential is gage-dependent: replacing $\mathbf{A}$ by $\mathbf{A} + \nabla\chi$, where $\chi$ is a scalar gage function, leaves $\mathbf{B}$ unchanged. The family includes directional components such as the [radial vector potential](name:radial_vector_potential) and [poloidal vector potential](name:poloidal_vector_potential), as well as the [perturbed vector potential].

Sign convention: Positive when a specified gage-fixed component points along its corresponding positive direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ basis, where $R$ increases away from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ increases toroidally, and $Z$ increases vertically.

Kinetic energy density of the ion population is the local translational kinetic energy per unit volume, summed over all ion species and charge states. It includes random particle motion and directed bulk-flow motion and is the ion-specific component of [kinetic energy density].

$$
w_{i,\mathrm{kin}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_s \int \frac{1}{2} m_s |\mathbf{v}|^2 f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

Here $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $s$ indexes ion species and charge states, $m_s$ is the particle mass, and $f_s$ is the corresponding phase-space distribution. The quantity excludes neutral and electron populations. It is distinct from [runaway-electron kinetic energy density], which describes the kinetic energy density of a runaway-electron population.

Poloidal perturbed magnetic flux at a measurement position due to wave-particle interaction is the signed change in the poloidal magnetic flux function evaluated at the effective measurement position relative to the corresponding reference position obtained without that interaction. It expresses a displacement of the sampled location in poloidal-flux space, not a perturbation of the equilibrium poloidal magnetic flux itself.

The quantity is defined as the difference between two evaluations of the same equilibrium poloidal magnetic flux function:

$$
\delta\psi = \psi_\mathrm{WPI} - \psi_\mathrm{ref}
$$

where $\psi_\mathrm{WPI}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux function evaluated at the effective measurement position including the wave-particle interaction, and $\psi_\mathrm{ref}$ is the same flux function evaluated at the corresponding reference position obtained without that interaction. The difference vanishes when the interaction does not displace the effective measurement position, so that both positions lie on the same flux surface.

This quantity is the wave-particle-interaction-attributed form of [poloidal perturbed magnetic flux at a measurement position](name:poloidal_perturbed_magnetic_flux_at_measurement_position_due_to_wave_particle_interaction) and parallels the suprathermal-electron-attributed [poloidal perturbed magnetic flux at a measurement position](name:poloidal_perturbed_magnetic_flux_at_measurement_position_due_to_wave_particle_interaction). Its angular counterpart is the [poloidal perturbed suprathermal electron angle at a measurement position](name:poloidal_perturbed_suprathermal_electron_angle_at_measurement_position). It is distinct from any absorbed or emitted wave power and from geometric position offsets that are not expressed as a difference of the poloidal magnetic flux function.

Sign convention: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux function at the wave-particle-interaction-shifted measurement position exceeds its value at the corresponding reference position.

The tilt angle of a plasma filament is the signed inclination $\beta$ of the beta-angle side of a plasma-filament parallelogram cross-section. The angle lies in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height, and is referenced to the upward $+Z$ direction.

For the ordered parallelogram, let $\mathbf{u}_\beta = u_R\hat{R}+u_Z\hat{Z}$ be the unit vector along the beta-angle side, directed from the reference vertex shared with the base side toward the adjacent beta-side vertex. The signed angle is defined by:

$$
\beta = \operatorname{atan2}(-u_R, u_Z)
$$

where $u_R$ and $u_Z$ are the components of $\mathbf{u}_\beta$ along $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$, and $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ returns the principal branch $-\pi < \beta \le \pi$.

The beta-angle side terminology follows the same angle-labeled parallelogram convention as [length of iron-core segment](name:minor_length_of_iron_core_segment), identifying a side by its inclination angle rather than by an ordinal label. The directed-edge and branch conventions make $\beta$ unique: translating to the opposite parallel edge leaves the value unchanged, while reversing the side direction is excluded. This angle complements cross-section size quantities such as [plasma-filament width](name:plasma_filament_width) and [thickness of plasma filament]; it is not a filament-current direction or a magnetic-field pitch angle.

Sign convention: Positive when the directed beta-angle side is rotated counterclockwise from the upward $+Z$ direction in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, drawn with $R$ increasing to the right.

The maximum neutron energy of a detector band is the upper kinetic-energy boundary used to classify energy-resolved neutron counts. It is an instrumental band limit, not the maximum energy present in the neutron population.

The selected energy interval is bounded by

$$
E_{\min} \leq E_n \leq E_{\max}
$$

where $E_n$ is neutron kinetic energy, $E_{\min}$ is the lower band boundary, and $E_{\max}$ is this quantity. The lower boundary is represented by [lower-bound neutron-detector energy]; [neutron-detector energy] denotes a band boundary without specifying which edge.

This quantity is the signed radial displacement of a beamlet-group center from its nominal static position during a position variation. It describes only the major-radius component of the group's displacement, not the complete position vector or the injector's own reference position.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ frame, the offset is defined by:

$$
\Delta R_{\mathrm{bg}} = R_{\mathrm{bg}} - R_{\mathrm{bg},0}
$$

Here $R_{\mathrm{bg}}$ is the beamlet-group center's major-radius coordinate and $R_{\mathrm{bg},0}$ is its nominal static reference coordinate; $R$ is measured from the machine symmetry axis and increases outward.

For dynamic beam tilting, the offset describes the group's positional variation and is distinct from the [radial coordinate of the neutral beam injector](name:radial_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector), which refers to the injector reference position. Related angular variation is described by the [perturbed beam tilt angle of the neutral beam injector].

Sign convention: Positive when the beamlet-group center lies at larger major radius than its nominal reference position.

Volume-averaged krypton density divided by volume-averaged electron density is the plasma-volume krypton abundance ratio formed from the same averaging volume for krypton and electrons. The krypton density is the species-level krypton number density summed over all charge states, including neutral through fully stripped krypton.

The ratio is defined by the quotient of the two volume averages:

$$
f_{\mathrm{Kr},V} = \frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V} = \frac{V_p^{-1}\int_{V_p}\sum_{q=0}^{Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}} n_{\mathrm{Kr},q}(\mathbf{x})\,dV}{V_p^{-1}\int_{V_p} n_e(\mathbf{x})\,dV}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{Kr},V}$ is this krypton abundance ratio, $\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged krypton density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density), $\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), $V_p$ is the averaging plasma volume, $n_{\mathrm{Kr},q}$ is the krypton number density in charge state $q$, $q=0$ denotes neutral krypton, $q=Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ denotes fully stripped krypton, $Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the nuclear charge of krypton, $n_e$ is the electron number density, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, and $dV$ is an infinitesimal volume element.

This quantity applies to the krypton and electron populations inside the same plasma volume $V_p$. Its aggregation convention is volumetric averaging for both numerator and denominator; because krypton density is an extensive per-volume species amount, the species-level krypton density is charge-state-summed before the volume average is taken.

It is not normalized by the maximum local electron density and is not a krypton-to-electron density ratio at a single position. It is also distinct from [line-averaged krypton density](name:line_averaged_krypton_density), which averages krypton density along a path rather than over the plasma volume.

The numerator is exactly [volume-averaged krypton density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density), and the denominator is exactly [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density). Replacing the denominator by a maximum electron density gives the related but different [ratio of volume-averaged krypton density to maximum electron density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_krypton_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density).

The thickness is the through-material dimension of a plasma-facing component at its midplane, separating the plasma-exposed surface from the opposite material boundary. It is measured along the local thickness direction normal to the exposed surface.

$$
t_{\mathrm{PFC}} = d_{\perp}\left(S_{\mathrm{plasma}}, S_{\mathrm{back}}\right)\big|_{\mathrm{midplane}}
$$

Here, $t_{\mathrm{PFC}}$ is the component thickness, $d_{\perp}$ is the through-material normal separation, and $S_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ and $S_{\mathrm{back}}$ are the exposed and opposite material surfaces, respectively.

This is a geometric material dimension for the specified midplane section; it is not a plasma-to-wall separation such as the [gap at the plasma boundary], nor a surface thermal quantity.

Poloidal angular offset estimate of the electron cyclotron emission measurement position due to the presence of suprathermal electrons is the signed change in the assigned poloidal coordinate of that position relative to the thermal-electron emission reference. The poloidal angle $\theta$ is measured about the magnetic axis in a constant-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\theta=0$ is at the outboard midplane and $\theta$ increases from larger $R$ toward $+Z$.

The offset is the difference between the poloidal coordinate assigned when suprathermal emission is included and the thermal-electron reference coordinate:

$$
\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra} = \theta_\mathrm{meas,supra} - \theta_\mathrm{meas,thermal}
$$

where $\theta_\mathrm{meas,supra}$ is the assigned measurement-position poloidal angle with the suprathermal-electron contribution included, $\theta_\mathrm{meas,thermal}$ is the corresponding thermal-electron reference angle, and $\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra}$ is this quantity; all angular quantities are in radians.

This quantity is only the poloidal angular component of the suprathermal-electron offset at the measurement position; it is not a radial displacement, toroidal angular offset, or full spatial correction. It is distinguished from [poloidal_suprathermal_electron_perturbed_angle_of_ece_channel_emission_position](name:poloidal_perturbed_suprathermal_electron_angle_at_measurement_position), which applies to the ECE-channel emission position. No universal signed range, magnitude, or sign is implied by the name; the value is zero when the presence of suprathermal electrons leaves the assigned measurement position unchanged.

Poloidal angular offset estimate of the electron cyclotron emission measurement position due to the presence of suprathermal electrons is the signed change in the assigned poloidal coordinate of that position relative to the thermal-electron emission reference. The poloidal angle $\theta$ is measured about the magnetic axis in a constant-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\theta=0$ is at the outboard midplane and $\theta$ increases from larger $R$ toward $+Z$.

The offset is the difference between the poloidal coordinate assigned when suprathermal emission is included and the thermal-electron reference coordinate:

$$
\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra} = \theta_\mathrm{meas,supra} - \theta_\mathrm{meas,thermal}
$$

where $\theta_\mathrm{meas,supra}$ is the assigned measurement-position poloidal angle with the suprathermal-electron contribution included, $\theta_\mathrm{meas,thermal}$ is the corresponding thermal-electron reference angle, and $\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra}$ is this quantity; all angular quantities are in radians.

This quantity is only the poloidal angular component of the suprathermal-electron offset at the measurement position; it is not a radial displacement, toroidal angular offset, or full spatial correction. Neutral particle flux at the wall due to surface emission, summed over all emitting plasma-facing surfaces, is the total rate at which neutral atoms or molecules are released by material surfaces and enter the adjacent plasma-facing region. Here total denotes a global counting rate accumulated over the emitting wall area and over all included neutral species, rather than a local flux density.

The total emission rate is the surface integral of the local emitted neutral particle flux density over the emitting wall:

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{em}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wall}}} \gamma_{\mathrm{em}}(\mathbf{x}) \, dA
$$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{em}}$ is the total neutral emission rate in s$^{-1}$, $\gamma_{\mathrm{em}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local outward neutral particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ already summed over all neutral atomic and molecular species at surface position $\mathbf{x}$, $A_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the emitting plasma-facing wall area, and $dA$ is a surface area element in m$^2$.

This quantity counts only neutrals leaving the wall by surface emission; it excludes the incident neutral flux arriving at the wall carried by neutral_particle_flux_at_wall, which measures neutrals reaching the surface rather than being released from it. It is the neutral-species instance of the species-general integrated emission rate particle_flux_due_to_surface_emission and is numerically equivalent to the plasma source term [neutral_particle_source_rate_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission](name:total_neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission). Emission specifically from recombination at the surface, a subset of this total, is carried by [neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination).

Sign convention: Positive when neutral particles cross the material wall surface away from the wall and into the plasma-facing region.

The total plasma mass density is the local plasma mass per unit volume, representing the equilibrium value summed over the charged plasma rather than a first-order perturbation. It supplies the inertial density in the MHD momentum balance.

The mass density is defined by:

$$
\rho = \sum_s m_s n_s
$$

where $\rho$ is the total plasma mass density, $m_s$ is the particle mass of charged species $s$, and $n_s$ is its number density. The sum includes electrons, main-ion isotopes, and impurity charge states; neutral atoms and molecules are excluded.

This is the total equilibrium realization of the broader [plasma mass density](name:plasma_mass_density) concept, which also covers perturbations. It has the same physical scope as [mass density], with the aggregation made explicit.

Fast-ion charge-exchange spectral-line radiance is the photon radiance of a specified atomic transition emitted by the excited product formed when a fast ion undergoes charge exchange with a neutral atom. It is integrated along the viewing path and over the selected spectral line, and is defined per projected area perpendicular to the viewing direction, per solid angle, and per time. Physical values are non-negative.

The defining relation is the line integral of the local photon emissivity for that transition along the viewing path:

$$
\mathcal{R}_{\ell} = \int_{\Gamma} \varepsilon_{\ell}^{\mathrm{FICX}}\bigl(\mathbf{r}(l), \hat{\mathbf{n}}\bigr)\, dl
$$

where $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ is the radiance of transition $\ell$ with photon-radiance units, $\Gamma$ is the viewing path, $l$ is path length along $\Gamma$ with length units, $\mathbf{r}(l)$ is position on that path, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the dimensionless unit viewing direction, and $\varepsilon_{\ell}^{\mathrm{FICX}}$ is the local photon emissivity of transition $\ell$ from radiating charge-exchange products with photon-emissivity units. The emissivity includes the relevant relative-velocity-dependent charge-exchange or excitation rates and the radiative branching for the selected transition.

The selected-line qualifier means the photon radiance is integrated over the transition's spectral line and is not a wavelength-differential radiance. This quantity is the spectral-line counterpart of [fast-ion radiance due to charge exchange](name:fast_ion_radiance_of_spectral_line_due_to_charge_exchange) and is equivalent in meaning to [line-integrated fast-ion emissivity of a spectral line due to charge exchange](name:fast_ion_radiance_of_spectral_line_due_to_charge_exchange) when expressed as a path-integrated emissivity. It is distinct from [Motional Stark radiance at a spectral line], which describes radiation from beam-neutral Motional Stark emission rather than fast-ion charge-exchange products.

Helium-4 abundance ratio formed from mean densities inside the last closed flux surface is the quotient of the volume-averaged helium-4 ion number density and the volume-averaged electron number density. It is a global isotope-abundance measure for ionized helium-4 relative to electrons in the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface.

The ratio is defined from independent volume averages over the same enclosed plasma volume:

$$
f_{{}^4\mathrm{He},e}^{V} = \frac{\langle n_{{}^4\mathrm{He}}\rangle_V}{\langle n_e\rangle_V}, \qquad \langle n_s\rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_\mathrm{LCFS}}\int_{V_\mathrm{LCFS}} n_s(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $f_{{}^4\mathrm{He},e}^{V}$ is this helium-4 abundance ratio, the superscript $V$ denotes formation from volume averages, $\langle n_{{}^4\mathrm{He}}\rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged helium-4 density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density), $\langle n_e\rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), $n_s(\mathbf{x})$ is the local number density of species $s$ at position $\mathbf{x}$, $V_\mathrm{LCFS}$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface, and $dV$ is an element of that volume. For $s={}^4\mathrm{He}$, $n_s$ is the local helium-4 ion number density summed over all ion charge states; for $s=e$, $n_s$ is the local electron number density.

The semantic scope is species-level helium-4 ion density inside the last closed flux surface. The helium-4 numerator is summed over all ion charge states before averaging, while neutral helium-4 atoms and helium isotopes other than helium-4 are excluded. Because the numerator and denominator are averaged separately, this quantity is not the volume average of the local ratio $n_{{}^4\mathrm{He}}/n_e$.

For fully stripped helium-4 ions in a quasi-neutral plasma, $2 f_{{}^4\mathrm{He},e}^{V}$ represents the helium-4 ion contribution to the electron charge balance, apart from contributions of other ions and departures from full stripping. The isotope analog is [ratio of volume-averaged helium-3 density to volume-averaged electron density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_helium_3_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density), and the analogous elemental abundance quantity is [ratio of volume-averaged neon density to volume-averaged electron density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_neon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density). It is related to [ratio of volume-averaged helium-4 ion density to electron density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_helium_4_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density) by the shared helium-4 numerator species, while this name explicitly normalizes by the independently volume-averaged electron density.

The fast-ion critical energy $E_c$ separates two collisional energy-loss regimes for suprathermal ions decelerating in a thermal plasma. Above $E_c$, fast ions lose energy predominantly to thermal electrons via Coulomb drag; below $E_c$, energy is deposited preferentially in the bulk thermal ion population, directly controlling the electron-to-ion power balance in transport modeling.

The critical energy follows from equating the electron and ion frictional forces on the decelerating fast ion:

$$
E_c = T_e \left(\frac{3\sqrt{\pi}}{4}\right)^{2/3} \left(\frac{m_f}{m_e}\right)^{1/3} \left(\sum_i \frac{n_i Z_i^2}{n_e} \frac{m_f}{m_i}\right)^{2/3}
$$

where $T_e$ is the electron temperature, $m_f$ and $m_e$ are the fast-ion and electron masses, $n_i$, $Z_i$, and $m_i$ are the density, charge number, and mass of background ion species $i$, and $n_e$ is the electron density.

The critical energy varies radially through its dependence on local $T_e$ and plasma composition and is computed from kinetic plasma data rather than measured directly. For NBI-injected deuterons at $T_e \approx 3$–$8$ keV, $E_c$ falls in the range 30–150 keV; for fusion alpha particles, it reaches several hundred keV at reactor-relevant temperatures.

This quantity is the ion-specific form of [fast_particle_critical_energy](name:fast_ion_critical_energy), which spans both electron and ion fast-particle populations. The equivalent name with the thermalization mechanism made explicit is [critical_fast_particle_energy_due_to_thermalization](name:fast_ion_critical_energy). The thermal-plasma heating power that accumulates as fast ions slow through $E_c$ is quantified by [thermal_particle_heating_power_due_to_thermalization_of_fast_particles](name:thermal_particle_power_due_to_thermalization).

This quantity is the radial rate of change of the poloidal cross-sectional area enclosed by a closed magnetic flux surface, parameterized by the dimensionful toroidal flux coordinate. It describes how neighboring flux-surface cross sections change along that coordinate.

For a nested family of flux surfaces, it is defined by

$$
\frac{dA}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $A(\rho_{\mathrm{tor}})$ is the poloidal cross-sectional area enclosed by the flux surface labeled by $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal flux coordinate.

The scope is the enclosed poloidal cross-sectional area of a closed magnetic flux surface in an equilibrium, with no averaging or summation over flux surfaces. It is a local geometric derivative along the nested-surface family, not the area of the three-dimensional toroidal surface.

This quantity is a derivative specialization of [area of a flux surface]. It is distinct from the [derivative with respect to normalized poloidal flux coordinate of area of a flux surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_area_of_flux_surface), which uses a normalized poloidal-flux coordinate, and from the [derivative with respect to toroidal flux coordinate of volume of a flux surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface), which differentiates enclosed volume rather than cross-sectional area.

Ion-state mean ionization potential is the concentration-weighted mean cumulative ionization energy required to produce the charge states represented by an ion charge state bundle from the neutral ground state. It represents ionization energy only, not the total internal, kinetic, or thermal energy of the ions.

For charge states $z$ in an ion charge state bundle $\mathcal{B}$, the ion-state mean ionization potential is defined by

$$
E_{\mathrm{ion}} = \sum_{z \in \mathcal{B}} x_z \sum_{k=0}^{z-1} \epsilon_k
$$

where $\mathcal{B}$ is the set of represented charge states, $x_z$ is the fractional concentration of charge state $z$ within the bundle with $\sum_{z \in \mathcal{B}} x_z = 1$, and $\epsilon_k$ is the successive ionization energy required to remove one electron from charge state $k$. The inner sum starts at the neutral ground state and accumulates the ionization energy needed to reach charge state $z$.

The quantity excludes electronic excitation energy, kinetic energy, thermal energy, radiation losses, and any other non-ionization contribution. The [maximum ion charge number](name:ion_state_maximum_charge_number) identifies the highest charge state included in a bundle; the corresponding change quantity is [change in ion-state mean ionization potential].

The normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary is the value of the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) on the closed flux surface selected as the plasma boundary. It is the linear normalized poloidal flux, labeling the boundary's radial position between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface.

Its value is the poloidal flux difference from the magnetic axis normalized to the axis-to-separatrix flux difference:

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{boundary}} = \frac{\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{sep}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) on the selected plasma-boundary surface, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and $\psi_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the separatrix (last closed flux surface).

The label equals zero at the magnetic axis and equals one when the selected plasma boundary coincides with the separatrix; a value below one selects an internal closed flux surface. Its defining role is to specify, for fixed-boundary equilibrium representations, which closed flux surface is taken as the plasma boundary, commonly a surface just inside the separatrix so that the boundary remains strictly closed.

This is the linear normalized poloidal flux value itself, not its square root, and it is a flux-surface label rather than a signed poloidal-flux value or a geometric minor-radius measure. It is distinct from the toroidal-flux-based boundary label [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary), and it belongs to the same locus-valued family as the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor] and the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal).

The strap-current amplitude is the non-negative peak magnitude of the radio-frequency current associated with electromagnetic-wave excitation at a specified location along an ion-cyclotron-heating antenna strap.

For the oscillatory current represented by a complex phasor, the amplitude is defined as

$$
I_{\mathrm{amp}} = |\widetilde{I}|
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{amp}}$ is the strap-current amplitude and $\widetilde{I}$ is the complex phasor of the strap current at the specified location.

This quantity applies to one antenna strap within one antenna module and is evaluated at the relevant position along that strap. It characterizes the radio-frequency excitation associated with the module's wave current; it is not summed or averaged over multiple straps, modules, or the complete antenna system. The amplitude is non-negative and therefore excludes the sign and phase information of the instantaneous current.

As the amplitude form of [wave current of antenna strap], it retains the parent quantity's strap locus and wave-current meaning while selecting its peak magnitude. It is distinct from the instantaneous signed current and from a root-mean-square representation of the same oscillatory current.

The quantity is the signed plasma-induced change in effective optical path length accumulated along one interferometer-beam line of sight. It captures the integrated refractive effect of the plasma along that path rather than a local geometric displacement.

The defining difference is

$$
\Delta L = L_{\mathrm{plasma}} - L_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\Delta L$ is the plasma-induced optical path-length variation, $L_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the effective optical path length with the plasma contribution present, and $L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the corresponding effective optical path length for the same beam path with the plasma contribution removed.

The quantity applies to all plasma encountered along the complete propagation path of a single interferometer beam, with distributed contributions aggregated into one path-length difference. It has no local spatial, species-resolved, or charge-state-resolved meaning. It excludes the unvaried reference path length and is not the total [effective optical path length] of the beam.

This variation is the optical-path quantity associated with the interferometric phase shift and is used to relate the propagation path to the [line-integrated electron number density](name:line_integrated_electron_number_density). It remains a path-length difference and must not be identified with the electron column density itself.

Sign convention: Positive when the plasma increases the effective optical path length relative to the corresponding no-plasma reference path.

The equilibrium weight assigned to an interferometer-beam constraint is a nonnegative factor that sets the relative importance of its line-integrated electron-density residual in an equilibrium objective function. It applies to the constraint associated with one interferometer beam rather than to the electron density itself.

A weighted least-squares objective containing this constraint is defined by

$$
J = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i w_i^2 \left(\frac{y_i^{\mathrm{rec}} - y_i^{\mathrm{meas}}}{\sigma_i}\right)^2
$$

where $J$ is the equilibrium objective function, $i$ indexes individual constraints, $w_i$ is the equilibrium weight, $y_i^{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the reconstructed line-integrated electron density for constraint $i$, $y_i^{\mathrm{meas}}$ is its measured line-integrated electron density, and $\sigma_i$ is the standard deviation assigned to its measurement error.

For this quantity, $i$ denotes an interferometer-beam line-integrated electron-density constraint. The weight is specific to that individual constraint; the objective function aggregates all constraint contributions through the summation. It is not the line-integrated electron density, either its measured or reconstructed value, and it is distinct from the [calibration coefficient of an interferometer beam](name:spectral_calibration_factor_at_line_of_sight), which characterizes signal calibration rather than equilibrium-objective weighting.

This quantity has the same objective-function role as the [equilibrium weight of a flux loop] and the [equilibrium weight of a poloidal magnetic-field probe]; those related weights differ by the physical measurement constraint to which they apply.

The toroidal flux-surface-averaged metric is the geometric coefficient obtained by averaging the reciprocal of major radius over each nested magnetic flux surface. It is the toroidal member of the metric family represented by [flux_surface_averaged_metric](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_metric) and is distinct from the radial-radial coefficient [radial_flux_surface_averaged_metric](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_metric).

The coefficient $g_\phi(\psi)$ is defined by

$$
g_\phi(\psi) = \left\langle \frac{1}{R} \right\rangle_\psi
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\psi$ labels the magnetic flux surface, and the brackets denote the flux-surface average.

This is the average of the reciprocal radius, not the reciprocal of the [flux-surface-averaged major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_major_radius).

This quantity is the binormal component of the oscillatory magnetic perturbation carried by a coherent electromagnetic wave. It excludes equilibrium and other static magnetic-field contributions.

For a harmonic-wave phasor representation, the component amplitude is defined by projection on the local binormal unit vector:

$$
\widetilde{B}_{\mathrm{wave,bi}}(\mathbf{r},\omega)=\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{r},\omega)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{bi}}(\mathbf{r})
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is position, $\omega$ is angular frequency, $\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the complex amplitude of the [wave magnetic field], $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{bi}}$ is the local binormal unit vector, and $\widetilde{B}_{\mathrm{wave,bi}}$ is the complex amplitude of the binormal component. The corresponding physical time-dependent component is obtained from the real part of the phasor convention; real- and imaginary-part quantities are phase-resolved representations, not alternate definitions of this field.

The binormal direction is tangent to a magnetic flux surface and perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic-field direction, distinguishing this quantity from the [parallel wave magnetic field](name:parallel_wave_magnetic_field). It is the magnetic-field analog of the [binormal wave electric field](name:binormal_wave_electric_field).

Sign convention: Positive when the wave magnetic-field projection is along the declared positive binormal unit vector.

Radial outline of a flux surface is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of a point on a contour of constant poloidal magnetic flux. The contour is described in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a point whose Cartesian coordinates are $(x,y,z)$ in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, the corresponding major-radius coordinate is

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are Cartesian coordinates in the plane perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis.

This quantity is the radial coordinate component of the flux-surface outline, paired with the [vertical outline of a flux surface]. It is a specialization of [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) to points on a poloidal magnetic-flux level set and does not denote the flux label, a flux-surface-normal displacement, or the radial component of a vector field.

The ion-charge-state particle convection velocity is the effective coefficient of the density-proportional, convective contribution to transport of a specified ion charge state across magnetic flux surfaces. It is the ion-charge-state specialization of [particle convection velocity], not a velocity magnitude.

The convective particle flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_s^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_s v_s^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\Gamma_s^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective particle flux of the specified ion charge state, $n_s$ is its particle number density, and $v_s^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is this convection velocity.

This quantity excludes density-gradient-driven diffusive transport and is not summed over other ion charge states. The magnitude-only counterpart [ion-state particle convection velocity magnitude](name:ion_state_particle_convection_velocity_magnitude) removes the directional sign.

Sign convention: Positive when the convective particle flux of the specified ion charge state follows the positive orientation assigned to the underlying transport coordinate.

A spectrometer-channel logarithmic spectral signal-to-noise ratio is the logarithmic power-ratio contrast, for one spectrometer channel, between spectral power assigned to a selected signal wavelength interval and spectral power assigned to a line-free reference wavelength interval. It is a band-integrated spectral quantity: each band contribution is formed by integrating the channel spectral power density over its wavelength interval before the ratio is taken.

For signal wavelength interval $B_s$ and reference wavelength interval $B_n$, it is defined by

$$
L_{\mathrm{SNR}} = 10 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P_s}{P_n}\right), \qquad P_s = \int_{B_s} S(\lambda)\,d\lambda, \quad P_n = \int_{B_n} S(\lambda)\,d\lambda
$$

where $L_{\mathrm{SNR}}$ is the logarithm of the spectral signal-to-noise ratio of the channel, $P_s$ is the integrated signal-band spectral power, $P_n$ is the integrated reference-band spectral power, $B_s$ is the selected signal wavelength interval, $B_n$ is the line-free reference wavelength interval, $S(\lambda)$ is the channel spectral power density as a function of wavelength, and $\lambda$ is wavelength.

The scope is one spectrometer channel and one selected pair of wavelength intervals. The aggregation convention is integration over each selected wavelength interval before forming the logarithmic ratio; no wavelength averaging and no aggregation over multiple spectrometer channels is implied. The reference interval is line-free with respect to the spectral feature defining the signal interval, and a finite value requires $P_s>0$ and $P_n>0$.

This quantity is a power-ratio logarithm, not an amplitude-ratio logarithm, not a pointwise value of $S(\lambda)$, and not an unlogged linear ratio $P_s/P_n$. It denotes the same logarithmic power-ratio quantity as the [spectral signal-to-noise ratio of a spectrometer channel]; the explicit logarithm wording makes the logarithmic scaling unambiguous. The value is zero when $P_s=P_n$, positive when $P_s>P_n$, and negative when $P_s<P_n$.
documents.after:

Particle diffusivity is an effective Fickian coefficient describing the diffusive part of particle transport driven by a particle-number-density gradient. It may be resolved by transport direction or by the particle population being transported.

For each resolved direction $i$, the diffusive particle flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{p,i}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{p,i}\,\frac{\partial n_p}{\partial x_i}
$$

where $\Gamma_{p,i}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive particle flux, $D_{p,i}$ is the corresponding diffusivity component, $n_p$ is the particle number density, and $x_i$ is the coordinate along the resolved transport direction. The minus sign defines down-gradient diffusive transport for a positive coefficient.

This parent quantity does not specify a particle population, charge-state aggregation, transport direction, or microscopic mechanism. Population- and direction-specific instances include [neutral particle diffusivity](name:neutral_particle_diffusivity) and [poloidal particle diffusivity].

Hydrogenic-density-derived quantities quantify the abundance of hydrogen-isotope particles with the included isotopic species and charge states. Depending on the derivative, the total density is averaged along a line, averaged over a volume, or used as the reference denominator for a neutral-state composition fraction.

The underlying [hydrogenic density](name:hydrogenic_density) is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{H}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{H}} \sum_q n_{s,q}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the total hydrogenic number density, $\mathcal{H}$ is the set of included hydrogen-isotope species, $q$ is charge state, and $n_{s,q}$ is the number density of species $s$ in state $q$.

The [line-averaged total hydrogenic density] and [volume-averaged total hydrogenic density] retain density character under their respective averaging operations. The [neutral-state density ratio](name:ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density) is instead a composition fraction formed by dividing a neutral charge-state density by $n_{\mathrm{H}}$, and is therefore not itself a density.

The heat-flux vector represents the net transport of plasma energy through space, including convective, conductive, cross-field, field-aligned, and fluctuation-driven contributions when included in the energy balance.

For an oriented surface $S$, the transported power is defined by

$$
P_S = \int_S \mathbf{q} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\,dA
$$

where $\mathbf{q}$ is the heat-flux vector, $P_S$ is the crossing power in W, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the chosen unit normal, and $dA$ is a surface element in m$^2$. The [parallel heat flux](name:parallel_heat_flux) is its projection along the local magnetic-field direction. Convective transport may be parameterized by the [ratio of heat flux to product of particle flux and particle temperature due to convection].

Sign convention: Positive when the local component of $\mathbf{q}$ points along the chosen oriented surface normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$.

This quantity is the local geometric derivative of the area enclosed by a closed magnetic flux surface’s poloidal cross-section with respect to the surface’s signed poloidal magnetic-flux label.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{dA}{d\psi}
$$

where $A$ is the enclosed poloidal cross-sectional area and $\psi$ is the signed poloidal magnetic flux labeling the nested surface.

The derivative applies to each closed flux surface in the nested equilibrium region and is not a volume or toroidal-surface average. It describes the poloidal cross-sectional area only; it excludes the total area of the three-dimensional toroidal surface and derivatives with respect to a toroidal-flux coordinate.

This is the derivative specialization of the geometric quantity [area of a flux surface]. It is mathematically analogous to the derivative of enclosed volume with respect to poloidal magnetic flux, [derivative with respect to poloidal magnetic flux coordinate of volume of flux surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface), with area replacing volume.

Sign convention: Positive when the enclosed poloidal cross-sectional area increases in the direction of increasing signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$; for positive plasma current, this direction is toward the magnetic axis because $\psi$ decreases outward.

Curvature of an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror is the local radius of curvature of the reflecting surface along one specified mirror-local tangential direction. The selected direction is associated with either the [first local tangential coordinate](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) or the [second local tangential coordinate](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror); these are intrinsic tangent directions of the mirror surface.

The radius of curvature in a selected local tangential direction $u$ is the reciprocal of the normal curvature of the surface curve tangent to that direction:

$$
R_u = \frac{1}{\kappa_u}
$$

where $R_u$ is the local radius of curvature and $\kappa_u$ is the normal curvature of the mirror surface along the selected tangential direction.

This quantity is a radius of curvature, not a reciprocal-radius curvature; a locally planar direction corresponds to zero normal curvature and an unbounded radius, so the quantity is defined only for mirror geometry types that are curved in the selected direction. A smaller radius corresponds to stronger geometric focusing or defocusing of the reflected electron-cyclotron beam in that direction. The associated [first local tangential width](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and [second local tangential width](name:second_local_tangential_width_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) describe the finite surface extent along the same tangent axes and are not curvature radii; the mirror orientation itself is described by the [mirror angle].

Signed inclination of the second side of a parallelogram-shaped oblique cross-section of a ferritic element is the $\beta$ orientation angle of that side in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is measured from the vertically upward $+Z$ direction.

Let $\mathbf{t}_\beta$ be the directed vector along the second side, with radial component $\Delta R_\beta$ along $\hat{R}$ and vertical component $\Delta Z_\beta$ along $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The angle is defined by:

$$
