This quantity is the signed difference between the Doppler-displaced wavelength of a neutral-beam spectral line and its unshifted [reference wavelength of the spectral line]. It represents the bulk neutral-beam velocity projected along the viewing line of sight.

The displacement is defined by

$$
\Delta\lambda_{\mathrm{D}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{D}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{ref}} \simeq \lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}\frac{v_{\mathrm{los}}}{c}
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{D}}$ is the Doppler-displaced wavelength, $\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference wavelength, $v_{\mathrm{los}}$ is the signed bulk velocity component along the line of sight, and $c$ is the speed of light. The approximation applies when the projected velocity is small compared with $c$.

The quantity excludes the distinct wavelength displacement produced by the Lorentz shift from the motional Stark electric field; that effect is represented by [difference of fast neutral beam motional Stark wavelength and fast neutral beam reference wavelength of spectral line](name:difference_of_fast_neutral_beam_motional_stark_wavelength_and_fast_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line).

Sign convention: Positive when the Doppler-displaced wavelength exceeds the reference wavelength, corresponding to a redshift.

Number density of oxygen ions at the plasma boundary is the local, intensive particle count per physical volume for the oxygen-ion population evaluated on the last closed magnetic flux surface. The plasma boundary is the limiting closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off-layer region.

The local charge-state-summed oxygen ion density at a boundary point is the zeroth velocity moment of the oxygen-ion distribution functions:

$$
n_{\mathrm{O}}(\mathbf{x}_b,t)=\sum_{z=1}^{8}\int f_{\mathrm{O}^{z+}}(\mathbf{x}_b,\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{O}}$ is the oxygen-ion number density, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a point on the last closed magnetic flux surface, $t$ is time, $z$ is the positive oxygen ionization state, $f_{\mathrm{O}^{z+}}$ is the phase-space distribution function for that state, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

This quantity applies specifically to oxygen ions and sums the populations from singly ionized through fully stripped oxygen. It excludes neutral oxygen and other ion species, and it is a local boundary value with no averaging over the boundary surface or over a volume.

It is the oxygen-specific instance of [density at the plasma boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). The [flux-surface-averaged oxygen density at the plasma boundary] represents the same charge-state-summed oxygen-ion content averaged over the last closed magnetic flux surface rather than evaluated locally.

This quantity is the toroidal projection of the angular-momentum source density produced by the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic response of the plasma. Without a species or charge-state qualifier, it denotes the aggregate contribution to the bulk momentum balance.

The toroidal projection is defined by

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}} = \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{dia}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the full angular-momentum source-density vector due to diamagnetic drift, consistent with [torque density due to diamagnetic drift](name:toroidal_torque_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector.

This local source density is distinct from [ion charge-state momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), which represents momentum transport across a surface, and from species-resolved torque densities.

Sign convention: Positive when the diamagnetic torque density points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Gyro-Bohm-normalized contribution of the perturbed parallel magnetic field to the parallel component of the toroidal gyrocenter momentum flux of a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode is the dimensionless laboratory-frame flux contribution associated with $\delta B_\parallel$. The toroidal direction is defined by increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and the parallel component is the part associated with gyrocenter motion along the equilibrium magnetic field.

The normalized contribution is defined by

$$
\Pi_{\phi,\parallel,N}^{\delta B_\parallel} = \frac{\Pi_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel}}{\Pi_{\mathrm{GB}}}
$$

where $\Pi_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel}$ is the laboratory-frame contribution of the [perturbed parallel magnetic field] to the parallel component of the toroidal gyrocenter momentum flux, and $\Pi_{\mathrm{GB}}$ is the Gyro-Bohm reference used to normalize toroidal gyrocenter momentum flux.

This quantity includes only the $\delta B_\parallel$ contribution to the parallel component; it excludes electrostatic, perturbed-perpendicular-magnetic-field, and other field-channel contributions. The corresponding sum over field-channel contributions is the [parallel normalized gyrocenter momentum flux].

Sign convention: Positive when the $\delta B_\parallel$ contribution gives flux of positive toroidal gyrocenter momentum in the flux-surface-normal direction toward increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ (normalized toroidal flux radius), where positive toroidal momentum corresponds to motion in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the scalar field-aligned component of the conventional plasma current generated by electromagnetic-wave–particle interactions. It represents the wave-driven contribution to current flowing along the magnetic field on a magnetic flux surface.

For a magnetic flux surface labeled by the poloidal flux coordinate $\psi$, the flux-surface-averaged parallel current density is defined by

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{FSA}}(\psi) = \frac{\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wave}} \cdot \mathbf{B} \right\rangle_{\psi}}{B_0(\psi)}
$$

where $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{FSA}}$ is this scalar current-density quantity, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the conventional current-density contribution generated by wave–particle interactions, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes averaging over the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $B_0(\psi)$ is the reference magnetic-field magnitude used for the parallel-current normalization.

The quantity applies to the wave-driven current contribution from the plasma populations participating in the electromagnetic-wave interaction and uses a flux-surface average rather than a local value. It excludes inductive current and current contributions from non-wave mechanisms, and it is distinct from the full vector [flux-surface-averaged wave-driven current density].

It is the magnetic-field-aligned scalar projection of that vector parent, retaining only the component parallel to the local magnetic field; [parallel current density due to ohmic current drive](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ohmic_current_drive) instead represents the inductive resistive contribution.

Sign convention: Positive when the wave-driven conventional current flows in the direction of the magnetic field, so that $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wave}} \cdot \mathbf{B} > 0$.

This quantity is the retained neutral-particle inventory accumulated through net exchange between the plasma and the wall. It is not the instantaneous number of neutral particles present at the wall.

The inventory is defined by the time-integrated net particle flux across the wall surface:

$$
N_{\mathrm{wall}}(t)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{wall}}}\left[\Gamma_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathbf{x},t')-\Gamma_{\mathrm{out}}(\mathbf{x},t')\right] \,\mathrm{d}A\,\mathrm{d}t'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the accumulated neutral inventory, $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the wall surface, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{out}}$ are the inward and outward neutral-particle flux densities. The inward contribution is related to the [neutral particle flux at wall], while recombination provides one process-resolved contribution to outward flux through [neutral particle flux at wall due to recombination](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination). The accumulation is for the selected neutral species and represents net exchange rather than a global gas-injection inventory.

The equivalent-electron source rate is defined by

The parallel neutral momentum diffusion coefficient is the effective coefficient for diffusive transport of neutral-particle momentum along the magnetic-field direction. It represents the field-aligned component of the anisotropic momentum-diffusion description for the aggregate neutral population.

The diffusive neutral momentum flux density along the magnetic field is governed by:

$$
\Pi_{\mathrm{diff},\parallel} = -\rho_n D_{\mathrm{mom},\parallel} \frac{\partial u_{n,\parallel}}{\partial s_\parallel}
$$

where $\Pi_{\mathrm{diff},\parallel}$ is the neutral momentum flux density parallel to the magnetic field, $\rho_n$ is the neutral mass density, $D_{\mathrm{mom},\parallel}$ is this parallel momentum diffusion coefficient, $u_{n,\parallel}$ is the neutral flow-velocity component parallel to the magnetic field, and $s_\parallel$ is distance along a magnetic field line measured in the field direction.

This coefficient applies to the aggregate neutral population, with momentum contributions summed over all resolved neutral internal states. It is not a coefficient for a selected internal state, a radial or poloidal component, or neutral particle-number transport.

As the field-aligned component of the [neutral momentum diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient), it supplies the parallel branch of the anisotropic neutral momentum-transport description. It is distinct from the [radial neutral momentum diffusion coefficient], which governs cross-field radial transport, and from the [parallel neutral species particle diffusivity](name:parallel_neutral_species_particle_diffusivity), which governs particle-number rather than momentum transport.

Poloidal neutral internal-state particle diffusivity is the effective Fickian transport coefficient for diffusive particle transport of a specified neutral internal-state population along the poloidal coordinate $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. The neutral state is an internal population of a neutral species, not an ion charge state or an aggregate over neutral states.

The Fickian relation for neutral internal state $s$ is

$$
\Gamma_{\theta,s}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{\theta,s}\,\frac{\partial n_s}{\partial \ell_\theta}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\theta,s}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the poloidal diffusive particle-flux component of neutral internal state $s$, $D_{\theta,s}$ is this diffusivity, $n_s$ is the number density of neutral internal state $s$, and $\ell_\theta$ is arc length in the direction of increasing $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$.

This coefficient is resolved for a single neutral internal state and excludes summation or averaging over distinct neutral internal states. The effective neutral internal-state diamagnetic drift velocity is the fluid-level velocity of a neutral species population occupying a defined internal quantum state, restricted here to its toroidal component and diamagnetic contribution. The velocity due to diamagnetic drift is a pressure-gradient-driven fluid velocity contribution associated with a plasma population, charge state, or internal state. It retains the drift vector before a component-specific projection, such as the one represented by [toroidal ion velocity due to diamagnetic drift](name:toroidal_ion_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

For a charged species, the diamagnetic-drift velocity is defined by

$$
\mathbf{v}_{\ast s}=-\frac{\nabla p_s\times\mathbf{B}}{q_s n_s B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\ast s}$ is the species diamagnetic-drift velocity, $p_s$ is its partial pressure, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $q_s$ is its signed charge, $n_s$ is its number density, and $B=|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic-field magnitude. A component is the projection of this vector onto the specified direction; aggregation over species uses the weighting defined for the corresponding population, as in [velocity due to diamagnetic drift].

This fluid transport contribution is distinct from a guiding-center particle drift and from the diamagnetic current.

Sign convention: Positive when a reported projection points in the positive sense of its specified component direction.

Effective coefficient relating the radial diffusive flux of electron particles to the radial gradient of electron number density is the scalar Fickian closure coefficient for radial electron particle diffusion in the edge plasma. It describes the diffusive, cross-field radial part of electron particle transport.

The radial diffusive electron particle flux is related to the radial density gradient by

$$
\Gamma_{e,r}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{e,r}^{\mathrm{eff}}\,\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial r}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,r}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the radial diffusive electron particle flux, $D_{e,r}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is this effective radial electron diffusivity, $n_e$ is the [electron number density], and $r$ is the radial transport coordinate.

The scope is electron particles in the edge plasma and the radial component of the diffusive particle-flux closure. It excludes the convective or advective part of electron particle flux, particle sources and sinks, parallel transport along the magnetic field, and the total electron particle flux.

It is the radial member of the direction-dependent [effective electron diffusivity](name:effective_electron_diffusivity). The broader [electron diffusion coefficient](name:electron_diffusion_coefficient) denotes electron particle diffusion without the radial effective-component restriction, while the [radial electron diffusion coefficient] denotes the corresponding radial coefficient when the effective-closure distinction is not made. With the minus sign in the defining relation, a positive $D_{e,r}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ produces diffusive electron particle flux down the gradient of $n_e$; an effective negative value represents an up-gradient flux contribution in the same closure.

Poloidal neutral-state velocity due to diamagnetic drift is the signed poloidal component of particle-flow velocity assigned to a specified neutral atomic or molecular state and attributed to the diamagnetic, pressure-gradient part of transport. For an uncharged neutral state, it denotes an effective contribution in a modeled velocity decomposition rather than a direct single-particle Lorentz-force drift. It refines [neutral-state velocity due to diamagnetic drift] to the poloidal projection.

The scalar component is the projection of the effective neutral-state diamagnetic velocity vector onto the unit vector tangent to increasing poloidal angle in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$:

$$
v_{a,\theta}^{\mathrm{dia}} = \mathbf{e}_{\theta} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{a}^{\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $a$ labels the neutral state, $\mathbf{v}_{a}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the effective diamagnetic velocity contribution for that state, and $\mathbf{e}_{\theta}$ is the unit vector tangent to increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed flux label $\rho$ and toroidal angle $\phi$.

The poloidal projection is distinct from the radial $\hat{R}$, toroidal $\hat{\phi}$, and vertical $\hat{Z}$ components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, and from the field-parallel projection along the magnetic field. It is not the full effective neutral-state diamagnetic velocity vector and not a speed magnitude.

This quantity is the normalized toroidal flux label assigned to the point on a line of sight that approaches the magnetic axis most closely. Its sign records whether that closest point lies above or below the magnetic axis.

The signed closest-approach value is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{LOS}} = \operatorname{sgn}(Z_* - Z_{\mathrm{axis}})\,\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x}_*),
\qquad
\mathbf{x}_* = \underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathrm{LOS}}{\operatorname{arg\,min}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{LOS}}$ is this signed line-of-sight value, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), $\mathbf{x}$ is a point on the line of sight, $\mathbf{x}_*$ is the closest-approach point, and $\mathrm{LOS}$ denotes the line of sight. The function $\operatorname{sgn}$ supplies the sign of its argument; $Z_*$ is the vertical coordinate of the closest-approach point and $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis. Here $R$, $\phi$, and $Z$ are the major-radius, toroidal-angle, and vertical coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The quantity applies to one line of sight and uses only the selected closest-approach point; it is not a line average, line integral, flux-surface average, or volume aggregate. Unlike [normalized toroidal flux coordinate of measurement position], it does not describe the coordinate at an arbitrary single measurement point.

It is obtained from the parent [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) by evaluating that magnetic-surface label at the closest-approach point and appending the above/below-axis sign. The underlying unsigned label increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the equilibrium boundary.

Sign convention: Positive when the closest point on the line of sight lies above the magnetic axis, meaning $Z_* > Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

Parallel diffusion coefficient for total ion energy transport is the effective scalar diffusivity that multiplies the parallel gradient of total ion energy density in a Fickian closure. It is the parallel component of the [total ion energy diffusion coefficient], where total ion energy is summed over all ion species and charge states.

A local diffusive closure for the parallel total-ion-energy flux is

$$
q^{\mathrm{diff}}_{i,\parallel} = -D^{E_i}_{\parallel}\,\nabla_{\parallel} W^{\mathrm{tot}}_i
$$

where $q^{\mathrm{diff}}_{i,\parallel}$ is the diffusive flux of total ion energy along the magnetic-field direction, $D^{E_i}_{\parallel}$ is this coefficient, $\nabla_{\parallel} = \hat{b}\cdot\nabla$ is the derivative along the magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$, and $W^{\mathrm{tot}}_i$ is the total ion energy density summed over all ion species and charge states.

This coefficient represents only the diffusive parallel contribution; advective, convective, source, sink, and cross-field transport terms are outside its definition. It is directionally distinct from the [poloidal total ion energy diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_total_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient).

Sign convention: Positive when the diffusive total-ion-energy flux is directed down the parallel gradient of total ion energy density.
documents.after:

A local diffusive closure for the parallel total-ion-energy flux is

Poloidal ion energy flux is the signed component of ion energy-flux density normal to a poloidal-oriented surface. It gives the rate at which energy carried by a specified ion population crosses the surface per unit area in the poloidal direction, including convective, conductive, or other channels only when they belong to the stated ion-energy reservoir.

For a surface whose chosen unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the local poloidal direction, the scalar poloidal ion energy flux $F_{E,i}^{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the projection of the ion energy-flux-density vector $\mathbf{q}_{E,i}$:

$$
F_{E,i}^{\mathrm{pol}} = \mathbf{q}_{E,i} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_{E,i}$ is the vector density of energy transport for the selected ion population and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

Poloidal ion energy flux is a species- and charge-state-resolved or aggregated specialization of [ion energy flux](name:ion_energy_flux) and an ion specialization of [energy flux]. When an ion species is represented without explicit charge-state resolution, the flux is summed over the charge states included in that species population. [Total ion energy flux](name:total_ion_energy_flux) aggregates all ion species and charge states, while [parallel ion energy flux](name:parallel_ion_energy_flux) uses the local magnetic-field direction for its projection. The quantity is distinct from ion energy density, a volumetric energy source or sink, and ion velocity.

Sign convention: Positive when the ion energy-flux-density vector has a component in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

The magnetic-field magnitude is the nonnegative strength of the local magnetic induction at the pressure-pedestal top on the low-field side. It is the magnitude transformation of [magnetic field at the low-field-side pressure-pedestal top], with no directional component selected.

The magnitude is defined from the local field components by

$$
B = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_\phi^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $B$ is the magnetic-field magnitude and $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are the radial, toroidal, and vertical components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The quantity is nonnegative and is distinct from signed component quantities such as the toroidal magnetic field.

Short-wavelength boundary of the spectral sensitivity band accepted by a visible-camera detector channel is the minimum photon wavelength included in the specified detector response interval. It defines an interval endpoint of the spectral sensitivity band, not the value of the detector response at that endpoint.

Together with the [upper-bound wavelength], it delimits the nominal accepted wavelength interval. Photons with wavelengths shorter than this lower bound are outside the specified interval; photons within the interval remain subject to the detector spectral response function. It is distinct from the [central wavelength] and the [wavelength bandwidth], which summarize the interval rather than define its short-wavelength edge.

Etendue is the geometric extent of the spectrometer optical system: its phase-space acceptance for radiation transmitted through the collecting aperture from accepted directions.

The defining relation is

$$
G = A\Omega
$$

where $G$ is the etendue, $A$ is the effective collecting area, and $\Omega$ is the accepted solid angle.

This quantity describes the instrument-level geometric acceptance, excluding wavelength-dependent transmission losses represented by [efficiency of a spectrometer channel](name:viewing_efficiency_of_spectrometer_channel). It is distinct from the channel-level [viewing etendue of a spectrometer channel].

Full toroidal angular width of a spectrometer-channel spatial-resolution region is the non-negative span in toroidal angle covered by the region associated with that channel, including its effective spatial-resolution broadening. The toroidal angle $\phi$ is the angular coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\phi$ increases counterclockwise when viewed from the $+\hat{Z}$ side.

For a channel $c$ with spatial-resolution region $\Omega_c$, the width is

$$
\Delta\phi_c = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega_c} \tilde{\phi}(\mathbf{x}) - \min_{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega_c} \tilde{\phi}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\Delta\phi_c$ is the toroidal angular width, $\Omega_c$ is the spatial-resolution region of channel $c$, and $\tilde{\phi}(\mathbf{x})$ is a continuously unwrapped toroidal angle of point $\mathbf{x}$ over that region.

It is an angular extent, not a center coordinate, orientation, or signed toroidal displacement. If the region crosses a toroidal-angle branch cut, the unwrapped angle is chosen so the expression gives the full physical span of the region; this width may be used as a geometric factor in [viewing étendue], but it is not an étendue.

where $\Delta\phi_c$ is the toroidal angular width, $\Omega_c$ is the spatial-resolution region of channel $c$, and $\tilde{\phi}(\mathbf{x})$ is a continuously unwrapped toroidal angle of point $\mathbf{x}$ over that region.

It is an angular extent, not a center coordinate, orientation, or signed toroidal displacement. If the region crosses a toroidal-angle branch cut, the unwrapped angle is chosen so the expression gives the full physical span of the region; this width may be used as a geometric factor in viewing étendue, but it is not an étendue.

This quantity is the flux-surface average of the magnitude of the total equilibrium magnetic-field vector. It represents the mean field strength on a magnetic surface, rather than a component or a vector average.

The flux-surface average is defined by

$$
\left\langle \lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert \right\rangle_{\psi} = \frac{\oint_{\psi} \lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert\,\mathrm{d}S/\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}{\oint_{\psi} \mathrm{d}S/\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total equilibrium magnetic-field vector, $\psi$ is the scalar label of the magnetic flux surface, $\mathrm{d}S$ is the surface-area element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of that surface label. The aggregation is the normalized surface integral with weighting $\mathrm{d}S/\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert$.

The quantity applies to all components of the equilibrium field on the selected magnetic flux surface and is non-negative. It excludes any signed field component, any species or source decomposition, and the magnitude of a vector obtained by averaging $\mathbf{B}$ before taking its modulus.

It is the flux-surface-averaged transformation of [magnetic-field magnitude]. It differs from [flux-surface-averaged square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), which averages the squared field strength rather than the field strength itself.

This quantity is the normalized radial component of the wave vector associated with a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode. It characterizes the radial scale of the corresponding perturbation in a local flux-tube description.

The normalized component is defined by

$$
\widehat{k}_x = k_x \rho_{\rm ref}
$$

where $k_x$ is the radial component of the wave vector, $\rho_{\rm ref}$ is the positive reference Larmor radius, and $\widehat{k}_x$ is the dimensionless normalized component.

The quantity describes radial spectral structure and is distinct from the [normalized frequency of a gyrokinetic eigenmode] and its [normalized linear growth rate].

Photon-count line radiance is the photon emission rate from one identified transition accumulated along the emitting line of sight, resolved by projected collecting area and viewing solid angle.

The defining photon-count radiance is

$$
L_{\gamma,\ell} = \frac{d^3 N_{\gamma,\ell}}{dt\,dA_{\perp}\,d\Omega}
$$

where $L_{\gamma,\ell}$ is the line radiance, $N_{\gamma,\ell}$ is the number of photons from transition $\ell$, $\ell$ identifies the emission transition, $t$ is time, $A_{\perp}$ is collecting area projected normal to the viewing direction, and $\Omega$ is viewing solid angle.

The quantity applies to one identified emission transition without imposing a particular emitting species, charge state, or line-splitting mechanism. Photon counts are integrated across the selected spectral-line interval and accumulated along the viewing path; the result is not resolved per wavelength.

Integrating [photon-number spectral radiance] over wavelength across the selected line interval gives this line radiance under matching projected-area and solid-angle conventions. The qualified [motional-Stark photon radiance at a spectral line] is a specialized instance restricted to an identified motional-Stark-split component. Unlike energy radiance, this quantity counts photons without weighting them by photon energy; conversion to energy radiance requires applying that energy weighting before integration.

This quantity is the direction-resolved effective Fickian diffusivity for neutral-particle transport. It retains directional components that are not represented by the scalar [neutral diffusivity].

For each resolved direction $k$, the diffusive particle flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{n,k}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{n,k}^{\mathrm{eff}}\,\partial_k n_n
$$

where $\Gamma_{n,k}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the neutral-particle diffusive flux component, $D_{n,k}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the corresponding effective diffusivity component, $\partial_k$ is the spatial derivative in direction $k$, and $n_n$ is the neutral-particle number density.

The quantity excludes convective transport and particle sources or sinks. Its radial component is represented by [radial effective neutral diffusivity](name:radial_effective_neutral_diffusivity); passive down-gradient diffusion has nonnegative effective coefficients.

Effective ion diffusivity is the vector of directional effective Fickian coefficients for particle transport of the ion population summed over all charge states. Each component relates the diffusive total-ion particle flux projected along one resolved physical direction to the physical gradient of the total ion number density along that direction.

The component definition is

$$
\Gamma_{i,a}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{i,a}^{\mathrm{eff}}\left(\hat{e}_a \cdot \nabla n_i\right)
$$

where $a$ labels one resolved physical direction, $\hat{e}_a$ is the normalized direction vector, $D_{i,a}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the corresponding effective ion diffusivity component, $\Gamma_{i,a}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive total-ion particle flux component, and $n_i$ is the total ion number density. The projection $\hat{e}_a \cdot \nabla n_i$ is the metric-scaled physical gradient along $a$, not a bare derivative with respect to a coordinate label.

The charge-state aggregation is defined through the flux-gradient relation: $n_i$ and $\Gamma_{i,a}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ are sums over all ion charge states before the effective coefficient is formed. Therefore $D_{i,a}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is not generally a density-weighted mean of [charge-state-resolved ion diffusivities](name:ion_charge_state_diffusivity). The quantity includes only the diffusive, gradient-driven coefficient; it excludes advective or convective particle transport, source terms, and off-diagonal cross-gradient elements of a rank-two tensor. Concrete directional specializations of this effective quantity include [radial effective ion diffusivity](name:radial_effective_ion_diffusivity); related non-effective [ion diffusivity] is not a specialization of this effective parent.

Sign convention: Positive when the diffusive ion particle flux component is opposite to the total-ion density gradient along the same resolved direction.

Effective electron diffusivity is an effective scalar transport coefficient for diffusive electron-particle transport along a specified transport direction in a magnetized plasma. It is the direction-specific coefficient appearing in a macroscopic particle-transport closure for electrons.

The directional constitutive relation is

$$
\Gamma_{e,\alpha}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{e,\alpha}^{\mathrm{eff}}\,\nabla_\alpha n_e
$$

where $\alpha$ labels the specified oriented transport direction, $\Gamma_{e,\alpha}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the component of the diffusive electron particle-flux vector along that direction, $D_{e,\alpha}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective electron diffusivity for the same direction, $\nabla_\alpha n_e$ is the component of the gradient of electron number density along $\alpha$, and $n_e$ is electron number density. The minus sign denotes down-gradient diffusive transport when $D_{e,\alpha}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is positive.

This quantity applies to electron particles in the magnetized plasma and has no isotope or charge-state aggregation. It describes the diffusive contribution only and excludes convective particle fluxes, particle sources, and sinks; the qualifier effective identifies a reduced coefficient for the represented diffusive flux component, not a microscopic collision-only diffusion coefficient or a species-independent particle diffusivity.

This is the effective branch of [electron diffusivity]. The directional specialization [radial effective electron diffusivity](name:radial_effective_electron_diffusivity) is the specialization for the $\hat R$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity is the collection of discrete mode labels that identifies a coherent wave perturbation through its periodic phase dependence. It is a mode-index vector, not a spatial wavevector, physical displacement vector, or full linear-MHD eigenmode label.

For a coherent perturbation represented by a single Fourier phase in periodic coordinates, the wave mode-number vector is defined by

$$
\tilde{q}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}, t) = \hat{q}\,\exp\!\left[i\left(\mathbf{N}_w \cdot \boldsymbol{\alpha} - \omega t\right)\right]
$$

where $\tilde{q}$ is the coherent wave perturbation of a field quantity, $\hat{q}$ is its complex amplitude, $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ is the set of periodic coordinates used to label the phase, $\mathbf{N}_w$ is the wave mode-number vector, and $\omega$ is the angular frequency.

This parent covers Fourier harmonic labels of coherent waves, such as the [toroidal wave mode number](name:toroidal_wave_mode_number) associated with toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It does not by itself assert a radial branch index or a poloidal harmonic; those belong only to more specific quantities when explicitly defined, and distinguish it from the broader linear-MHD [mode number].

Sign convention: Positive when increasing the associated periodic coordinate at fixed time increases the Fourier phase in the representation above.

This quantity is the cumulative inventory of neutral hydrogen atoms delivered by gas injection after plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Hydrogen contributes one equivalent electron per atom because its atomic number is one.

$$
N_{H,mathrm{gas}}(t)=Z_H\,\int_{t_{\mathrm{bd}}}^{t}\dot{N}_H(t')\,dt'
$$

where $N_{H,\mathrm{gas}}$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count, $Z_H=1$ is hydrogen's atomic number, $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the plasma-breakdown time, and $\dot{N}_H$ is the neutral-hydrogen injection rate. The corresponding instantaneous rate is [hydrogen source rate due to gas injection](name:hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection).

The accumulation begins at breakdown and excludes hydrogen introduced during prefill; it represents delivered hydrogen inventory rather than the number of free plasma electrons or the ionization-state distribution. It is the post-breakdown component of [hydrogen count due to gas injection], distinct from [accumulated hydrogen prefill count](name:accumulated_hydrogen_prefill_count).

Accumulated impurity-radiation energy is the total energy carried away by photons produced through electron interactions with impurity ions over the disruption interval. It is a cumulative quantity, distinct from the instantaneous [impurity-radiation power].

$$
E_{\mathrm{imp}}(t_0,t_1)=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}P_{\mathrm{imp}}(t)\,dt
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{imp}}$ is the accumulated radiated energy, $P_{\mathrm{imp}}(t)$ is the total radiative power attributed to electron–impurity interactions in W, and $t$, $t_0$, and $t_1$ are times in s. The integration interval spans the defined disruption duration. The quantity includes the impurity-radiation channels represented in $P_{\mathrm{imp}}$ and excludes radiation not attributed to impurity interactions; it is therefore not equivalent to [total plasma radiated power](name:total_plasma_radiated_power).

The particle convection velocity is the effective coefficient of the density-proportional, convective contribution to particle transport. It represents directed drift, pinch, or outward convection after density-gradient-driven diffusive transport has been separated, and it is the shared quantity represented by [particle convection velocity].

The convective particle flux is defined by

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{conv}} = n\,\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective particle-flux vector, $n$ is particle number density, and $\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the particle convection-velocity vector.

This parent quantity is independent of species and directional component; specific children may resolve it for a selected population or component, as in [parallel neutral particle convection velocity](name:parallel_neutral_particle_convection_velocity). It excludes density-gradient-driven diffusive transport.

Sign convention: Positive when a reported component of convective particle transport points along its positive direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ basis, or along the specified magnetic-field direction for a parallel component.

The linear neutral internal-state momentum flux density is the vector-valued transport of linear momentum carried by neutral particles restricted to one specified atomic, molecular, charge, or excitation state. It describes momentum transport rather than particle-number transport or a local momentum source.

For an oriented surface, the momentum-flux vector is defined by

$$
\mathbf{F}_{\Pi}^{(s)}(\hat{n}) = \boldsymbol{\Pi}^{(s)} \cdot \hat{n} = \int m_s\mathbf{v}\, (\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{n}) f_s(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $s$ identifies the internal state, $\hat{n}$ is the oriented surface normal, $m_s$ is the particle mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $f_s$ is the state-resolved velocity distribution, and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{(s)}$ is the corresponding momentum-flux tensor.

This is the linear-momentum form of the parent [neutral internal-state momentum flux]. Projection onto a specified direction produces components such as [poloidal linear neutral internal-state momentum flux](name:poloidal_linear_neutral_internal_state_momentum_flux); no particular radial, poloidal, toroidal, vertical, or magnetic-field-parallel direction is implied here.

Sign convention: Positive when particles cross the oriented surface in its positive normal direction while carrying linear momentum in the selected positive direction.

This quantity is the normalized perturbed gyrocenter current-density vector: the charge-weighted first velocity moment of a perturbed gyrocenter distribution. It represents the vector current response, distinct from density and pressure moments.

The charge-weighted moment and its normalization are defined by

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{gc}}^{\delta}=\sum_s q_s\int \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{gc}}\,\delta f_{\mathrm{gc},s}\,d^3\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{gc}},\qquad \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{gc}}^{\delta}=\frac{\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{gc}}^{\delta}}{J_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $q_s$ is the charge of species $s$, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{gc}}$ is gyrocenter velocity, $\delta f_{\mathrm{gc},s}$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution, and $J_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the positive reference current-density scale. The vector may be resolved into directional projections; [parallel normalized gyrocenter perturbed current density](name:parallel_normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_current_density) is one such field-aligned component. The [normalized gyrocenter perturbed density](name:normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_density) is the corresponding zeroth moment, while [normalized gyrocenter perturbed pressure] is a second moment.

Sign convention: Positive when a projected component of the charge-weighted perturbed gyrocenter flow points along its assigned positive basis direction.

Fast-electron collisional torque density is the vector rate of angular-momentum transfer to the fast-electron population through Coulomb momentum exchange with other plasma species. It is the fast-population specialization of [electron collisional torque density](name:electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

For position vector $\mathbf{r}$ relative to the chosen torque origin and collisional force density $\mathbf{F}_{e,f}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ acting on fast electrons, the torque density is

$$
\boldsymbol{\tau}_{e,f}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{r}) = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}_{e,f}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{r})
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{e,f}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the fast-electron collisional torque density, $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector, and $\mathbf{F}_{e,f}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional force density.

Electron collisional torque is the volume-integrated angular-momentum transfer to an electron population caused by Coulomb collisions with other plasma species. It represents collisional momentum exchange rather than a local torque density.

The defining relation is

$$
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}_{e,\mathrm{coll}} = \int_V \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{f}_{e,\mathrm{coll}}\,dV
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}_{e,\mathrm{coll}}$ is the total collisional torque, $V$ is the plasma volume, $\mathbf{r}$ is displacement from the torque origin, and $\mathbf{f}_{e,\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional force density acting on electrons. The quantity excludes torque from external sources and noncollisional interactions. Its components include the [toroidal thermal-electron torque](name:toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions), while [toroidal fast-electron torque] resolves the corresponding exchange for a nonthermal population; the family is represented by [electron torque due to collisions](name:electron_torque_due_to_collisions).

Sign convention: Positive when a component points along the corresponding positive direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis.

Collisionally transferred net torque on the electron population is the volume-integrated rate of angular-momentum transfer caused by Coulomb collisions with other plasma populations. It is the electron-specific member of the broader [torque due to collisions](name:torque_due_to_collisions) family and parallels [fast torque due to collisions](name:fast_torque_due_to_collisions).

The defining relation is

$$
\tau_{e,\mathrm{coll}} = \frac{dL_{e,\mathrm{coll}}}{dt}
$$

where $\tau_{e,\mathrm{coll}}$ is the net collisional torque on the electron population, $L_{e,\mathrm{coll}}$ is its volume-integrated angular momentum transferred by collisions, and $t$ is time.

Sign convention: Positive when collisions increase the electron population's angular momentum in the positive rotational sense about the torque axis.

Current density $\mathbf{J}$ is the vector density of conventional electric-charge flux at a point. It represents the signed flow of electric charge carried by charged particles, with direction defined by positive charge transport.

A kinetic definition is the charge-weighted first velocity moment of the particle distribution functions:

$$
\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_s q_s \int \mathbf{v}\, f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $t$ is time, $s$ indexes charged species, $q_s$ is the species charge, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $f_s$ is the velocity-space distribution function, and $d^3v$ denotes integration over velocity space.

Unless a narrower restriction is specified, the sum includes all charged-particle contributions. In quasistatic equilibrium, current density is the source in Ampere's law, $\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0\mathbf{J}$ when displacement current is neglected, and steady charge conservation gives $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}=0$. It is distinct from scalar electric current, which is the flux of $\mathbf{J}$ through a specified surface. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, geometric projections include [toroidal current density]; orbit-restricted forms such as [toroidal counter-passing current density](name:toroidal_counter_passing_current_density) remain instances of this quantity. The parent [current density](name:current_density) excludes displacement-current density.

Sign convention: Positive when the stated component or scalar projection of $\mathbf{J}$ is aligned with the positive direction of the basis vector or unit vector defining that component or projection.

Runaway-electron current density $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the vector density of conventional electric charge flux carried by suprathermal electrons beyond the collisional drag limit. Because electron charge is negative, its direction is opposite to the net runaway-electron particle flux.

It is defined by the charge-weighted first velocity moment of the runaway-electron distribution:

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{RE}}(\mathbf{x},t)=q_e\int_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{RE}}}\mathbf{v}\,f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $t$ is time, $q_e$ is electron charge, $\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity, $f_e$ is the electron velocity-space distribution, and $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the velocity-space subset beyond the collisional drag limit.

As a population-restricted form of [current density](name:current_density), it excludes thermal and nonrunaway electrons, ion contributions, and displacement-current density. The vector precedes geometric projection and volume averaging; its field-aligned projection is [parallel runaway-electron current density](name:parallel_runaway_electron_current_density), while [volume-averaged runaway-electron current density] represents its volume average. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, components are projections onto the corresponding basis directions.

Sign convention: Positive when a stated component or scalar projection of $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ aligns with the positive direction of its defining basis vector or unit vector.

Plasma pressure imaginary part is the scalar coefficient multiplying the imaginary unit in a complex representation of isotropic plasma pressure. It represents the imaginary phase quadrature of that pressure representation and is not the complete complex pressure quantity.

A complex plasma-pressure quantity is decomposed into real and imaginary quadratures as:

$$
p = p_\mathrm{R} + i\,p_\mathrm{I}
$$

where $p$ is the complex plasma-pressure quantity, $i$ is the imaginary unit, $p_\mathrm{R}$ is its real-part quadrature, and $p_\mathrm{I}$ is the plasma pressure imaginary part defined here.

This parent quantity applies to any complex scalar representation of isotropic plasma pressure. It does not by itself specify perturbation order, Fourier mode number, reference phase, eigenfunction normalization, or spatial dependence.

The perturbation-specific [perturbed plasma pressure imaginary part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part) is a specialization of this parent in which $p$ is restricted to the complex first-order plasma-pressure perturbation eigenfunction. The quantity is distinct from [plasma pressure], which denotes the pressure scalar itself rather than the imaginary quadrature of a complex representation.

Sign convention: Positive when the pressure phasor projects onto the $+i$ direction of the complex plane.

Ratio of the square of the toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to the square of the local magnetic-field magnitude is a local scalar magnetic-geometry coefficient. It expresses how the spatial metric of the toroidal flux coordinate is weighted by the magnetic-field strength at the same position.

The coefficient $K_{\rho B}$ is defined pointwise by:

$$
K_{\rho B}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{|\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}(\mathbf{x})|^2}{|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})|^2}
$$

where $K_{\rho B}$ is this ratio, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate, $\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is its spatial gradient, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $|\mathbf{B}|$ is the [magnetic-field magnitude].

This quantity is the unaveraged, pointwise ratio evaluated where the toroidal flux coordinate is differentiable and the magnetic-field magnitude is nonzero. It does not include a flux-surface, volume, or time average, and it is distinct from an averaged geometry coefficient.

The numerator is the [square of the toroidal flux-coordinate gradient magnitude](name:square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude), and the denominator is the square of the local magnetic-field magnitude at the same position. The [flux-surface-averaged ratio](name:flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude) is obtained by applying a flux-surface average to this local quotient itself, not by separately averaging the numerator and denominator.

Collisional torque density is the local angular-momentum transfer rate imparted to a specified plasma population by collisional interactions, divided by volume. It applies to electron, ion, charge-state, and orbit-class populations, including the specific cases represented by [electron collisional torque density](name:electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) and [ion collisional torque density](name:ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

For a resolved scalar torque component, the defining relation is

$$
\tau_{s,\mathrm{coll}} = \left.\frac{\partial \ell_s}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{coll}}
$$

where $\tau_{s,\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional torque density, $\ell_s$ is the corresponding angular-momentum density of population $s$, and the subscript indicates that only collisional transfer is included.

The quantity excludes torque caused by electromagnetic forces, pressure forces, or other noncollisional processes. More specific population and orbit restrictions, such as [co-passing fast-ion charge-state collisional torque density], refine the recipient population without changing the underlying definition.

Sign convention: Positive when collisions increase the resolved angular momentum of the recipient population.

Ohmic current density is the vector electric-current contribution generated by the plasma's collisional response to an inductive electric field. It represents the inductive, resistive part of the plasma current rather than the total current density.

The constitutive relation is

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\rm ohm} = \boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\rm ind}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\rm ohm}$ is the ohmic current-density vector, $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ is the plasma conductivity tensor, and $\mathbf{E}_{\rm ind}$ is the inductive electric field. The field-aligned, flux-surface-averaged instance is [parallel current density due to ohmic current drive](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ohmic_current_drive). This quantity excludes bootstrap and externally driven non-inductive contributions, which are represented by [parallel current density due to non-inductive current drive](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive), and is a density counterpart to [current due to ohmic induction].

Torque density due to Coulomb collisions with electrons is the local toroidal angular-momentum transfer rate per volume to a specified plasma population caused by Coulomb collisional momentum exchange with electrons. It is the torque density about the vertical symmetry axis associated only with electron collision partners.

The scalar torque density is the moment arm times the toroidal component of the Coulomb-collisional force density from electrons in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
\tau_e^{\mathrm{C}} = R f_{\phi,e}^{\mathrm{C}}
$$

where $R$ is major radius and $f_{\phi,e}^{\mathrm{C}}$ is the toroidal component, along $\hat{\phi}$, of the force density on the receiving population due to Coulomb collisions with electrons.

This parent quantity does not specify the receiving population; species-specific children such as [electron torque density due to Coulomb collisions with electrons] identify that population. It excludes torque density from collisions with ions or neutrals, from external fields or waves, and from any non-Coulomb momentum-transfer mechanism.

Sign convention: Positive when the Coulomb-collisional force density from electrons on the receiving population points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the species-independent rotational contribution produced by electric-field cross magnetic-field drift. Its vector form retains directional components, while a change form represents variation of the same drift-induced rotation.

The underlying drift velocity is defined by

$$
\mathbf{v}_{E\times B} = \frac{\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector. For a specified rotational direction, the corresponding angular frequency is the drift-velocity component divided by its local lever arm. The toroidal instance, [toroidal rotation frequency due to electric-field cross magnetic-field drift](name:toroidal_rotation_frequency_due_to_e_cross_b_drift), uses the local major radius as that lever arm.

This parent includes the direct drift-induced rotation and its variation, represented by [change in rotation frequency due to electric-field cross magnetic-field drift]. It excludes species-dependent drifts and rotation contributions from other physical processes.

Sign convention: Positive when each resolved component points along its corresponding positive direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the effective vector velocity associated with convective, or advective, transport of a plasma quantity. It describes the motion of the transported quantity rather than diffusive spreading or the transported flux itself.

For a transported density $Q$, the convective flux is defined by

$$
\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{conv}}_Q = Q\,\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{conv}}_Q$ is the convective flux, $Q$ is the local density of the transported quantity, and $\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{conv}}$ is this velocity. For vector or tensor quantities, the product is interpreted componentwise or as the corresponding dyadic flux.

The same parent quantity is specialized by the transported channel in [energy velocity due to convection](name:energy_velocity_due_to_convection), [internal-state velocity due to convection], and [momentum velocity due to convection]. It excludes diffusive transport contributions.

Sign convention: Positive when a vector component points along the corresponding positive basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity is a geometric coefficient in toroidal plasma equilibrium whose scale contains the reciprocal square of the [major radius]. It includes both direct inverse-square radius factors and geometric factors formed from a flux-coordinate gradient divided by the squared major radius.

Its common form is

$$
G = \frac{g}{R^2}
$$

where $G$ is the geometric coefficient, $R$ is the major radius, and $g$ is a dimensionless geometric factor. For [inverse_of_square_of_major_radius](name:inverse_of_square_of_major_radius), $g=1$; for [ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius](name:ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius), $g$ is the squared magnitude of the gradient of the toroidal flux coordinate.

The quantity is a metric factor for flux-coordinate equilibrium and transport formulations, not the major radius or its square itself. Its specific numerator is determined by the concrete member of this geometric-coefficient family.

The common base relation is

$$
B^2 = \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{B}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total equilibrium magnetic-field vector and $B$ is its magnitude, corresponding to the [total magnetic-field magnitude].

The quantity applies to equilibrium magnetic geometry and is defined either pointwise or after the aggregation specified by a concrete form: flux-surface averaging, reciprocal formation, or ratio formation. It is not the magnetic-field magnitude itself; it is a derived expression constructed from its squared magnitude and may therefore represent different geometric factors while retaining the same magnetic-field basis.

Reciprocal major radius is the inverse of the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. It is a geometric quantity used to represent the radial dependence of toroidal equilibrium relations.

$$
R^{-1} = \frac{1}{R}
$$

where $R$ is the [major radius], namely the radial coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

At the parent level, the quantity is evaluated pointwise or at a specified geometric location and has no averaging or integration implied. It is positive wherever the major radius is positive, and it is distinct from the major radius itself because it reverses the radial dependence rather than specifying the distance from the symmetry axis.

A flux-surface-averaged instance applies the flux-surface averaging operation to this reciprocal quantity; [flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius) is the corresponding geometric coefficient obtained by averaging over a magnetic flux surface.

This quantity is the instantaneous global power-balance residual available to account for energy leaving the plasma confinement system. It corrects the total plasma heating power for transient changes in the plasma’s stored energy.

It is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{loss}} = P_{\mathrm{heat,total}} - \frac{dW_{\mathrm{plasma}}}{dt}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ is the power-balance residual represented by this quantity, $P_{\mathrm{heat,total}}$ is the [total plasma heating power], $W_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the total stored energy of the plasma, and $t$ is time.

The quantity is global and aggregated over all heating contributions included in total plasma heating power and over the complete stored plasma-energy reservoir. It is not the heating input itself, a single-source heating contribution, or a regional radiation measurement; [radiated power over the core region](name:radiated_power_over_core_region) is a specific loss channel rather than this balance residual. A positive value means heating exceeds the instantaneous increase in stored energy, while a negative value means stored energy is increasing faster than the heating input.

This residual is the loss-power term in the conventional energy-confinement relation $\tau_E = W_{\mathrm{plasma}}/P_{\mathrm{loss}}$, where $\tau_E$ is the energy confinement time; transient storage changes are therefore excluded from the inferred loss power rather than counted as losses.
documents.after:

Charge-state-averaged ion bulk-flow velocity projected onto the local magnetic-field direction and divided by the local magnetic-field magnitude is the signed ratio of field-parallel ion velocity to magnetic-field magnitude. The underlying ion velocity is the density-weighted first velocity moment over all ion charge states.

The ratio is defined from the field-parallel projection of the charge-state-averaged ion velocity:

$$
\frac{V_{i,\parallel}}{|\mathbf{B}|} = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{b}}\cdot\mathbf{V}_i}{|\mathbf{B}|},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{b}} = \frac{\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $V_{i,\parallel}$ is the [parallel ion velocity], $\mathbf{V}_i$ is the [ion velocity](name:ion_velocity), $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic-field vector, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is the [magnetic-field magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude), and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{B}$.

This species-level intensive quantity applies to the ion population represented collectively, not to a single charge state; the charge-state aggregation is a density-weighted mean over all ionization charge states. It is the field-parallel component divided by magnetic-field magnitude, not a perpendicular velocity component, the standalone ion velocity, or the standalone magnetic-field magnitude.

Multiplying this ratio by the local [magnetic-field magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude) recovers the [parallel ion velocity] for the same ion population and location; that velocity is the projection of [ion velocity](name:ion_velocity) onto $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

Sign convention: Positive when the charge-state-averaged ion bulk flow points in the direction of the local magnetic-field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

This quantity is the temporal rate of change of the electron number density after volume averaging over the confined plasma volume. Positive values indicate increasing mean electron density, while negative values indicate decreasing mean electron density.

For a fixed averaging volume, the defining relation is

$$
\frac{d\langle n_e\rangle_V}{dt} = \frac{1}{V}\int_V \frac{\partial n_e}{\partial t}\,dV
$$

where $n_e$ is the local electron number density, $V$ is the confined plasma volume, and $\langle n_e\rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density).

The volume-average operation is applied to the electron density before time differentiation. This distinguishes the quantity from the more general [time derivative of electron density], which does not specify volume averaging.

This quantity is the instantaneous neutral-gas throughput supplied to the vessel by gas injection, expressed as an equivalent-electron rate. It combines all injected neutral species rather than representing one gas species.

For the set of injected species, the equivalent-electron rate is defined by:

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} Z_s\,\dot{N}_s
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the total equivalent-electron source rate, $\mathcal{S}$ is the set of injected neutral gas species, $\dot{N}_s$ is the particle injection rate of species $s$, and $Z_s$ is the equivalent-electron weighting per injected particle. For an atomic species, $Z_s$ is its atomic number; for a molecule, it is the sum of the atomic numbers of its constituent atoms.

The quantity applies to the vessel-level gas input and is aggregated by summing over all injected neutral species. It is an instantaneous rate, not a time-integrated inventory, and excludes ionization and subsequent plasma particle sources. Species-resolved rates such as the [hydrogen source rate due to gas injection](name:hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) provide individual contributions to this total. Unlike the [total lower gas source rate of the vacuum vessel due to gas injection](name:total_lower_gas_source_rate_of_vacuum_vessel_due_to_gas_injection), it is not restricted to the lower vessel region.

The corresponding accumulated quantity, such as the [accumulated hydrogen count due to gas injection], is obtained by time integration and represents delivered inventory rather than instantaneous throughput.

Electron emissivity is the local electromagnetic radiation power emitted by the electron population per unit volume. It represents an emission source attributable to electrons, not the net energy change of the electron population.

At position $\mathbf{x}$, the emissivity is defined by

$$
\varepsilon_e(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{dP_e^{\mathrm{rad}}}{dV}
$$

where $\varepsilon_e$ is electron emissivity, $P_e^{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the radiation power emitted by electrons, $V$ is volume, and $\mathbf{x}$ is position.

A particular radiation mechanism may be selected by the surrounding physical context, but no mechanism is implied by this name. The quantity excludes absorbed power and differs from [power density due to radiation](name:power_density_due_to_radiation), which is not electron-specific, and from [electron power density], which denotes net energy transfer in the electron energy balance.

Change in ion-state mean ionization potential is the signed difference in the [ion-state mean ionization potential] of an ion charge-state bundle across a specified state change. The base quantity is the concentration-weighted mean of the cumulative successive ionization energies required to reach, from the neutral ground state, the charge states represented in the bundle.

The change is defined as the value after the change minus the value before the change:

$$
\Delta \bar{E}_{\mathrm{ion},s} = \bar{E}_{\mathrm{ion},s}^{\mathrm{after}} - \bar{E}_{\mathrm{ion},s}^{\mathrm{before}}
$$

where $\bar{E}_{\mathrm{ion},s}^{\mathrm{after}}$ and $\bar{E}_{\mathrm{ion},s}^{\mathrm{before}}$ are the [ion-state mean ionization potentials] of the same ion-state bundle after and before the change.

This quantity accounts only for the change in the mean cumulative ionization energy associated with the represented charge-state composition. It excludes thermal internal energy, excitation energy, radiation losses, and kinetic energy exchanged during ionization or recombination.

This quantity is the incoming, process-resolved energy flux density crossing a plasma-facing wall surface into the wall and attributed to eddy-current processes. It is the incident component of the wall-energy-flux decomposition, evaluated locally at each wall-surface element.

The incident flux is the inward normal projection of the energy-flux vector attributed to eddy-current processes:

$$
q_{\mathrm{inc}}^{\mathrm{EC}} = -\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{EC}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{w}}
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{inc}}^{\mathrm{EC}}$ is the incident eddy-current energy flux density, $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{EC}}$ is the energy-flux vector attributed to eddy-current processes, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{w}}$ is the unit normal directed outward from the wall toward the plasma-facing side.

The scope is restricted to the wall region, to energy entering the wall, and to the eddy-current process attribution. No spatial integration, averaging, maximum, or other aggregation over wall elements is implied; the quantity is local to each wall-surface element. It excludes energy emitted outward from the wall after current-driven dissipation and excludes incident contributions attributed to other processes.

The incident component is a directional refinement of [energy flux at the wall due to eddy current]. In the corresponding process-resolved balance, net wall energy flux is the incident contribution minus the outward emitted contribution; therefore this quantity must not be interpreted as the net or emitted wall flux.

Sign convention: Positive when energy flows from the plasma-facing side into the wall.

Non-negative major-radius coordinate $R$ of a point on a ferritic element outline in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is the distance of that point from the toroidal symmetry axis. It specializes the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) to ferritic-element outline points and is paired with the [vertical outline coordinate] for the same outline point.

The major radius is equivalently the norm of the horizontal Cartesian position vector:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are horizontal Cartesian coordinate components in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$ parallel to the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$.

This coordinate denotes an outline-point location and is not a signed radial displacement, aggregate radial size, centroid position, or maximum radial boundary coordinate. The aggregate radial size is represented by [width of ferritic element](name:width_of_ferritic_element), the centroid position by [radial coordinate of ferritic element centroid](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), and the maximum radial boundary coordinate by [outer radius of ferritic element](name:outer_radius_of_ferritic_element).

Volume-integrated rate of neutron production from fusion reactions in the plasma, summed over all neutron-producing fusion reaction channels and all reacting-population classes: thermonuclear (thermal-thermal), beam-thermal, and beam-beam reactions. Neutrons born in non-fusion processes, such as photoneutron production or material activation, are excluded.

The defining aggregation is

$$
\Gamma_n^{\mathrm{fusion}} = \int_{V} S_n^{\mathrm{fusion}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV = \sum_{\alpha} \Gamma_{n,\alpha}
$$

where $\Gamma_n^{\mathrm{fusion}}$ is this quantity, $S_n^{\mathrm{fusion}}$ is the local neutron production rate density summed over all fusion channels, $V$ is the plasma volume, $\alpha$ runs over the neutron-producing reaction-channel and reacting-population classes, and $\Gamma_{n,\alpha}$ is the class-resolved volume-integrated production rate; the thermonuclear contribution to the integrand is the local [fusion neutron emissivity].

Each class-resolved summand $\Gamma_{n,\alpha}$ corresponds to a [neutron flux] scoped to a specified fusion-reaction class; this quantity is the sum of those class-resolved rates. The thermonuclear summand alone is the [total neutron source rate due to thermal fusion](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion), and channel- and population-resolved members such as the [deuterium-tritium beam-beam neutron production rate] are components of the sum, not additional totals. Despite the word flux in the name, this quantity is a global source strength (a count rate), not a particle flux crossing a surface.

Accumulated total gas count at midplane due to gas injection is the cumulative unweighted count of neutral gas particles introduced by all gas-injection valves assigned to the equatorial-midplane valve group. It aggregates all injected species and all valves in that group; each gas particle contributes one count to the total inventory.

The accumulation over a specified time interval is the time integral of the unweighted total midplane gas-particle source rate:

$$
N_{\mathrm{gas,mid}}(t_1;t_0) = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{gas,mid}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{gas,mid}}$ is the accumulated dimensionless count, $t_0$ and $t_1$ are the interval endpoints in seconds, $t'$ is the integration time in seconds, and $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{gas,mid}}$ is the [total gas source rate at midplane due to gas injection](name:total_gas_source_rate_at_midplane_due_to_gas_injection) in particles per second, summed over all midplane gas-injection valves and all injected species.

For a post-breakdown accumulated inventory, $t_0$ is the plasma-breakdown time; for a prefill inventory, the interval is the pre-breakdown gas-fill interval. This quantity is the midplane contribution to the all-position [accumulated total particle count due to gas injection](name:accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection), not a per-valve count and not an equivalent-electron inventory. Species-specific inventories such as [accumulated neon count due to gas injection], [accumulated nitrogen count due to gas injection], and [accumulated carbon count due to gas injection] are separate components of the injected species inventory.

This quantity is the cumulative net electron particle source enclosed by a magnetic flux surface. It includes particle production and removal within the enclosed volume rather than the local source density.

$$
S_{e,\mathrm{inside}}(\psi)=\int_{V(\psi)} s_e(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

Here $\psi$ is the magnetic-flux-surface label, $V(\psi)$ is the volume enclosed by that surface, $s_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local electron particle source rate density, and $dV$ is the volume element. The quantity is the enclosed counterpart of the global [electron source rate](name:cumulative_inside_flux_surface_electron_particle_source_rate); [ion particle source rate](name:ion_particle_source_rate) is the analogous ion quantity.

Sign convention: Positive when the enclosed electron population has a net particle gain.

This quantity is the photon-number radiance of discrete spectral-line emission generated by charge exchange involving impurity ions. It describes photons emitted in the selected transition rather than the corresponding emitted energy.

The wavelength-integrated photon radiance is defined by

$$
L_{\mathrm{ph}}(\ell)=\int_{\ell}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}N_{\gamma}}{\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}A_{\perp}\,\mathrm{d}\Omega\,\mathrm{d}\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda
$$

where $N_{\gamma}$ is the photon count, $t$ is time, $A_{\perp}$ is area projected normal to the viewing direction, $\Omega$ is solid angle, $\lambda$ is wavelength, and $\ell$ is the selected spectral-line interval.

The quantity includes only charge-exchange line emission and excludes continuum radiation and line emission from other production processes. The corresponding [ion radiance of a spectral line due to charge exchange] applies the same photon-radiance definition at the ion-population scope, while [fast-ion radiance of a spectral line due to charge exchange] restricts the emitting population to fast ions.

The toroidal coordinate identifies the azimuthal location of the geometric center of the Bragg crystal around the machine symmetry axis. It describes position, not the crystal’s orientation or the direction of an incident beam.

In the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$ aligned with the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$, the toroidal angle is defined by

$$
\phi_c = \operatorname{atan2}(y_c, x_c)
$$

where $x_c$ and $y_c$ are the Cartesian coordinates of the crystal center and $\phi=0$ is the facility-defined reference direction. Together with the [vertical coordinate of the Bragg crystal], this coordinate locates the crystal center geometrically.

Sign convention: Positive when the angle increases in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$.

Electron pressure at the separatrix is the local scalar pressure associated with the random kinetic motion of the electron population on the last closed magnetic flux surface. It characterizes the electron contribution to the total plasma pressure at the boundary between confined plasma and the open-field-line scrape-off layer.

For an isotropic electron population, the pressure is defined by

$$
p_e = n_e k_B T_e
$$

where $p_e$ is electron kinetic pressure, $n_e$ is electron number density, $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant, and $T_e$ is the electron thermodynamic temperature.

This quantity is evaluated locally at the separatrix and is not a flux-surface average, a pressure gradient, or a pedestal-top value. It applies only to electrons; no ion, neutral, or impurity contribution is included, and no charge-state aggregation applies. The related [electron-pressure derivative at the pedestal top] describes a spatial slope at a different edge-plasma locus rather than the pressure value defined here.

Toroidal fast-particle torque density due to Coulomb collisions with electrons is the local rate of transfer of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume to the fast-particle population caused by Coulomb collisions with background electrons. The toroidal direction is the $\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining relation to the corresponding collisional force density is

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow e}^{\mathrm{C}} = R\,\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow e}^{\mathrm{C}}\cdot\hat{\phi}
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow e}^{\mathrm{C}}$ is this torque density, $\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow e$ identifies transfer to the fast-particle population from electrons, superscript $\mathrm{C}$ identifies the Coulomb-collisional contribution, and $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow e}^{\mathrm{C}}$ is the corresponding force density exerted on the fast-particle population by electrons.

The scope is the local fast-particle recipient population and the background-electron collision partner. The value is integrated over fast-particle velocity space and is an angular-momentum transfer rate per unit volume; it is not a single-particle torque and is not resolved by energy, pitch, or orbit class unless an orbit-class qualifier is present. The [toroidal co-passing fast-particle torque density due to Coulomb collisions with electrons] is the co-passing orbit-class-resolved member of the same electron-partner channel.

This quantity excludes torque density transferred to electrons, collisions with non-electron partners, non-Coulomb momentum exchange, and externally applied torques. As an electron-partner contribution, it adds with corresponding non-electron partner terms to form the [toroidal fast-particle torque density due to Coulomb collisions]. The reaction torque density on electrons for the same pair interaction is a different recipient quantity and has the opposite sign when both are expressed along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

Sign convention: Positive when the Coulomb-collisional torque on the fast-particle population is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.
documents.after:

This quantity is the local volumetric abundance of one selected atomic species in the material composing an individual shattered-pellet fragment.

It is defined by

$$
n_s = \frac{N_s}{V_f}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of the selected atomic species, $N_s$ is its number of constituent atoms in the fragment, and $V_f$ is the physical volume occupied by the fragment.

The scope is restricted to one fragment and one specified atomic species in the fragment material. The quantity is species-selective rather than summed over different species, and it describes pellet composition rather than the number density of particles in the surrounding plasma. No plasma ionization-state aggregation or charge-state resolution is implied.

Multiplying this density by the fragment volume gives the corresponding constituent-atom count. It therefore provides a fragment-local density counterpart to the whole-pellet inventory represented by [atomic count of pellet], while [fast neutral internal state number density](name:fast_neutral_internal_state_number_density) describes a plasma-particle population distinguished by internal state.
