Electron particle flux due to surface emission is the number of electrons emitted from a plasma-facing wall and crossing the wall surface toward the plasma. It represents the emitted electron population only, rather than the incident population arriving from the plasma.

The local emitted electron particle flux density is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{emit}} = \frac{dN_{e,\mathrm{emit}}}{dA\,dt}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{emit}}$ is the emitted electron particle flux density, $N_{e,\mathrm{emit}}$ is the number of surface-emitted electrons crossing the surface, $A$ is the wall-surface area, and $t$ is time. The subscript $e$ identifies electrons and $\mathrm{emit}$ identifies the surface-emission contribution.

The quantity applies locally to the plasma-facing wall surface and counts emitted electrons without energy weighting or summation over other particle species. It excludes electrons incident on the wall, photons, ions, and any other non-electron emission products.

The net electron particle flux received by the wall is obtained by subtracting this emitted contribution from the incident electron particle flux. This quantity is a process-resolved component of the broader [flux at wall] concept; its energy-carrying counterpart is the [electron kinetic energy flux at wall due to surface emission](name:electron_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission).
documents.after:

Poloidal current density due to diamagnetic drift is the signed poloidal scalar projection of the pressure-gradient-driven current described by [current density due to diamagnetic drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). It includes the poloidal projection of both the perpendicular pressure-gradient drive and any field-aligned closure or return-current contribution included in the parent vector.

The projection is defined by

$$
j_{\mathrm{dia,pol}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{dia,pol}}$ is this scalar projection, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the [current density due to diamagnetic drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the unit tangent in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed flux-surface label $\rho$ and toroidal angle $\phi$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

This quantity applies to the aggregate plasma current-density contribution associated with diamagnetic drift in plasma transport regions where the parent decomposition is defined. The aggregation convention is that all contributions included in $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}$, including field-aligned closure contributions when present, are combined in the parent vector before the poloidal projection is taken.

It is not the complete vector [current density due to diamagnetic drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), not the [toroidal current density due to diamagnetic drift](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), not the [parallel current density due to diamagnetic drift](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and not the [Pfirsch-Schlueter current density due to diamagnetic drift](name:pfirsch_schlueter_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). It is also distinct from [diamagnetic current density] when that name denotes a magnitude rather than a signed component.

Sign convention: Positive when $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ has a component in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

Second local tangential front-surface radius of an optical element is the non-negative principal radius of curvature of the optical element's front surface along the second local tangential axis $X_2$ in the right-handed local optical-element frame $(X_1, X_2, z_\mathrm{loc})$. In this frame, $X_1$ and $X_2$ are the first and second local surface-tangent axes and $z_\mathrm{loc}$ is the local surface-normal axis.

The radius is the reciprocal of the magnitude of the corresponding signed principal curvature:

$$
R_2 = \frac{1}{|\kappa_2|}
$$

where $R_2$ is the second local tangential front-surface radius of the optical element and $\kappa_2$ is the signed principal curvature of that front surface along $X_2$.

This quantity is defined for a single front surface of a single optical element when that surface form has a specified principal curvature in the second local tangential direction, including cylindrical and toroidal surfaces. It is not aggregated over multiple optical elements or over multiple surfaces, and it excludes the first local tangential front-surface radius, any back-surface radius, aperture size, and position coordinates.

The second local tangential direction is object-local and must not be reinterpreted as a laboratory vertical direction unless the optical element's local frame is independently aligned that way. Together with the [first local tangential front-surface radius], when that counterpart is defined, this radius specifies the two principal curvature radii of the front surface; a flat second tangential direction corresponds to an unbounded radius, not to a negative value.

This quantity is the outward kinetic-energy flux density carried by electrons released from a plasma-facing wall through surface-emission processes. It represents energy transported by the emitted electron population after sheath transmission.

The emitted electron kinetic-energy flux density is related to the emitted particle flux and the mean kinetic energy per emitted electron by

$$
q_{\mathrm{e,kin}}^{\mathrm{em}} = \Gamma_{\mathrm e}^{\mathrm{em}}\,\overline{E}_{\mathrm{kin,e}}
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{e,kin}}^{\mathrm{em}}$ is this kinetic-energy flux density, $\Gamma_{\mathrm e}^{\mathrm{em}}$ is the [electron particle flux due to surface emission](name:electron_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission), and $\overline{E}_{\mathrm{kin,e}}$ is the mean kinetic energy carried by each emitted electron.

The quantity applies specifically to emitted electrons at the wall surface and is aggregated over the emitted electron population, rather than representing an individual electron energy or a spatial maximum. It excludes energy carried by incident electrons, emitted ions, emitted photons, and non-kinetic energy of emitted electrons.

It is the electron kinetic contribution to the broader [energy flux at the wall due to surface emission](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission), which also includes other emitted energy channels. It is distinct from the incident wall energy represented by [energy flux at the wall] and from the corresponding emitted-ion quantity [ion kinetic energy flux at the wall due to surface emission](name:ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission).

Sign convention: Positive when kinetic energy is carried away from the wall into the plasma.

Total plasma pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure summed over all represented plasma particle species and populations in a fluid or magnetohydrodynamic description. It represents the aggregate equilibrium mechanical stress of the included particle populations, rather than a pressure perturbation.

The total pressure is defined by the isotropic part of the aggregate kinetic pressure tensor:

$$
p_{\mathrm{tot}} = \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_s p_s
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total plasma pressure, $\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the combined kinetic pressure tensor of the represented plasma particle populations, $\operatorname{tr}$ denotes the tensor trace, $s$ indexes those species and populations, and $p_s$ is the isotropic kinetic-pressure contribution from population $s$.

The quantity applies locally to the equilibrium plasma and aggregates all represented kinetic particle contributions, including thermal and nonthermal populations. The total qualifier denotes summation over the included populations; it does not denote normalization, volume integration, or addition of magnetic pressure.

It excludes magnetic pressure, dynamic ram pressure, anisotropic pressure-tensor components, and first-order pressure perturbations. [Plasma pressure] is the corresponding unqualified equilibrium kinetic-pressure concept, while [thermal plasma pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure) restricts the aggregation to thermal electron and ion populations and [perturbed plasma pressure] describes a first-order variation about equilibrium.

The quantity denotes radio-frequency wave power launched toward the plasma by an ion-cyclotron resonance heating antenna at the antenna reference plane. It is the net launched component after accounting for the forward and reflected traveling-wave components.

For a single antenna, the launched power is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{launched}} = P_{\mathrm{fwd}} - P_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{launched}}$ is the launched radio-frequency power, $P_{\mathrm{fwd}}$ is the forward incident power traveling from the generator toward the antenna, and $P_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reflected power traveling from the antenna toward the generator.

This quantity applies to one ion-cyclotron heating antenna at its reference plane and represents a net directional power, not a sum over an antenna set. It excludes the reflected component and the power subsequently absorbed by the plasma.

Within the broader [power of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:launched_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) quantity, this is the launched-power specialization. The [forward power](name:forward_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) and [reflected power](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) are the components combined by the defining relation, whereas [power due to ion-cyclotron heating] denotes power coupled from the waves into the plasma.

This quantity is the total neutron production rate associated with the neutron-producing deuterium–deuterium beam–beam fusion branch. It represents reactions between deuterons belonging to beam populations, rather than reactions involving the thermal deuteron population.

The rate is defined as the volume integral of the local beam–beam neutron-production rate:

$$
S_{DD,bb} = \int_{V_{\rm plasma}} \varepsilon_{DD,bb}(\mathbf{x})\,d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where $S_{DD,bb}$ is the integrated neutron production rate, $\varepsilon_{DD,bb}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neutron-production rate from beam–beam deuterium–deuterium fusion, $V_{\rm plasma}$ is the plasma volume included in the aggregation, and $\mathbf{x}$ is the spatial position. The subscripts $DD$ and $bb$ identify the deuterium–deuterium reaction and beam–beam fusion branch, respectively.

The scope is restricted to the neutron-producing deuterium–deuterium branch and to reactions between beam-origin deuterons. It is a single volume-integrated total over the plasma and excludes thermal deuterium–deuterium fusion, beam–thermal fusion, other fusion reaction channels, and the local volumetric emissivity represented by [deuterium-deuterium emissivity due to fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion).

This branch-resolved rate contributes to [neutron flux], which aggregates neutron production over the applicable fusion reaction channels. It is distinct from [deuterium-deuterium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion], whose corresponding contribution arises from the thermonuclear deuterium–deuterium branch.

The subscripts $DD$ and $bb$ identify the deuterium–deuterium reaction and beam–beam fusion branch, respectively.

The scope is restricted to the neutron-producing deuterium–deuterium branch and to reactions between beam-origin deuterons. It is a single volume-integrated total over the plasma and excludes thermal deuterium–deuterium fusion, beam–thermal fusion, other fusion reaction channels, and the local volumetric emissivity represented by [deuterium-deuterium emissivity due to fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion).

This branch-resolved rate contributes to neutron flux, which aggregates neutron production over the applicable fusion reaction channels. It is distinct from deuterium-deuterium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion, whose corresponding contribution arises from the thermonuclear deuterium–deuterium branch.

Viewing efficiency is the geometric fraction of radiation emitted locally at a specified point that is collected by the optical system of a spectrometer channel. It characterizes spatial light collection for non-pinhole optics, rather than the probability that a detector registers an incident photon.

For a point at position $mathbf{r}$, the viewing efficiency is defined by

$$
\eta_{\mathrm{view}}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{collected}}(\mathbf{r})}{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{local}}(\mathbf{r})}
$$

where $\eta_{\mathrm{view}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the viewing efficiency, $\mathbf{r}$ is the spatial emission point, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{collected}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local emission contribution collected by the optical system, and $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{local}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the corresponding local emitted radiation considered by the collection model.

The quantity is evaluated separately at each point defining a region of interest and is a fraction bounded between zero and one. It represents spatial collection and is not summed or averaged over the region-of-interest points. It is not a wavelength-resolved efficiency and excludes detector-registration probability or other spectral detector response.

Viewing efficiency is related to the optical phase-space acceptance described by [etendue of a spectrometer channel], but it is a pointwise collection fraction rather than an etendue. It is distinct from [spectral efficiency of a hard X-ray detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector), which is an energy-dependent photon-registration probability.

The instantaneous radial width-change rate of a neoclassical tearing-mode magnetic island quantifies whether the island is expanding or contracting. The width is the full radial extent in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, measured along increasing $R$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The rate is defined by

$$
\frac{dW_r(t)}{dt} = \dot{W}_r(t)
$$

where $W_r(t)$ is the full radial width of the island, $t$ is physical time, and $\dot{W}_r(t)$ is its instantaneous time derivative; the subscript $r$ identifies the radial width.

This quantity applies to one identified neoclassical tearing-mode island at its resonant magnetic surface. It describes the complete island width rather than a half-width, radial position, phase, or an aggregate over multiple modes or islands; no summation or averaging is implied.

It is the NTM-specific radial realization of the generic [mode width] change-rate concept. It is distinct from the [rotation frequency of a neoclassical tearing mode](name:rotation_frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode), which describes helical phase motion rather than radial size evolution.

Sign convention: Positive when the full radial island width increases with physical time.

Effective neutral energy diffusion coefficient is the scalar coefficient in a Fickian closure for diffusion of aggregate neutral thermal energy driven by the gradient of aggregate neutral thermal-energy density. It represents a direction-agnostic effective closure parameter for the neutral thermal-energy channel rather than a resolved spatial component.

The defining closure is

$$
\mathbf{q}_{E,n}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{E,n}^{\mathrm{eff}} \nabla w_{E,n}
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_{E,n}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive flux of aggregate neutral thermal energy, $D_{E,n}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is this effective neutral-energy diffusion coefficient, $\nabla$ is the spatial-gradient operator, and $w_{E,n}$ is the aggregate neutral thermal-energy density. The subscript $E,n$ denotes neutral thermal energy, and the superscript $\mathrm{eff}$ denotes an effective closure coefficient.

The scope is the aggregate neutral population and its thermal-energy density; aggregation is performed at the closure level by using one effective coefficient for the aggregate energy-density gradient. It does not select a particular neutral species, internal state, or spatial direction, and it excludes convective or advective neutral-energy transport.

This quantity is distinct from the [neutral-energy diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient), which belongs to the temperature-gradient, density-normalized neutral-energy diffusion family. The [radial neutral-energy diffusion coefficient] and [poloidal neutral-energy diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient) are direction-specific members of that temperature-gradient family; the radial member is along the cylindrical $\hat{R}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with $R$ major radius, $\phi$ toroidal angle, and $Z$ vertical height. Those direction-specific coefficients are not components of $D_{E,n}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ unless a separate physical closure explicitly equates the energy-density-gradient and temperature-gradient formulations.

The effective ionic charge at the separatrix is a dimensionless measure of the charge composition of the local plasma ion mixture. It weights each ionic population by the square of its charge and relates the resulting charge-weighted ion density to the local electron density.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{\sum_i n_i Z_i^2}{n_e}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective ionic charge, $i$ indexes each included ion species and charge-state population, $n_i$ is the number density of that population, $Z_i$ is its ionic charge number, and $n_e$ is the local electron number density.

The quantity is evaluated locally at the separatrix, the last closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off-layer region. The numerator is summed over the contributing ion species and charge states; the quantity is not a single-species or single-charge-state charge number, and it is not averaged over the separatrix surface.

The corresponding [flux-surface-averaged effective charge at the plasma boundary] averages the local effective-charge field over the boundary surface, and is therefore distinct from this local separatrix value.

This quantity is the retained neutral-particle inventory accumulated through net exchange between the plasma and the wall. It is not the instantaneous number of neutral particles present at the wall.

The inventory is defined by the time-integrated net particle flux across the wall surface:

$$
N_{\mathrm{wall}}(t)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{wall}}}\left[\Gamma_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathbf{x},t')-\Gamma_{\mathrm{out}}(\mathbf{x},t')\right] \,\mathrm{d}A\,\mathrm{d}t'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the accumulated neutral inventory, $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the wall surface, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{out}}$ are the inward and outward neutral-particle flux densities. The inward contribution is related to the [neutral particle flux at wall], while recombination provides one process-resolved contribution to outward flux through [neutral particle flux at wall due to recombination](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination). The accumulation is for the selected neutral species and represents net exchange rather than a global gas-injection inventory.

Flux-surface average of tritium ion number density evaluated at the plasma boundary is the value obtained by applying the flux-surface-average operator to the local tritium ion number density on the last closed magnetic flux surface. The plasma boundary is the separatrix bounding the confined plasma.

The average at the boundary flux value $\psi_b$ is defined in flux coordinates $(\psi, \theta, \phi)$ by the Jacobian-weighted surface integral:

$$
\langle n_T \rangle_{\psi_b} = \frac{\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{2\pi} n_T(\psi_b,\theta,\phi)\,\mathcal{J}(\psi_b,\theta,\phi)\,d\theta\,d\phi}{\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{2\pi} \mathcal{J}(\psi_b,\theta,\phi)\,d\theta\,d\phi}
$$

where $n_T$ is the local [tritium ion number density at the plasma boundary](name:tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary), $\psi_b$ is the boundary value of the poloidal magnetic flux, $\theta$ and $\phi$ are the poloidal and toroidal coordinates in the flux-coordinate tuple $(\psi, \theta, \phi)$, and $\mathcal{J}$ is the positive coordinate Jacobian of the flux-coordinate mapping. Equivalently, $\mathcal{J}\,d\theta\,d\phi$ is the flux-surface measure $dS/|\nabla\psi|$ at fixed $\psi$.

The species-level tritium density is summed over all charge states of tritium ions. It excludes neutral tritium atoms and tritium-bearing molecules, and is distinct from [flux-surface-averaged total ion density], which aggregates over all ion species.

Flux-surface-averaged number density of deuterium-tritium pseudo-species ions at the plasma boundary (separatrix) is the particle density of the effective deuterium-tritium fuel species averaged over the last closed magnetic flux surface. The pseudo-species represents the deuterium-tritium fuel mixture as a single ion constituent with effective mass number 2.5; as a species-level density, it is summed over all charge states.

Using the poloidal-contour representation of a flux-surface average in an axisymmetric equilibrium, the boundary value is defined by:

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{DT}} \rangle_b =
\frac{\oint_{\psi=\psi_b} n_{\mathrm{DT}}(l)\, dl / B_p(l)}
{\oint_{\psi=\psi_b} dl / B_p(l)}
$$

where $\langle n_{\mathrm{DT}} \rangle_b$ is this boundary average, $\psi_b$ labels the plasma-boundary flux surface, $l$ is poloidal arc length along that surface, and $B_p$ is the [poloidal magnetic-field magnitude]. The local pseudo-species density is $n_{\mathrm{DT}} = n_{\mathrm{D}} + n_{\mathrm{T}}$, where $n_{\mathrm{D}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{T}}$ are the corresponding charge-state-summed deuterium and tritium ion densities.

This quantity is the plasma-boundary member of [flux-surface-averaged deuterium-tritium density](name:flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary) and the flux-surface-averaged counterpart of [deuterium-tritium density at the plasma boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary), which retains variation around the same boundary surface. The single-isotope boundary analog [flux-surface-averaged deuterium density at the plasma boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary) separates one isotope contribution, while [volume-averaged deuterium-tritium density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density) averages the same effective fuel population over the confined-plasma volume. It excludes scrape-off-layer and material-limiter densities, including [deuterium-tritium density at a limiter](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_limiter).

The ion particle convection velocity is the effective coefficient of the density-proportional, convective contribution to ion particle transport. It is the ion specialization of [particle convection velocity] and the vector parent whose resolved projections include the [radial ion particle convection velocity](name:radial_ion_particle_convection_velocity); it is not a velocity magnitude.

The convective ion particle flux is defined by

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_i \mathbf{v}_i^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective ion particle flux, $n_i$ is the ion particle number density, and $\mathbf{v}_i^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is this ion particle convection velocity.

This quantity excludes density-gradient-driven diffusive transport and applies specifically to ions, not to electrons, neutrals, or neutral internal states. As a species-level intensive transport coefficient, it is the density-weighted mean over all ion charge states; the charge-state-resolved counterpart is the [ion-charge-state particle convection velocity](name:ion_charge_state_particle_convection_velocity). Component or projection names specify the direction used to resolve the vector, for example along increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame for the radial ion component.
documents.after:

Kinetic energy density is the translational kinetic energy carried by a defined particle population per unit volume. It includes random thermal motion and directed or nonthermal motion represented within that population.

The local kinetic energy density is defined from the particle velocity distribution by

$$
K_{\mathrm{kin}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \int \varepsilon_{\mathrm{kin},s}(\mathbf{v})\, f_s(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $K_{\mathrm{kin}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the kinetic energy density at position $\mathbf{r}$, $\mathcal{S}$ is the set of included particle species or states, $s$ identifies one member of that set, $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kin},s}(\mathbf{v})$ is the translational kinetic energy of a particle with velocity $\mathbf{v}$, and $f_s(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{v})$ is its velocity-distribution density.

The population and aggregation are defined by the specific application: species and charge states may be summed, while a designated population such as runaway electrons may be represented by its population mean. The quantity may be evaluated locally or resolved by magnetic flux surface; neither spatial representation changes its kinetic-energy definition. The [ion kinetic energy density](name:ion_kinetic_energy_density) is the ion-population instance, while the [runaway electron kinetic energy density](name:runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density) is the runaway-electron instance.

This component of [energy density] includes translational particle motion only. It excludes magnetic, electric, potential, and non-translational internal-state energy, while random thermal motion remains included when it belongs to the specified particle population.

Radial coordinate of an annulus center is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric center of an annular element. It is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to that center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies to annuli used to represent finite material or conductor cross-sections, including passive conducting, ferritic, or antenna-strap annular elements. For each annulus it denotes the center coordinate of that individual annular cross-section; it is not an average over multiple annuli.

It distinguishes the annulus-center locus from the radial coordinate of an inner edge, outer edge, boundary point, node, or arbitrary measurement position. Size quantities such as annulus width, thickness, or boundary radii describe the extent of the annulus and do not change the meaning of this center coordinate.

Together with the [height of annulus center], this quantity locates the annulus center in the $(R,Z)$ poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The toroidal angle $\phi$ is not part of this scalar center coordinate.

This quantity is the peak radio-frequency voltage amplitude associated with one transmission-line feed serving one ion-cyclotron-heating antenna module. It represents the magnitude of the oscillating feed voltage rather than its instantaneous signed value or phase.

For a voltage waveform, the peak amplitude is defined by

$$
V_{\mathrm{amp}} = \max_t |V(t)|
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{amp}}$ is the peak voltage amplitude, $V(t)$ is the instantaneous signed voltage between the ordered feed terminals, and $t$ is time.

The quantity applies to a single transmission-line feed of a single antenna module. It is not a module-averaged or antenna-system-aggregated voltage, and it excludes the instantaneous waveform and phase information represented by the underlying [voltage of the ion-cyclotron-heating antenna].

The amplitude is the magnitude transformation of that parent voltage quantity: the parent defines the terminal potential difference, while this quantity retains its peak magnitude for radio-frequency power and reflection analysis. It is distinct from reflected power, which characterizes returned wave energy rather than feed voltage.

Signed logarithmic derivative of a selected particle-species density with respect to normalized minor radius is the local derivative of that species density's natural logarithm along the normalized minor-radius coordinate. It represents the relative change of the selected species density with respect to that coordinate.

The derivative is defined by

$$
G_{n_s} = \frac{\partial \ln n_s}{\partial \rho} = \frac{1}{n_s}\frac{\partial n_s}{\partial \rho}
$$

where $G_{n_s}$ is this logarithmic derivative, $n_s$ is the density of the selected particle species $s$, and $\rho$ is the [normalized minor radius], the radial coordinate in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

The scope is one selected particle species at the position where the derivative is evaluated. When the selected species represents a charge-state-aggregated ion population, $n_s$ is the charge-state-summed density over all charge states; it is not a density-weighted charge-state mean and not a total over unrelated species.

This quantity is the derivative of the logarithmic density with respect to $\rho$, not the density itself, not the logarithm alone, and not a coordinate-specialized value of a logarithm-of-density quantity. Logarithmic-gradient conventions that add an extra minus sign or differentiate with respect to an unnormalized minor-radius coordinate denote different quantities.

Sign convention: Positive when $\ln n_s$ increases with increasing normalized minor-radius coordinate $\rho$.

Electron power is the volume-integrated net rate at which energy is transferred to or from the electron population. It is the aggregate electron-recipient source or sink for the selected plasma volume.

$$
P_e = \int_V p_e(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_e$ is electron power, $p_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local [electron power density] at physical position $\mathbf{x}$, $V$ is the selected plasma volume, and $dV$ is its differential volume element.

The scope is the electron population throughout the specified plasma volume, with all applicable source and sink channels assigned to the electron energy balance. The aggregation convention is a net volume integral; this quantity is not a local density, an individual process contribution, a flux-surface average, or stored electron energy. It excludes energy assigned to ion or neutral recipients and is distinct from [power density due to radiation](name:power_density_due_to_radiation), which represents emitted electromagnetic radiation.

This quantity is obtained by integrating [net electron power density] over the selected volume. Unlike [power at the inside flux surface](name:power_at_inside_flux_surface), it does not encode a specific flux-surface boundary in its name; unlike [thermal electron power at the inside flux surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface), it is not restricted to thermal-electron wave absorption.

Sign convention: Positive when the included balance terms increase the energy of the electron population.

This quantity is the local geometric derivative of the area enclosed by a closed magnetic flux surface’s poloidal cross-section with respect to the surface’s signed poloidal magnetic-flux label.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{dA}{d\psi}
$$

where $A$ is the enclosed poloidal cross-sectional area and $\psi$ is the signed poloidal magnetic flux labeling the nested surface.

The derivative applies to each closed flux surface in the nested equilibrium region and is not a volume or toroidal-surface average. It describes the poloidal cross-sectional area only; it excludes the total area of the three-dimensional toroidal surface and derivatives with respect to a toroidal-flux coordinate.

This is the derivative specialization of the geometric quantity [area of a flux surface]. It is mathematically analogous to the derivative of enclosed volume with respect to poloidal magnetic flux, [derivative with respect to poloidal magnetic flux coordinate of volume of flux surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface), with area replacing volume.

Sign convention: Positive when the enclosed poloidal cross-sectional area increases in the direction of increasing signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$; for positive plasma current, this direction is toward the magnetic axis because $\psi$ decreases outward.

Tungsten-ion number density at the plasma boundary represents the local population of positively charged tungsten ions on the separatrix, the last closed magnetic flux surface. The same physical quantity may also be evaluated as a flux-surface average over that boundary surface; the local and averaged forms are distinct.

The charge-state-summed local density is defined from the velocity distributions by:

$$
n_{\mathrm{W}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{Z=1}^{Z_{\max}} \int f_{\mathrm{W}}^{Z}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{W}}$ is the tungsten-ion number density, $\mathbf{x}$ is a position on the separatrix, $Z$ is the positive tungsten ion charge state, $Z_{\max}$ is the highest included charge state, $f_{\mathrm{W}}^{Z}$ is the velocity distribution of that charge state, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

This quantity applies to tungsten ions evaluated at the plasma boundary and sums over all positive ionization states. It excludes neutral tungsten and does not select an individual charge state. The local form is evaluated at a boundary position, whereas the [flux-surface-averaged tungsten density at the plasma boundary] averages the same charge-state-summed density over the boundary flux surface.

The flux-surface-averaged quantity is therefore an aggregation of this local density over the same separatrix, not a different species or charge-state convention. It is distinct from [volume-averaged tungsten density](name:volume_averaged_tungsten_density), which averages tungsten-ion density over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface.

This quantity is the full transverse width of the neutron detector’s collimating aperture along its first local tangential direction. It describes the aperture opening rather than the external detector body, housing, or shielding.

The width is defined by

$$
w_1 = x_{1,\max} - x_{1,\min}
$$

where $w_1$ is the first local tangential aperture width, and $x_{1,\max}$ and $x_{1,\min}$ are the positions of the two aperture edges along the first local tangential axis.

This quantity applies only to a rectangular aperture and represents the complete edge-to-edge opening dimension, not a radius or half-width. The other transverse dimension is represented by the [second local tangential width of the neutron detector], whereas a circular opening is characterized by the [radius of the neutron detector](name:radius_of_neutron_detector) rather than by rectangular widths.

Incident neutral particle flux at the wall is the wall-integrated rate at which neutral particles of one specified species arrive at plasma-facing material from the plasma side. It counts incoming neutral particles crossing the material boundary toward the wall, not particles emitted by the wall.

The wall-integrated arrival rate is the surface integral of the corresponding local incident flux:

$$
\dot{N}_{n,\mathrm{wall}}^{\mathrm{inc}} = \int_{A_\mathrm{wall}} \Gamma_{n,\mathrm{wall}}^{\mathrm{inc}}(\mathbf{x})\, dA
$$

where $\dot{N}_{n,\mathrm{wall}}^{\mathrm{inc}}$ denotes this incident neutral particle flux at the wall, $A_\mathrm{wall}$ is the plasma-facing wall surface included in the total, $\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{wall}}^{\mathrm{inc}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the incident component of the local [neutral particle flux at the wall] for the same neutral species at wall position $\mathbf{x}$, and $dA$ is the surface-area element.

The quantity is species-resolved for one neutral species and aggregated over wall position by surface integration. It is not the local per-area [neutral particle flux at the wall] at a given wall position, and it is not a signed net balance between incoming and outgoing neutrals.

Wall-emitted neutral particles belong to the opposite direction of exchange and are represented separately by quantities such as [neutral particle flux at the wall due to surface emission](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission). Contributions from disjoint wall regions add to form the global incident rate.

The radial ion momentum diffusivity $D_{[3m\mathrm{rad}}^i$ is the effective diffusion coefficient characterizing down-gradient redistribution of the radial component of momentum across magnetic flux surfaces within the total ion population summed over all charge states. It is the radial component of the broader [ion momentum diffusivity].

The flux-surface-integrated diffusive radial ion momentum flux is represented by

$$
\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{mom},i,r}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -V'\mathcal{M}_iD_{\mathrm{rad}}^i\left\langle \left|\nabla\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\right|^2 \right\rangle \frac{d v_{r,i}}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{mom},i,r}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive flux of radial ion momentum through a flux surface, $V'$ is the derivative of enclosed volume with respect to the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, $\mathcal{M}_i$ is the total ion mass density, $v_{r,i}$ is the radial component of the mean ion fluid velocity, $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient, and angle brackets denote a flux-surface average.

The coefficient applies to the total ion population, with contributions summed over ion species and all charge states. Here radial denotes the flux-surface transport direction associated with increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, not a cylindrical-$R$ projection; parallel and poloidal momentum channels are distinct quantities. Unlike [ion-state momentum diffusivity], this quantity is not resolved by charge state.

Replacing the radial momentum component with the poloidal component gives the corresponding [poloidal ion momentum diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_momentum_diffusivity); both are directional components of [ion momentum diffusivity], while the minus sign expresses down-gradient diffusive transport.

Vertical coordinate of an arc-of-circle center is the $Z$ coordinate of the point that is the center of the circle whose circumference contains the arc defining a curved conductor element. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an arc-of-circle center with position vector $\mathbf{x}_c$, the coordinate is

$$
Z_c = \mathbf{x}_c \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_c$ is the vertical coordinate of the arc-of-circle center, $\mathbf{x}_c$ is the position vector of that center relative to the coordinate origin, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical basis direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies only to the center of the supporting circle for an arc-of-circle element. It is not the vertical coordinate of an arbitrary point on the conductor, nor the [vertical coordinate of a coil conductor element](name:vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor_element) when that name denotes the element location itself rather than the center of the circle defining an arc.

Together with the [radial coordinate of the arc-of-circle center](name:radial_coordinate_of_arc_of_circle_center) and the [toroidal angle of the arc-of-circle center], it specifies the same circle center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Sign convention: Positive when the arc-of-circle center is displaced in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction from the origin of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity represents the energy-weighted parallel motion carried by the perturbed gyrocenter population. It is evaluated in the field-aligned parallel direction and includes first-order Bessel weighting.

The normalized moment is defined by

$$
\widehat{q}_{\parallel,J_1}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{N}_q}\int \frac{1}{2}m v_{\parallel}v^2 J_1\,\delta f_g^{(1)}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\widehat{q}_{\parallel,J_1}$ is the normalized parallel heat-flux moment, $\mathcal{N}_q$ is the normalization factor for the corresponding heat-flux moment, $m$ is the gyrocenter particle mass, $v_{\parallel}$ is the velocity component parallel to the magnetic field, $v$ is the particle-speed magnitude, $J_1$ is the first-order Bessel weighting factor at the prescribed gyrokinetic argument, $\delta f_g^{(1)}(\mathbf{v})$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function, $\mathbf{v}$ is the velocity-space coordinate, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

The integral applies to the perturbed gyrocenter distribution associated with a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode and aggregates the represented distribution over velocity space. It excludes the equilibrium or unperturbed distribution and is not an unweighted heat-flux moment.

The parallel projection distinguishes this quantity from the perpendicular heat-flux moment [perpendicular gyrocenter heat perturbed flux normalized of gyrokinetic eigenmode]. It belongs to the same first-Bessel-weighted perturbed gyrocenter moment family as [normalized perturbed parallel gyrocenter current density bessel 1](name:normalized_perturbed_parallel_gyrocenter_current_density_bessel_1), but uses the energy-weighted heat-flux kernel rather than the current-density kernel.

This quantity is the geometric arclength of one magnetic field line traced during plasma initiation. It characterizes the distribution of individual field-line lengths associated with the evolving magnetic topology.

For a field-line trajectory parameterized by $(s)$, its length is

$$
L = \int_{s_0}^{s_1} \left\lVert \frac{d\mathbf{r}}{ds} \right\rVert ds
$$

where $L$ is the field-line length, $(s)$ is the position vector along the traced magnetic field line, $s$ is a tracing parameter, and $s_0$ and $s_1$ delimit the traced segment.

The quantity applies separately to each traced magnetic field line during the plasma-initiation phase; it is not an average, sum, or charge-state aggregation. It does not impose the open-field-line averaging and closed-line replacement convention of [connection length](name:connection_length), and it is distinct from [field-line fraction], which describes the fraction of lines that are open.

The set of individual lengths provides a geometric characterization of magnetic topology, while the open-line fraction identifies the prevalence of open field lines within the same traced population.

Major length of a plasma filament is the Euclidean length of the oblique parallelogram side associated with the major-radius direction.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the side lies in the poloidal $R$-$Z$ cross-section and is defined by

$$
L_{\mathrm{major}} = \sqrt{(\Delta R)^2 + (\Delta Z)^2}
$$

where $L_{\mathrm{major}}$ is the major oblique-side length, $\Delta R$ is the difference in major-radius coordinates between the side endpoints, and $\Delta Z$ is the corresponding difference in vertical coordinates.

This quantity applies to one discrete plasma current-carrying filament element and describes only its major oblique side. It is an individual geometric length, not a sum, average, or aggregate over filament elements, and it excludes the other oblique side represented by the [minor length of a plasma filament](name:minor_length_of_plasma_filament).

It is the major-qualified component of [length of a plasma filament], selecting the side associated with the major-radius direction rather than defining an additional length to be added to the parent quantity. Its inclination is described separately by the [inclination angle of a plasma filament](name:alpha_angle_of_plasma_filament).

The minor oblique parallelogram-side length of a plasma-filament element is the Euclidean length of the side inclined at angle beta to the vertical height direction. It characterizes one side of the element's oblique cross-sectional geometry.

The side length is defined by the separation of its two endpoints:

$$
\ell_\beta = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_{\beta,2} - \mathbf{x}_{\beta,1} \right\rVert
$$

where $\ell_\beta$ is the minor side length, $\mathbf{x}_{\beta,1}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\beta,2}$ are the position vectors of its endpoints, and $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ denotes the Euclidean norm. The inclination angle $\beta$ is measured relative to the vertical height direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to one discrete plasma current-carrying filament element and is neither summed nor averaged over elements. It excludes the complementary major oblique side and therefore is distinct from [major length of the plasma filament](name:major_length_of_plasma_filament).

This quantity specializes [length of the plasma filament] by selecting its minor, beta-inclined side. The paired major-length quantity selects the complementary oblique side of the same element.

Plasma-volume-averaged volumetric production rate of runaway electrons is the spatial average, over the plasma volume, of the local total rate at which electrons enter the runaway population. The total rate includes generation by Dreicer, avalanche, hot-tail, Compton, and tritium-decay mechanisms.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\left\langle S_{\mathrm{RE,total}}\right\rangle_V = \frac{1}{|\Omega_p|}\int_{\Omega_p} S_{\mathrm{RE,total}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $\left\langle S_{\mathrm{RE,total}}\right\rangle_V$ is the volume-averaged total runaway electron source rate, $S_{\mathrm{RE,total}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the [total runaway electron source rate] at position $\mathbf{x}$, $\Omega_p$ is the plasma-volume domain, $|\Omega_p|$ is the volume measure of that domain, and $dV$ is the volume element.

This quantity applies to the runaway-electron population within the plasma volume and uses an unweighted volume average of the total local volumetric production rate. The mechanism sum is part of the quantity definition; the total includes component production rates such as the [Dreicer runaway electron source rate](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) and the [hot-tail runaway electron source rate](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail), but is not restricted to either component.

It is the plasma-volume-averaged counterpart of the [total runaway electron source rate]. It is a production-rate density averaged over volume, not the absolute number of runaway electrons and not a current-density measure; in particular it is distinct from the [volume-averaged parallel runaway electron current density](name:volume_averaged_parallel_runaway_electron_current_density), which describes charge transport by the runaway population.

Absorbed neutral-beam injection power is the total power transferred from neutral beams to the plasma through beam ionization and subsequent thermalization. It represents deposited plasma power rather than power that merely enters the vacuum vessel.

$$
P_{\mathrm{abs}} = f_{\mathrm{dep}} P_{\mathrm{launched}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{abs}}$ is the absorbed neutral-beam power, $f_{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the fraction of launched beam power deposited in the plasma through ionization and thermalization, and $P_{\mathrm{launched}}$ is the [launched neutral-beam injection power](name:launched_power_due_to_neutral_beam_injection).

The quantity is aggregated over the neutral-beam injection contribution to the plasma and includes deposited power from all represented beam components. It excludes neutral-beam shine-through and energy carried away by fast ions lost from their confining orbits; it is therefore distinct from launched beam power and from undeposited beam power.

This quantity specializes [power due to neutral-beam injection] to the absorbed, deposited component. The deposition fraction relates it to [launched neutral-beam injection power](name:launched_power_due_to_neutral_beam_injection), while the excluded shine-through and orbit-loss terms account for launched power that does not remain deposited in the plasma.

Vertical focal length of a beamlet group is the path length along the neutral-beam line from the beamlet group's ion source to the group vertical focus. The group vertical focus is the location at which the collective beamlet envelope has its minimum vertical extent, with vertical measured parallel to $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Using an along-beam coordinate $s$ that increases from the ion source along the neutral-beam line, the focal length is defined by

$$
f_v = s_f - s_0, \qquad w_v(s_f) = \min_s w_v(s)
$$

where $f_v$ is the vertical focal length of the beamlet group, $s_0$ is the ion-source position on the along-beam coordinate, $s_f$ is the vertical-focus position, and $w_v(s)$ is the collective vertical envelope extent of the beamlet group at position $s$.

The quantity applies to one beamlet group and aggregates all beamlets in that group through their collective vertical envelope. It is not a per-beamlet focal length and not a whole-unit focal length formed by combining multiple groups; the distance is along the beam-line path rather than a vertical separation.

It is distinct from the source-surface vertical width of a beamlet group and from any vertical extent at locations other than the focus; those are transverse extents, whereas this quantity is the along-beam separation to the location of the minimum. It is the vertical counterpart of the [horizontal focal length of a beamlet group], which uses the minimum horizontal extent instead of the minimum vertical extent.

Eddy-current-attributed energy flux is the areal rate at which energy generated by Joule dissipation of induced eddy currents is transferred across a surface. It is a process-attributed scalar energy flux: the process is fixed to eddy currents, while more specific names may add a locus such as a wall surface.

The scalar flux is defined as the surface density of eddy-current-attributed power:

$$
F_{\mathrm{eddy}} = \frac{dP_{\mathrm{eddy}}}{dA}
$$

where $F_{\mathrm{eddy}}$ is the eddy-current-attributed energy flux, $P_{\mathrm{eddy}}$ is the power associated with Joule dissipation of induced eddy currents, and $A$ is the area over which that power is distributed.

The scope is the eddy-current contribution in conducting plasma-facing structures; if several induced-current paths contribute to the same surface element, their eddy-current-attributed power contributions are summed before division by area. This quantity excludes total wall heat flux and energy-flux contributions attributed to radiation, particle impact, externally applied heating, or non-eddy-current mechanisms, and it does not by itself specify that the evaluation locus is the wall.

[Energy flux due to eddy current] is the explicitly energy-qualified form of this same process-attributed flux. [Flux at wall due to eddy current](name:flux_at_wall_due_to_eddy_current) is a locus-specialized form evaluated at a plasma-facing wall; the present quantity retains only the shared eddy-current mechanism attribution, not that child locus.

Spectral photon radiance is the photon-number emission rate associated with a specified viewing direction, projected emitting area, and wavelength interval. It describes the angular and spectral distribution of plasma radiation before integration over wavelength or solid angle.

The defining differential relation is

$$
L_\lambda(\lambda,\Omega) = \frac{d^3 N_\gamma}{dA_\perp\,dt\,d\Omega\,d\lambda}
$$

where $L_\lambda$ is the spectral photon radiance, $N_\gamma$ is the number of emitted photons, $A_\perp$ is the projected emitting area, $t$ is time, $\Omega$ is solid angle about the viewing direction, and $\lambda$ is photon wavelength.

This generic quantity includes the photon-number contributions from all unresolved emitting populations and mechanisms within the specified spectral and angular element. Its aggregation is differential in wavelength and solid angle, and it is not restricted to a particular species, reaction, or plasma region. It is not a volumetric photon-production rate and is not integrated over a spectral line, wavelength band, or viewing solid angle.

Integrating the spectral radiance over a selected emission-line interval gives the corresponding [photon radiance at a spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line). The free-free contribution is represented by the mechanism-specific [spectral bremsstrahlung rate], while this quantity includes that contribution only as part of the total emission when no mechanism qualifier is present.

The neutron emissivity due to fusion $\varepsilon_n^{\mathrm{fus}}$ is the local number of neutrons produced per unit volume per unit time from all included fusion reactions. Each contributing neutron-producing branch adds its local neutron yield, so this quantity is the reaction-channel-aggregated fusion neutron source rather than a single-channel contribution.

For included binary fusion reaction branches, the emissivity is defined by:

$$
\varepsilon_n^{\mathrm{fus}} = \sum_{(\{a,b\},r)\in\mathcal{C}} \nu_{ab,r}^{(n)} \frac{n_a n_b}{1+\delta_{ab}} \langle \sigma v \rangle_{ab,r}
$$

where $\varepsilon_n^{\mathrm{fus}}$ is the neutron emissivity due to fusion, $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of included unordered reacting-species pairs and fusion reaction branches, $a$ and $b$ identify the reacting ion species, $r$ identifies a reaction branch, $\nu_{ab,r}^{(n)}$ is the number of neutrons produced by one reaction in that branch, $n_a$ and $n_b$ are the local number densities of the reacting ion populations, $\delta_{ab}$ is the Kronecker delta for identical reacting species, and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{ab,r}$ is the velocity-averaged fusion reactivity for that branch.

This quantity is local to each point in the plasma and is summed over the included neutron-producing fusion branches and their reacting ion populations. The factor $1+\delta_{ab}$ counts unordered pairs of identical reactants once, so identical-population reactions such as deuterium-deuterium are not double-counted. It represents neutron production only; it excludes charged fusion products, radiation other than neutrons, and the released fusion energy represented by [power_density_due_to_fusion](name:power_density_due_to_fusion).

The related quantity [emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:neutron_emissivity_due_to_fusion) is already restricted to fusion neutron production; this quantity should not be interpreted as a neutron-only component of a broader all-product emissivity. Single-channel contributions are represented by [deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion) and [deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion); summing the included channel contributions gives this reaction-aggregated emissivity. Volume integration of $\varepsilon_n^{\mathrm{fus}}$ gives neutron_rate with the same reaction-channel aggregation.

Radial coordinate of a rectangle center is the major-radius coordinate \(R_{\mathrm{rect,c}}\) of the geometric center of a rectangular cross-section. It is measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame, whose basis \((\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})\) satisfies \(\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}\); \(R\) is major radius, \(\phi\) is toroidal angle, and \(Z\) is vertical height.

The relation between this coordinate and Cartesian coordinates of the same center point is

$$
R_{\mathrm{rect,c}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{rect,c}}^{2} + y_{\mathrm{rect,c}}^{2}}
$$

where \(R_{\mathrm{rect,c}}\) is the radial coordinate of the rectangle center, and \(x_{\mathrm{rect,c}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{rect,c}}\) are the first and second Cartesian coordinates of that center in the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})\) frame whose \(\hat{z}\) direction is vertical and whose origin lies on the toroidal symmetry axis.

This quantity applies to the center point of the rectangle as a whole; for an axisymmetric rectangular element, that point is the center of the generating rectangle in a surface of constant \(\phi\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame. It is not the rectangle's inner radius, outer radius, radial width, corner coordinate, boundary coordinate, or a centroid of a non-rectangular object, and no area or volume averaging is implied.

The companion [height of the rectangle center] gives \(Z_{\mathrm{rect,c}}\), the vertical coordinate of the same center; the pair \((R_{\mathrm{rect,c}},Z_{\mathrm{rect,c}})\) locates the center in a surface of constant \(\phi\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame. As a major-radius coordinate, \(R_{\mathrm{rect,c}}\ge 0\) and is not a signed radial offset from another reference point.

The total magnetic-field magnitude is the nonnegative Euclidean norm of the local magnetic-induction vector at the pressure-pedestal top on the high-field side. It represents the complete field at that location rather than a selected directional component.

The defining relation is

$$
B = |\mathbf{B}| = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_\phi^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-induction vector, $B$ is its magnitude, and $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are its signed projections onto the right-handed cylindrical basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity is evaluated locally at the high-field-side pressure-pedestal top and includes all magnetic-field components through the Euclidean norm. It excludes component-specific or perturbation-only fields and is not a signed projection. It is the magnitude transformation of the parent total magnetic-field vector [magnetic field at the high-field-side pedestal top], so the parent vector and this scalar contain the same local field information in vector and magnitude representations, respectively.

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-induction vector, $B$ is its magnitude, and $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are its signed projections onto the right-handed cylindrical basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity is evaluated locally at the high-field-side pressure-pedestal top and includes all magnetic-field components through the Euclidean norm. It excludes component-specific or perturbation-only fields and is not a signed projection. It is the magnitude transformation of the parent total magnetic-field vector magnetic field at the high-field-side pedestal top, so the parent vector and this scalar contain the same local field information in vector and magnitude representations, respectively.

Signed local derivative of fitted electron pressure with respect to the normalized poloidal flux coordinate at the H-mode pedestal top is the local rate of change of the fitted electron-pressure function with the flux coordinate $\psi_N$ at the pedestal-top locus. It is not the derivative of the scalar [electron pressure at the H-mode pedestal top](name:electron_pressure_at_pedestal_top); that scalar is the pressure value at the same locus.

The derivative is defined by differentiating the fitted electron-pressure function with respect to $\psi_N$ and evaluating the result at the pedestal top:

$$
D_{p_e,\mathrm{ped\ top}} = \left.\frac{\partial p_e}{\partial \psi_N}\right|_{\mathrm{ped\ top}}
$$

where $D_{p_e,\mathrm{ped\ top}}$ is this quantity, $p_e$ is [electron pressure](name:electron_pressure), and $\psi_N$ is the normalized poloidal flux coordinate, with $\psi_N=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\psi_N=1$ at the plasma boundary.

This quantity is a local pedestal-top derivative. It excludes the steepest pressure-gradient value over a pedestal interval, represented by [gradient of electron pressure], and it is distinct from electron-density derivatives such as [derivative with respect to normalized poloidal flux coordinate of electron density at pedestal maximum].

The quantity is the Fourier-mode coefficient of the total surface current associated with an ion-cyclotron-heating antenna. It combines the current contributions from the antenna straps and passive components before resolving their poloidal and toroidal variation.

For the Fourier convention used here, the coefficient for poloidal mode number $m$ and toroidal mode number $n$ is

$$
\widetilde{I}_{mn}=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi} I_s(\theta,\phi)e^{-i(m\theta+n\phi)}\,d\theta\,d\phi
$$

where $\widetilde{I}_{mn}$ is the modal surface-current coefficient, $I_s(\theta,\phi)$ is the signed total surface-current distribution, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, $m$ and $n$ are integer poloidal and toroidal mode numbers, respectively, $i$ is the imaginary unit, and $\pi$ is the circle constant.

The quantity is aggregated over all straps and passive components belonging to the antenna, while each pair $(m,n)$ identifies one Fourier component rather than a sum over mode numbers. It is therefore distinct from [wave current of an antenna strap], which describes current confined to an individual strap, and from [wave current of an antenna strap amplitude](name:wave_current_of_antenna_strap_amplitude), which describes the peak magnitude of that strap current. The coefficient's sign and phase follow the chosen positive surface-current direction, angular origins, and Fourier convention shown above.

The energy-flux limiter coefficient for ions is a dimensionless factor that sets the maximum allowed energy flux density carried by ions relative to their collisionless free-streaming bound.

The limiting relation is

$$
|q_E| \leq \alpha_E q_{E,\mathrm{fs}}
$$

where $q_E$ is the energy flux density carried by ions, $\alpha_E$ is this ion energy-flux limiter coefficient, and $q_{E,\mathrm{fs}}$ is the corresponding collisionless free-streaming energy-flux bound.

The coefficient applies to ion energy transport summed over all ion charge states; it is not restricted to a specified charge state and does not limit electron, neutral, momentum, or particle flux. It is the ion specialization of the broader [energy flux-limiter coefficient](name:energy_flux_limiter_coefficient). The related [ion-state energy flux-limiter coefficient] applies instead to ions in a specified charge state, while the [ion momentum flux-limiter coefficient](name:ion_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient) limits momentum-flux density rather than energy-flux density.

Electron particle flux limiter coefficient is a dimensionless closure coefficient that sets the upper bound on the magnitude of the modeled electron particle transport flux as a fraction of the electron free-streaming particle flux. It specifies the multiplier used to cap the particle flux in an electron-density transport closure.

The corresponding limiting relation is

$$
\left|\Gamma_e^{\mathrm{lim}}\right| \le \alpha_{\Gamma,e}\, n_e\, v_{\mathrm{th},e}
$$

where $\alpha_{\Gamma,e}$ is the electron particle flux limiter coefficient, $\Gamma_e^{\mathrm{lim}}$ is the limited [electron particle flux](name:electron_particle_flux), $n_e$ is the [electron density](name:electron_density), and $v_{\mathrm{th},e}$ is the electron thermal speed used in the free-streaming estimate.

This quantity applies to the electron population in the particle component of an electron-density transport closure. It has no species, charge-state, spatial, surface, or volume aggregation by itself; the coefficient denotes a local multiplier for the closure where it is applied.

It is distinct from [electron particle diffusivity], which relates a density gradient to an unconstrained diffusive particle flux, and from [electron particle flux](name:electron_particle_flux), which is the signed flux being limited. It does not define a heat-flux limiter or a momentum-flux limiter.

The coefficient multiplies the free-streaming estimate $n_e v_{\mathrm{th},e}$; decreasing it lowers the permitted magnitude and increasing it raises the permitted magnitude. The limiting operation is a magnitude cap, so an unconstrained modeled flux whose magnitude exceeds the cap is reduced to the cap while retaining its original sign.
documents.after:

Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of the hard X-ray detector is the $Z$ coordinate of that center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. In this frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The coordinate is the projection of the detector-center position onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
Z_\mathrm{det} = \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{det} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{det}$ is the vertical coordinate of the hard X-ray detector geometric center, $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{det}$ is the position vector of that center relative to the coordinate origin, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies only to the geometric center of the hard X-ray detector as a detector-location coordinate. It is not the vertical coordinate of an aperture, viewing chord, collimator, sensitive-area point, or any local orientation axis of the detector.

Together with the [radial coordinate of the hard X-ray detector] and the [toroidal angle of the hard X-ray detector], it specifies the detector-center position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Sign convention: Positive when the detector geometric center lies in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction from the coordinate origin.

This quantity is the signed position of an individual optical-fiber center along the first local-tangential axis of its fiber bundle. It describes the fiber-bundle geometry in the local $(X_1, X_2)$ coordinate frame, not a machine-coordinate position.

For a fiber center, the coordinate is defined by

$$
x_1 = (\mathbf{r}_f - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1
$$

where $x_1$ is the first local-tangential coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_f$ is the position vector of the individual fiber center, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the origin of the fiber-bundle local frame, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ is the oriented unit vector along its first local-tangential axis.

The quantity applies to individual fibers belonging to the fiber bundle. Each fiber center has its own coordinate; no summation, averaging, or replacement by the bundle geometric center is implied. It is distinct from the bundle's machine-frame [vertical coordinate], which uses the vertical direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The local-coordinate meaning is shared with [first local-tangential coordinate of a reflector](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_reflector), but the intrinsic owning object here is the fiber bundle and the coordinate refers to fiber centers rather than reflector-outline vertices.

Sign convention: Positive when the fiber-center displacement from the local-frame origin has a component in the direction of the oriented first local-tangential axis.

The vertical coordinate identifies the height of a point on the cryostat centerline, where the centerline represents the middle of the annular vessel layer. It applies specifically to the annular cryostat unit's centerline rather than to the inner or outer layer boundary.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{c}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{c}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the position vector of the centerline point, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The quantity is pointwise for each centerline point and is not an average over the centerline or an aggregate over cryostat units. It excludes contour points describing the annular layer boundaries; those are represented by the [vertical outline of the cryostat], which describes a different geometric locus.

Sign convention: Positive when the centerline point lies in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

This quantity is the cumulative post-breakdown inventory of carbon atoms delivered by gas injection, represented as an equivalent-electron count. It excludes carbon introduced during the plasma prefill phase and does not represent an instantaneous source rate or a charge-state-resolved ion inventory.

The equivalent-electron count is defined by

$$
N_{\mathrm{C,eq}}(t)=6N_{\mathrm{C}}(t)=6\int_{t_{\mathrm{bd}}}^{t}\dot{N}_{\mathrm{C}}^{\mathrm{gas}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{C,eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron count, $N_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the cumulative number of injected carbon atoms, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{C}}^{\mathrm{gas}}$ is the carbon injection rate, $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the plasma breakdown time, and $t$ is the evaluation time. The factor 6 is carbon's atomic number. This is the post-breakdown component of [carbon count due to gas injection] and is distinct from [carbon prefill count due to gas injection](name:carbon_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection).

This quantity is the geometric derivative of the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to the dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate. It describes how rapidly the enclosed region expands as the flux-surface label changes.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{dV}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $V$ is the [volume enclosed by a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface) and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate labeling the nested surfaces.

The quantity applies to the three-dimensional region inside each selected nested magnetic flux surface. The volume is cumulative, beginning at the magnetic axis and extending to the specified surface; this is not a local plasma-population quantity and carries no species weighting. It is the derivative with respect to the toroidal-flux coordinate, not the volume itself or the derivative of the enclosed poloidal area.

As the derivative of [volume enclosed by a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface), it provides the volume increment associated with a change in toroidal-flux coordinate and serves as a geometric coefficient in flux-surface-averaged transport relations. The [derivative of area with respect to the toroidal-flux coordinate] is the analogous area derivative, while [the temporal derivative of this volume derivative](name:time_derivative_of_derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate) describes its change in time.

This quantity is the number density of tungsten ions averaged over the last closed magnetic flux surface, with all positive ionization states included and neutral tungsten excluded. It is the surface-averaged counterpart of the local [tungsten density at the plasma boundary](name:tungsten_density_flux_surface_averaged_at_plasma_boundary).

The flux-surface average at the plasma-boundary flux label is defined by

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{W}} \rangle_{\psi_b} = \frac{\oint_{\psi=\psi_b} n_{\mathrm{W}}\,d\ell_p/B_p}{\oint_{\psi=\psi_b} d\ell_p/B_p}
$$

where $\psi_b$ is the flux label of the plasma boundary, $n_{\mathrm{W}}$ is the local summed tungsten-ion density, $d\ell_p$ is poloidal contour length, and $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude. The quantity is distinct from [volume-averaged tungsten density](name:volume_averaged_tungsten_density), which averages over the enclosed plasma volume.

A spectrometer-channel logarithmic spectral signal-to-noise ratio is the logarithmic power-ratio contrast, for one spectrometer channel, between spectral power assigned to a selected signal wavelength interval and spectral power assigned to a line-free reference wavelength interval. It is a band-integrated spectral quantity: each band contribution is formed by integrating the channel spectral power density over its wavelength interval before the ratio is taken.

For signal wavelength interval $B_s$ and reference wavelength interval $B_n$, it is defined by

$$
L_{\mathrm{SNR}} = 10 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P_s}{P_n}\right), \qquad P_s = \int_{B_s} S(\lambda)\,d\lambda, \quad P_n = \int_{B_n} S(\lambda)\,d\lambda
$$

where $L_{\mathrm{SNR}}$ is the logarithm of the spectral signal-to-noise ratio of the channel, $P_s$ is the integrated signal-band spectral power, $P_n$ is the integrated reference-band spectral power, $B_s$ is the selected signal wavelength interval, $B_n$ is the line-free reference wavelength interval, $S(\lambda)$ is the channel spectral power density as a function of wavelength, and $\lambda$ is wavelength.

The scope is one spectrometer channel and one selected pair of wavelength intervals. The aggregation convention is integration over each selected wavelength interval before forming the logarithmic ratio; no wavelength averaging and no aggregation over multiple spectrometer channels is implied. The reference interval is line-free with respect to the spectral feature defining the signal interval, and a finite value requires $P_s>0$ and $P_n>0$.

This quantity is a power-ratio logarithm, not an amplitude-ratio logarithm, not a pointwise value of $S(\lambda)$, and not an unlogged linear ratio $P_s/P_n$. It denotes the same logarithmic power-ratio quantity as the [spectral signal-to-noise ratio of a spectrometer channel]; the explicit logarithm wording makes the logarithmic scaling unambiguous. The value is zero when $P_s=P_n$, positive when $P_s>P_n$, and negative when $P_s<P_n$.
documents.after:

B = |\mathbf{B}| = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_\phi^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-induction vector, $B$ is its magnitude, and $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are its signed projections onto the right-handed cylindrical basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity is evaluated locally at the high-field-side pressure-pedestal top and includes all magnetic-field components through the Euclidean norm. It excludes component-specific or perturbation-only fields and is not a signed projection. It is the magnitude transformation of the parent total magnetic-field vector magnetic field at the high-field-side pedestal top, so the parent vector and this scalar contain the same local field information in vector and magnitude representations, respectively.

q_{E,\mathrm{max}}^{L} = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in S_L} q_E(\mathbf{x})

Normalized count at detector pixel is the detector-pixel count divided by a positive count-equivalent reference from the same acquisition frame. The reference is a relative scale for that frame and must be common to the detector pixels whose normalized values are compared.

The defining ratio for detector pixel $p$ is

$$
C_\mathrm{norm}(p) = \frac{C(p)}{C_\mathrm{ref}}, \qquad C_\mathrm{ref} > 0
$$

where $C_\mathrm{norm}(p)$ is the normalized count, $C(p)$ is the [count at detector pixel], and $C_\mathrm{ref}$ is the positive count-equivalent reference for the same acquisition frame.

The same definition applies to count rates or exposure-normalized count-equivalent signals only when $C(p)$ and $C_\mathrm{ref}$ use identical time or exposure normalization. The quantity is a relative normalization; it does not specify whether $C_\mathrm{ref}$ is a total-frame, peak, mean, or externally specified reference count, and it is distinct from an absolute calibration factor.

The normalized electron Larmor radius is the dimensionless gyroradius of the electron population evaluated at the low-field-side pressure-pedestal top. It characterizes electron orbit scale relative to the macroscopic length prescribed by the normalization convention.

The defining relation is

$$
\rho_e^* = \frac{\rho_e}{L_{\mathrm{ref}}} = \frac{m_e v_{\perp,e}}{|q_e| B_{\mathrm{LFS}} L_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $\rho_e$ is the electron Larmor radius, $L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the prescribed macroscopic normalization length, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v_{\perp,e}$ is the characteristic electron speed perpendicular to the magnetic field, $q_e$ is the electron charge, and $B_{\mathrm{LFS}}$ is the local magnetic-field magnitude at the low-field-side pressure-pedestal top. The field magnitude is the quantity represented by the [low-field-side pedestal-top magnetic-field magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude_at_pedestal_top_low_field_side).

The quantity applies specifically to electrons and to the low-field-side pressure-pedestal-top location. It is a local dimensionless scale ratio, not an unnormalized Larmor radius, a magnetic-field component, or a quantity aggregated over particle species.

The corresponding high-field-side value, [normalized electron Larmor radius at the pedestal top on the high-field side], uses the same normalization concept at the high-field-side pedestal-top location; the two values differ through their local magnetic-field evaluation.

This quantity is the signed, normalized term in turbulent energy flux produced by the perturbed parallel electromagnetic vector potential $\delta A_\parallel$. It isolates the energy transport associated with this electromagnetic field contribution rather than representing the total turbulent energy flux.

The field-attributed flux decomposition is represented by

$$
Q_{E,\mathrm{norm}} = Q_{E,\mathrm{norm}}^{(\phi)} + Q_{E,\mathrm{norm}}^{(A_\parallel)} + Q_{E,\mathrm{norm}}^{(\delta B_\parallel)}
$$

where $Q_{E,\mathrm{norm}}$ is the normalized turbulent energy flux, $Q_{E,\mathrm{norm}}^{(\phi)}$ is the electrostatic-potential contribution, $Q_{E,\mathrm{norm}}^{(A_\parallel)}$ is this quantity, and $Q_{E,\mathrm{norm}}^{(\delta B_\parallel)}$ is the contribution from perturbed parallel magnetic-field fluctuations. The vector potential component $\delta A_\parallel$ is parallel to the equilibrium magnetic field and is distinct from its modulus, represented by the [parallel normalized perturbed vector-potential amplitude]. The decomposition complements the [normalized energy flux due to perturbed parallel magnetic field](name:energy_flux_normalized_due_to_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field) and the [normalized energy flux due to E cross B drift].
