Dimensionless imaginary part of the complex linear gyrokinetic eigenmode frequency, divided by the positive reference angular frequency, is the normalized temporal growth rate of a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode at a specified wavevector perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field in the local flux-tube approximation. It identifies the exponential amplitude change of that eigenmode in linear gyrokinetic theory.

The defining normalization is

$$
\gamma_\mathrm{norm} = \frac{\operatorname{Im}\omega}{\omega_\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\omega$ is the complex eigenfrequency for time dependence $\exp(-i\omega t)$ and $\omega_\mathrm{ref}>0$ is the reference angular frequency used for the normalized eigenfrequency. When the reference angular frequency is written as $v_{\mathrm{th,ref}}/L_\mathrm{ref}$, this is equivalently $\gamma_\mathrm{norm}=\gamma L_\mathrm{ref}/v_{\mathrm{th,ref}}$, with $\gamma=\operatorname{Im}\omega$, $v_{\mathrm{th,ref}}$ the reference thermal speed, and $L_\mathrm{ref}$ the reference length scale.

This quantity is for one linear gyrokinetic eigenmode at one specified perpendicular wavevector, not for a spectrum-averaged rate, nonlinear turbulent growth, or finite-amplitude envelope evolution. It is the imaginary-part counterpart to the [normalized_frequency_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode](name:frequency_normalized_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode), which uses the real part of the same $\omega$; the eigenmode-specific scope distinguishes it from [normalized_growth_rate](name:linear_growth_rate_normalized_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode), which does not by itself require a linear gyrokinetic eigenvalue.

Sign convention: Positive when the eigenmode amplitude increases exponentially with time.

Normalized parallel momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel magnetic field is the dimensionless, parallel-velocity-weighted electromagnetic contribution to turbulent radial transport of toroidal angular momentum.

The normalized quantity is defined by

$$
\widehat{\Pi}_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel} = \frac{\Pi_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel}}{\Pi_{\mathrm{GB}}}
$$

where $\Pi_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel}$ is the toroidal momentum flux in the parallel velocity-space channel driven by the perturbed parallel magnetic field, and $\Pi_{\mathrm{GB}}$ is the gyro-Bohm reference momentum-flux scale. The perturbation $\delta B_\parallel$ is the magnetic-field-magnitude fluctuation along the equilibrium magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$.

This is the parallel component of the aggregate [momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel magnetic field](name:normalized_momentum_flux_due_to_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field), complementary to the [normalized perpendicular momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel magnetic field]. It excludes contributions attributed to the electrostatic potential and the perturbed parallel vector potential, including the [normalized parallel momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel vector potential]. The normalization follows the gyrokinetic reference based on outboard-midplane electron density and temperature.

Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal angular momentum flux is directed outward across magnetic flux surfaces, away from the magnetic axis.

$$
\widehat{\Gamma}_{r,A_\parallel}=\frac{\Gamma_{r,A_\parallel}}{\Gamma_{\rm GB}}
$$

Normalized toroidal momentum flux from the perturbed parallel electromagnetic vector potential in gyrokinetic turbulence, restricted to the parallel velocity-space channel, is the gyro-Bohm-normalized flux-surface-normal transport of toroidal angular momentum associated with magnetic-flutter correlations from $\delta A_\parallel$. Toroidal angular momentum is referenced to motion in the direction of increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The normalized total parallel-channel contribution is defined by the aggregate gyrokinetic flux moment normalized by the gyro-Bohm momentum-flux scale:

$$
\widehat{\Pi}^{\mathrm{tot}}_{\phi,\delta A_\parallel;\parallel}
=
\frac{1}{\Pi_{\mathrm{gB}}}
\sum_s \sum_{\mathbf{k}}
\left\langle
\int m_s R v_\parallel b_\phi\,
v^{\mathrm{fl}}_{\chi,\delta A_\parallel}\,
\delta f_{s,\mathbf{k}}\,d^3v
\right\rangle
$$

where $s$ labels species, $\mathbf{k}$ labels fluctuation-wavevector contributions, $m_s$ is species mass, $v_\parallel$ is gyrocenter velocity parallel to the magnetic field, $b_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the magnetic-field unit vector, $v^{\mathrm{fl}}_{\chi,\delta A_\parallel}$ is the flux-surface-normal magnetic-flutter velocity produced by $\delta A_\parallel$ for magnetic-flux label $\chi$, $\delta f_{s,\mathbf{k}}$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution contribution, and angle brackets denote the flux-surface and turbulence average. The gyro-Bohm scale is $\Pi_{\mathrm{gB}}=n_{\mathrm{ref}}T_{\mathrm{ref}}R_{\mathrm{ref}}(\rho_{\mathrm{ref}}/a_{\mathrm{ref}})^2$, with $n_{\mathrm{ref}}$ the reference density, $T_{\mathrm{ref}}$ the reference temperature, $R_{\mathrm{ref}}$ the reference major radius, $\rho_{\mathrm{ref}}$ the reference gyroradius, and $a_{\mathrm{ref}}$ the reference minor radius.

This quantity has the same parallel velocity-space projection as the [normalized parallel momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel vector potential], while the word total denotes aggregation over species and fluctuation contributions within that projection. It excludes the [normalized perpendicular momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel vector potential](name:perpendicular_normalized_momentum_flux_due_to_perturbed_parallel_vector_potential), whose velocity-space projection is perpendicular to the magnetic-field direction, and is not the algebraic sum of the parallel and perpendicular projections.

Sign convention: Positive when toroidal angular momentum for motion in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ is transported in the flux-surface-normal direction toward increasing magnetic-flux label in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
documents.after:

This quantity is the normalized total pressure moment of a perturbed physical-particle distribution associated with a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode. It combines the parallel and perpendicular pressure contributions while preserving their signed or complex perturbation amplitude.

The normalized pressure is defined by

$$
\widetilde{p}_{\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{\widetilde{p}_{\parallel} + \widetilde{p}_{\perp}}{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $\widetilde{p}_{\parallel}$ and $\widetilde{p}_{\perp}$ are the parallel and perpendicular perturbed particle pressure moments, and $p_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the positive reference pressure specified by the eigenmode normalization.

The numerator is an algebraic sum, not a magnitude or absolute value. Its component contributions are resolved by [parallel normalized particle perturbed pressure] and [perpendicular normalized particle perturbed pressure](name:perpendicular_normalized_particle_perturbed_pressure); it is distinct from the gyrocenter quantity [normalized gyrocenter perturbed pressure].

Flux-surface-averaged parallel current density at a specified constraint position is the signed plasma current density associated with the component of conventional current flowing along the local magnetic field, averaged over the corresponding closed magnetic flux surface.

The defining field-aligned flux-surface average is

$$
j_{parallel}^{\mathrm{FS}}(\psi_c)=\frac{\left\langle\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle_{\psi_c}}{B_0(\psi_c)}
$$

where $j_{\parallel}^{\mathrm{FS}}(\psi_c)$ is this averaged parallel current density, $\mathbf{j}$ is the conventional plasma current-density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic-field vector, $\psi_c$ is the flux-surface label selected by the constraint position, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi_c}$ denotes averaging over that magnetic flux surface, and $B_0(\psi_c)$ is the reference magnetic-field magnitude used to normalize the field-aligned projection.

The quantity applies to the total plasma current-density field on the selected closed magnetic surface, with all current-carrying populations and mechanisms included unless a narrower physical qualifier is supplied. Its aggregation is over the complete flux surface, so it is not a pointwise parallel current density.

It is not restricted to a particular current-drive mechanism and is therefore distinct from the [parallel current density due to ohmic current drive](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ohmic_current_drive) and the [parallel flux-surface-averaged current density due to wave-driven current drive].

The underlying vector quantity is [current density](name:current_density); this name applies its magnetic-field-aligned projection and then performs a flux-surface average. The [toroidal flux-surface-averaged current density at a constraint position] instead uses the geometric toroidal projection before averaging.

Sign convention: Positive when the conventional current-density vector has a component along the local magnetic-field vector.

This quantity is the scalar field-aligned component of the conventional plasma current generated by electromagnetic-wave–particle interactions. It represents the wave-driven contribution to current flowing along the magnetic field on a magnetic flux surface.

For a magnetic flux surface labeled by the poloidal flux coordinate $\psi$, the flux-surface-averaged parallel current density is defined by

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{FSA}}(\psi) = \frac{\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wave}} \cdot \mathbf{B} \right\rangle_{\psi}}{B_0(\psi)}
$$

where $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{FSA}}$ is this scalar current-density quantity, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the conventional current-density contribution generated by wave–particle interactions, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes averaging over the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $B_0(\psi)$ is the reference magnetic-field magnitude used for the parallel-current normalization.

The quantity applies to the wave-driven current contribution from the plasma populations participating in the electromagnetic-wave interaction and uses a flux-surface average rather than a local value. It excludes inductive current and current contributions from non-wave mechanisms, and it is distinct from the full vector [flux-surface-averaged wave-driven current density].

It is the magnetic-field-aligned scalar projection of that vector parent, retaining only the component parallel to the local magnetic field; [parallel current density due to ohmic current drive](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ohmic_current_drive) instead represents the inductive resistive contribution.

Sign convention: Positive when the wave-driven conventional current flows in the direction of the magnetic field, so that $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wave}} \cdot \mathbf{B} > 0$.

Normalized parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular-momentum flux of a gyrokinetic eigenmode due to $E\times B$ drift is the normalized spectral contribution, evaluated in the rotating frame, of the perturbed electrostatic potential's $E\times B$ drift to the parallel gyrocenter part of toroidal angular-momentum flux. The toroidal component is the $\hat{\phi}$ component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The normalization is defined relative to the reference momentum-flux normalization for the same eigenmode:

$$
\widehat{\Pi}_{\parallel,\phi}^{E\times B} = \frac{\Pi_{\parallel,\phi}^{E\times B}}{\Pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $\widehat{\Pi}_{\parallel,\phi}^{E\times B}$ is this normalized contribution, $\Pi_{\parallel,\phi}^{E\times B}$ is the corresponding unnormalized parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular-momentum-flux contribution from the perturbed electrostatic-potential $E\times B$ drift in the rotating frame, $\Pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference momentum-flux normalization, $E$ is the perturbed electric field associated with the electrostatic potential, $B$ is the magnetic field, the subscript $\parallel$ denotes the part associated with gyrocenter motion parallel to $B$, and the subscript $\phi$ denotes toroidal angular momentum about the symmetry axis.

The quantity applies to one specified linear gyrokinetic eigenmode and to the rotating-frame representation of that mode; it is not summed over eigenmodes, wave-number spectrum, or transport channels. Its aggregation convention is a single-channel normalized eigenmode contribution, not a total turbulent momentum flux.

It is the electrostatic-potential $E\times B$ channel in the additive decomposition of the normalized parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular-momentum flux. The [perturbed parallel vector-potential channel] and the [perturbed parallel magnetic-field channel](name:parallel_gyrocenter_momentum_flux_normalized_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode_due_to_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field) are separate contributions and are excluded from this quantity.

Sign convention: Positive when the $E\times B$-drift contribution transports positive parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular momentum across a magnetic flux surface toward increasing flux label, with positive toroidal angular momentum corresponding to the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

Gyro-Bohm-normalized contribution of the perturbed parallel magnetic field to the parallel component of the toroidal gyrocenter momentum flux of a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode is the dimensionless laboratory-frame flux contribution associated with $\delta B_\parallel$. The toroidal direction is defined by increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and the parallel component is the part associated with gyrocenter motion along the equilibrium magnetic field.

The normalized contribution is defined by

$$
\Pi_{\phi,\parallel,N}^{\delta B_\parallel} = \frac{\Pi_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel}}{\Pi_{\mathrm{GB}}}
$$

where $\Pi_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel}$ is the laboratory-frame contribution of the [perturbed parallel magnetic field] to the parallel component of the toroidal gyrocenter momentum flux, and $\Pi_{\mathrm{GB}}$ is the Gyro-Bohm reference used to normalize toroidal gyrocenter momentum flux.

This quantity includes only the $\delta B_\parallel$ contribution to the parallel component; it excludes electrostatic, perturbed-perpendicular-magnetic-field, and other field-channel contributions. The corresponding sum over field-channel contributions is the [parallel normalized gyrocenter momentum flux].

Sign convention: Positive when the $\delta B_\parallel$ contribution gives flux of positive toroidal gyrocenter momentum in the flux-surface-normal direction toward increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ (normalized toroidal flux radius), where positive toroidal momentum corresponds to motion in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Normalized parallel momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel magnetic field is the gyro-Bohm-normalized, parallel-velocity-weighted electromagnetic contribution to turbulent transport of toroidal angular momentum across magnetic flux surfaces. The toroidal angular momentum is the component associated with the toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The normalized quantity is defined by

$$
\widehat{\Pi}_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel} = \frac{\Pi_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel}}{\Pi_{\mathrm{GB}}}
$$

where $\widehat{\Pi}_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel}$ is the normalized parallel momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel magnetic field, $\Pi_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel}$ is the corresponding unnormalized toroidal momentum flux in the parallel velocity-space channel, and $\Pi_{\mathrm{GB}}$ is the gyro-Bohm reference momentum-flux scale. The unnormalized term $\Pi_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel}$ is the bilinear turbulent-flux contribution formed from the $\delta B_\parallel$ electromagnetic perturbation and the parallel-velocity part of the toroidal-momentum weight; $\delta B_\parallel$ is the fluctuation of magnetic-field magnitude along the equilibrium magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$, and $\hat{b}$ is that unit vector.

This is the parallel-velocity component of the aggregate [normalized momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel magnetic field], complementary to the [normalized perpendicular momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel magnetic field](name:perpendicular_momentum_flux_normalized_due_to_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field). Here parallel refers to the particle-velocity component along $\hat{b}$ in the momentum weight, not to a projection of the transport direction. It excludes contributions attributed to the electrostatic potential and to the perturbed parallel vector potential, including the [normalized parallel momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel vector potential](name:parallel_momentum_flux_normalized_due_to_perturbed_parallel_vector_potential).

The quantity is evaluated in a frame rotating about the symmetry axis with the reference equilibrium rotation: particle velocities and toroidal angular-momentum weights entering $\Pi_{\phi,\parallel}^{\delta B_\parallel}$ are relative to that frame, so the background rotation defining the frame is not an additional turbulent flux contribution. For turbulent-spectrum aggregates, same-channel contributions are additive over the included wave-vector components; flux-surface and time averaging do not change the channel definition. The normalization follows the gyrokinetic reference based on outboard-midplane electron density and temperature.

Sign convention: Positive when positive toroidal angular momentum in the rotating frame, associated with motion in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, is transported across magnetic flux surfaces toward increasing flux label, away from the magnetic axis.

Parallel per-toroidal-mode current density due to wave-driven current drive is the component of the current-density contribution from one toroidal Fourier harmonic that is parallel to the local magnetic field. It represents the field-aligned part of the non-inductive current generated by wave-driven current drive for the specified harmonic.

The defining projection is

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{wcd}}^{(n_\phi)} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{wcd}}^{(n_\phi)} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{wcd}}^{(n_\phi)}$ is the parallel per-toroidal-mode current density due to wave-driven current drive, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{wcd}}^{(n_\phi)}$ is the vector [per-toroidal-mode current density due to wave-driven current drive], $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, and $n_\phi$ is the integer toroidal Fourier mode index associated with variation in toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height.

This quantity is a field-aligned scalar projection, not the vector current density and not the $\hat{\phi}$ component that defines [toroidal current density] in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It includes only the wave-driven non-inductive contribution for the specified $n_\phi$; it excludes inductive, bootstrap, neutral-beam-driven, and other non-wave current-density contributions. It is distinct from the integrated [per-toroidal-mode current due to wave-driven current drive](name:current_per_toroidal_mode_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive) and the [toroidal current due to wave-driven current drive](name:toroidal_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive).

Sign convention: Positive when the wave-driven current-density contribution from the specified toroidal harmonic points along $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

Launched power of a lower-hybrid antenna is the nonnegative RF power entering the vacuum vessel from one selected antenna row, resolved jointly over toroidal and poloidal refractive-index coordinates. It is the mode-resolved component of the per-antenna quantity [launched power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna).

The joint power density is defined by

$$
S(n_{\mathrm{tor}},n_{\mathrm{pol}}) = \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}P_{\mathrm{launched}}}{\mathrm{d}n_{\mathrm{tor}}\,\mathrm{d}n_{\mathrm{pol}}}
$$

where $S$ is the launched-power density over the two refractive-index coordinates, $P_{\mathrm{launched}}$ is the net launched power of the antenna, $n_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal component of the lower-hybrid wave refractive-index vector, and $n_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is its poloidal component. These components correspond to the [toroidal launched wave index of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:toroidal_launched_wave_index_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) and [poloidal launched wave index of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:poloidal_launched_wave_index_of_lower_hybrid_antenna); they are refractive-index coordinates rather than integer Fourier harmonic numbers.

The quantity applies to one selected lower-hybrid antenna row at a given time. It is resolved over both refractive-index coordinates, is not aggregated over antenna rows or antennas, and is not a time average.

Because the underlying launched power is net power after accounting for reflected power, this quantity is distinct from [forward power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:forward_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) and [reflected power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna). It represents power entering the vacuum vessel, not generator output, incident forward power, returning reflected power, or power absorbed by the plasma.

Integrating $S$ over $n_{\mathrm{tor}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{pol}}$ recovers the corresponding [launched power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna), while integrating over $n_{\mathrm{pol}}$ gives the [per-toroidal-mode launched power of a lower-hybrid antenna].

The quantity is the Fourier-mode coefficient of the total surface current associated with an ion-cyclotron-heating antenna. It combines the current contributions from the antenna straps and passive components before resolving their poloidal and toroidal variation.

For the Fourier convention used here, the coefficient for poloidal mode number $m$ and toroidal mode number $n$ is

$$
\widetilde{I}_{mn}=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi} I_s(\theta,\phi)e^{-i(m\theta+n\phi)}\,d\theta\,d\phi
$$

where $\widetilde{I}_{mn}$ is the modal surface-current coefficient, $I_s(\theta,\phi)$ is the signed total surface-current distribution, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, $m$ and $n$ are integer poloidal and toroidal mode numbers, respectively, $i$ is the imaginary unit, and $\pi$ is the circle constant.

The quantity is aggregated over all straps and passive components belonging to the antenna, while each pair $(m,n)$ identifies one Fourier component rather than a sum over mode numbers. It is therefore distinct from [wave current of an antenna strap], which describes current confined to an individual strap, and from [wave current of an antenna strap amplitude], which describes the peak magnitude of that strap current. The coefficient's sign and phase follow the chosen positive surface-current direction, angular origins, and Fourier convention shown above.

Toroidal mode current due to wave-driven current drive is the cumulative toroidal plasma current enclosed by a magnetic flux surface and attributed to one toroidal Fourier mode. It represents the wave-particle-interaction contribution only; inductive and non-wave non-inductive current sources are excluded.

The cumulative mode current inside the surface labeled by normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is defined by:

$$
I_{\mathrm{wcd},n}(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}) = \int_{S(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}})} \widetilde{\mathbf{j}}_{\mathrm{wcd},n}(R,Z) \cdot \hat{\phi}\,dR\,dZ
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{wcd},n}$ is the mode-resolved current, $n$ is the dimensionless toroidal Fourier mode number, $\widetilde{\mathbf{j}}_{\mathrm{wcd},n}$ is the corresponding wave-driven current-density coefficient in A m$^{-2}$, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector, $R$ is major radius in m, $Z$ is vertical height in m, and $S$ is the enclosed poloidal cross-section.

At the outer closed surface, this quantity is the single-mode contribution to [current due to wave-driven current drive](name:current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive). Unlike [toroidal current due to wave-driven current drive](name:toroidal_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive), it is not summed over toroidal Fourier modes; its local density counterpart is [per-toroidal-mode current density due to wave-driven current drive].

Sign convention: Positive when the specified mode's net current contribution flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The perpendicular channel denotes the velocity-space contribution perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field, not a cylindrical spatial projection. This scalar quantity represents the aggregate turbulent contribution of that channel to radial momentum transport across magnetic flux surfaces. It is the perpendicular component of the aggregate [normalized momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel magnetic field], complementary to the [parallel momentum flux normalized due to the perturbed parallel magnetic field](name:parallel_momentum_flux_normalized_due_to_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field). This quantity is the magnitude of the local time-averaged electromagnetic power-flow component perpendicular to the local magnetic-field direction, normalized by the beam’s initial launch power. It measures transverse power flow and is not a signed projection onto a selected perpendicular direction.

$$
p_{\perp} = \frac{\left\lVert \mathbf{P} - (\mathbf{P}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}})\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right\rVert}{P_0}
$$

where $\mathbf{P}$ is the local beam power-flow vector, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, and $P_0$ is the initial launch power. The magnitude makes $p_{\perp}$ non-negative. Together with the signed [parallel normalized beam power], it characterizes the local power-flow decomposition relative to the magnetic field; [initial beam power](name:initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam) supplies the normalization reference.

p_{\perp} = \frac{\left\lVert \mathbf{P} - (\mathbf{P}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}})\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right\rVert}{P_0}
$$

where $\mathbf{P}$ is the local beam power-flow vector, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, and $P_0$ is the initial launch power. The magnitude makes $p_{\perp}$ non-negative. Together with the signed parallel normalized beam power, it characterizes the local power-flow decomposition relative to the magnetic field; [initial beam power](name:initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam) supplies the normalization reference.

Poloidal angular offset estimate of the electron cyclotron emission measurement position due to the presence of suprathermal electrons is the signed change in the assigned poloidal coordinate of that position relative to the thermal-electron emission reference. The poloidal angle $\theta$ is measured about the magnetic axis in a constant-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\theta=0$ is at the outboard midplane and $\theta$ increases from larger $R$ toward $+Z$.

The offset is the difference between the poloidal coordinate assigned when suprathermal emission is included and the thermal-electron reference coordinate:

$$
\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra} = \theta_\mathrm{meas,supra} - \theta_\mathrm{meas,thermal}
$$

where $\theta_\mathrm{meas,supra}$ is the assigned measurement-position poloidal angle with the suprathermal-electron contribution included, $\theta_\mathrm{meas,thermal}$ is the corresponding thermal-electron reference angle, and $\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra}$ is this quantity; all angular quantities are in radians.

This quantity is only the poloidal angular component of the suprathermal-electron offset at the measurement position; it is not a radial displacement, toroidal angular offset, or full spatial correction. It is distinguished from [poloidal_suprathermal_electron_perturbed_angle_of_ece_channel_emission_position](name:poloidal_suprathermal_electron_angle_perturbed_at_measurement_position), which applies to the ECE-channel emission position. No universal signed range, magnitude, or sign is implied by the name; the value is zero when the presence of suprathermal electrons leaves the assigned measurement position unchanged.

Sign convention: Positive when $\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra}$ shifts the assigned electron cyclotron emission measurement position in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$, from the outboard midplane toward $+Z$ in the constant-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The radial normalized wave-vector component is the signed direction cosine of the electromagnetic wave vector along a beam-tracing ray. It describes the fraction of the local wave-vector direction projected onto the cylindrical radial direction.

At each point along the ray, it is defined by

$$
k_{r,\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{k_R}{|\mathbf{k}|} = \frac{\mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}}{|\mathbf{k}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the local electromagnetic wave vector, $k_R$ is its projection onto the radial unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$, and $|\mathbf{k}|$ is the wave-vector magnitude. The projection is taken in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity is evaluated pointwise along a single beam-tracing ray and is not an aggregate or average over rays, channels, wave sources, or propagation paths. It is dimensionless and bounded between negative and positive unity; it is distinct from the unnormalized [radial wave vector](name:radial_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), which retains the signed radial component itself.

The [normalized toroidal wave vector](name:normalized_toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and [vertical normalized wave vector] are the analogous direction cosines for the toroidal and vertical projections, respectively.

Sign convention: Positive when the wave vector points toward increasing major radius $R$.

The instantaneous radial width-change rate of a neoclassical tearing-mode magnetic island quantifies whether the island is expanding or contracting. The width is the full radial extent in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, measured along increasing $R$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The rate is defined by

$$
\frac{dW_r(t)}{dt} = \dot{W}_r(t)
$$

where $W_r(t)$ is the full radial width of the island, $t$ is physical time, and $\dot{W}_r(t)$ is its instantaneous time derivative; the subscript $r$ identifies the radial width.

This quantity applies to one identified neoclassical tearing-mode island at its resonant magnetic surface. It describes the complete island width rather than a half-width, radial position, phase, or an aggregate over multiple modes or islands; no summation or averaging is implied.

It is the NTM-specific radial realization of the generic [mode width] change-rate concept. It is distinct from the [rotation frequency of a neoclassical tearing mode](name:rotation_frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode), which describes helical phase motion rather than radial size evolution.

Sign convention: Positive when the full radial island width increases with physical time.

Flux-surface-averaged toroidal bulk-flow velocity of elemental argon ions describes the toroidal component of their collective motion over the plasma-boundary flux surface. It includes the argon ion population rather than a single charge state.

The boundary flux-surface average is defined by:

$$
\left\langle v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ar}}\right\rangle_{\psi_b}
= \frac{\displaystyle\int_{S_{\psi_b}} v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ar}}\,dS/|\nabla\psi|}{\displaystyle\int_{S_{\psi_b}} dS/|\nabla\psi|}
$$

where $\psi$ is a scalar magnetic-flux label, $\psi_b$ is its value on the plasma boundary, $S_{\psi_b}$ is the complete boundary flux surface, $dS$ is its surface-area element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of the flux label. The component $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ar}}$ is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$; $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For charge-state index $z$, with density $n_{\mathrm{Ar},z}$ and bulk velocity $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ar},z}$, the local elemental-argon velocity is the density-weighted mean $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ar}}=\sum_z n_{\mathrm{Ar},z}\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ar},z}/\sum_z n_{\mathrm{Ar},z}$. Thus, this quantity differs from the local, unaveraged [toroidal argon velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) and parallels the charge-state aggregation used for [toroidal flux-surface-averaged deuterium velocity at the plasma boundary].

Sign convention: Positive when the argon bulk-flow component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The quantity is the toroidal component of the oxygen impurity-ion bulk velocity on the last closed magnetic flux surface, with oxygen ionization states combined by density weighting. It is a surface average rather than the velocity at a particular poloidal location.

The toroidal direction is $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The defining density-weighted average is:

$$
\overline{V}_{\phi,\mathrm{O}}^{\mathrm{LCFS}} = \frac{\left\langle \sum_q n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}} V_{\phi,\mathrm{O}^{q+}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{LCFS}}}{\left\langle \sum_q n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{LCFS}}}
$$

where $q$ indexes the included oxygen ionization states, $n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}}$ is the local number density of state $q$, $V_{\phi,\mathrm{O}^{q+}}$ is its toroidal bulk-flow velocity, and angle brackets denote flux-surface averaging on the last closed flux surface. The quantity excludes other ion species; the corresponding all-ion quantity is [toroidal flux-surface-averaged ion velocity at plasma boundary]. The local, non-averaged counterpart is [toroidal oxygen velocity at plasma boundary](name:toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

Sign convention: Positive when the oxygen-ion bulk flow has a component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

Flux-surface-averaged total plasma momentum in the toroidal direction at the plasma boundary is the flux-surface average, on the last closed magnetic flux surface, of the cumulative toroidal component of plasma linear momentum enclosed by that surface. The cumulative momentum includes electrons and all ion species and is treated as a flux-surface scalar before averaging.

The cumulative boundary value is defined by the enclosed-volume integral; writing the flux-surface average explicitly gives:

$$
P_{\phi,\mathrm{FSA}}^{\mathrm{b}}
=
\frac{\oint_{\psi=\psi_\mathrm{b}} P_\phi(\psi_\mathrm{b})\, dA/|\nabla\psi|}
     {\oint_{\psi=\psi_\mathrm{b}} dA/|\nabla\psi|}
=
\int_{V_\mathrm{b}} \sum_s m_s n_s(\mathbf{x})\, v_{\phi,s}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\phi,\mathrm{FSA}}^\mathrm{b}$ is this quantity, $P_\phi(\psi_\mathrm{b})$ is the [toroidal total plasma momentum](name:toroidal_total_plasma_momentum) associated with the boundary flux label, $\psi_\mathrm{b}$ is the boundary value of the [poloidal magnetic-flux label](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface), $dA/|\nabla\psi|$ is the flux-surface averaging measure normalized by the denominator, $V_\mathrm{b}$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface, $dV$ is the volume element, $s$ runs over electrons and all ion species, $m_s$ is species mass, $n_s$ is species number density, and $v_{\phi,s}=\mathbf{v}_s\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal velocity component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The product $m_s n_s v_{\phi,s}$ is the toroidal momentum density contribution of species $s$, so the flux-surface average is applied to the enclosed total $P_\phi(\psi_\mathrm{b})$, not directly to this local density.

This quantity is not a boundary-surface integral of local toroidal momentum density, not the flux-surface average of the local density $g_\phi=\sum_s m_s n_s v_{\phi,s}$ alone, and not a major-radius-weighted angular-momentum measure. It is the flux-surface-averaged representation of [toroidal total plasma momentum at the plasma boundary]; the analogous cumulative value at the pedestal top is [toroidal plasma momentum at the pedestal top](name:toroidal_plasma_momentum_at_pedestal_top).

Sign convention: Positive when the enclosed total toroidal momentum is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Toroidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the signed toroidal direction cosine of the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point. It is the projection of the local unit wave vector onto the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The normalized toroidal component is defined by

$$
k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\phi}}{\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert} = \frac{k_\phi}{\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert}
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$, $k_\phi=\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the [toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), and $\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert$ is the wave-vector magnitude.

This is a launch-point quantity, not an integral or average over a beam path. It is distinct from the [normalized toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:normalized_toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), which denotes the same toroidal direction cosine evaluated along a traced beam rather than specifically at launch. For real nonzero $\mathbf{k}$ it satisfies $-1 \leq k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}} \leq 1$; together with the [radial normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:radial_wave_vector_normalized_of_beam_tracing_beam) and the [vertical normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam], the cylindrical direction cosines obey $k_{R,\mathrm{norm}}^2+k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}}^2+k_{Z,\mathrm{norm}}^2=1$. The [poloidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam] is instead a related projection in the meridional plane spanned by $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$.

Sign convention: Positive when the projection of $\mathbf{k}$ onto $\hat{\phi}$ is along the local $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the plasma-volume average of the local critical momentum threshold for avalanche-driven runaway-electron generation. It characterizes the boundary between collisional drag-dominated and net-accelerated electron dynamics.

The volume average is defined by

$$
p_{c,\mathrm{av}} = \frac{1}{V}\int_V p_c(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $p_{c,\mathrm{av}}$ is the averaged threshold, $V$ is the plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, and $p_c(\mathbf{r})$ is the local [critical momentum due to avalanche] at position $\mathbf{r}$.

This quantity is an unweighted volume average, not the momentum carried by the runaway-electron population and not a volume average of electron momentum. It is the spatially aggregated form of the local avalanche threshold and is distinct from the broader [momentum due to avalanche], which need not denote a critical threshold.

Electron density at pedestal maximum is the electron number density evaluated at the pedestal maximum, the steep mid-pedestal locus whose position is given by the [normalized poloidal-flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal). It is a local density value of the electron population at that flux-coordinate position.

The defining evaluation is

$$
n_{e,\mathrm{ped,max}} = n_e(\psi_{N,\mathrm{ped}})
$$

where $n_{e,\mathrm{ped,max}}$ is the electron density at pedestal maximum, $n_e(\psi_N)$ is the [electron density](name:electron_density) as a function of normalized poloidal-flux coordinate $\psi_N$, and $\psi_{N,\mathrm{ped}}$ is the [normalized poloidal-flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal).

The scope is the free-electron population in the pedestal region at this single locus. The value is local rather than averaged over the pedestal or integrated over a flux surface or volume, and no ion charge-state aggregation is part of this electron quantity.

It is distinct from the pedestal-top electron density and from a maximum value of $n_e$ over the pedestal; the word maximum denotes the pedestal-gradient locus, not an extremum of electron density. It is also distinct from the signed gradient or slope of electron density with respect to $\psi_N$.

The associated [derivative of electron density at pedestal maximum with respect to normalized poloidal-flux coordinate] is $\partial n_e/\partial \psi_N$ evaluated at the same pedestal maximum locus; that derivative characterizes the local gradient, whereas $n_{e,\mathrm{ped,max}}$ is the value being differentiated.

The velocity due to diamagnetic drift is a pressure-gradient-driven fluid velocity contribution associated with a neutral population. It retains the drift vector before a magnitude-specific reduction.

The corresponding magnitude is defined by

$$
v_{\ast,n}^{\mathrm{mag}} = \left|\mathbf{v}_{\ast,n}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\ast,n}$ is the neutral-population velocity contribution due to diamagnetic drift and $v_{\ast,n}^{\mathrm{mag}}$ is its scalar magnitude.

The scope is the neutral-population contribution to momentum convection, retaining all directional information rather than selecting a component or summing over ionic charge states. It includes only the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic contribution and excludes unrelated drift or independent flow contributions.

This quantity is the neutral-population specialization of the broader [velocity due to diamagnetic drift]. The derived [neutral velocity magnitude due to diamagnetic drift] removes the vector direction by applying the norm shown above.

The quantity is the flux-surface average over the separatrix of the toroidal component of the helium-4 ion bulk-flow velocity. The helium-4 value includes all helium-4 charge states through a density-weighted mean, rather than a sum of their velocities.

For charge-state-resolved density $n_{4,q}$ and toroidal velocity $v_{\phi,4,q}$, the species velocity is defined by

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{FS}} = \left\langle \frac{\sum_q n_{4,q}v_{\phi,4,q}}{\sum_q n_{4,q}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{sep}}
$$

where $q$ indexes helium-4 charge state, $n_{4,q}$ is its number density in m$^{-3}$, $v_{\phi,4,q}$ is its toroidal velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{sep}}$ denotes the flux-surface average over the separatrix. The toroidal component is taken along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This averaged quantity is distinct from the local [toroidal helium-4 velocity at the plasma boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_plasma_boundary); the corresponding isotope-specific construction for helium-3 is [toroidal flux-surface-averaged helium-3 velocity at the plasma boundary].

This quantity is the normalized poloidal-flux coordinate assigned to the closed magnetic surface where the magnitude of the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) is globally smallest inside the last-closed flux surface. It identifies the radial location of the minimum safety factor rather than the minimum safety-factor value itself.

The coordinate of this surface is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{p},q_{\min}} = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0 \le \rho_{\mathrm{p}} \le 1} \left|q(\rho_{\mathrm{p}})\right|
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{p},q_{\min}}$ is the normalized poloidal-flux coordinate at the minimum-safety-factor surface, $\rho_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the normalized poloidal-flux coordinate, and $q(\rho_{\mathrm{p}})$ is the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) evaluated on the closed flux surface labeled by $\rho_{\mathrm{p}}$.

The minimization is global over nested closed magnetic flux surfaces in the confined plasma. The coordinate follows the convention of [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), increasing from zero at the magnetic axis to one at the last-closed flux surface. It is a single locus value, not a flux-surface average, volume average, or integral. If multiple surfaces attain the same global minimum of $|q|$, the arg-min is non-unique unless an additional tie-breaking convention is supplied.

The minimand is the magnitude $|q|$, so this quantity locates the minimum of the safety-factor magnitude rather than the minimum of signed $q$. It must not be confused with the value of $q_{\min}$ itself or with the dimensional flux on the same surface, given by [poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor]. The corresponding toroidal-flux coordinate is [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_absolute_safety_factor).

Poloidal angular offset estimate of the electron cyclotron emission measurement position due to the presence of suprathermal electrons is the signed change in the assigned poloidal coordinate of that position relative to the thermal-electron emission reference. The poloidal angle $\theta$ is measured about the magnetic axis in a constant-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\theta=0$ is at the outboard midplane and $\theta$ increases from larger $R$ toward $+Z$.

The offset is the difference between the poloidal coordinate assigned when suprathermal emission is included and the thermal-electron reference coordinate:

$$
\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra} = \theta_\mathrm{meas,supra} - \theta_\mathrm{meas,thermal}
$$

where $\theta_\mathrm{meas,supra}$ is the assigned measurement-position poloidal angle with the suprathermal-electron contribution included, $\theta_\mathrm{meas,thermal}$ is the corresponding thermal-electron reference angle, and $\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra}$ is this quantity; all angular quantities are in radians.

This quantity is only the poloidal angular component of the suprathermal-electron offset at the measurement position; it is not a radial displacement, toroidal angular offset, or full spatial correction. It is distinguished from [poloidal_suprathermal_electron_perturbed_angle_of_ece_channel_emission_position](name:poloidal_suprathermal_electron_angle_perturbed_at_ece_channel_emission_position), which applies to the ECE-channel emission position. No universal signed range, magnitude, or sign is implied by the name; the value is zero when the presence of suprathermal electrons leaves the assigned measurement position unchanged.

Sign convention: Positive when $\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra}$ shifts the assigned electron cyclotron emission measurement position in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$, from the outboard midplane toward $+Z$ in the constant-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Flux-surface-averaged parallel current density at a specified constraint position is the signed plasma current density associated with the component of conventional current flowing along the local magnetic field, averaged over the corresponding closed magnetic flux surface.

The defining field-aligned flux-surface average is

$$
j_{parallel}^{\mathrm{FS}}(\psi_c)=\frac{\left\langle\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle_{\psi_c}}{B_0(\psi_c)}
$$

where $j_{\parallel}^{\mathrm{FS}}(\psi_c)$ is this averaged parallel current density, $\mathbf{j}$ is the conventional plasma current-density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic-field vector, $\psi_c$ is the flux-surface label selected by the constraint position, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi_c}$ denotes averaging over that magnetic flux surface, and $B_0(\psi_c)$ is the reference magnetic-field magnitude used to normalize the field-aligned projection.

The quantity applies to the total plasma current-density field on the selected closed magnetic surface, with all current-carrying populations and mechanisms included unless a narrower physical qualifier is supplied. Its aggregation is over the complete flux surface, so it is not a pointwise parallel current density.

It is not restricted to a particular current-drive mechanism and is therefore distinct from the [parallel current density due to ohmic current drive](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ohmic_current_drive) and the [parallel flux-surface-averaged current density due to wave-driven current drive].

The underlying vector quantity is [current density](name:current_density); this name applies its magnetic-field-aligned projection and then performs a flux-surface average. The [toroidal flux-surface-averaged current density at a constraint position] instead uses the geometric toroidal projection before averaging.

Sign convention: Positive when the conventional current-density vector has a component along the local magnetic-field vector.

This quantity is the plasma-volume average of the local field-aligned conventional current density carried only by runaway electrons. It selects the magnetic-field-parallel contribution of the runaway-electron current before applying the same volume averaging represented by [volume-averaged runaway-electron current density].

$$
\left\langle j_{\parallel,\mathrm{RE}} \right\rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{RE}}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the local conventional current-density vector of the runaway-electron population, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the local unit vector in the magnetic-field direction, $V_p$ is the selected plasma volume, and $dV$ is its volume element. Contributions from thermal electrons, ions, and non-runaway populations are excluded. Because this is conventional current, its direction is opposite to the motion of negatively charged runaway electrons.

Sign convention: Positive when the local conventional runaway-electron current component points along the local magnetic-field direction.

Flux-surface-averaged toroidal bulk-flow velocity of elemental argon ions describes the toroidal component of their collective motion over the plasma-boundary flux surface. It includes the argon ion population rather than a single charge state.

The boundary flux-surface average is defined by:

$$
\left\langle v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ar}}\right\rangle_{\psi_b}
= \frac{\displaystyle\int_{S_{\psi_b}} v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ar}}\,dS/|\nabla\psi|}{\displaystyle\int_{S_{\psi_b}} dS/|\nabla\psi|}
$$

where $\psi$ is a scalar magnetic-flux label, $\psi_b$ is its value on the plasma boundary, $S_{\psi_b}$ is the complete boundary flux surface, $dS$ is its surface-area element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of the flux label. The component $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ar}}$ is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$; $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For charge-state index $z$, with density $n_{\mathrm{Ar},z}$ and bulk velocity $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ar},z}$, the local elemental-argon velocity is the density-weighted mean $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ar}}=\sum_z n_{\mathrm{Ar},z}\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ar},z}/\sum_z n_{\mathrm{Ar},z}$. Thus, this quantity differs from the local, unaveraged [toroidal argon velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) and parallels the charge-state aggregation used for [toroidal flux-surface-averaged deuterium velocity at the plasma boundary].

Sign convention: Positive when the argon bulk-flow component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The root-mean-square spectral width is the wavelength spread of a spectrometer channel’s instrumental response about its reference vacuum wavelength. It characterizes broadening produced by the channel rather than the intrinsic width of the incident spectral line.

For a monochromatic input, the width is the second-moment spread of the channel response:

$$
w_{\lambda,\mathrm{rms}} = \left[\frac{\int (\lambda-\lambda_0)^2 R(\lambda)\,d\lambda}{\int R(\lambda)\,d\lambda}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $w_{\lambda,\mathrm{rms}}$ is the root-mean-square spectral width, $\lambda$ is vacuum wavelength, $\lambda_0$ is the channel reference vacuum wavelength, and $R(\lambda)$ is the channel spectral response.

This quantity applies to one spectrometer channel and aggregates the complete spectral response over wavelength through its second moment. It excludes physical broadening of the incident spectral line and is not an interval obtained by integrating the response.

The RMS width is the statistical form of [spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:root_mean_square_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel); for a Gaussian response, it is the Gaussian standard deviation used by that parent quantity. It is distinct from the [effective spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel), which is a response-equivalent wavelength interval rather than an RMS spread.

Flux-surface-averaged toroidal krypton velocity is the density-weighted mean over all krypton ionization states on the plasma boundary, identified with the last closed magnetic flux surface. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

\left\langle v_{\phi,\mathrm{Kr}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS},b} = \frac{\displaystyle\oint_{\psi=\psi_b} \left(\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}} v_{\phi,\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}\right)\frac{dl}{B_p}}{\displaystyle\oint_{\psi=\psi_b} \left(\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}\right)\frac{dl}{B_p}}
$$

This species-resolved quantity differs from the total-ion quantity [toroidal flux-surface-averaged ion velocity at the plasma boundary]; its locus differs from [toroidal krypton velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).

The root-mean-square wave current is the effective magnitude of the oscillatory radio-frequency current carried by one ion-cyclotron-heating antenna strap during wave excitation. It is a non-negative scalar that represents the current waveform over an RF cycle.

For an RF period, the RMS current is defined by

$$
I_{\mathrm{RMS}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{RF}}}\int_{0}^{T_{\mathrm{RF}}} i^2(t)\,dt}
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{RMS}}$ is the RMS wave current, $i(t)$ is the instantaneous wave current in the strap, $t$ is time, and $T_{\mathrm{RF}}$ is the RF period. The time origin is arbitrary within the period.

The quantity applies to a single antenna strap and averages over one RF period; it is not a sum over straps or antenna modules. It describes the strap-conductor current associated with the launched wave and excludes plasma current and non-wave direct current.

It is the RMS transformation of the underlying [wave current of antenna strap]. Unlike that parent quantity, it does not retain instantaneous sign or phase. For sinusoidal excitation, it equals the peak current magnitude divided by the square root of two and therefore differs from the [wave current of antenna strap amplitude].

I_{\mathrm{RMS}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{RF}}}\int_{0}^{T_{\mathrm{RF}}} i^2(t)\,dt}
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{RMS}}$ is the RMS wave current, $i(t)$ is the instantaneous wave current in the strap, $t$ is time, and $T_{\mathrm{RF}}$ is the RF period. The time origin is arbitrary within the period.

The quantity applies to a single antenna strap and averages over one RF period; it is not a sum over straps or antenna modules. It describes the strap-conductor current associated with the launched wave and excludes plasma current and non-wave direct current.

It is the RMS transformation of the underlying [wave current of antenna strap](name:wave_current_of_antenna_strap). Unlike that parent quantity, it does not retain instantaneous sign or phase. For sinusoidal excitation, it equals the peak current magnitude divided by the square root of two and therefore differs from the wave current of antenna strap amplitude.

Flux-surface-averaged parallel current density is the scalar current-density quantity defined on a magnetic flux surface by averaging the scalar product of the plasma current-density vector with the magnetic-field vector and normalizing by a single global reference magnetic-field scalar. It describes the current density parallel to the magnetic field only through this flux-surface-averaged, reference-field-normalized definition.

For a magnetic flux surface $S$, the defining relationship is

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{fs}}(S) = \frac{\left\langle \mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle_S}{B_0}
$$

where $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{fs}}(S)$ is the flux-surface-averaged parallel current density on $S$, $\mathbf{j}$ is the [plasma current-density vector](name:current_density), $\mathbf{B}$ is the [magnetic-field vector](name:magnetic_field), $\left\langle \cdot \right\rangle_S$ denotes the flux-surface average over $S$, and $B_0$ is a single global reference magnetic-field scalar.

The scope is magnetic flux surfaces in the plasma for which a flux-surface average is defined. The aggregation convention is to average $\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}$ over each surface first and then divide by the same $B_0$ for every surface; $B_0$ is not a function of the flux-surface label.

This quantity is not the local [parallel current density] and is not the flux-surface average of that local component, because the definition normalizes by $B_0$ rather than by the local magnetic-field magnitude. Multiplying this quantity by $B_0$ gives the flux-surface average $\left\langle \mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle_S$.

Sign convention: Positive when $\left\langle \mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle_S$ has the same sign as the global reference magnetic field $B_0$.

This quantity is the toroidal component of the lithium-ion bulk-flow velocity, flux-surface averaged over the separatrix, which is the last closed magnetic flux surface at the plasma boundary. Lithium ions comprise Li+ through Li3+, combined using their particle densities.

$$
\left\langle v_{\phi,\mathrm{Li}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}} = \frac{\sum_{q=1}^{3}\left\langle n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}v_{\phi,\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}}{\sum_{q=1}^{3}\left\langle n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}}
$$

Here, $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}$ is the toroidal bulk-flow velocity of lithium charge state $q$, $n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}$ is its number density, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes averaging over the separatrix. The toroidal component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The related [flux-surface-averaged lithium density at the plasma boundary] supplies the corresponding charge-state-summed density, not a velocity.

Net ion-cyclotron radio-frequency power is the power delivered through a specified ion-cyclotron heating antenna into the vacuum vessel toward the plasma. It is a launcher-boundary quantity, not the power ultimately absorbed by plasma particles.

The defining net-power relation is:

$$
P_{\rm launched}=P_{\rm forward}-P_{\rm reflected}
$$

where $P_{\rm launched}$ is the net power launched toward the plasma, $P_{\rm forward}$ is the incident radio-frequency power traveling toward the antenna as described by [forward power of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:forward_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna), and $P_{\rm reflected}$ is the radio-frequency power returned from the antenna toward the source as described by [reflected power of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna).

The quantity applies to one specified ion-cyclotron heating launcher and represents its launcher-associated power. It has no species, charge-state, or volumetric deposition resolution and is not an all-antenna aggregate.

Reflected power is excluded from the launched result, as are power losses upstream of the antenna boundary and power subsequently absorbed by plasma particles. The launcher-resolved quantity is the per-launcher counterpart of [power due to ion-cyclotron heating](name:net_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating); summing corresponding launcher values gives [total power due to ion-cyclotron heating](name:total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating), while [launched power of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:launched_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) expresses the same boundary power with the antenna as the explicit object locus.

Flux-surface-averaged wave-driven current density is the vector average, on a magnetic flux surface, of the conventional plasma current density generated non-inductively by electromagnetic-wave–particle interactions. It retains the vector character of the local current-density contribution while averaging its resolved components over the surface.

The flux-surface average is defined componentwise by

$$
\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wd}} \right\rangle_{\psi}
=
\frac{\displaystyle\int_{S_{\psi}} \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wd}}\,\frac{dS}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}}
{\displaystyle\int_{S_{\psi}}\frac{dS}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wd}}$ is the local conventional current-density vector generated by wave–particle interactions, $\psi$ is the scalar magnetic-flux label, $S_{\psi}$ is the corresponding magnetic flux surface, $dS$ is its surface-area element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of the flux label.

The quantity applies to the plasma current on one magnetic flux surface and includes the wave-driven contributions of the charged-particle populations represented in the conventional current. Its aggregation convention is a complete flux-surface average, not a local value, volume average, toroidal current integral, or Fourier-mode-resolved contribution.

It excludes inductive current density and current contributions generated by bootstrap, ohmic, or other non-wave current-drive mechanisms. No field-aligned or other directional projection is imposed at this parent level.

This quantity is obtained by applying flux-surface averaging to the local [wave-driven current density](name:current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive). The [parallel flux-surface-averaged wave-driven current density] is a specialization that retains only the component projected along the magnetic-field direction before or within the averaging operation.

Sign convention: Positive when a resolved current-density component points in the corresponding positive direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ basis, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, consistent with conventional positive-charge transport.

Strain of a strain gage is a signed scalar component of the small mechanical strain of the structural component to which the gage is attached. It represents local deformation along one gage measurement axis for a single-axis gage, or one component of the in-surface strain tensor resolved in the first and second local tangential measurement directions of a rosette gage.

The in-surface small-strain tensor components are defined by the symmetrized displacement gradient in the local tangential coordinates:

$$
S_{\alpha\beta} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial u_\alpha}{\partial x_\beta} + \frac{\partial u_\beta}{\partial x_\alpha}\right), \qquad \alpha,\beta \in \{1,2\}
$$

where $S_{\alpha\beta}$ is the strain component for the ordered local directions $\alpha$ and $\beta$, $u_\alpha$ is the structural displacement component along local tangential direction $\alpha$, $x_\alpha$ is the corresponding local tangential coordinate, and $1$ and $2$ label the first and second local tangential measurement directions.

The supported component set comprises the single-axis normal strain along the gage axis and, for a rosette gage, the three independent in-surface tensor components $S_{x_1x_1}$, $S_{x_1x_2}$, and $S_{x_2x_2}$. The first local tangential direction $x_1$ and second local tangential direction $x_2$ are ordered object-local measurement axes on the component; they are not components of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is not a gage factor, an electrical resistance change, or an orientation unit-vector component. It must not be restricted to single-axis gages and does not exclude rosette shear strain; $S_{x_1x_2}$ is the symmetric tensor shear component, with $S_{x_1x_2}=S_{x_2x_1}$.

For a single-axis gage with gage-axis unit vector $\hat{a}$, the reported normal strain is the tensor projection $S_{\hat{a}\hat{a}}=\hat{a}\cdot\mathbf{S}\hat{a}$, where $\mathbf{S}$ is the small-strain tensor. The local measurement directions are related to direction-vector component quantities such as the [z component of the first measurement-direction unit vector] and the [x component of the second measurement-direction unit vector] in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame with $\hat{z}$ vertical.

Sign convention: Positive when the reported normal component corresponds to extension along its local measurement direction, and when $\frac{1}{2}(\partial u_1/\partial x_2+\partial u_2/\partial x_1)>0$ for the rosette shear component $S_{x_1x_2}$.

This quantity is the geometric derivative of the area enclosed by a nested, closed magnetic flux surface in a poloidal cross-section. It describes how neighboring flux surfaces differ in enclosed poloidal-plane area.

$$
\frac{dA}{d\psi}
$$

where $A(\psi)$ is the area enclosed by the flux surface labeled by signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$. The area is measured in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to the cumulative enclosed area of each nested closed flux surface and is not a local area density, toroidal surface area, or enclosed-volume derivative. The corresponding [derivative of volume of flux surface with respect to poloidal magnetic flux coordinate](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate) differentiates enclosed volume rather than cross-sectional area, while the [derivative of area of flux surface with respect to toroidal flux coordinate] uses the toroidal magnetic flux coordinate instead of $\psi$.

Sign convention: Positive when the enclosed poloidal-plane area increases in the direction of increasing signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, with positive flux oriented by the $+Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Nuclear fusion reaction energy deposition rate integrated over a specified plasma region or material component is the rate at which energy whose ultimate source is fuel-ion fusion reactions is transferred to matter within that region or component. It is an extensive deposited-power quantity, so energy is assigned to the place where it is deposited, which may differ from the place where the fusion reaction occurred.

For a specified region or component $\Omega$, the quantity is defined by the local fusion-origin deposition rate density:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fusion,dep}}(\Omega) = \int_{\Omega} q_{\mathrm{fusion,dep}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{fusion,dep}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local rate density of energy deposited at position $\mathbf{x}$ by fusion products, fusion-neutron interactions, and secondary nuclear radiation, and $dV$ is the volume element of $\Omega$.

Each reaction channel contributes according to the partition of its released energy among products. For the deuterium-tritium channel, approximately one fifth of the fusion energy is born in the alpha particle and four fifths in the neutron; this birth partition does not imply local deposition. Charged-product energy is included in a plasma region only for the fraction actually deposited there during slowing down, while escaping charged products or neutrons contribute where they subsequently deposit energy through interactions and secondary radiation.

This name is distinct from [power density due to fusion](name:power_density_due_to_fusion), which denotes local fusion energy release rate before nonlocal transport, and from [neutron power], which tracks energy carried by neutrons rather than deposited energy in $\Omega$. [Power due to neutron interaction] is the neutron-interaction contribution when the interacting neutrons originate from fusion. The divertor specializations [deposited power of divertor due to fusion](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_divertor) and [power of divertor due to fusion](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_divertor) restrict $\Omega$ to the divertor; non-fusion heat loads such as conduction, plasma radiation, charge-exchange neutrals, and externally supplied heating are excluded.

Plasma energy is the volume-integrated internal kinetic energy carried by all confined electron and ion populations, including thermal and suprathermal populations. It is the all-population stored particle energy of the confined plasma, not a thermal-only component.

A pressure-tensor definition gives the stored particle energy without assuming isotropic distributions:

$$
W_\mathrm{p} = \int_{V_\mathrm{p}} \sum_a \frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{P}_a\, dV
$$

where $W_\mathrm{p}$ is the plasma energy, $V_\mathrm{p}$ is the confined plasma volume, $a$ labels the electron, ion, and modeled suprathermal populations included in the confined plasma, $\mathbf{P}_a$ is the pressure tensor of population $a$ in its local mean-flow frame, and $dV$ is the scalar volume element. For isotropic populations this reduces to the pressure-sum relation with energy density $3p_\mathrm{tot}/2$, where $p_\mathrm{tot}=\sum_a p_a$; for a gyrotropic anisotropic population the contribution is $p_{\perp a}+p_{\parallel a}/2$.

This quantity excludes electromagnetic-field energy, electrostatic-field energy, rest-mass energy, and organized macroscopic bulk-flow energy. [Electron energy](name:electron_energy), [thermal plasma energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), and [fast-particle energy](name:fast_particle_energy) are component contributions, while [total plasma energy] and [total particle energy] denote the corresponding all-population stored particle-energy concept when the naming emphasizes totality.
